RESEARCH ARTICLE
A comparative study on porous activated carbon derived
from waste biomass with varying oxygen functionalities as
supercapacitor electrodes
Atika | R. K. Dutta
Department of Chemistry, Indian Institute
of Technology Roorkee, Roorkee, India
Correspondence
R. K. Dutta, Department of Chemistry,
Indian Institute of Technology Roorkee,
Roorkee 247667, India.
Email:
r.dutta@cy.iitr.ac.in
Funding information
UGC-DAE-CSR-KC/CRS/19/
TE09/1077/1093
Abstract
Activated carbon derived from biomasses with different oxygen-bearing chemi-
cal constituents has been explored as supercapacitor electrode. The rice straw
(RS) and eucalyptus wood biomasses were selected owing to their contrasting
composition of cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin contents. The activated car-
bons of these biomasses are obtained by pyrolysis at 550
/C14 C followed by thermal
activation (700 /C14 C) after treatment with optimized KOH. The specific capaci-
tance of RS-based activated carbon (ACRS-700), measured from galvanostatic
charging-discharging studies at 0.5 A g /C0 1, is much higher (eg, 365 F g /C0 1) than
that of ACEW-700 (168 F g /C0 1). The higher specific capacitance of ACRS-700 is
attributable to: (i) significantly higher surface area (3345 m 2 g/C0 1) comprising
of interconnected micro- and mesoporous structure; (ii) porosity of about
2.0 cm
3/g; and (iii) oxygen-rich hemicellulose contents. The possible charge
storage mechanism in ACRS-700 has been discussed. The real-time application
of ACRS-700 has been demonstrated by lighting up red LEDs using ACRS-
700//ACRS-700 symmetric supercapacitor device, operated with aqueous and
freshly synthesized [Bu 4N+][NO3
/C0 ] ionic liquid as electrolytes. The maximum
energy density (42.7 Wh kg /C0 1) and the power density (1.9 kW kg /C0 1) for ionic
liquid electrolyte are favourable for supercapacitor applications.
KEYWORDS
biomass, charge storage mechanism, porousactivated carbon, supercapacitor electrode,
symmetric supercapacitor device
1 | INTRODUCTION
About 50 billion tonnes of biomasses are generated annu-
ally and these are mostly derived from agriculture and
forestry sources. Management of such huge quantities of
waste biomasses has been a challenging task from envi-
ronment and climate change perspective. There has been
a continuous effort for finding sustainable technology to
utilize this organic carbon-rich waste for generating
wealth, including valuable technological products.
1 In
this regard, conversion of plant-derived waste biomasses
intoactivated carbon has been a lucrative option. This has
been well-studied as adsorbent for environmental
applications.2,3 Lately, porousactivated carbon from
waste biomasses has revealed very promising result as
carbon-based supercapacitors (SCs) to meet the drastic
demand in the energy sector.
4-6 The carbon-based SCs
offer promising futuristic prospect as efficient energy-
storage device(s) due to their fast charging-discharging,
durable cycle life, high-power delivery capabilities, and

environmental friendliness. 7-9 These types of carbon
materials as SCs correspond to electrical double-layer
capacitors (EDLCs) and store charge via adsorption/
desorption of electrolytic ions at the electrode-electrolyte
interface and offer high power density.
10 The favorable
features of activated carbon (AC) as SCs are associated
with relatively higher electrical conductivity, large spe-
cific surface area with tunable pores, favorable electro-
chemical and thermal stability, and mechanical
properties.
11 The carbon materials, operated at higher
potential as compared to the transition metal-based mate-
rials such as metal oxides(CoO), metal
sulfides(Cu
2MoS4), metal carbides (Fe 3Mo3C/Mo2C), and
metal borides (CoB, NiB, NiCoB). 12-15 Moreover, the scal-
able manufacturing of porousactivated carbon from bio-
mass waste is a feasible option that is lucrative for
production of largescale SCs to meet the requirement of
energy production. In this scheme, one can avoid the
commonly employed strategy of managing large quanti-
ties of agro and forestry wastes via open field burning,
which leads to environmental pollution.
Some of the common biomasses used for developing
supercapacitor electrodes include eucalyptus wood, bam-
boo, rice husk, rice straw, tea leaves, coconut husk,
bagasse from sugarcane, and eucalyptus bark.
16-20 Among
them, rice straw contains some traces of silica along with
cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin. The silica is expected
to combine with lignocellulose to produce matrix of high
chemical and thermal stability.
21 While on the other
hand, eucalyptus wood-derived AC with hierarchical
porous structure has also been explored for preparation
for supercapacitor application. It is one of the most com-
mon and widely planted species found in 90 countries of
our world due to its rapid growth rate and renewable
availability.
22 Though several methods including
microwave-based heating are available for the prepara-
tion of AC, but direct heating of biomasses for carboniza-
tion at higher temperature has been a preferred one
owing to its ability to process large quantities of bio-
mass.
23 The electrochemical studies of these ACs are pri-
marily focussed on the effect of pore dimensions and
consequential increase in specific surface area as salient
factors for EDLC-type SCs. However, the chemical com-
position of the AC tends to vary due to differences in the
constituents of their source biomasses. This may impact
on the structural and morphological features of the AC,
which consequently alter their electrochemical proper-
ties. For example, lignin-rich biomasses are rich in oxy-
gen functionalities and may act as natural oxygen
dopants in the corresponding AC and might improve
electronic conductivity, surface wettability, and electro-
chemical reactivity at the carbon electrode/electrolyte
interface for accessing electrolyte ion and favor the
charge accumulation capacity.
24 This is consistent with
higher specific capacitances exhibited by carbonaceous
materials doped with heteroatoms, owing to higher
charge densities in dopants of higher electronegativity
than carbon.
25 These studies are mostly based on
nitrogen-doped carbon materials. While supercapacitor
electrodes made with oxygen-functionalized carbona-
ceous materials are less studied. Moreover, the oxygen
functionalities might offer additional redox property-
based pseudocapacitive characteristics for further
enhancing the charge storage process and could also
improve charge migration due to more polar electrode
surface and enhanced wettability of the electrolytes.
26
Looking at these advantages, biomasses with different
chemical composition were chosen for synthesizing
oxygen-rich AC as supercapacitor electrode materials.
The porous and oxygen-enriched AC of these biomasses
were obtained by carbonization method via direct heating
in inert condition. It is followed by alkali-treated thermal
activation. KOH activation is chosen for laboratory scale
due to its low activation temperature and it produces AC
with well-defined micropore distribution, large micro-
pore volume, and a very high surface area. Moreover,
metallic potassium in the carbon matrix expands the
space between carbon atomic layers, and leads to the pro-
duction of more porosity.
27 Several studies on porous AC
obtained from rice straw show high specific capacitance
and the results are attributed to favourable EDLC-based
charge storage owing to formation of very high surface
area. It is however not very clear why rice straw-based
AC exhibits such high surface area while AC derived
from other biomass sources does not. It could be due to
variation in the chemical composition of the biomasses,
particularly in terms of their cellulose, hemicellulose, lig-
nin, ash, and extractives. It is worth studying the correla-
tion of AC derived from strikingly different compositions
of biomasses with their charge storage properties. In view
of this, we have selected two biomasses, that is, rice straw
and eucalyptus wood of strikingly different composition
with respect to lignin, cellulose, and hemicellulose to pre-
pare AC for understanding the correlation between com-
position of biomasses and their effect on charge storage
property.
The electrochemical properties of AC obtained from
rice straw and eucalyptus wood biomasses are studied in
a three-electrode set-up. The neutral aqueous electrolyte
(2 M NaCl) has been used, as the acidic and alkaline elec-
trolytes are associated with evolution of H
2 or O 2 gases
when operated at larger potential window and may affect
the stability of the electrode materials in device opera-
tion.28 Besides, ionic liquid-based non-aqueous electro-
lyte has been explored here to achieve higher energy
density requirement by virtue of their ability to operate

groups use imide-based ionic liquids as non-aqueous
electrolytes due to their better thermal and chemical sta-
bility, and lesser inflammable and environmentally
benign nature.
29 Here, we have synthesized tetraalkylam-
monium based ionic liquid (IL) ([Bu 4N+][NO3
/C0 ]) as non-
aqueous electrolyte for supercapacitor applications. The
charge storage and charge transfer mechanism in terms
of ion resistances and electrode-electrolyte resistances
has been characterized by measurements employing elec-
trochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS). The applica-
tions of the optimized batch of AC have been explored by
fabricating symmetric supercapacitors (SSCs) devices,
operated with optimized aqueous (2 M NaCl) and non-
aqueous ([Bu
4N+][NO3
/C0 ] ionic liquid) electrolytes,
respectively. The charge storage capacity of the as-
fabricated SSC device is further demonstrated by lighten-
ing up of red-light emitting diodes (LEDs) forming
“IITR” pattern.
2 | EXPERIMENTAL METHOD
2.1 | Preparation of porous activated
carbon (AC) from biomasses
Batch of dried and grinded rice straw biomass is taken in
a pre-cleaned silica boat and kept in a tube furnace
(Nabertherm) at 550
/C14 C for 2 h in the presence of N 2 gas
for carbonization. The heating rate is optimized to 10 /C14 C
min/C0 1. The as-obtained carbonized sample is further
thermally activated after treatment with KOH at 1:3
weight ratio. The temperature for thermal treatment is
kept at 600, 700, and at 800 /C14 C. The heating is continued
for 2 h in a tube furnace with 100 mL min /C0 1 flow rate of
N2 gas rate. The respective samples are further grinded
using agate mortar and pestle and then soaked in HCl
solution (0.5 N) for 12 h. The separated AC is then
cleaned with de-ionized (DI) water for several times until
the pH of the washed solution becomes neutral. The
finally cleaned AC is oven-dried at 120
/C14 C for overnight.
Based on the activation temperature, the AC samples
obtained from rice straw are named as ACRS-600, ACRS-
700, and ACRS-800. Similarly, the AC sample obtained
from eucalyptus wood is named as ACEW-600, ACEW-
700, and ACEW-800. The production yield of these sam-
ples is determined, for example, the yield of ACRS-700
and ACEW-700 were 5.6-5.8 wt% and 8.6-8.9 wt%, respec-
tively. A schematic representation of the methodology for
the preparation of porous AC from rice straw and euca-
lyptus wood biomass is presented in Scheme
1A. The
chemical reagents used for the preparation of respective
porous AC and the techniques used for their
characterization are given in Section S1, as Supporting
Information.
2.2 | Electrochemical analysis
All electrochemical studies (eg, CV, GCD, and EIS) of the
respective AC samples are carried out in a three-electrode
system using a Multi Autolab/M204 electrochemical
workstation (Metrohm Autolab B.V., The Netherlands).
The respective AC samples are used as working electrode.
A saturated calomel electrode is taken as a reference elec-
trode. A platinum electrode has been used as an auxiliary
electrode. The working electrode is prepared as follows:
80 wt% of the AC (ie, ACRS or ACEW) is thoroughly
mixed with 10 wt% carbon black and 10 wt% Polyvinyli-
dene fluoride binder. The mixture is then magnetically
stirred in N-methyl-2-pyrrolidinone solvent for 12 h until
a sticky slurry is formed. The slurry is casted on a cleaned
flexible graphite sheet of dimension 1 cm /C2 1 cm and
then dried at 80
/C14 C overnight to form the respective work-
ing electrode. The weight of the active material in the
working electrode is about 1 mg, which is accurately
measured in a microbalance. The thickness of working
electrodes is 1 mg cm
/C0 2. The EIS measurements are per-
formed at a frequency range between 10 /C0 2 and
2 /C2 104 Hz with an amplitude of 5 mV. The cyclic studies
for the best-performing batches, for example, ACRS-700
and ACEW-700 are performed at 10.0 A g
/C0 1 for
8000 cycles. The NaCl (2 M) solution has been used as
neutral aqueous electrolyte for all electrochemical mea-
surements at ambient temperature. The specific capaci-
tance is determined from GCD measurement using the

3 | RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
3.1 | Optimization of porous activated
carbon materials and its characterization
The CV and GCD plots of the batches of AC derived from
the biomass of rice straw, for example, ACRS-600, ACRS-
700, and ACRS-800 as supercapacitor electrodes are given
in Figure
S1, (Section S2, given as Supporting Informa-
tion). The specific capacitances of these batches activated
at different temperatures are obtained from their respec-
tive GCD measurements recorded at an arbitrary current
density of 1.0 A g
/C0 1 is found in the order of ACRS-700
(258 F g /C0 1) > ACRS-600 (205 F g /C0 1) > ACRS-800
(166 F g /C0 1), as determined from Equation ( 1). Notably,
the batch of ACRS-700 exhibited maximum specific
capacitance, which is higher than various types of ACs
prepared from different sources. 30,31 The role of texture,
morphology, and concentration of major constituents
might play a role for the variation in their charge storage
properties. In view of this, a comprehensive study has
been performed on AC derived from the rice straw
(ACRS-700) and eucalyptus wood (ACEW-700) bio-
masses, both activated at 700
/C14 C under nitrogen gas flow
after treating with 3 M KOH.
The CV curves of ACRS-700 and ACEW-700 recorded
after running initial 50 cycles at variable scan rates are
given in Figure 1A, B , respectively. The respective GCD
plots of ACRS-700 and ACEW-700 are given in
Figure 1C, D . The CV depicted a rectangular-shaped plot
for both the batches at all the scan rates and current den-
sities, and the GCD appeared a triangle-shaped plot.
These profiles are typically observed for SCs,
4,5 and corre-
spond to capacitive behavior in carbon-based SCs with
fast charging-discharging capability. 32 The coulomb effi-
ciency of ACRS-700 is more than 100% at lower current
density, for example, at 0.5 A g /C0 1, which has been
discussed in Section S3, Supporting Information. With
increase in scan rate, the area of CV curve increases and
it is consistent with the Randles-Sevcik equation. The
specific capacitance ( Csp) of ACRS-700 and ACEW-700
are determined using Equation ( 1). The specific capaci-
tance of ACRS-700 determined from the GCD measure-
ments is maximum at 0.5 A g /C0 1 (365 F g /C0 1), which is
about 1.5 times greater than that of ACEW-700
(168 F g /C0 1 at 0.5 A g /C0 1, Table 1). The corresponding volu-
metric capacitances are also given in Table 1. The specific
capacitance decreased with increase in current density.
This is attributable to the time constraint for the electro-
lyte ions to access all the active sites of the electrode. The
potential drop at the beginning of the discharge stage in
GCD profile is negligible at lower current densities (ie, at
0.5, 1.0, and 2.0 A g
/C0 1) and it increased gradually
at higher current densities up to 10.0 A g /C0 1. This might
be attributable to the limited electrolyte diffusion
kinetics.
It is worthwhile to investigate the structural, mor-
phological, textural, and compositional parameters of
the two materials to account for the variation in their
specific capacitances. The structural property of ACRS-
700 and ACEW-700 has been studied from XRD and
Raman spectroscopy. Both the batches exhibit two
broad diffraction peaks in the XRD spectra, correspond-
ing to (002) and (101) lattice plane reflections of gra-
phitic structure, respectively (Figure
2A). The more
intense peak corresponding to (002) plane reveals
graphitization and carbonization of the sample, while
the minor peak corresponding to the (101) facet is
indicative of a partial crystalline nature in the AC
formed due to KOH activation process.
33 These broad-
ened XRD peaks indicate partial amorphous and disor-
dered structure in both the batches of AC. The (002)
plane of ACRS-700 is observed at 23.8 /C14 , which appeared
at a lesser 2 θ value than that of ACEW-700
(2θ = 25.1/C14 ). This indicates larger interlayer distance in
the ACRS-700 than ACEW-700. It is attributable to
higher concentration of non-planar hemicellulose com-
ponent in ACRS-700 than that in ACEW-700 (men-
tioned later in proximate analysis discussion). Our

incorporated with enhanced oxygen functionalities. 34
The graphitic nature in both the batches of AC is also
revealed from the Raman spectroscopy investigation. The
typical D and G bands of graphitic structure are observed
at 1365 cm
/C0 1 and at 1590 cm /C0 1 for ACRS-700, respec-
tively (Figure 2B). Compared to ACRS-700, the D and G
bands of ACEW-700 are observed at lesser energies, that
is, at 1353 and 1589 cm
/C0 1, respectively (Figure 2B). The
D-band is attributable to any structural defect in the gra-
phitic plane comprising the sp3 hybridized carbon atoms,
while G-band is attributable to the bond stretching with
sp
2 hybridization in graphitic plane. Such bands are
reported in polyaromatic hydrocarbons and also in gra-
phene.35,36 In addition, a broad hump comprising of 2D
band (overtone of D vibration mode) and D + G band
are observed in both ACRS-700 and in ACEW-700
(Figure 2B), which are associated with sp2 carbon in gra-
phitic system. 37 The higher graphitized nature in the
batch ACRS-700 is indicated from its greater IG/ID ratio
(1.1), as compared to that of ACEW-700 ( IG/ID = 1.03).
Furthermore, the surface microstructure in ACRS-700
and ACEW-700 are determined from BET surface area
measurements. The nitrogen adsorption-desorption iso-
therm plots of ACRS-700 and ACEW-700 represent a typ-
ical Type-I isotherm (Figure
2C, D , respectively). This
type of adsorption isotherm for carbon-based materials is
obtained in the mixed micro- and mesoporous struc-
ture.38 The BET surface area of ACRS-700 (3345 m 2 g/C0 1)
is significantly greater than that of ACEW-700
(1253 m2 g/C0 1). The pore sizes in ACRS-700 are deter-
mined as 1.8 and 3.4 nm, while the pore sizes in ACEW-
700 are found to be 1.2 and 2.0 nm (given in the insets of
Figure
2C, D , respectively). The pore volume for ACRS-
700 is significantly higher (2.0 cm 3/g) as compared to that
of ACEW-700 (0.5 cm 3/g). This is attributable to intercon-
nected porous network structure in ACRS-700. 39 The
order of BET surface area of ACRS-700 and ACEW-700
are consistent with their order of specific capacitances
(Table
1).
The morphological characteristics of as-prepared
ACRS-700 and ACEW-700 are investigated in detail using
scanning electron microscopy analysis. The FESEM
micrographs of ACRS-700 recorded at different magnifi-
cations and their energy dispersive x-ray spectrum are
given in Figure
3A-C. Similarly, the FE-SEM images of
ACEW-700 recorded at different magnifications and their
energy dispersive x-ray spectrum are given in Figure 3D-
F. Better morphological features of ACRS-700 and
ACEW-700 are reflected from higher resolution transmis-
sion electron microscopy images (Figure 4A-C and in
Figure 4D-F, respectively). The HR-TEM images reveal
randomly interconnected porous graphitic layered struc-
ture, particularly for ACRS-700, and the results are

The porous structure in AC is mainly achieved by
thermal activation of KOH-treated pyrolyzed biomasses.
During the KOH activation process, the pyrolyzed bio-
mass reacts with KOH and tends to liberate a series of
CO (g), H
2 (g), CO2 (g), and H 2O (g) leading to the forma-
tion of pores and the intermediate products such as
K
2CO3 and K 2O. The produced K 2CO3 and CO 2 react
with carbon to form potassium and release CO, which is
also responsible for the formation of additional pores.
The as-obtained potassium intercalates into the carbon
matrix, which is removed during washing with dilute
HCl and DI water producing large fraction of micropo-
rous structure. The tentative chemical reactions involved
in the formation of pores have already been discussed in
our earlier published work.
24 Quantitatively, large frac-
tion of pores are obtained in ACRS-700 as compared to
those in ACEW-700. The variation in the porous struc-
ture and surface area in the respective batches is likely to
be due to chemical composition of the respective

eucalyptus wood biomass are determined from proximate

40 The rice straw biomass constitutes 16.5% acid-
insoluble lignin, 2.4% acid-soluble lignin, 32.7% cellulose,
21.8% hemicellulose, 7.8% moisture, and 19.1% ash. The
eucalyptus wood biomass constitutes 33.1% acid-
insoluble lignin, 39.5% cellulose, 11.6% hemicellulose,
7.7% moisture, and 0.3% ash. These compositions are
given as weight percent. The significant variation in the
concentration of lignin, hemicellulose, and cellulose,
along with their respective molecular structures might
play a role in the formation of pores during pyrolysis and
alkali activation at higher temperature. The literature
suggests the decomposition or condensation of hydroxyl
groups in cellulose and hemicellulose produces large
amount of CO, CO
2, and H 2O even at lower temperature
leading to the formation of pores. 41 On the other hand,
lignin comprises of aromatic rings that are not readily
decomposed and hence the pore sizes or volumes are
lesser in ACEW-700 than in ACRS-700. The ultimate
CHNS analysis of the of ACRS-700 revealed 46.0% car-
bon, 3.7% hydrogen, 0.2% nitrogen, 0.06% sulphur, and
50.0% oxygen. While, CHNS analysis of ACEW-700
revealed 60.8% carbon, 3.8% hydrogen, 0.2% nitrogen,
0.01% sulphur, and 35.1% oxygen. Notably, the chemical
analysis suggested that the batch ACRS-700 comprised of
larger concentrations of oxygen group than the batch
ACEW-700.
The composition of ACRS-700 and ACEW-700 is fur-
ther deduced from XPS and FT-IR analysis. The survey
scan of the batch ACRS-700 confirmed the presence of C
(1s), O (1s), and Si (2p) with atomic percentage of 63.2 at
%, 28.3 at% and 8.5 at%, respectively (Figure
5A). The
high-resolution binding energy spectrum of C 1s of
ACRS-700 exhibits two strong peaks at 284.6 and
285.8 eV and a weak broad peak at 289.3 eV (Figure 5B).
The peak at 284.6 eV corresponds to sp2 carbon in C =C.
The peak at 285.8 eV due to C-O-C (ether) and/or C-C
group, while the small peak at 289.3 eV is attributable to
less populated O-C =O (carboxylic/ester) in the struc-
ture.
24 Similarly, the O 1s binding energy spectrum
showed three peaks at 532.6, 533.2, and 534.8 eV, respec-
tively (Figure 5C). The strong peak at 533.2 eV corre-
sponds to C-O groups and the broad peak at 534.8 eV is
attributable to O-C =O (carboxylic/ester) group. However,
the weak peak at 532.6 eV is obtained, which is attribut-
able to the Si-O/C-O-C species, which indicates SiO
2 and
ether groups on the surface of ACRS-700. The SiO 2 com-
ponent in ACRS-700 is also revealed from the binding
energy spectrum of Si 2p (Figure
5D), in which the peak
at 104 eV is attributed to Si-O bond. 42 In the case of
ACEW-700, C (1s) and O (1s) constitute 89.3 at% and
10.7 at%, respectively. The batch ACEW-700 comprises of
C=C, C-O-C/C-C, and COOH groups as evident from the
peaks at 284.7, 286.0, and 288.4 eV, respectively in C1s
spectrum. Similarly the functionalities (C =O, C-O, and
COOH) are also reflected from the peaks at 530.9, 532.7,
and 534.4 eV in O1s spectrum of ACEW-700. Notably,

The FT-IR spectrum of ACRS-700 (Figure 6) reveals

The presence of aromatic benzene ring is further sup-
ported by the characteristic C =C stretching (1436 cm /C0 1,

For realizing practical applications, it is necessary
that the supercapacitor electrode material should be elec-
trochemically stable over a number of cyclic studies. The
stability of ACRS-700 and ACEW-700 for 8000 cycles has
been evaluated at a current density of 10.0 A g
/C0 1 and the
cyclic GCD plots are given in Figure 7G. The batches
ACRS-700 and ACEW-700 exhibit exceptionally high
capacitance retention, which is attributable to the grad-
ual activation of carbon electrode generating more active
sites for charge storage. In addition, the wetting of porous
active electrode (ACRS-700 and ACEW-700) with the
electrolytic ions endowed better accessibility of electro-
lyte ions towards the micro- and meso-porosity of the
electrode during prolonged charge-discharge process
which resulted in the initial increase of charge retention.
Similar exceptional capacitance retention higher than its
original value are reported in some of the porous carbon-
based electrodes.
49
Compared to ACEW-700, the enhanced specific
capacitance in ACRS-700 is mainly attributable to several
factors in ACRS-700, for example, (a) higher surface area
which could enhance the electrode-electrolyte interaction
and favor the charge accumulation phenomenon;
(b) higher extent of graphitization, which favour mobility
of electrolyte ions through the pores of active material
and access the entire surface for the charge storage;
(c) abundant redox-active oxygen functionalities at the
surface of ACRS-700 might favour redox transformations
in charging-discharging process for more efficient charge
storage phenomenon
10; (d) better electrode-electrolyte
interactions due to enhanced polarity and surface wetta-
bility of the electrode surface because of presence of
abundant carbon-oxygen functionalities; and (e) low ion
transport resistance in three dimensional interconnected
micro-mesoporous structure reflected from decrease in
the W
R and Rct across ACRS-700/electrolyte interface
in EIS measurement. The lower values of resistances ( Rct
and WR) are favourable for ion transportation and
enhance the specific capacitance of ACRS-700.
The detailed structural characterization and electro-
chemical investigation revealed that the batch ACRS-700
is the best-performing efficient electrode material and is
further used for the fabrication of aqueous and non-
aqueous based SSC.

and non-aqueous electrolyte

profile. The specific capacitance ( C
sp) of the SSC device

g/C0 1. The specific capacitances measured at higher current
densities, for example, 1.5, 2.0, 3.0, and 4.0 A g /C0 1 were
lesser, (ie, 78, 60, 42, and 24 F g /C0 1, respectively). From

oxygen contents is a better supercapacitor electrode mate-
rial than that of eucalyptus wood. Compared to the AC
prepared from eucalyptus wood (ie, ACEW-700), the
enhanced specific capacitance in AC from rice straw (ie,
ACRS-700) has been discussed on the basis of several fac-
tors, for example, (a) high surface area; (b) high propor-
tion of graphitization; (c) abundant redox-active oxygen
functionalities at the surface of ACRS-700; (e) low ion
transport resistance due to micro-mesoporous structure.
The detailed charge storage mechanism has been dis-
cussed. The difference in the charge storage property has
been attributed to higher hemicellulose contents and
lower lignin content in rice straw biomass than those of
eucalyptus wood biomass, which resulted in much higher
surface area and suitable micro-mesoporous material in
AC of rice straw. The application of ACRS-700 as elec-
trode material has been revealed by illuminating “IITR”
electric panel using as-fabricated SSCs devices, operated
with aqueous (2 M NaCl) and non-aqueous (ie, tetraalky-
lammonium based ionic liquid) electrolytes. The specific
energy (42.7 W h kg
/C0 1) and specific power (1.9 kW kg /C0 1)
at 1.0 A g /C0 1 obtained for the ionic liquid-based ACRS-
700//ACRS-700 SSC are promising for real applications.

Biomass Porous Carbon Derived from Celery Leaves with
High Capacitance for Supercapacitor
Jiaqi Wu, Zihan Ma, Guangning Wang,* and Tingting Chen*
[a]
To develop environmentally friendly and high-performance
supercapacitors, the low-cost, high-capacitance renewable
electrode material is at present viewed as one of the most
challenging tasks for obtaining the next-generation of energy
storage devices. Therefore, in this study, Celery leaves, a
common biomass vegetable, are used to prepare activated
carbon for high voltage and high-capacity supercapacitors
through a simple method. Due to their high surface area and
abundant nitrogen and sulfur heteroatoms, hierarchically
porous carbon materials can simultaneously realize high
capacity and long-cycling durability. The specific capacitance
has been recorded to be up to 753.0 F g
� 1
at 0.5 A g
� 1
with
capacity retention as high as 96.7 % even after 5,000 cycles.
Also, the assembled symmetric cell provided a high energy
density of 17.36 Wh kg
� 1
at 250 W kg
� 1
. The effects of yellow
and green colors and different activation temperatures on the
properties of electrode materials were systematically studied.
The results showed an excellent electrochemical performance
in biomass carbon electrode materials, which would facilitate
the development of a high-quality energy system and a green
supercapacitor.
Introduction
With the worsening of the environment and depletion of
resources, the human society is in crisis. Therefore, there is a
critical need to develop high energy conversion efficiency
storage devices. Supercapacitors (SCs) have attracted attention
because of the merits of large power density, good cycling
stability, fast charging, and discharging.
[1]
Thus, the super-
capacitor is being used in various ways for electronics as well
as electric vehicles with hybrid drive and pulse technology.
[2]
However, the SCs have low energy density, which limits the
range of the original application. Generally, it is proportional to
the supercapacitor’s energy density with capacitance and
voltage window.
[3]
The potential window can be increased by
assembling an asymmetric supercapacitor. Although high
capacitance electrode materials have been widely used in the
positive electrode of the asymmetric supercapacitor, it is
difficult to obtain negative electrodes that have high capaci-
tance. Generally, carbon materials with large negative potential
windows are used as negative electrode.
[4]
Carbon materials,
such as, graphene, carbon nanotubes, porous carbon, etc. are
versatile. They are not only non-toxic, chemically stable, and
readily conduct electricity, but also have peculiar properties
can accelerate electrolyte ions diffusion.
[5]
However, the low
capacitance of traditional carbon materials reduces the energy
density of SCs. Finding a negative electrode with high
capacitance remains a challenge, which limits the development
of SCs. Specifically, increasing the specific surface areas (SSA)
can improve the capacitance and rate performance by adjust-
ing the pore distribution of carbon.
[6]
The wettability can be
increased by doping heteroatoms on the carbon surface, and
the electrolyte-accessible areas can be enlarged.
[7]
However,
these electrode materials are usually prepared using expensive
and unsustainable raw materials.
[8]
Given all these require-
ments, biomass is seen as a high-efficiency carbon precursor
because of its economical and continuable potential. Using
special processes, well-distributed pore size and physicochem-
ical stability were exhibited in some biomass-derived carbons.
[9]
They have the advantages of large potential windows, stable
physicochemical properties, easy synthesis, and are often used
as a positive pole in asymmetric SCs.
[10]
Additionally, biochar
raw materials tend to contain a mass of oxygen-containing
functional groups, such as C � O, C = O, and carboxyl groups,
improving their performance over traditional carbon
materials.
[11]
For example, Wu et al. used albizia flowers to
prepare hierarchical porous carbon microrods for SCs. The
specific capacitance (Cs) reached 406 F g
� 1
at a current density
of 0.5 A g
� 1
in a 6 M KOH electrolyte.
[12]
It could improve
capacitance performance and energy storage in SCs by
selecting suitable biomass precursors and catalysts. Regarding
SCs, biomass is a promising electrode material. However, there
are still many factors preventing its further use: finiteness of
geographical distribution, production, and transportation.
[13]
Celery, which is widely planted in China, naturally has several
elements that can be doped, and people always eat celery
stalks but discard celery leaves as garbage. Celery stem had
been used to prepare porous carbon in supercapacitors with
good charge storage capacity, but unfortunately it was
prepared by expensive freeze-drying and the SSA was only
507.73 m
2
g
� 1
.
[14]
Celery stem is usually eaten and celery leaves
are wasted, and celery leaves and celery stems have different
morphology. Therefore, the biomass porous carbon derived

be used as waste but also have high SSA and charge storage
capacity.
Therefore, a quick absent template method was developed
to efficiently synthesize porous carbon by carbonizing celery
leaves and activating them with KOH (Scheme 1). In this view,
the effects of activator and carbonization temperature on the
formation of biomass carbon pores were investigated. Also, the
impact of yellow leaves and green leaves on the electro-
chemical performance of SCs was investigated in detail.
Results and Discussion
Materials characterization. Scanning electron microscopy
(SEM) was used to study the morphology of celery-derived
porous carbon. The SEM images of five samples were
compared. Figure 1a-b show random distribution of some
pores on the surface of the carbon material that green leaves
with 800 ° C activation temperature (aGCL-800). Several pores
were derived from the development of gases, such as H
2
and
CO
2
in the carbon layers during the fission of KOH. Figure 1c-d
show the magnified SEM images of porous carbonized at
different conditions. When carbonized green leaves at 700 ° C,
aGCL-700 (Figure 1c) has only some nanopoles due to low
carbonization temperature and graphitization. Due to the lack
of activator action, many pores were not formed in the GCL-
800 that green leaves with 800 ° C activation temperature
absence with activator (Figure 1d). Combined with BJH desorp-
tion, the average pore diameter of aGCL-800 and aGCL-900
(Figure S1a) aYCL-800 (Figure S1b) carbonized yellow leaves
with 800 ° C activation temperature is 3.942, 3.941 and
3.938 nm, respectively. The Transmission Electron Microscope
(TEM) images (Figure S1c) indicate the presence of micropores
that were randomly distributed and irregularly shaped. The
TEM images (Figure S1d) also explain the deficiency of any
graphitic domains, revealing the non-crystalline property of
aGCL-800.
[15]
Therefore, suitable temperature and activator
action promote aGCL-800 to have a large number of pore size
structure at the same time, which successfully improves the
SSA of the electrode material and is conducive to the electro-
lyte and electrode material adequately contact.
The powder X-ray diffraction (XRD), Raman spectra, X-ray
photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), and the Brunauer-Emmett-
Teller (BET) were used to show the chemical structure of the
GCL-800, aGCL-800, and aYCL-800. In Figure S2, XRD was used
to investigate the crystal structure of the graphitized porous
carbon material. All XRD patterns demonstrate two character-
istic peaks at 2θ of 22 ° (002) and 43 ° (100). There was a broad
diffraction peak of carbon in XRD patterns which confirmed the
amorphous carbon structure.
[16]
The Raman spectra of GCL-800, aGCL-800, and aYCL-800
indicate two peaks (Figure 2a). G implies graphite carbon, and
D implies defects and disordered carbon located at about
1595 cm
� 1
and 1350 cm
� 1
, respectively.
[17]
Generally, the inten-
sity ratio of two peaks (I
D
/I
G
) expresses defected degree of the
carbon materials.
[18]
The I
D
/I
G
values of aYCL-800, GCL-800, and
aGCL-800 were calculated to be 2.255, 2.603, and 2.729,
respectively. The higher I
D
/I
G
ratios of aGCL-800 indicated more
sites for ion accommodation and good electrochemical
performance.
[19]
The N
2

to characterize the porosity parameters of these carbon
samples. Based on Figure 2b–c, aGCL-800 was found to mainly
have micro-pores and meso-pores which worked in enlarging
the specific SSA and ion transport.
[20]
Compared with GCL-800
and aYCL-800, aGCL-800 presented a highly SSA of

[21]
Thus, aGCL-800 could effectively
quicken ion movement, resulting in high capacitance and

the coulombic efficiency of the device was recorded to be
99.9 % efficient, supporting its efficiency and reproducibility.
This proves that the electrode material has excellent practical
performance. Besides, it showed 91–99.8 % energy efficiency
when assembled SSC device indicated low energy loss during
the discharging process in Figure S11. The Nyquist plots of the
aGCL-800 SSC was showed in Figure S12 and it showed that
aGCL-800 SSC has a small Rct and Rs (0.39 Ω and 1.619 Ω)
indicating its excellent conductivity in aqueous electrolyte.
The remarkable electrochemical performance of aGCL-800
for SCs could be ascribed to the following aspects: 1) celery leaf
itself also showed excellent capability since it is rich in fiber
and elements. These advantages guaranteed the fabrication of
pores and improvement of surface wetting ability; 2) due to the
activation of KOH, pores of all sizes were distributed in original
starting material so that the ions could continue to flow rapidly
resulting in a high Cs; 3) More importantly, aGCL-800 has some
factors of heteroatom doped, high graphitization degree and
hierarchical porous structure so that it showed excellent
electrochemical performance. Many doped heteroatoms (N, O,
S) could be considered profitable for enhancing capacitance
through increased ion adsorption sites and offer extra faradaic
pseudo-capacitance. Improvements to the graphitization re-
sulted in further improvement in the electrical chemical proper-
ties of the active material and increasing the conductivity of
the material. When large-scale ions proceed discharge/charge,
several macropores played an important part in buffering
them, meanwhile the main function of the micropores was to
increase the capacitance of the double layer. With the large
SSA (1409.728 m
2
g
� 1
), aGCL-800 contained various electric
charges, by shortening the diffusion length to implement the
acceleration of the charging process while the effective
reduction of the current resistance by the interconnection was
one of the reasons for its high capacitance. Consequently, the
aGCL-800 electrode displayed an impressive Cs (753.0 F g
� 1
at
0.5 A g
� 1
) and stable cycling performance (86 % even after 10
000 cycles). The as-prepared aGCL-800 samples could serve as
potential sustainable electrodes for the production of high-
performance SCs.
Conclusion
Here, a simple strategy was developed using pyrolysis and KOH
activation to activate porous carbon SCs. The different heter-
oatoms in the material, carbonization temperature, and
introduction of activator played a great role in the improve-
ment of subsequent electrochemical performance. As previ-
ously mentioned, the aGCL-800 showed many excellent
features: the structure of hierarchical porous, large SSA, higher
degree of graphitization, and Cs. Moreover, the SSC showed
that the Cs reached 125 F g
� 1
at 0.5 A g
� 1
and the Cs showed
minimal change after 10000 cycles, demonstrating an excellent
cycling stability. The supercapacitance performances of aGCL-
800 were much better than most studies reporting carbon-
based material from biomass. This study offers a useful way to
produce finely hierarchical porous carbonaceous substances via
a simply chemical activation-assisted pyrolysis process. It could
turn biomass into modern energy storage equipment and
could be used in other energy storage materials and equip-
ment.
Experimental Section
All the reagents and solvents were purchased from chemical
suppliers and used without any further purification.
Synthesis of the celery leaves-derived porous carbon: The waste
celery leaves that were collected from the canteen of Harbin
Normal University washed multiple times with deionized water to
remove visible mud. The cleaned green celery leaves were placed
in a cool, ventilated place and dried naturally. Then the dried celery
leaves were put into a tube furnace and calcined at a temperature
of 600 ° C for 1 h under the protection of nitrogen. The carbonated
samples were mixed with KOH at the mass ratio of 1 : 4 in an
aqueous solution. The dried celery leaves/KOH mixture was then
heated at 800 ° C under a nitrogen atmosphere. The product was
washed with 1 M HCl and distilled water thoroughly for several
times until the pH = 7 and then it was dried at 80 ° C and named it
aGCL-800 which the figure is activation temperature. For compar-
ison, the different activation temperature (700 ° C, 900 ° C) were also
investigated in the above process. The samples were denoted as
aGCL-700 and aGCL-900. What’ s more, in order to study the effect
of activator on the properties of the prepared samples, the GCL-
800 absence with activator was also investigated in above process.
The yellow celery leaves which procedure was similar with aGCL-
800 were named as aYCL-800.
Preparation of the working electrode: The working electrode was
prepared by pressing a homogeneous paste of 80 % (wt.) active
material, 10 % (wt.) carbon black and 10 % (wt.) polyvinylidene
fluoride (PVDF) onto carbon paper followed by overnight drying at
60 ° C. The mixture was brushed evenly onto the carbon paper with
a pipettor. And the area of each electrode piece was 1 cm × 1 cm =
1 cm
2
. The thickness of the working electrode is about 60 μm.
Before used, the electrodes were vacuum dried at 80 ° C for 12 h
thus the mass loading of the active material of electrode was about
2.00 mg cm
� 2
. The mass of positive and negative active material
aGCL-800 are 2.040 mg and 2.872 mg, respectively. So, the total
mass of active material for device case is 4.912 mg when assembled
device.

Elementally doped biomass‑derived activated 
carbon (Sm‑doped MS‑AC) for enhanced 
supercapacitor performance
Muhammad Moeez1, B. M. Alotaibi2, Haifa A. Alyousef2, Albandari W. Alrowaily2, Rizwan Ul Hassan3,*, 
Hussain Sawwan4, and Reda A. Haggam5
1 Department of Chemistry, Government Graduate College for Boys, Taunsa Sharif 32100, Pakistan
2 Department of Physics, College of Science, Princess Nourah bint Abdulrahman University, 84428, 11671 Riyadh, Saudi Arabia
3 Department of Chemical and Biological Engineering, Gachon University, Seongnam‑Si, Gyeonggi‑Do 13120, Republic of Korea
4 Department of Chemical Engineering, College of Engineering, King Khalid University, 61411 Abha, Saudi Arabia
5 Department of Chemistry, Faculty of Science, Islamic University of Madinah, 42351 Madinah, Saudi Arabia
ABSTRACT
The development of sustainable and effective electrode materials is essential to 
the advancement of high-performance supercapacitors. In this study, we report a 
low-cost, eco-friendly way of producing samarium-doped activated carbon from 
mosambi peel (sweet lime) waste using the KOH activation process for utilization 
in supercapacitors. The addition of samarium to the biomass carbon framework 
increased the number of active sites and enhanced the material’s characteristics. 
Electrochemical analysis demonstrates that the samarium-doped mosambi peel-
activated carbon (Sm-doped MS-AC) electrode achieves a remarkable specific 
capacitance  (Cs) of 560 F/g at 1 A/g current density. The material demonstrates 
a high energy and power densities of 68.80 Wh/kg  (Ed) and 470 W/kg  (Pd). Fur-
thermore, the electroactive material revealed excellent kinetic features with a low 
solution resistance  (Rs) of 0.6 Ω and retained exceptional cycling stability over 
6500th cycles. The practical capabilities of the material were evaluated through 
two-electrode symmetric studies. These analyses yielded  Cs of 182 F/g,  Ed of 
20.54 Wh/kg, and  Pd of 1800 W/kg. These results demonstrate the crucial role 
that heteroatom engineering plays in improving the electrochemical behaviour 
of carbons derived from biomass, offering an adaptable approach for sustainable 
energy storage devices.

1 Introduction
The global utilisation of conventional fuel brought 
about by the industrial revolution caused a significant 
negative influence on environment [1 ]. Fossil fuels 
are running out, there is an enhanced requirement to 
develop sustainable sources. However, external factors 
must be constantly focussed on the impact of renew-
able energy sources like water, wind, and solar [2 ]. 
These resources also have a number of serious draw-
backs, such as their complete reliance on nature for 
example, the need for wind to produce electricity or 
inability to utilise solar cells at night [3 , 4]. In recent 
decades, researchers have emphasized their efforts 
creating energy conserving and storage applications. 
Batteries, capacitors, and supercapacitors  (SCs) are 
example of energy storing electronic devices that are 
essential for overcoming these obstacles. Nevertheless, 
fuel cells and batteries are much more costly, have less 
ion mobility and limited durability than  SCs [5, 6].
As a result,  SCs contributed to closing the gap 
between minor energy density  (Ed) of capacitors and 
lower power density  (Pd) of batteries.  SCs are viewed 
as one of the leading prospects for energy storage 
innovations due to its quick charging, long lifespan, 
high  Pd and environmental safety [ 7, 8]. As a result, 
 S Cs are a superior choice for electronic devices that 
demand a constant supply of energy, together with 
portable electrical appliances and other electric vehi-
cles such as hybrid electric cars [9 , 10]. These  SCs are 
categorised as electric double-layer capacitor (EDLC), 
pseudo capacitor (PC), or hybrid supercapacitors rely-
ing on charge storage approach [11]. In order to store 
charges, the EDLC gathers double-layer charges at 
electrode/electrolyte interface [12]. In EDLC, carbo-
naceous substances containing carbon, graphene and 
graphite are typically used electroactive materials [13, 
14]. However, PC enable charge storage through redox 
reactions that include electron transport between elec-
trode and electrolyte [ 15]. Furthermore, because of 
their enormous  Ed and ability attained by integrating 
complementary qualities of PC and EDLC with high 
voltage hybrid supercapacitor (HSC) believed to be 
efficient of preserving energy [16].
Moreover, carbon materials having special qualities, 
such as their affordability, chemical inactivity, high 
surface area and modifiable pore size provide attrac-
tive options for  SCs. Activated carbon (AC) is most 
effective adsorbent in world and surface accumula-
tion is one of the most used techniques for recovering

biomass-based activated carbon for enhanced elec-
trochemical performance. The incorporation of Sm 
effectively improves electric double layer and faradic 
behaviour, leading to significant increase in  Cs and  Ed. 
This study offers a cost effective, eco-friendly strategy 
for high-performance supercapacitor design.
The objectives of this study, to explore effect of Sm 
doping on biomass-derived AC for improved SC per-
formance. The different physical analyses techniques 
were employed to investigate the structural, morpho-
logical and surface area of the studies, while electro-
chemical results exhibits higher  Cs (560 F/g),  Ed (68.80 
Wh/Kg) and  Pd (470 W/Kg). These findings demon-
strate the Sm-doped MS-AC is a prospective electrode 
material for advanced SC.
2  Experimentalanalyses
2.1  Reagentsutilised
Chemicals utilised for fabrication of Sm-doped 
MS-AC composite were samarium nitrate (III) hexa-
hydrate (Sm(NO 3)3.6H2O, 98%), potassium hydrox-
ide (KOH, 99.9%), citric acid  (C6H8O7, 99%) ethanol 
 ( C2H5OH, 99.4%), hydrochloric acid (HCl, 37%), poly 
(vinylidene fluoride) (PVDF, 99.9%) all are acquired 
from Sigma–Aldrich, while mosambi peel gathered 
from local market.
2.2  Fabricationofmosambipeel(sweetlime)
activatedcarbon(MS‑AC)
Waste mousambi peel biomass was converted into 
porous hard carbon using chemical and physical acti-
vation approaches. Peels from biomass, cleaned using 
ethanol and distilled water eliminate of contaminants 
and dehydrated for 12 h at 100 °C. 10 g of already-pre-
pared mosambi peel powder were mixed with KOH 
in ratio of 1:3 and calcined for 4 h at 500 °C in order 
to produce AC. Derived material first purified using 
distilled  H2O. After being drying at 80 °C to create AC 
and stored for further characterization [31].
2.3  SynthesisofSm‑dopedMS‑AC
nanocomposite
1 g of mosambi peel (sweet lime) activated carbon (MS-
AC) was dissolved in 50 mL of distilled  H2O in order 
to create Sm-doped MS-AC using a hydrothermal 
method. For half an hour, this dispersion was agitated. 
0.3 g Citric acid used to make the carbon more porous 
with a hierarchical structure [32] followed by 0.03 g of 
samarium nitrate hexahydrate [Sm(NO 3)3.6H2O] cor-
responding to 3 wt.% weight of activated carbon. This 
combination shifted to autoclave and heated for 4 h at 
180 °C. Once precipitates collected, they repeatedly 
purified with distilled  H2O. After that, precipitates 
dried for 24 h at 80 °C, display in scheme 1 [33].
2.4  Fabricationoftheelectrode
Nickel-foam (Ni-foam) was cut into (1 × 1  cm2) small 
pieces and cleaned via sonication with HCl, ethanol 
and then distilled water. The nanocomposite (0.015 g), 
carbon black (0.0025 g) used to increase the conduc-
tion, PVDF (0.0025 g) act as a binder used to bind the 
material on Ni-foam, and binder solution n-methyl-
epyroledone (75 μL) were mixed for 2 h in an HPLC 
tube to create the required slurry. The resulting slurry 
was then applied to Ni- foam utilising the drop-cast-
ing approach with help of a micropipette. Finally, the 
deposited nickel foam was then dried at 90 °C.
2.5  Characterizationtechnique
The XRD (X-ray Diffraction) technique was utilised 
to observe crystalline attributes of generated sub-
stance activated carbon (MS-AC) and Sm-doped 
MS-AC. This was determined using the D8 Advance 
Bruker X-ray diffractometer with Cu-Kα source 
(40 kV, 100 mA, λ = 1.5418 A°) with 2θ in 10° to 70°. 
Brunauer–Emmett–Teller (BET), a surface area ana-
lyser technique, is used to look at a certain surface 
area utilising Nova-2200 Quantachrome instrument. 
A Zeiss Sigma-500VP scanning electron microscopy 
(SEM) equipment utilised to take SEM images, while 
FT-IR confirmed the position of functional groups uti-
lising FT-IR spectrometer (Thermo Scientific Systems 
Nicolet-6700).
2.6  Electrochemicalcharacterizationtechnique
Cyclic voltammetry (CV), galvanostatic charge–dis-
charge (GCD), electrochemical surface area (ECSA), 
electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS), and 
chronoamperometry (CA) executed on three-electrode 
setup in 3 M KOH using lab’s CS Corrtest 350 M equip-
ment. Ag/AgCl were employed as reference electrodes, 
Pt wires as auxiliary electrodes, and Sm-doped MS-AC

3  Resultsanddiscussion
Crystalline structure and phase composition of syn-
thesised material assessed by XRD. Figure 1a displays 
diffractogram for both the pristine activated carbon 
(MS-AC) and Sm-doped MS-AC nanocomposite over a 
2θ degrees range of 10° to 70°. Since, samarium nitrate 
hexahydrate precursor was incorporated on to the 
biomass-derived carbon without undergoing a sub-
sequent annealing step, the XRD pattern is primarily 
characterized by prominent hydroxide related peaks 
rather than oxide phases. However, the presence of 
minor peaks corresponding to samarium oxide sug-
gest a thermal effect occurred during hydrothermal 
preparation process. This combination of phases con-
firms the successful incorporation of samarium into 
the MS-AC framework [ 34]. In addition to prevent-
ing the collapse of porosity and large surface area of 
activated carbon, lack of annealing helps maintain 
electrolyte penetration and redox activity [35]. The 
diffraction peaks of Sm(OH)3 at 41.35° and 50.04° cor-
respond to the hexagonal Sm(OH)3 hkl values of (201) 
and (300), which reliable with standard JCPDS card 
No. 00–006-0117 and hkl values for cubic  Sm2O3 were 
(411) and (541), which match the diffraction peaks of 
 S m2O3 at 34.8° and 54.3°, respectively which consist-
ent with standard JCPDS card No. 00–015-0813. XRD 
pattern shows a large MS-AC peak at roughly 2θ = 25° 
and 42°, which correspond to (002) and (100) planes, 
similarly, that consistent with conventional pattern 
(JCPDS # 75–0444) [36, 37]. XRD pattern of Sm-doped 
MS-AC shows both discrete peaks from pure samar-
ium salt and broad MS-AC peak. That indicates that 
Sm was successfully integrated into MS-AC matrix 
while preserving amorphous character of MS-AC. 
The diffraction peak slightly shifts and broadens as 
a result of Sm doping, indicating lattice distortion 
and charge in structural, increased in crystalline size 
ordering within the MS-AC matrix [38]. Additional 
peaks that correspond to Sm-based phases (Sm(OH) 3

and  Sm2O3) show that the inclusion of Sm species was 
successful. Overall, the change in the peaks is a reflec-
tion of the strain and defect creation caused by Sm 
doping, which altered the carbon structure. Because 
Sm doping may reduces the distance between the lay-
ers in the material, the peak shifts to the right. The 
XRD peaks naturally shift to a higher 2θ location as 
the spacing decreases [39]. The crystallite sizes of Sm-
doped MS-AC nanocomposite were measured to be 
21.5 nm, by using the Scherrer Eq. (1) [40].
Here, D stands for crystallite size, θ for Bragg’s 
angle, β for full width at half maximum, λ for Kα 
radiation wavelength (0.15406 nm), and K (Scherrer 
constant) was 0.9. According to XRD patterns, MS-AC 
exhibits a broader diffraction peak at 2θ = 25°, that 
aligns to (002) plane. Following the doping, the peak 
shifts to a higher angle, causing the interlayer space 
to reduce from 0.40 nm (MS-AC) to 0.30 nm (doped). 
These demonstrate the addition of Sm to the MS-AC 
matrix. Additionally, broad diffraction peaks indicate 
a disorder after doping.
FT-IR of synthesised MS-AC and Sm-doped 
MS-AC was analysed in the 400–4000  cm−1 range 
to observe functional groups, as shown in Fig. 1b. 
These FT-IR findings clearly demonstrate the rela-
tionship between pure and doped activated carbon. 
Typically, carbonaceous features dominate the pure 
MS-AC spectra. For instance, the presence of a peak 
(1)D = O.9/u1D706
/u1D6FDcos/u1D703
between 1200 and 1350  cm−1 indicates the bonding 
with carbon O–C–O or C–OH, while several peaks 
between 1350 and 1600 represent the C=O, C–O func-

3.1  Electrochemicalcharacterisation
The electrochemical properties of activated carbon 
(MS-AC) and Sm-doped MS-AC composite were 
examined using electrolytic analysis in a three-elec-
trode configuration. However, as shown in Fig. 3a, b, 
CV voltammogram at a potential of -0.25 to 0.8 was 
shown at different sweep rates (5–60 mV/s). Sm-doped 
MS-AC performs better electrochemically than pure 
MS-AC, as seen by the cyclic voltammetry curves’ big-
ger CV area, anodic and cathodic peak current, and 
more noticeable redox characteristic. These improve-
ments show that in addition to activated carbon’s 
intrinsic double-layer capacitance, Sm incorporation 
improves the number of electroactive sites, enhances 
electron transport, and promotes faradic behaviour. 
The collaborative effect of Sm doping on the biomass-
derived activated carbon is demonstrated by the CV 
comparison in Fig. 3c. However, the EDLC character-
istic is predominantly displayed by the pure MS-AC.

4  Conclusion
In the present research, biomass-derived activated 
carbon (AC) from mosambi (sweet lime) peels was 
hydrothermally combined with samarium salt to 
create Sm-doped MS-AC, which resulted in high SC 
electrode productivity. Based on GCD tests, electro -
chemical characterisation revealed that the Sm-doped 
MS-AC composite electrode had a higher  Cs of 560 
F/g at 1 A/g, with  Ed of 68.80 Wh/kg and  Pd of 470 W/
kg. The Nyquist plot illustrates doped electrodes with 
 Rs values of 0.60 Ω, while an excellent cyclic stability 
over 6500th cycles. For the creation of MS-AC nano-
structures, the usage of samarium offers a number of 
benefits. Increased faradic sites on the MS-AC matrix 
within the nanostructures, reduced  Rs, and improved 
conduction are all benefits of Sm doping. As a result, 
the addition of Sm stabilize the MS-AC nanostruc-
ture which is confirmed by its consistent performance 
across several charge–discharge cycles. While sym -
metric study demonstrates  Cs,   Ed and  Pd of Sm-doped 
MS-AC was 182 F/g, 20.54 Wh/kg and 1800 W/kg, simi-
larly. These results indicate that our created Sm-doped 
MS-AC nanocomposite material can also be employed 
in other energy storage applications like batteries.

Journal of Porous Materials (2023) 30:2113–2120 
https://doi.org/10.1007/s10934-023-01487-3
Potassium gluconate‑assisted synthesis of biomass derived porous 
carbon for high‑performance supercapacitor
Yu Feng1 · Ge Li1 · Xiaoliang Wu1 
Published online: 20 June 2023 
© The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Science+Business Media, LLC, part of Springer Nature 2023
Abstract
Porous carbon has attracted enormous attentions as electrode materials for supercapacitor due to its sufficient porosity and 
large specific surface area. In this paper, we reported a convenient approach for the preparation of activated porous carbon 
(APC) by one-step activation method using bacterial cellulose as carbon source and potassium gluconate as activator. The 
obtained porous carbon possesses a unique porous framework with suitable specific surface area and rich oxygen content. 
Benefiting from the unique structure, the obtained electrode shows a high specific capacitance of 437 F  g−1  at 0.5 A  g−1  
and excellent electrochemical stability. More interestingly, the constructed APC-700//APC-700 symmetrical supercapacitor 
exhibits a high energy density of 23.5 Wh  kg−1  and good cycling stability in 1 M  Na2SO4 aqueous electrolyte. Therefore, the 
work provides a new and facile method to prepare porous carbon-based electrode materials from biomass for supercapacitor.
Keywords Bacteria cellulose · Potassium gluconate · Hierarchical porous carbon · Supercapacitor
1 Introduction
Along with the fast increasing of portable electronic devices 
and new energy vehicles, high-efficiency energy storage 
devices have become a promising choice. Among current 
energy storage equipment, supercapacitors have gained 
extensive research as a result of their high power density, 
fast charging and discharging rate and good electrochemical 
stability [1 –5]. Porous carbon with excellent conductivity 
and high specific surface area are often the first choice for 
commercialized electrode materials [6 –9]. But traditional 
porous carbon materials are often derived from non-renew-
able fossil energy. In recent years, for the sustainable devel-
opment, biomass porous carbon materials, which have the 
advantages of wide source, green and low cost as a suitable 
alternative material are widely used in electrode materials, 
such as eggshell [10], plant straw [11], poplar catkins [12] 
and various pollens [13].
Bacterial celluloses (BCs), a porous network nanoscale 
biopolymer synthesized by microbial fermentation, can be 
efficiently produced by metabolism of acetic acid bacteria 
[14]. In addition, bacterial cellulose has a natural porous net-
work nanostructure. This network porous structure ensures 
high specific surface area and low electron transport resist-
ance of carbon electrode materials [15–18]. Recently, bacte-
rial cellulose-derived electrode materials have been studied 
by researchers. Such as, Wang et al. prepared a new type of 
flexible electrode by using bacterial cellulose as a biologi-
cal template with KOH as activator. The prepared electrode 
exhibits a specific capacitance of 241.8 F  g−1  [19]. Pei et al. 
synthesized nanobelt-carbonized bacterial cellulose nano-
composite by activating bacterial cellulose with  V2O5. The 
prepared electrodes display a specific capacitance of 281 
F  g−1  at 0.25 A  g−1  [20]. However, the traditional way to 
activate bacterial cellulose is mainly through alkaline acti-
vators. This method is mainly activated by external etching 
under high temperature conditions. Therefore, the obtained 
carbon materials often have uneven pore distribution in the 
microstructure and poor connectivity between pores, further 
restricting the electrochemical property of the materials. The 
obtained electrode has a specific capacitance usually low 
300 F  g−1 , which is far from meeting the needs of practi-
cal applications. Accordingly, it is worth looking forward 
to exploring an efficient, convenient and economical way 
to prepare high performance bacterial cellulose electrode 
materials.

Herein, we  developed a convenient method for the 
preparation of porous carbon by one-step activation method 
using bacterial cellulose as carbon source and potassium 
gluconate as activator. The optimized electrode possesses 
a distinct hierarchical porous structure with suitable spe -
cific surface area and rich oxygen content. Benefiting from 
the unique structure, the obtained electrode exhibits high 
specific capacitance and excellent electrochemical stabil-
ity. More interestingly, the constructed APC-700//APC-700 
symmetrical supercapacitor exhibits high energy density and 
good cycling stability.
2  Experimental sections
2.1  Synthesis of the porous carbon
The bacterial cellulose was added into distilled water and 
stirred for 24 h, followed by freezing and evacuating in the 
vacuum freeze dryer. After drying, 1 g bacterial cellulose 
were added into 0.5 mol  L−1  potassium gluconate solution 
and stirred magnetically for 12 h. The obtained product was 
filtered and freeze-dried. The dried product was pyrolyzed 
at 600 °C, 700 °C and 800 °C for 2 h with a heating rate 
of 5 °C   min−1  in  N2 atmosphere, respectively. Then, the 
obtained product was dried after washed with 2 M HCl for 
12 h and deionized water. Then, the samples were named 
as APC-x (which x represents the activation temperature). 
For comparison, the bacterial cellulose was directly carbon-
ized at 700 °C in  N2 for 2 h, and the obtained sample was 
recorded as PC.
Characterization ways and electrochemical characteriza-
tion were recorded in supporting information.
3  Results and discussions
Scheme  1 illustrates the synthetic route of APC-x. The dried 
BC was soaked in 0.5 mol  L−1  potassium gluconate solu-
tion, and activated at high temperature after freeze drying. 
After removing impurities with dilute HCl, the hierarchical 
porous framework was formed. The microstructures of the 
obtained materials were explored by scanning/transmission 
electron microscopy (SEM/TEM). As seen in Fig. S1a, the 
materials from the direct carbonization of bacterial cel -
lulose (PC-700) shows a big block-like structure without 
obvious pore structure. After introducing potassium gluco-
nate as activator, the SEM images of the APC-700 materi-
als (Fig.  1a, b) reveal a three-dimensional interconnected 
hierarchical porous structure compose of rich micrometer 
sized macropores between carbon skeleton, which can as 
ion-buffering regions to shorten the diffusion distance of 
ions. As reported in the literature [21], potassium gluconate 
is used as an activator, when the temperature is below 500, 
it is mainly the decomposition of organic matter. when the 
temperature is above 600, the generated potassium carbon-
ate will enhance its activation ability with the increase of 
temperature, further generating potassium oxide and carbon 
dioxide, further enlarging the pore structure. In addition, as 
shown in Fig.  1c, d, TEM further confirms that the APC-
700 samples possess the three-dimensional interconnected 
porous structure with massive macropores. The APC-600 
(Fig. S1b) and APC-800 samples (Fig. S1c) possess the 
similar three-dimensional interconnected porous structure 
with APC-700. Furthermore, as shown in Fig. S2b, c, the 
corresponding elements mapping images regarding SEM 
show that the samples are composed of C and O elements.
The crystal structure of the obtained carbon materials 
was explored through X-ray diffraction (XRD). As seen 
in Fig.  2a, all materials have a weak peak at 43.5° and a 
broad peak at 23.6°, representing the 002 and 101 crystal 
planes of carbon, respectively [22, 23]. As the temperature 
increases, the (002) crystal plane reflection intensity of the 
samples gradually decreases, indicating that the degree of 
graphitization reduces gradually and the increase of tem-
perature causes more amorphous and disordered structures 
in the carbon samples [ 24]. The element compositions of 
the obtained samples were tested by X-ray photoelectron 
spectroscopy (XPS). As shown in Fig.  2b, it is obviously 
evident that all the APC samples are composed of C and O 
elements. As the temperature increases, the oxygen content 
decreases from 13.84 at% (APC-600) to 11.24 at% (APC-
700) and finally to 8.86% (APC-800). The C 1 s spectra of 
APC-700 (Fig.  2c) consists of four different peaks centering

In order to evaluate the supercapacitive performance of 
the obtained porous carbon, cyclic voltammetry (CV) and

electrode system in 6 M KOH aqueous electrolyte. Figure 4a

ing typical double layer capacitance characteristics. Moreo-
ver, the quasi-rectangular profile of the wide hump is repre-
sented by the CV curves of APC-600 and APC-700 samples, 
which indicates that massive oxygen-containing functional 
groups can provide extraordinary pseudocapacitance. It is 
obviously found that the APC-700 electrode has the largest 
CV curve integral area, suggesting the highest specific 
capacitance among all electrodes. As shown in Fig.  4b, the 
GCD curve of APC-700 owns the longest charge–discharge 
time, further demonstrating the largest capacitance for APC-
700 with the same consequence of CV curve. Meanwhile, 
the GCD profiles of all electrodes exhibits nearly isosceles

as shown in Fig.  4c, the charge–discharge curve of APC-

relevance between the total response current (i) and the 
scan rate (v) can be evaluated by i  = avb, where the b is an 
important index for showing the charge storage kinetics. 
when b value approaches 0.5, the reaction is controlled by a 
slow kinetic process as a result of pseudocapacitance, while 
the b value of 1.0 represents that the reaction is controlled 
by EDLC-controlled fast reaction kinetics. For APC-700, 
the obtained b-value is 0.95, indicating that this reaction is 
mainly controlled by EDLC (Fig.  5a). Moreover, the contri-
bution of EDLC and pseudocapacitance in the capacitance 
can be analyzed according to the equation: i(v) = k1v + k2v1/2, 
where k1v represents the contribution of EDLC-controlled 
fast kinetics and k2v1/2 corresponds to the slow kinetic pro-
cess dominated by pseudocapacitance. Figure  5b and Fig. 
S4 exhibit the kinetic process of EDLC-controlled behavior 
(green region) and pseudocapacitance-controlled behavior 
(blue region) at different scanning rates. As the scanning rate 
increases, the pseudocapacitance-controlled kinetic process 
gradually decreases and this variation is usually attributed 
to the restriction of ion diffusion. In addition, the large dis-
tribution of green regions further confirms the good dou-
ble layer properties of the carbon-based material and the 
still remained blue regions confirms the pseudocapacitance 
coming from the rapid redox reaction of oxygen. Accord-
ing to the Fig.  5c, APC-700 electrode shows an EDLC con-
trolled contribution rate of 74.01% at a low scanning rate of 
2 mV   s−1  and increased to 94.91% at 100 mV   s−1 , demon-
strating the outstanding ion storage capacity of hierarchical 
porous carbon at high scanning rate.
To further test the practicability and operation stabil -
ity of APC-700 electrode materials, a symmetric superca-
pacitor was constructed by using two APC-700 electrodes 
with equal mass as positive and negative electrodes in 1 M 
 Na2SO4 electrolyte due to  Na2SO4 electrolyte can provide 
wider decomposition voltage region (1.6 V) than KOH 
electrolyte. Figure  6a clearly shows that the voltage win-
dow of the assembled symmetric supercapacitor could be 
enormously extended to 1.8 V and anodic current without 
increase evidently. As shown in Fig.  6b, when the scanning 
speed reaches 200 mV   s−1  with the increase of voltage scan-
ning speed, the CV curve still maintains a rectangular with-
out appearing obvious distortion, meaning outstanding rate 
performance. The GCD cruves (Fig.  6c) of the APC-700//
APC-700 symmetric supercapacitor present a nearly sym-
metric triangular shape at different current densities, indi-
cating superior electrochemical invertibility. Moreover, the 
reason for the large deviations in linearity of GCD curves at 
0.25 A  g−1  is due to the presence of the pseudo-capacitance 
attributed to the quick redox reactions at the electrode–elec-
trolyte interface with the rich oxygen content [43]. Accord-
ing to the Fig.  6d, the specific capacitance of the APC-700//
APC-700 symmetric supercapacitor is 52.2 F  g−1  at 0.25 A 
 g−1 . Duing to the wide potential region and high specific 
capacitance, the energy density of the APC-700//APC-700 
symmetric supercapacitors (Fig.  6e) can reach 23.5 Wh 
 kg−1 , which is higher than previously reported carbon-based 
symmetric supercapacitors [44–50]. The Nyquist plot of the 
symmetric supercapacitor (Fig. S5) displays a low equivalent 
series resistance of 0.87 Ω in the highest frequency and a 
nearly vertical line in the low frequency, revealing excel-
lent electric conductivity and rapid electron/ions migration. 
Finally, the electrochemical stability of the APC-700//ACP-
700 symmetric supercapacitor was also measured by CV. 
The results exhibit that the capacitance retention rate of the 
10,000th cycle is 99.7% of the initial cycle. And the above 
test results further confirm that APC-700 electrode possesses 
good cycle durability and practicability.
4  Conclusion
In summary, we have developed a convenient way for the prep-
aration of porous carbon by one-step activation method using 
bacterial cellulose as carbon source and potassium gluconate 
as activator. The obtained porous carbon possesses a unique 
hierarchical porous structure with suitable specific surface area

Biomass‑derived carbon electrodes from sugarcane bagasse 
for supercapacitor applications
Kajal Gautam1 · Mohit Bhatt2 · Akarsh Verma3  · Anil Kumar Sinha2
Received: 21 January 2025 / Revised: 8 March 2025 / Accepted: 19 March 2025 / Published online: 26 March 2025 
© The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer-Verlag GmbH Germany, part of Springer Nature 2025
Abstract
This research investigates the application of carbon materials derived from sugarcane bagasse, a form of biomass, for the 
advancement of supercapacitor electrodes. Carbon electrodes were synthesized by carbonizing biomass waste at 500 °C with 
varying durations (3, 4, 5, and 10 h) and pre-treatment using glacial acetic acid, HCl, and NaOH. The resulting materials were 
designated as C-1, C-2, C-3, and C-4 respectively. X-ray diffraction (XRD) was employed to analyze the structural properties 
of the materials, while Fourier-transform infrared (FT-IR) spectroscopy and photoluminescence (PL) spectroscopy were used 
to evaluate their optical characteristics. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) was performed to examine the morphology and 
structural characteristics of all samples. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) was conducted to surface chemistry, and 
elemental composition of materials. Electrochemical performance was assessed using cyclic voltammetry (CV), charging 
discharge, and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS). Sample C-4, synthesized at 500 °C for 10 h, exhibited the 
best electrochemical performance, with high specific capacitances of 226.7 F/g at 1 mV/s, excellent rate capability with 65% 
capacitance retention at 100 mV/s, and excellent cyclic stability and coulombic efficiency of 100% over 5000 cycles. These 
findings underscore the effectiveness of biomass-derived carbon electrode for high performance supercapacitor applications.
Keywords Biomass-derived carbon · Sugarcane bagasse · Supercapacitors · Electrochemical performance
1 Introduction
Supercapacitors, also known as electrochemical capacitors, 
have gained substantial recognition for their exceptional 
power density, rapid charge–discharge capabilities, and 
impressive cycle life, positioning them as critical compo-
nents in energy storage technologies [1 ]. Unlike conven-
tional batteries, supercapacitors excel in applications that 
demand swift energy delivery and high-power output, such 
as regenerative braking systems in electric vehicles, grid 
energy storage, and various consumer electronics [2 , 3]. 
Supercapacitors, unlike the conventional capacitors, deliver 
significantly more energy density because of adsorption of 
charges during charging cycle. This is unlike the storage 
mechanism in conventional capacitors, which store energy 
only by the electrical polarization of dielectric [4]. Carbon-
based materials are extensively employed as electrodes in 
supercapacitors due to their high electrical conductivity, 
large surface area, and excellent electrochemical stability 
[5–7]. These properties are crucial for achieving high capac-
itance and efficient charge storage. Various forms of carbon, 
like activated carbons [8], carbon nanotubes (CNT) [9], gra-
phene [10], reduced graphene oxide [11], and carbon-based 
composites [5 ], have been used as electrodes for superca-
pacitors, each offering unique advantages and limitations [5, 
12]. Activated carbons, derived from various sources includ-
ing biomass, are the most common electrode materials for 
supercapacitors. Activated carbon, also known as activated 
charcoal or activated coal, is highly porous form of carbon 
with high surface area exceeding 2000  m2/g [13], tuneable 
pore morphology, and amenable for surfaces functionalized,
