which enables substantial charge storage through electro-
static interactions and double-layer capacitance [14– 16]. 
Additionally, these materials find applications in water/air 
purification [17, 18], odor remover [19], and as catalyst [20]. 
Carbon nanotubes and graphene offer superior electrical 
conductivity and mechanical strength, making them suit -
able for high-performance supercapacitors [5 , 21, 22]. The 
sustainability of energy storage materials is an increasing 
concern, and biomass-derived carbon materials are emerging 
as an eco-friendly alternative [15, 23]. Sugarcane bagasse, a 
by-product of sugar industries, is an abundant and low-cost 
biomass source that can be converted into carbon materials 
through carbonization. This process not only recycles agri-
cultural waste but also reduces the environmental impact 
associated with conventional carbon production methods 
[24, 25]. Biomass-derived carbon materials offer several 
advantages over traditional carbon sources. First, they are 
derived from bio-waste, which contributes to sustainability 
and reduces material cost [26]. Second, the synthesis process 
allows morphology engineering like pore size and surface 
functionalisation to maximize device charge storage capac-
ity. Finally, the use of biomass reduces environmental impact 
by lowering carbon footprints and mitigating greenhouse 
gas emissions associated with traditional carbon production 
[24, 27].
Biomass-derived carbon materials, such as those 
obtained from sugarcane bagasse, grass, wood, and other 
plant-based sources, have emerged as promising electrode 
materials for supercapacitors due to their high surface area, 
abundant functional groups, and sustainable nature [ 23, 28, 
29]. These biomass-derived carbons often possess a hierar -
chical porous structure, which enhances ion diffusion and 
electrolyte accessibility, leading to superior electrochemi-
cal performance [30]. Additionally, the intrinsic heteroatom 
doping (e.g., oxygen, nitrogen, sulfur) in these materials 
improves charge storage capacity by introducing pseudo-
capacitive behavior and increasing electrical conductivity 
[31]. Studies have demonstrated that sugarcane bagasse-
derived activated carbon exhibits a high specific capaci-
tance and excellent cyclic stability, making it a competitive 
alternative to conventional carbon-based electrodes [13, 
15]. Furthermore, grass-derived biochar has been shown to 
deliver outstanding electrochemical performance due to its 
high graphitic content and tunable porosity [32]. The renew-
able and cost-effective nature of biomass-derived carbons 
makes them highly attractive for sustainable energy stor -
age applications in supercapacitors [ 28, 32]. In this quest, 
Anand et al. [33] synthesized heteroatom-doped activated 
carbon from walnut shells, achieving a high specific sur -
face area and a hierarchical pore structure that enhanced 
ion transport and electrochemical performance. Their mate-
rial exhibited a gravimetric capacitance of 271.4 F/g at 0.5 
A/g. In another work, Alwi et al. [34] investigated waste 
sugarcane bagasse (WSB) as a cost-effective and sustain-
able precursor for porous carbon in supercapacitors. To 
enhance its electrochemical performance, they hybridized 
WSB-derived carbon with silicon dioxide (SiO₂), a low-cost 
pseudocapacitive material. The optimized nanocomposite 
electrode demonstrated a high specific capacitance of 362.3 
F g⁻ 1 at 0.25 A/g, demonstrating the potential of WSB-
derived composites for high-performance energy storage 
applications. Singh et al. [35] developed a series of highly 
porous sulfur-doped activated carbon (WSC/S) derived 
from sugarcane bagasse. The WSC/S exhibited a large 
specific surface area with high mesoporosity, enhanced 
wettability, and abundant redox-active sites, which con-
tributed to superior supercapacitor performance. The high 
mesopore content facilitated efficient ion transport, ena -
bling the WSC/S electrode to achieve a remarkable spe-
cific capacitance of 282.25 F g⁻ 1 at 0.1 A g⁻ 1 with excel-
lent cycling stability, retaining over 96% capacitance after 
10,000 cycles. These materials demonstrate the potential of 
biomass-derived materials as efficient energy storage solu-
tions for energy storage applications. In this study, activated 
(AC) carbon electrodes were synthesized from sugarcane 
bagasse by treatment with glacial acetic acid, hydrochloric 
acid, and sodium hydroxide to remove impurities from the 
raw material and then carbonizing the biomass at 500 °C 
for different time durations 3, 4, 5, and 10 h. The resulting 
electrode materials were designated as C-1 (500 °C, 3 h), 
C-2 (500 °C, 4 h), C-3 (500 °C, 5 h), and C-4 (500 °C, 
10 h). The structural properties of the carbon materials 
were analyzed using X-ray diffraction (XRD), revealing a 
graphitic structure of material. Fourier-transform infrared 
(FTIR) provided insights into the functional groups and 
photoluminescence (PL) provides optical characteristics of 
the materials. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) con-
firmed that sample C-4, synthesized at 500 °C for 10 h, 
exhibits a crossed sheet-like morphology. This morphol-
ogy is consistent with the characteristics of hard carbon, 
which is beneficial for enhancing ion transport and elec-
trochemical performance in energy storage devices such 
as batteries or supercapacitors. Hard carbon typically has 
a disordered structure with micro- and mesopores, facili-
tating the insertion and extraction of ions during charge 
and discharge cycles. The crossed sheet-like morphology 
provides a large surface area, improving electrolyte access 
and reducing the diffusion path for ions, thereby enhancing 
electrochemical performance. Electrochemical tests dem-
onstrated that sample C-4 achieved specific capacitances 
of 226.71 F/g at 1 mV/s and 147.80 F/g at 10 A/g, surpass-
ing the performance of several other biomass-derived car -
bon materials reported in the literature (shown in Table  1). 
Carbon electrodes derived from agricultural residues gen-
erally exhibit lower capacitance compared to the perfor -
mance of our materials [36]. Additionally, carbon materials

derived from sugarcane bagasse have shown competitive 
performance compared to more expensive carbon materi -
als such as graphene and CNTs, which have higher specific 
capacitances, but at a higher cost and complexity [3 , 12, 
37, 38]. This study underscores the potential of utilizing 
biomass-derived carbon materials, specifically from sug-
arcane bagasse, as effective electrodes for supercapacitors. 
The optimization of synthesis conditions has demonstrated 
that these materials can achieve high electrochemical per -
formance, making them a viable and sustainable alternative 
to traditional carbon sources. By leveraging the advantages 
of biomass resources, this approach not only contributes to 
the development of high-performance energy storage solu-
tions but also promotes environmental sustainability.
2  Preparation of sugarcane bagasse‑derived 
activated charcoal
Step 1: Initial charcoal preparation
Sugarcane bagasse-derived activated carbon was treated 
to remove impurities and reduce ash content. The procedure 
involved mixing 1 g of the charcoal with 3 mL of glacial ace-
tic acid. This mixture was left to react, allowing the acetic 
acid to dissolve impurities and ash components. After the 
reaction, the charcoal was filtered, washed thoroughly with 
deionized water to remove residual acid, and then oven-dried 
at 100 °C for 2 h. Schematic of synthesis procedure has 
shown in Fig.  1.
Step 2: Chemical activation
The dried charcoal underwent chemical activation to 
improve its porosity and surface characteristics. An equimo-
lar solution of sodium hydroxide (NaOH) and hydrochloric 
acid (HCl) was prepared, ensuring balanced molarity. The 
charcoal was immersed in this solution, allowing the chemi-
cals to react with the carbon structure. The mixture was then 
heated in an oven at 100 °C for 3 h to facilitate activation.
Step 3: Carbonization
Following chemical activation, the treated charcoal was 
transferred to a ceramic boat for carbonization. The boat was 
placed inside a tubular furnace under a nitrogen atmosphere 
to prevent oxidation during the carbonization process. The 
furnace was heated at a controlled rate of 5 °C/min until 
reaching the target temperature of 500 °C. The carboniza-
tion was conducted at this temperature for varying durations 
to study the effect of time on the properties of the activated 
charcoal.
Step 4: Post-carbonization treatment
After the carbonization process was completed, the 
furnace was allowed to cool naturally to room tempera-
ture while maintaining the nitrogen atmosphere. This step 
ensured that the samples did not oxidize upon cooling. The 
resulting activated charcoal samples were then collected and 
labeled based on the carbonization time:

3  Characterization
The carbonized samples were characterized using several 
advanced techniques. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM, 
Make: JEOL, Model: JSM-7610 F Plus) was utilized to 
observe the surface morphology, and energy-dispersive 
X-ray (EDX) analysis was conducted for elemental composi-
tion analysis. X-ray diffraction (XRD, Make: Bruker, Model: 
D8 Advanced ECO) provided information on the crystalline 
structure, while photoluminescence (PL, Model: LAMBDA, 
Make: Perkin Elmer) analysis was used to study the optical 
properties. Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR, 
PerkinElmer Frontier) was employed to identify the func-
tional groups present on the carbon surface. Additionally, 
X-ray Photoelectron Spectroscopy (XPS, Make: Thermo 
Fisher Scientific, Model: K-Alpha) was used to analyze 
the surface chemical composition and bonding states of 
the material. For electrochemical analysis, cyclic voltam-
metry (CV) was used to measure specific capacitance and 
assess the electrochemical stability. These electrochemical 
measurements were carried out using a biologic potentiostat 
(Model: SP-150e) in a three-electrode setup.
4  Electrode preparation
The working electrode was prepared by mixing active mate-
rial, carbon black, and PVDF in an 8:1:1 ratio, respectively 
using a mortar and pestle. The mixture was then dispersed 
in ethanol and subjected to sonication for 8 h to ensure uni-
form dispersion. After proper mixing, a viscous solution 
was obtained and drop-casted onto a carbon paper substrate 
(1 × 1  cm2) using a pipette. The coated electrodes were then 
dried in a vacuum oven at 80 °C overnight to remove resid-
ual solvent. Once dried, the electrodes were directly used 
as working electrodes for electrochemical measurements. 
Platinum mesh served as the counter electrode, and a calo-
mel electrode was used as the reference electrode in 1 M 
KOH electrolyte.

5.3  Scanning electron microscopy (SEM)
SEM for all samples (C-4, C-3, C-2, and C-4 have shown in 
Fig.  4a, b, c, and d respectively) was employed to analyze the 
morphology of the activated carbon material, revealing the 
influence of synthesis time on their structural characteristics. 
SEM imaging provides detailed views of surface features at 
a microscale, which is crucial for evaluating electrode mor-
phology [62]. The SEM images demonstrate that longer syn-
thesis times result in the development of layered structure in 
the carbon electrodes (sample C-4) as shown in Fig. 4a. This 
layered morphology is particularly advantageous for super-
capacitor applications due to its significant enhancement of 
the surface area available for ion adsorption and improved 
ion transport efficiency, leading to better electrochemical 
performance. The stability of this layered structure is nota-
ble, contributing to consistent and reliable electrochemical 
behavior over multiple charge–discharge cycles. In contrast, 
shorter synthesis times fail to produce a well-defined layered 
structure and instead lead to considerable agglomeration of 
the material as shown in Fig.  4a, forming large clusters that 
block ion movement and reduce the effective surface area 
for electrochemical reactions. This can be further verified 
by the electrochemical performance evaluation, which shows 
that the agglomerated structure compromises overall perfor-
mance. Thus, extended synthesis durations are essential for 
achieving a stable morphology that supports enhanced and 
consistent electrochemical efficiency. Figure  4 (EDX-(a)) 
presents the EDX mapping of the activated carbon material 
(sample C-4), specifically highlighting the elemental compo-
sition. The EDX analysis indicates that the material consists 
of 62.77% carbon, 31.27% oxygen, and 5.95% nitrogen. The 
incorporation of nitrogen during the carbonization process 
plays a crucial role in enhancing the performance of the 
material. Nitrogen doping introduces additional active sites, 
improves the conductivity, and enhances the wettability of 
the carbon surface, which collectively contribute to better 
electrochemical performance. The presence of nitrogen can 
also enhance the pseudo capacitance, further boosting the 
overall energy storage capability of the material.
5.4  X‑ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS)
The XPS analysis of the C-4 sample provides insights into 
its surface chemical composition and bonding states, as 
depicted in Fig.  5a for the C 1 s spectrum and Fig.  5b for the 
O 1 s spectrum. The deconvoluted C 1 s spectrum reveals a 
primary peak at 284.4 eV, corresponding to the C–C bond, 
indicative of graphitic carbon [63]. Additionally, the pres-
ence of oxygen-containing functional groups is evident, with 
peaks at 285.6 eV assigned to C–O bonds from hydroxyl or 
carboxyl functionalities, and at 287.8 eV, corresponding to 
C = O bonds from quinone and carbonyl species [63]. The 
O 1 s spectrum exhibits two distinct peaks: one at 531.5 eV, 
attributed to C–O bonding, and another at 533.0 eV, associ-
ated with C = O functionalities [63]. Elemental composition 
from XPS reveals 64.8% carbon and 38.2% oxygen, whereas 
EDX analysis shows 62.77% carbon and 31.23% oxygen. 
The slight variation between XPS and EDX results can 
be attributed to the differences in surface sensitivity, with 
XPS primarily detecting the outermost atomic layers while 
EDX provides a bulk composition analysis. These findings, 
in conjunction with FTIR results, confirm the presence of 
oxygen-functionalized carbon structures, which significantly 
influence the electrochemical properties of the material.
5.5  Photoluminescence (PL)
For CDs, which have crystallite sizes smaller than the size 
of the exciton radius, the PL originates from the conju-
gated π domains, and the PL wavelengths are size depend-
ent. These emissions are from carbon core band to band 
transitions and have photon energies > 3.5 eV [64]. But in 
many cases, PL depends on the transitions from the sur -
face states originating from the synergistic hybridisation 
between the  sp2 carbon and the functional groups, surface 
defects, and heteroatom doping [65]. For application of 
biochar produced carbon in electrochemical energy storage, 
the surface defects and surface functionalisation are impor-
tant; we have used excitation photon energy of 375 nm 
(= 3.3 eV < core excitation energy of 3.5 eV), to selectively 
excite the surface state transitions. Figure  6 shows the PL 
spectra of all the samples (C-1 to C–4). In Fig.  6a–d, the 
PL spectra are fit with Gaussian peaks. For sample C–1 
(Fig.  6a), we find three PL emissions at 430, 484, and 
548 nm. The emission at 430 nm is attributed to nitrogen 
related functional groups [64, 65] attached to the carbon

are easily attached to the carbon core, giving significant

transitions from -NH2 and Pyridine-N related surface states 
to carbon core HOMO states [65]. The emission at 484 nm 
is identified with the oxygen related function groups, spe-
cifically the C = O related surface states [65]. The broad 
emission observed at 548 nm (~ 2.2 eV) is not well identi-
fied in literature [64, 65]. However, the green emission 
may be because of the transition from the dangling bond 
related surface states to the carbon core HOMO states. 
Three emission peaks are observed in peak fit for sample 
C-2, shown in Fig.  6b. The emissions are observed at 429, 
482, and 544 nm and are close to the emissions shown by 
sample C-1 and are similarly attributed to transitions from 
surface states related to  NH2/Pyridine-N (429 nm), C = O 
(482 nm), and the dangling bonds (544 nm) to the core 
HOMO states. Figure  6c depicts the PL peak fits for sample 
C-3, with longer carbonization (5 h). PL for these sample 
also shows 3 peaks at 427.7, 488, and 570 nm. These are 
red shifted compared to the emission wavelengths for sam-
ples C-1 and C-2. The red shift in the emission wavelength 
is attributed to two main reasons: the increase in the crys-
tallite size of the carbon dots and the formation of amor -
phous shell around carbon core [66]. From the analysis of 
the peak broadening of XRD peaks (discussed earlier in 
3.1), the crystallite sizes of all the samples are in the range 
40 ± 10 nm. So, the red shift in sample C-3 may be attrib-
uted to the formation of amorphous shell around crystalline 
core, due to prolonged carbonization. For the sample C-4, 
only one prominent emission is observed around 490 nm 
(Fig.  6d). Quenching of PL may be because of increased 
defects/functional groups along with increased amorphous 
shell and non-radiative recombination.
5.6  Electrochemical measurements (ECs)
ECs were conducted using a biologic VMP-128 potentiostat, 
employing a three-electrode setup. The working electrode 
was prepared from sugarcane-derived carbon material, while 
a platinum mesh (1 × 2  cm2) served as the counter electrode, 
and a saturated calomel electrode (Hg/HgCl) was used as the 
reference electrode. The electrolyte used was 1 M KOH, cho-
sen for its effective ionic conductivity and stability. Specific 
capacitance was calculated using the following Eq. 2 [67].
where Csp is the specific capacitance in F/g, I is the discharge

material in gm. This formula was applied to data obtained 
from CV tests to determine the specific capacitance of the 
electrodes.

5000 cycles, with results shown in Fig.  8b. Electrochemi-
cal Impedance Spectroscopy (EIS) measurements were 
carried out over a frequency range of 100 Hz to 100 kHz to 
evaluate the charge transfer resistance and overall imped-
ance characteristics of the electrodes.
The sugarcane-derived activated carbon electrode, par -
ticularly sample C-4, demonstrated exceptional electrochem-
ical performance compared to other samples. C-4 achieved a 
high specific capacitance of 226.7 F/g at 1 mV/s and 147.7 
F/g (65.15%) at 100 mV/s, surpassing the performance of 
many biomass and biochar-derived materials reported in 
the literature [68, 69]. Furthermore, it retained 65.15% of 
its specific capacitance at 100 mV/s, showcasing its excel-
lent stability and retention of capacitance over a high scan 
rate. Other biomass-derived materials, such as corn cob and 
rice husk biochar, exhibit lower specific capacitance values 
than our reported material [70– 73]. The superior specific 
capacitance of C-4 highlights its enhanced charge storage 
capabilities, likely due to its optimized porous structure and 
high surface area.
In the CV profiles of carbon electrodes, as shown in 
Fig.  7a, the appearance of multiple peaks during both oxi-
dation and reduction processes can be attributed to the com-
plex structure and surface chemistry of the carbon material. 
Biomass-derived carbons often contain a variety of oxygen-
containing functional groups, such as hydroxyl, carbonyl, 
and carboxyl groups, which undergo redox reactions at dif-
ferent potentials [74, 75]. These functional groups contribute 
to the distinct peaks observed in the CV curves, as each 
group reacts at a specific potential.
Figure  8a compares all four samples, highlighting the 
trend in specific capacitance behavior with an increasing 
scan rate from 1 to 100 mV/s, with sample C-4 demon-
strating the best performance among them. The stability of 
sample C-4 is shown in Fig.  8b; at a current density of 2.5 
A/g, C-4 exhibited an initial specific capacitance of 138.5 
F/g. After 100 cycles, the capacitance reduced to 87.5 F/g, 
and after 2000 cycles, it further decreased to 60.4 F/g. After 
5000 cycles the capacitance reached 36.45 F/g. Moreover, 
the coulombic efficiency of the material remained nearly 
100% throughout the cycling process, indicating excellent 
charge–discharge reversibility (shown in Fig.  8b). Thus, 
relatively high capacitance retention of C-4 over extended 
cycling demonstrates its good durability and stability, though 
further optimization could enhance long-term performance.
EIS is a powerful technique used to investigate the elec-
trochemical properties of materials by measuring their 
response to an applied AC voltage. In the context of superca-
pacitor electrodes, EIS provides insights into key parameters 
such as solution resistance (Rs) and charge transfer resistance 
(Rct), which are critical for evaluating the performance of the 
electrode material. Solution resistance (Rs) primarily reflects 
the resistance of the electrolyte and the electrode–electrolyte 
interface, where lower Rs values indicate better conductivity 
and efficient ion transport. Charge transfer resistance (R ct) 
is associated with the difficulty of electron transfer at the 
electrode surface during redox reactions. For carbon-based 
electrodes, minimizing Rct is crucial for enhancing specific 
capacitance and overall efficiency, as carbon materials often 
rely on surface reactions for energy storage [67, 76].
For sample C-4 (refer Fig.  8a), the solution resistance 
(Rs) before CV was recorded at 0.35 Ω, and it slightly 
increased to 0.38 Ω after CV (Fig.  9b), reflecting stable 
conductivity at the electrode–electrolyte interface. The 
charge transfer resistance (Rct) decreased significantly from 
0.47 to 0.33 Ω after CV, indicating improved charge transfer 
kinetics post-CV cycling. This improvement in charge trans-
fer reflects the activation of the material during cycling,

processes during CV, enhancing its electrical conductiv -
ity and reducing impedance. This reduction is critical as it 
directly correlates with improved ion transport and electron 
mobility within the electrode, making C-4 a highly efficient 
supercapacitor material.
Additionally, the stability testing for C-4 demonstrated that 
Rs exhibited minimal variation, increasing only slightly from 
0.37 Ω before stability testing to 0.38 Ω afterward, as shown 
in Fig. 9c. This slight increase indicates that the material main-
tains good conductivity even after prolonged cycling. Further-
more, the decrease in Rct from 2.77 to 2.14 Ω after stability 
testing suggests that the material not only retains its electro-
chemical performance but may even improve with cycling, 
likely due to enhanced connectivity within the porous struc-
ture or the activation of additional electroactive sites. The low 
impedance values, coupled with the high specific capacitance, 
underscore the strong correlation between the EIS results and 
the superior performance of C-4 as a supercapacitor electrode. 
The excellent electrochemical properties of C-4, demonstrated 
through both EIS and capacitance measurements, confirm its 
potential as a high-performance material for energy storage 
applications. While other samples also showed promising 
results, as indicated by the impedance values in Table 3, C-4 
stands out due to its optimized balance of low resistance, high 
capacitance, and stable performance over extended cycles. The 
sugarcane-derived carbon electrode (C-4) demonstrates excel-
lent electrochemical performance, with high specific capaci-
tance, competitive cycling stability, and lower charge transfer 
resistance compared to many reported biomass and biochar-
based electrodes. These findings underscore the potential of 
C-4 for high-performance supercapacitor applications and 
highlight its advantages over other similar materials.
6  Conclusions
This work demonstrates the potential of biomass-derived 
carbon electrodes synthesized from sugarcane bagasse, a 
waste material, for supercapacitor applications. Optimized 
carbonization conditions (500 °C for 10 h) resulted in a 
material (C-4) with superior electrochemical performance, 
including a specific capacitance of 226.7 F/g at 1 mV/s and 
147.80 F/g at 100 mV/s respectively, retaining 65% of its 
initial capacitance shows high retention at high scan rate. 
Structural analyses revealed a porous architecture and nitro-
gen doping that enhanced ion transport and charge storage 
capacity. Photoluminescence analysis revealed surface states 
and defect structures, with red-shifted emissions indicating 
amorphous shell formation, which enhances electrochemi-
cal behavior. EDX together with XPS shows an almost 
equal atomic percentage of identified elements, confirm -
ing the uniform composition of material. Additionally, the 
material exhibited excellent charge–discharge reversibility, 
maintaining nearly 100% coulombic efficiency over 5000 
cycles. Even after a long stability test over 5000 cycles, 40% 
capacitance was retained at 2.5 A/g, demonstrating the dura-
bility of electrode. These insights emphasize the synergistic 
effects of structural and surface chemistry modifications on 
the functional properties of material. Our study highlights 
the potential of sugarcane bagasse as a sustainable and cost-
effective precursor for high-performance supercapacitor 
electrodes, paving the way for greener energy storage tech-
nologies while addressing environmental concerns.

Construction of multifunctional cellulose nanofibers/reduced graphene 
oxide carbon aerogels by bidirectional freezing for supercapacitor 
electrodes and strain sensors 
Zhaoji Dong
a , b
, Li Zhong
b
, Yuhui Zhang
b
, Fei Liu
b

c
, Zhaoyang Xu
a , b , * 
a
Jiangsu Co-Innovation Center of Efficient Processing and Utilization of Forest Resources, Nanjing Forestry University, Nanjing 210037, China 
b
College of Materials Science and Engineering, Nanjing Forestry University, Nanjing 210037, China 
c
Jiangxi Academy of Forestry, Nanchang 330013, China   
ARTICLE INFO  
Keywords: 
Cellulose nanofibers 
Bidirectional freezing 
Carbon aerogel 
Supercapacitor electrodes 
Strain sensors 
ABSTRACT  
Carbon aerogel is an excellent conductive porous carbon material, but suffers from poor mechanical properties 
and fatigue resistance, which greatly limits its application as a flexible electronic device. Herein, the cellulose 
nanofibers/reduced graphene oxide carbon aerogel (BCRCA) with a unique layered structure was prepared by 
bidirectional freezing technique and thermal annealing. BCRCA's layered structure gives it ultra-low density 
(3.25 mg/cm
3
), high specific surface area (159.53 m
2
/g) and good compression properties (91.3 % stress 
retention, 100 cycles at 50 % compression). In addition, BCRCA for supercapacitor electrodes has a high specific 
capacity of 104.3 F g
� 1 
at 0.1 A g
� 1 
and a high capacitance retention rate of 93 % at 5000 cycles at 2 A g
� 1
. 
Notably, the BCRCA assembled into a wearable strain sensor exhibits a stable current signal for real-time 
monitoring of finger, wrist, and elbow joint movements. These advantages make BCRCA have broad applica -
tion prospects in the field of electronic energy storage devices and wearable strain sensors.   
1. Introduction 
Due to the rapid growth of unsustainable consumption and the 
increasing consumption of fossil fuels, environmental problems have 
become increasingly prominent, so new technologies closely related to 
new energy conversion and storage have attracted more and more 
attention [ 1 ]. Among them, the new technologies represented by flexible 
supercapacitors and strain sensors have caused extensive research in 
intelligent robots, intelligent textiles, wearable electronic devices, and 
other advanced fields [ 2 – 4 ]. Lightweight, high power and energy den -
sity, long cycle life, high mechanical flexibility, low cost, high sensitivity 
and fast response speed are the basic requirements of these electronic 
devices [ 5 – 8 ]. For example, smart textiles have high sensitivity and fast 
response ability as multifunctional sensors and heaters for personal 
health management, which was expected to enable disease diagnosis, 
early warning and personal hyperthermia [ 9 ]. 
Carbon aerogels (CAs) are an emerging carbon-based material, 
which is favored by many researchers because of its ultra-high specific 
surface area, rich pore structure and good electrical conductivity 
[ 10 – 12 ]. CAs are usually obtained by carbonizing aerogels in an inert 
atmosphere, and their unique porous structure makes them widely used 
in electromagnetic shielding [ 13 ], sensors [ 14 ], and supercapacitors 
[ 15 ]. However, these carbon aerogels usually have a disordered porous 
structure, which is easy to collapse, and it is difficult to obtain excellent 
compression properties and fatigue resistance [ 16 ]. This is not condu -
cive to the stability and durability of carbon aerogel in practical 
applications. 
Cellulose nanofiber (CNF) is a kind of environment-friendly natural 
polymer material with many advantages, such as stable chemical 
properties, high elastic modulus, and biodegradation [ 17 – 19 ]. The 
unique nanostructure of CNF enables it to be freeze-dried into CNF 
aerogel with a three-dimensional network structure [ 20 ]. After 
carbonization of CNF aerogel under inert gas, carbon aerogel materials 
with conductive properties can be obtained directly. However, pure CNF 
carbon aerogels not only undergo severe volume shrinkage and defor -
mation during the carbonization process, but also it is difficult to pro -
vide satisfactory capacitance by directly using it as an electrode material 
for supercapacitors [ 21 , 22 ]. To solve these problems, CNF is usually

2
combined with other materials (such as carbon materials [ 23 ], 
conductive polymers [ 24 ], metal compounds [ 25 ], etc.) to prepare 
composite carbon aerogels with excellent conductive and mechanical 
properties. Graphene is a two-dimensional honeycomb lattice structure 
carbon material, which stands out among many carbon materials 
because of its high conductivity and large specific surface area [ 26 ]. 
Unfortunately, the interaction of van der Waals forces and π - π bonds 
between graphene sheets tends to cause the sheets to stack and 
agglomerate [ 27 ]. This seriously hinders electrolyte ion diffusion and 
charge transfer, greatly limiting the further application of graphene in 
supercapacitors and sensor functional devices. Therefore, how to 
reasonably design and use the inherent characteristics and advantages of 
CNF and graphene to build high-performance electronic devices with 
special structures is still a huge challenge. 
Directional freezing is a method for synthesizing bionic porous ma -
terials and bionic layered composites [ 28 ]. Temperature gradient is an 
important factor in directional freezing because it can regulate the di -
rection of ice crystal growth [ 29 ]. Specifically, after the uniform 
colloidal suspension is cooled, the ice crystals gradually nucleate in the 
direction of the temperature gradient. At the same time, solute particles 
are pushed between ice crystals to obtain a oriented structure. In recent 
years, anisotropic aerogels prepared by directional freezing technology 
have been applied in various fields. Compared with traditional random 
freezing, directional freezing aerogels have a suitable microstructure 
and excellent properties [ 30 ]. In this paper, we have carefully designed a 
method to control the nucleation and growth of ice crystals under a 
double temperature gradient to achieve a highly ordered layered 
structure of carbon aerogel. Bidirectional carbon aerogel has more 
outstanding mechanical and electrochemical properties than random 
and single direction carbon aerogel. At the same time, this layered 
structure can generate more conductive paths under pressure, thus 
achieving high sensitivity. Therefore, the dual directional carbon aero -
gel can be effectively used for multifunctional applications in super -
capacitor electrodes and strain sensors. 
Herein, we have prepared a multifunctional nanocellulose/reduced 
graphene oxide carbon aerogel (BCRCA) through a simple bidirectional 
freezing, freeze-drying, and high temperature carbonization strategy. 
BCRCA has ultra-low density and good mechanical compression prop -
erties. Excellent performance is attributed to: (i) CNF acts as a physical 
spacer to effectively prevent the agglomeration of graphene sheets; (ii) 
The two-dimensional carbon skeleton of graphene oxide (GO) can 
reduce the excessive shrinkage of CNF during carbonization and give 
carbon aerogel excellent mechanical strength; (iii) The bidirectional 
freezing method is beneficial for obtaining parallel and ordered lamella, 
effectively achieving stress transfer and electrolyte ion transfer. BCRCA 
as electrode material for supercapacitors has excellent electrochemical 
properties. It also has good sensing performance, can easily monitor 
human activity and shows excellent signal stability. Therefore, the 
BCRCA has excellent application prospects in electrochemical energy 
storage materials and wearable electronic devices. 
2. Experimental section 
2.1. Materials 
CNF dispersion was purchased Zhongshan NanoFC bio-materials Co., 
Ltd. with a concentration of 2.5 %, a width of 35 nm, a length of 1 – 3 μ m, 
and a carboxyl content of 1.02 mmol/g. GO was purchased from Suzhou 
Carbon Peak Graphene Technology Co., Ltd. with a flake diameter of 
0.2 – 10 μ m and a thickness of ~1 nm. Deionized water was prepared by 
laboratory ultrapure water equipment. 
2.2. Preparation of bidirectional CNF/RGO carbon aerogel (BCRCA) 
CNF was first dispersed in deionized water and sonicated in an ice 
bath for 20 min using an ultrasonic cell crusher to obtain a concentration 
of 0.8 wt% CNF suspension. Then, the GO suspension (5 mg/ml) was 
added into the CNF suspension according to the mass ratio of CNF:GO =
1:1, stirring, and ultrasonic 30 min to obtain the mixed suspension. 
Transfer the mixture suspension to the cube plastic mold and place it on 
top of the bidirectional freezing device. The bidirectional freezing de -
vice consists of a curved copper plate immersed in liquid nitrogen at one 
end and hot water at the other (95 
◦
C) to create a temperature gradient. 
After complete freezing, the samples was frozen in a lyophilizer ( � 60 
◦
C, 
1 Pa) for 3 days to obtain CNF/GO aerogel (CGA). Finally, the CGA was 
heated in a tubular furnace at 800 
◦
C under argon for 120 min to obtain 
the layered bidirectional CNF/RGO carbon aerogel, named BCRCA. For 
comparison, unidirectional freezing CNF/RGO carbon aerogel was also 
prepared and named UCRCA (Unidirectional freezing was to place the 
mold on a copper plate and apply liquid nitrogen to the bottom, as 
shown in Fig. S1), and the non-directional CNF/RGO carbon aerogel 
prepared by random freezing in the refrigerator was named NCRCA. 
2.3. Characterization of materials 
The sample morphology was characterized by environmental scan -
ning electron microscopy (ESEM, Quanta 200, FEI, USA), and the 
microstructure of the sample was observed at an accelerated voltage of 
200 V-30 kV after gold spraying treatment. The diffraction pattern of the 
material was analyzed using a combined multifunctional horizontal X- 
ray diffractometer (XRD Ultima IV, Japan) with an X-ray generator 
power of 3KW, a 2 θ scan range of 10 to 50
◦
, and a sweep setting of 5
◦
/ 
min. An infrared spectrometer (Nicolet IS 50 FT-IR, Thermo Scientific, 
USA) was used to detect functional groups of the materials. The spectral 
acquisition range is 650 to 4000 cm
� 1
, and the spectral resolution is 
better than 0.09 cm
� 1
. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS, AXIS 
UltraDLD, England) was used to analyze the chemical components of the 
samples. Spectra were collected by testing in Al-K α monochromatic X- 
rays. The wide scanning residence time was 0.1 s, the narrow scanning 
residence time was 0.2 s, the vacuum degree is > 7 × 10
� 8 
Pa, and the 
power was 600 W. Raman spectra of the sample were obtained with a 
Raman spectrometer (RAMAN, DXR532, USA). Spatial resolution is 
better than 1um, spectral repeatability: ≤ ± 0.2 cm
� 1
, Raman frequency 
shift range: 50 – 3300 cm
� 1
. Thermogravimetric analyzer (TG 209 F3, 
GER) was used to study the thermal stability of the materials. Test range 
2 g, cooling rate < 20 min. The specific surface area and pore size dis -
tribution of the materials were measured using a specific surface area 
and pore size distribution meter (ASAP2020 HD88, Micromeritics, 
USA). Degassing temperature: 300 
◦
C, degassing time: 10 h. Samples 
were compressed and cycled using a mechanical tester equipped with a 
50 N sensor (SANS, Shenzhen Co. Ltd., China). 
2.4. Electrochemical performance measurements 
Electrochemical testing of three types of carbon aerogels BCRCA, 
UCRCA and NCRCA was performed using the electrochemical worksta -
tion of Tatsuwa CHI660E (Shanghai, China). The test system was a 
three-electrode system, and the electrolyte was selected from 1 M 
Na
2
SO
4
. Working electrode: carbon aerogel with a thickness of 2 mm; 
reference electrode: saturated calmel electrode; counter electrode: 
platinum electrode. Cyclic voltammetry (CV), galvanostatic charge/ 
discharge (GCD) and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) 
tests were performed on the two electrodes to compare their electro -
chemical performance excellence. The entire test was conducted at room 
temperature. 
2.5. Sensing performance measurements 
The BCRCA was placed between two copper foils with PE tape, 
assembled into a strain sensor, and connected to the human body's 
finger, wrist and elbow joint. The current change was recorded at the 
electrochemical workstation (CHI660E).

3. Results and discussion 
3.1. Preparation and characterization of materials 
The BCRCA synthesis process was shown in Fig. 1 . After evenly 
mixing CNF and GO suspension, BCRCA was prepared by bidirectional 
freezing, freeze-drying, and carbonization. The dual action of hydrogen 
bonding and electrostatic repulsion between CNF and GO results in their 
uniform dispersion in solution. Due to the temperature gradient gener -
ated by bidirectional freezing, the uniformly dispersed CNF and GO 
suspensions were repulsed by the growth of layered ice crystals. Sub -
sequently, these ice crystals were sublimated by freeze-drying to form 
CGA with a regular layered structure. As shown in Fig. 2 a, the pure CNF 
aerogel without GO has a serious volume shrinkage after carbonization, 
while the size shrinkage of CGA with GO was very low after carbon -
ization, which was almost negligible. It was proved that GO can be used 
as a carbon skeleton to prevent the severe volume shrinkage of CNF after 
high temperature carbonization. At the same time, CNF acts as a 
dispersant to prevent agglomeration between graphene sheets. After 
carbonization, the CGA was converted to black BCRCA and retains its 
original shape very well. It can be easily placed on the green leaf without 
making the leaf fall down, indicating that the BCRCA was very light with 
a density of only 3.25 mg/cm
3 
( Fig. 2 b). ESEM observed the detailed 
microstructure of the samples. Under the normal freezing condition of 
the refrigerator, ice crystals grow in both vertical and cross directions, so 
NCRCA exhibits a disordered porous structure inside ( Fig. 2 c). Unidi -
rectional freezing will promote the growth of ice crystals along the 
freezing direction from bottom to vertical. As shown in Fig. 2 d, UCRCA 
has a honeycomb structure with a pore size roughly in the range of 50- 
100 μ m. As expected, the bidirectional frozen BCRCA showed a layered 
structure, with the spacing between adjacent layers at 200 μ m ( Fig. 2 e, 
f), indicating that the problem of graphene sheet aggregation was well 
solved. 
Fig. 3 a showed XRD patterns of CNF, GO, CGA, and BCRCA. The 
diffraction peaks of CNF are 16.2
◦
and 22.3
◦
, corresponding to the 
typical (101) and (200) diffraction planes corresponding to the crystal 
structure of cellulose I, respectively [ 31 ]. The characteristic peak at 9.6
◦
of GO was similar to the diffraction peak reported in the literature [ 32 ]. 
CGA showed not only the characteristic peak of CNF but also the char -
acteristic peak of GO, which proved the successful preparation of CGA. 
After high temperature carbonization, the characteristic peak of GO at 
9.6
◦
was not observed in the XRD pattern of BCRCA, while a broad peak 
appeared near 2 θ = 24.7
◦
for the RGO (002) lattice plane [ 33 ]. This 
means that GO was highly reversible. 
The changes in functional groups of the materials were analyzed by 
FTIR spectroscopy ( Fig. 3 b). The characteristic peaks in the infrared 
spectrum of CNF at 3335, 2900, 1603, 1426, and 1053 cm
� 1 
correspond 
to O
–
H tensile vibration, saturated C
–
H tensile vibration, intra -
molecular hydrogen bond tensile vibration, aliphatic C
–
H tensile vi -
bration, and C
–
O tensile vibration [ 34 ]. For the GO infrared spectrum, 
five characteristic peaks appeared at 3223, 1729, 1622, and 1043 cm
� 1
, 
which were the tensile vibrations of O
–
H, C –
–
O, COOH, and C-O-C, 
which fully proved the existence of abundant oxygen-containing func -
tional groups in GO [ 35 ]. Similarly, oxygen-containing groups were 
abundant on the CGA, including O
–
H, C –
–
O, and C
–
O at 3342, 1620, 
and 1049 cm
� 1
. When the functional groups of CGA were compared 
with those of BCRCA, the oxygen-containing groups of BCRCA after 
carbonization at 800 
◦
C were significantly reduced, indicating that CNF 
becomes carbon nanofibers and GO becomes RGO.

Fig. 3 c shows characteristic peaks with binding energies of 284.5 eV and

mainly occurs at two stages: dehydration at 220

The specific surface area and pore structure of three carbon aerogels 
with different structures were further evaluated using a specific surface 
area and pore size distribution instrument. Fig. 3 h showed typical ni -
trogen adsorption-desorption isotherms. All carbon aerogels showed 
obvious type IV isotherms, indicating micropores and mesopores [ 40 ]. 
Their specific surface areas and dimensions are shown in Table S1. The 
specific surface area of BCRCA was 159.53 m
2
/g, which was larger than 
the other two carbon aerogels, indicating that more pore structures can 
be formed by the bidirectional freezing method. From the pore size 
distribution curves in Fig. 3 i, we can see that BCRCA's pore size distri -
bution was concentrated in the 2 – 20 nm range, showing a mesoporous 
structure. This pore structure provides rapid ion transport and diffusion, 
effectively reducing resistance and accelerating charge transport [ 41 ]. 
Compression tests investigated the compression properties of the 
carbon aerogel. Fig. 4 a showed the stress-strain curves of BCRCA, 
UCRCA and NCRCA at a strain of 70 %. The stresses of BCRCA, UCRCA 
and NCRCA were 22.7 kPa, 11.7 kPa and 1.5 kPa at 70 % strain. The 
compression properties of BCRCA were much higher than those of the 
other two, because the continuous layered structure formed by bidi -
rectional freeze casting gives carbon aerogel high compression proper -
ties. BCRCA exhibits good compressibility and elasticity at 10 % ~ 70 % 
strain ( Fig. 4 b). The stress-strain curve of BCRCA shows two 
characteristic stages: the first stage was the linear elastic region with ε <
50 %, in which the distance between the sheets decreases and the stress 
increases slowly due to the gradual compression of BCRCA. In the sec -
ond stage, in the densification region of ε > 50 %, the dense accumu -
lation inside BCRCA leads to a significant increase in stress [ 42 ]. Fig. 4 c 
showed cyclic curves for 100 load-unload cycles of BCRCA at 50 % 
strain. After 100 cycles, BCRCA had no obvious plastic deformation and 
stress reduction phenomenon, and the stress retention rate was 91.3 %, 
which indicated that BCRCA had good self-recovery performance and 
stability. Compared to aerogels reported in other literature [ 43 – 51 ], the 
layered BCRCA prepared in this paper exhibit excellent mechanical 
properties ( Fig. 4 d), and have potential application prospects in flexible 
supercapacitors and wearable strain sensors. 
3.2. Electrochemical performance of materials 
Tests were performed in a three-electrode system using BCRCA, 
UCRCA and NCRCA as independent electrodes without the addition of 
any binder or conductive agent. Fig. 5 a – c showed BCRCA, UCRCA and 
NCRCA CV curves at 0 – 1 V voltage window and scan rates of 5, 10, 20, 
50 and 100 mV s
� 1

the negative potential scanning direction of BCRCA, UCRCA and NCRCA 
electrodes moves in the positive direction, and the positive potential 
scanning direction moves in the negative direction. The peak current 
was positively correlated with the scanning rate. At the same time, the 
curves were almost symmetrical and approximately rectangular, which 
proves that all three electrodes have good sweep rate capability and 
electric double-layer capacitance performance [ 52 ]. Interestingly, the 
microstructure will affect the capacitive performance of the electrode.

EIS further compared the electrochemical properties of the samples. 
In Fig. 5 h, the Nyquist plots of the BCRCA, UCRCA and NCRCA elec -
trodes all consisted of semicircles in the high-frequency range and 
approximate vertical lines in the low-frequency range. This confirms the 
rapid diffusion of electrolyte ions and low charge transfer resistance, 
showing ideal capacitive performance [ 54 ]. The equivalent series 
resistance (ESR) was expressed as the intercept between the real part of 
the high frequency region and the Nyquist plot. The BCRCA electrode 
ESR of 1.61 Ω was lower than the ESR of 2.95 Ω for the UCRCA electrode 
and 3.26 Ω for the NCRCA electrode. This indicates that the lower in -
ternal resistance of the bidirectional freezing BCRCA electrode can be 
attributed to the layered network structure that promotes the charge 
transfer rate of electrolyte ions. 
Long-term cycle stability was particularly critical to the service life of 
supercapacitor electrode materials. Therefore, we tested the BCRCA 
electrode with 5000 GCD cycles at 2 A g

has 93 % capacitance retention after 5000 cycles. The better cycling 
stability of BCRCA electrodes was attributed to their large specific sur -
face area and layered properties. The excellent electrochemical prop -
erties and high stability indicate that BCRCA was a potential 
supercapacitor electrode material.

make it a promising material for strain sensors. A closed circuit was 
formed at a 9 V power supply, and the LED gradually became brighter as 
the BCRCA was compressed, and the diode became darker when pres -
sure was released ( Fig. 6 a). The reason was due to the gradual reduction

ends of the BCRCA in a mechanical test machine and connected to the 
electrochemical workstation with two copper wires (Fig. S4). In the 
range of 10 % ~ 70 % compressive strain, the current increases signif -

process, indicating that BCRCA had a fast compressive strain current 
response ( Fig. 6 b). As shown in Fig. 6 c, the strain rate was independent 
of the current BCRCA response because the current response remains at 
the same height at different rates, which was crucial for the sensor's

( Fig. 6 e), BCRCA's performance was more outstanding, making it a good 
candidate for strain sensors [ 55 – 60 ]. 
To demonstrate BCRCA's outstanding signal output stability and fa -
tigue, it was cyclically tested at 30 % compression strain. The results in 
Fig. 6 f showed that after 3500 cycles, the sensor signal attenuates very 
little, and the current signal remains almost the same current amplitude 
for each compression cycle. This demonstrates the long operating life 
and high stability of BCRCA for strain sensors, probably due to the high 
stability of the sheet structure. 
BCRCA strain sensor has superior sensing performance and can be 
assembled into a wearable sensor for monitoring the physiological ac -
tivities of the human body. Fig. 7 a showed a schematic diagram of a 
simple sensor device based on BCRCA assembly for human signal 
detection. As shown in Fig. S5, the sensing mechanism was based on the 
change in resistance of the BCRCA during compression. When pressure 
was applied to the BCRCA, the distance between adjacent sheet layers 
gradually decreases and the contact area continuously increases, 
resulting in a tighter conductive network [ 61 ]. The corresponding cur -
rent will increase and the resistance will decrease. When the pressure 
was released, the layer returns to the original structure, and the 
conductive network loosens and the resistance increases. As shown in

The higher the degree of finger curvature, the higher the strength of the

during continuous finger pressure ( Fig. 7 e). In addition, BCRCA showed 
a strong ability to recognize current signals during repeated bending 
movements of the human wrist, elbow, knee, and ankle, and could be 
repeated continuously ( Fig. 7 c, d, f, g). Continuous frowning also causes 
a regular current signal, indicating that BCRCA can also monitor small 
deformation movements ( Fig. 7 h). The above results showed that 
BCRCA strain sensor has great application prospects in human activity 
monitoring. 
4. Conclusion 
In summary, we have carefully designed and fabricated a layered 
ultra-light BCRCA with excellent mechanical properties using simple 
and effective bidirectional freeze drying and thermal annealing strate -
gies. BCRCA's rich layered structure facilitates stress transfer and 
diffusion of electrolyte ions. The use of BCRCA for supercapacitor 
electrode materials has good electrochemical properties (104.3 F g 
� 1 
at 
0.1 A g
� 1
) and excellent cycle stability (93 % capacitance retention after 
5000 cycles at 2 A g
� 1
). In addition, BCRCA can be used for strain 
sensors with excellent signal stability (3500 cycles) and to monitor 
human activity. In conclusion, this work provides a new way to prepare 
low-cost, sustainable lightweight elastic carbon aerogel, and makes it 
possible to apply it to electronic energy storage devices and wearable 
strain sensors.

Novel onion flower-derived biochar for high-performance sustainable 
supercapacitor applications
Felix A. Kwarteng
a

b

c

a
Materials Science and Engineering Program, School of Innovative Engineering, Egypt-Japan University of Science and Technology (E-JUST), 179 New Borg El-Arab City, 
Alexandria, Egypt
b
Institute of Basic and Applied Sciences, Egypt-Japan University of Science and Technology (E-JUST), 179 New Borg El-Arab City, Alexandria, Egypt
c
Environmental and Smart Technology Group, Faculty of Science, Fayoum University, Fayoum 63514, Egypt

Keywords:
Onion flower seed cover biochar
KOH-activation
Supercapacitor
ABSTRACT
Onions, scientifically known as Allium cepa L., are commonly used as a vegetable and offer a variety of health 
benefits. However, this study explored a novel part of the onion plant, such as the flower seed cover often 
regarded as waste, by converting it into biochar (BC) via pyrolysis. Through careful optimization and activation 
with potassium hydroxide, the resulting novel biochar exhibited a unique graphitic nanosheet-like structure with 
an impressive surface area of 2538.31 m
2
/g. To serve as a control, rice straw, one of the most commonly used 
biomasses, was also activated using the same protocol. Various techniques, including XPS, HRTEM, SAED, FTIR, 
BET, XRD, and Raman, were used to comprehensively understand the surface and structural properties of the 
biochar. When the novel biochar was tested as an energy storage material, it exhibited a specific capacitance of 
200.37 F/g at 1 A/g and 143.82 F/g at 5 A/g in a 1 M H
2
SO
4 
electrolyte with a three-electrode system. In a two- 
electrode system, it showed 158 F/g at 1 A/g and 102 F/g at 5 A/g, indicating its effectiveness at high rates. The 
long-term cyclic stability analysis demonstrated 100 % capacity retention over 1000 cycles in the three-electrode 
system, and 90.77 % and 74.40 % retention after 5000 cycles and 10,000 cycles, respectively, in the two- 
electrode system. The fabricated symmetric supercapacitor yielded a power density of 500 W/kg and an en -
ergy density of 21.94 Wh/kg at a current density of 1 A/g. These findings provide valuable insights into the 
valorization of biomass in addressing concerns regarding the current energy storage dilemma.
1. Introduction
It is reported that the natural world produces about 50 billion tons of 
land-based biomass each year. Out of this, about 16.7 billion tons are 
used for human purposes, such as feed for livestock, food, grazing, and 
specialized crops for other purposes. What is left off after the con -
sumption of these 16.7 billion tons is about 8.1 billion tons, which can be 
sustainably harvested and recycled into value-added products [ 1 ]. 
However, due to logistical and operational challenges, many of these 
biomasses are left untouched, eventually becoming a menace to the 
environment [ 2 ]. Owing to the high cost of commercially activated 
carbon and the vast tonnages of agricultural biomasses that pile up in the 
environment, scientists have resorted to the valorization of this agri -
cultural biomass waste into biochar to be more economical and sus -
tainable due to the abundance of biomass in the environment [ 3 ].
Biochar is a beneficial substance notably rich in carbon and lignin, 
produced under oxygen-deprived conditions via the thermochemical 
conversion of biomass [ 4 ]. Many plant-based agricultural residues are 
regarded as waste, and human approaches to dealing with this waste 
tend to pollute the environment. A practical and environmentally sus -
tainable way of managing these tons of agricultural waste is by pyro -
lyzing the waste in an anoxic environment to produce biochar [ 5 ]. The 
properties of biochar, such as its large surface area, surface functional 
groups, high porosity, and stability, make it a viable alternative for

energy applications [ 6 ]. These essential properties are predominantly 
established by the type of feedstock used, the treatment processes 
employed, and the conditions under which pyrolysis occurs.
Furthermore, the drastic depletion of non-renewable fossil fuels for 
energy has become a growing concern, and there is a massive advocacy 
to unearth the potential of renewable resources as a replacement for this 
fossil fuel [ 7 , 8 ]. However, this would need time to come to full light. In 
the meantime, supercapacitors have been introduced as the future of 
energy storage devices [ 9 ]. Many researchers have employed varieties of 
agricultural biomasses such as, corn straw [ 10 ], pinecone [ 11 ], rice 
straw [ 12 – 15 ] rice husk [ 16 ], and peanut shell [ 17 ] into forming biochar 
for supercapacitor applications [ 18 ]. Amongst these, rice straw is one of 
the most commonly used biomasses; hence, it was employed as a control 
sample in this study while detailed attention was given to the novel 
biomass. To strike a balance between cost and performance, agricultural 
biomass has been converted to activated carbon to fabricate electrodes, 
commonly referred to as electric double-layer capacitor (EDLC), for 
supercapacitor applications [ 19 ]. However, these biomass-derived 
electrodes suffer from low energy densities and low-rate capabilities 
but are powerful at possessing high power densities and good cycling 
stability [ 20 ] Additionally, the literature reveals significant variations in 
converting these biomasses into carbonaceous materials for super -
capacitor applications, resulting in prolonged processing times, 
increased energy consumption, relatively low capacitances, and the 
utilization of diverse chemicals for each technique.
For instance, a study conducted by Musyoka et al. [ 21 ] explored the 
transformation of onion peel first into hydrochar, followed by pre ‑ car -
bonization and finally activation using KOH in an argon environment. 
This process yielded porous carbon material that showed promise for 
applications in supercapacitors. Similarly, Dai et al. [ 22 ] investigated 
the synthesis of activated carbon from argy wormwood using two 
different chemicals, H
3
PO
4 
and KOH for supercapacitor applications. In 
a different approach also, García-Mateos et al. [ 23 ] developed activated 
carbon electrodes from lignin fibers through H
3
PO
4 
activation using an 
electrospinning technique. Subsequently, the electrodes underwent 
thermal stabilization at 200 
◦
C, carbonization at 900 
◦
C, and O
2 
treat -
ment under a moderately oxygen-containing N
2 
atmosphere. However, 
it should be noted that these sequential steps in the production process 
of activated carbon led to an increase in its energy consumption and 
lengthened the overall process.
To bridge the deficiencies in EDLC's several researchers have 
developed supercapacitors as a composite of biomass and metal oxides 
known as pseudocapacitors [ 24 – 26 ]. These developed pseudocapacitors 
also tend to increase production costs, and the incorporation of metal 
oxides is also non-renewable sources, thus having a mix of forward and 
backward steps towards attaining sustainable energy. Additionally, 
doping of biochar with heteroatoms such as nitrogen, boron, sulfur, and 
phosphorus also tend to improve the EDLC's energy density while 
maintaining its power densities. However, to some extent, these doping 
strategies distort the characteristic morphology of the developed bio -
char and do not largely improve capacitances in all cases. Hence, con -
stant research about the optimization of EDLC is imperative. To achieve 
optimal energy storage, it is important to have electrode materials that 
possess a high surface area, a good combination of micro and mesopores, 
and a characteristic morphology. This enables the electrode to have a 
large number of active sites, allows for fast transfer of ions from the 
electrolyte to the porous electrode, and provides good cycling proper -
ties, ultimately resulting in a high specific capacitance.
Recently, there has been a rise in the demand for fresh onions, both 
for consumption and medicinal purposes. As a result, onions have 
become the second most important horticultural crop, with around 47 
million tons cultivated annually [ 27 ]. However, onion cultivation also 
produces approximately 500,000 tons of waste each year in Europe [ 21 ]. 
Because onion peels have a strong smell and are unsuitable for landfill 
disposal, finding ways to use them is essential. Many researchers have 
focused on the peel of onions as agricultural waste, but the woody 
biomass that houses the flower seeds has been neglected. This results in 
waste from the flower seed covers, which could be transformed into a 
high-value-added product using optimal processing techniques. More -
over, despite the abundance of onion peels, they also have quite a good 
yield when pyrolyzed, and this could be an added reason for their wide 
usage. For example, Musyoka et al. [ 21 ] made porous carbon from onion 
peel by converting it to hydrochar, pre ‑ carbonizing it, and further 
activating it with KOH in an argon atmosphere for supercapacitor 
application. Krishnappa et al. [ 28 ] and Prajapati et al. [ 29 ] also 
employed onion peel biomass by converting it to biochar to treat a va -
riety of textile dyes, including MB, MO CR, and Cr (VI), of which it was a 
success. It is, therefore, essential to mention that there is currently no 
accurate data on the quantity of biomass generated by onion flower seed 
covers. However, it is known that waste is produced with every onion 
plant harvested. In future studies, research will be conducted to explore 
the potential of this unique biomass in greater detail, and accurate sta -
tistical data will be made available. Until then, this work lays the 
groundwork for fully exploring this unique agricultural biomass.
This study, therefore, explored the chemical activation of novel 
onion flower seed cover and rice straw biomasses via optimal temper -
ature, ramping rate, and mix ratio. The study investigated the suitability 
of the developed biochars as energy storage devices in a three-electrode 
and two-electrode setups. Various analytical techniques, including cy -
clic voltammetry (CV), galvanostatic charge/discharge (GCD), electro -
chemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS), capacitance retention, and 
response time, were thoroughly investigated. The study placed greater 
emphasis on the novel biochar's surface and structural properties, with 
rice straw serving as the control due to its common use as biomass. 
Consequently, this study makes noteworthy contributions to the field of 
converting innovative agricultural biomasses into high-performance 
supercapacitors for sustainable electrochemical energy storage.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Materials
Potassium hydroxide (KOH, 85 – 100 %), hydrochloric acid (30 – 33 % 
assay), sodium hydroxide (NaOH), sulphuric acid (H
2
SO
4
, 97 %), and N- 
Methyl-2-pyrrolidone (NMP, 98 %) were purchased from Loba Chemie. 
Graphite foil (99.8 %) was purchased from Thermo Fisher Scientific, 
Germany. Carbon black (super p Timcal) and polyvinylidene difluoride 
(PVDF) were also purchased from Sigma Aldrich, Germany. Electrolyte 
solutions, samples, and chemical reagents were cleaned using de-ionized 
water. Onion flower seed cover and rice straw were obtained from local 
supplies in Egypt.
2.2. Processing and development of biochar
After collecting the cover of onion flower seeds (OFSC) and rice straw 
(RS) biomasses, the two were cleaned using de-ionized water to elimi -
nate any dirt or other impurities. The cleaned samples were then dried 
for 24 h at 100 
◦
C in a Binder dry oven. Once dried, the samples were 
ground into fine particles using an RRH-500AK grinder and sieved 
through an aperture of 106 μ m. Next, 7 g of the samples were pre ‑ car -
bonized in a muffle furnace under continuous nitrogen gas at 10 
◦
C/min 
for 2 h at 600 
◦
C and designated as onion flower seed cover biochar 
(OFSCBC) and rice straw biochar (RSBC). After that, the samples were 
impregnated with KOH in a 5:1 ratio, sonicated, and refluxed at 65 
◦
C 
before being activated at 900 
◦
C for 2 h under a continuous nitrogen gas 
flow with the rate of heating set at 10 
◦
C/min. After activation, the 
samples were purified effectively using a rigorous 2-hour wash with 100 
ml of 2 M HCl, followed by rinsing with de-ionized water until the pH 
level reached neutrality. The biochars were then dried for 24 h at 100 
◦
C, 
resulting in the successful development of activated onion flower seed 
cover biochar (Act_OFSCBC) and activated rice straw biochar 
(Act_RSBC) ( Scheme 1 ).

2.3. Characterizations of the developed biochars
A thorough analysis of the activated biochars, examining both their 
surface properties and morphology, was conducted. The testing involved 
using the PerkinElmer 2400 Series II Elemental Analyzer (USA) to 
measure the percentages of active elements present in the biochar. To 
observe the biochar's surface morphology, SEM (JEOL JSM-6360LA, 
Japan) analysis was performed. Additionally, the HRTEM (JEOL, TEM- 
2100 Plus, Japan) combined with EDX analyzed the morphological 
and elemental distribution, as well as the selective area electron 
diffraction (SAED) of the obtained sample. The BET model determined 
the specific surface area and pore properties, employing the N
2 
gas 
adsorption and desorption techniques with the NOVA touch (4LX St 
1.17016062702). The activated biochar was thoroughly analyzed for its 
surface chemistry, elemental composition, and chemical bonding using 
advanced techniques such as XPS analysis with the Thermo Fisher ESCA 
Lab 250Xi X-ray photoelectron spectroscope. The study also utilized the 
Micro Raman Confocal Microscope Witec Alpha300 model to conduct 
Raman characterization, which identified defects and graphene-like 
structures in the materials. Additionally, the FTIR method (Shimadzu 
8400s, Japan) detected the functional groups of the synthesized mate -
rials, and the Bruker 2D phase XRD method was employed to analyze the 
samples' crystallinity using Cu- α radiation in the angle range of 10 – 80
◦
.
2.4. Electrode preparation and electrochemical analysis
A mixed ratio of 10:80:10 consisting of polyvinylidene difluoride 
(PVDF), biochar, and carbon black, respectively, was made into a slurry 
by the addition of 1 ml N -methyl-2-pyrrolidone (NMP). The obtained 
slurry was dropped cast unto a 1cm
2 
graphite sheet and dried under 
vacuum at 120 
◦
C for 12 h. The difference in mass before and after 
drying was recorded at 2 mg, which was used in the capacitance cal -
culations in Eqs. (1) and (2) . A three-electrode setup consisting of the 
biochar (working electrode), platinum (counter electrode), and Ag/AgCl 
(reference electrode) was put together and measured in a 1 M H
2
SO
4 
electrolyte using the VersaSTAT4 electrochemical workstation. Cyclic 
voltammetry measurements at an increasing scan rate (5 – 100 mV/s) and 
galvanostatic charge/discharge measurements at current densities of 1 
to 10 A/g were performed. Additionally, the electrochemical impedance 
spectroscopy, stability, and response time analysis were performed to 
identify the resistance, capacitance retention, and time taken for the 
activated-derived biochars to transition from a resistive to a capacitive 
mode, respectively.

Having identified that the structural and morphological properties of 
the pristine samples were inferior to the activated samples, the 
elemental compositions of the activated samples were analyzed using an 
elemental analyzer, and the results are documented in Table 2 . The 
activation process caused the biochars to react with KOH, which led to 
the consumption of organic elements and the creation of a porous 
structure, ultimately increasing the specific surface area [ 21 ]. The hy -
drophobic nature of Act_OFSCBC biochar is evident from its lower O/C

oxygenated functional groups. The Act_OFSCBC possesses a significantly 
higher aromaticity (H/C) in comparison to the control sample, giving it a 
higher tendency for efficient ion transport. It is important to note that 
different biomasses synthesized under common processing conditions 
can yield different characteristic features depending on the type of 
biomass.
The novel Act_OFSCBC was analyzed with a high-resolution trans -
mission electron microscope (HRTEM) to determine its structural and 
morphological characteristics. The chemical activation process in this 
study resulted in the graphitization of the OFSCBC, which functions as a 
framework of the activated porous carbon material. Fig. 3 (a) shows the 
evidence of crumpled layers and thin sheets of Act_OFSCBC, which was 
not so in the case of the TEM characterization of the Act_RSBC (Fig. S1). 
The HRTEM further reveals features of agglomerated crumpled nano -
sheets with voids distributed throughout the material, as seen in Fig. 3
(b). The formation of nanosheets in the activated novel material in -
creases its specific surface area, which suggests that the process of high- 
temperature pyrolysis with KOH modification is effective, as confirmed 
by Raman characterization in Fig. 2 (c). The nanosheets' large surface 
area structure and pore distribution over the sheet surface accelerate ion 
transport in multiple directions by providing abundant transport chan -
nels. Additionally, the varied micro and mesopore distribution act as 
reservoir for ion storage and favour ionic diffusion thereby enhancing 
electrochemical performance. This shortens transmission pathways and 
reduces charge-diffusion resistance, ultimately boosting electrochemical 
performance [ 19 , 36 , 37 ]. The lamellar structure of the novel biochar is 
depicted in a high-resolution micrograph in Fig. 3 (c). It is also possible 
that the transparent sheets with thinner wall structures in Fig. 3 (a) at 
higher activation temperatures resulted from the exfoliation of stacked 
onion-flower-seed-cover biochar after the intercalation of potassium 
(K). The graphitic lamellae in Fig. 3 (e) have a spacing of 0.35 nm, which 
is very near to the value reported in the literature (0.34), [ 38 ] indicating 
some level of crystallinity, which was affirmed by the selective area 
electron diffraction as seen in Fig. 3 (d). This can help with the accu -
mulation of charge in the electric double-layer, resulting in increased 
capacitance. Further, this observation implies that the structure of 
Act_OFSCBC material and its activation conditions are essential factors 
that determine the morphology of the resulting material. After analyzing 
Act_OFSCBC using SAED (Selected Area Electron Diffraction), some level 
of polycrystallinity was observed in the biochar, and this was evident by 
the unique broad diffraction ring shown in Fig. 3 (d). Interestingly, this 
diffraction ring is specific to the novel biochar meticulously synthesized 
and processed in this study. Furthermore, Fig. 3 (f) displays the results of 
HRTEM-EDX analysis, which showed that Act_OFSCBC contained a high 
amount of carbon even after KOH-activation, and this is also firmly 
supported by the elemental analysis displayed in Table 2 . Moreover, the 
analysis showed a significant amount of oxygen and a minimal quantity 
of nitrogen. The in-situ doping of nitrogen in the biochar may have been 
contributed by the thermal treatment performed under continuous ni -
trogen gas.

Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) was utilized to 
examine the ion and electron transfer kinetics of the developed elec -
trodes over a frequency range of 100 kHz to 10 mHz. The Nyquist plot 
depicted in Fig. 8 (a) revealed that the activated samples exhibited near- 
vertical curves closely aligned with the imaginary line on the y-axis. 
Notably, the Act_OFSCBC displayed more linear behaviour compared to 
the Act_RSBC, signifying a heightened capacitance behaviour. On the 
other hand, the pristine samples exhibit a significant deviation from the 
imaginary line at lower frequencies, resulting in notably low capaci -
tances. Furthermore, the point of intersection between the x-axis and the 
y- axis at higher frequencies indicates the combined resistances. These 
resistances stem from the interface between the electrode and electro -
lyte, the current collector and electrode, as well as the inherent resis -
tance of the electrode material, collectively referred to as the equivalent 
series resistance (ESR). Analysis of the Nyquist plot revealed the ESR for 
OFSCBC, RSBC, Act_RSBC and Act_OFSCBC to be 2.32 Ω , 2.74 Ω , 2.62 Ω 
and 2.83 Ω , respectively.
The resistance offered during ionic diffusion from the electrolyte to 
the electrode (known as charge transfer resistance or Rct), was identified 
by the semi-circles that appeared at high frequencies following the ESR. 
It has been noted that activated samples have smaller semi-circle di -
ameters compared to pristine ones. As semi-circle diameters decrease, 
Rct lowers, leading to faster and more efficient ionic migration from the 
electrolyte to the electrode, resulting in effective and efficient capaci -
tance contribution. According to the study, the Rct measurements for 
OFSCBC, RSBC, Act_RSBC, and Act_OFSCBC were 0.83 Ω , 3.70 Ω , 0.34 
Ω , and 0.16 Ω , respectively. Fig. 8 (b) displays the Bode phase plot for the 
activated samples. The phase angle at high frequencies is zero, while at 
lower frequencies, it becomes increasingly negative ( � 63 and � 69),

3.3. Two-electrode electrochemical configuration analysis of Act_OFSCBC
In the pursuit of validating the practical application of the 
Act_OFSCBC, a symmetric supercapacitor device was fabricated. The 
cyclic voltammograms depicted in Fig. 10 (a) by the Act_OFSCBC// 
Act_OFSCBC supercapacitor evidenced quasi-rectangular profiles within 
the range of 5 – 100 mV/s, thereby signifying an Electric Double-Layer 
Capacitor (EDLC) trait. The CV capacitance of the Act_OFSCBC// 
Act_OFSCBC supercapacitor was achieved at 194.4 F/g at 1 A/g current

curves illustrated in Fig. 10 (c) consistently demonstrated nearly trian -
gular profiles across all measured current densities (1 – 10 A/g). With 
increasing current density, a discernible reduction in discharge time was 
observed, resulting in diminished specific capacitances due to inade -
quate ion transfer time from the electrolyte to the electrode. The highest 
specific capacitance achieved was 158 F/g at 1 A/g and 102 F/g at 5 A/

Act_OFSCBC//Act_OFSCBC supercapacitor exhibited a notable deviation 
from the imaginary line on the y-axis in comparison to the 3-electrode 
system displayed in Fig. 8 (a), signifying a decrease in capacitance. 
This decline in capacitance can be attributed to the real-life application 
of the developed biochar. Notably, the observed 21.19 % reduction in 
capacitance from a 3-electrode to a 2-electrode system is a noteworthy 
achievement.
In the Nyquist plot shown in the insert of Fig. 11 (a), the intercept of 
the semicircle at the high-frequency region with the real axis represents 
the equivalent series resistance (ESR), which has been measured at 5.7 
Ω . This value emphasizes the combined resistances from the interface 
between the electrode and electrolyte, the current collector and elec -
trode, as well as the inherent resistance of the electrode material. 
Following the ESR, the subsequent semicircle portrays the charge 
transfer resistance (Rct). Smaller semicircles correlate with lower charge 
transfer resistance (Rct) values, indicating accelerated and more effi -
cient ionic migration from the electrolyte to the electrode, resulting in 
effective and efficient capacitance contribution. Notably, the 
Act_OFSCBC//Act_OFSCBC supercapacitor yielded an Rct value of 
0.001 Ω as displayed in Fig. 11 (b), underscoring an exceptionally rapid 
ionic migration and outstanding electrochemical performance. The cy -
clic stability test of the Act_OFSCBC//Act_OFSCBC supercapacitor de -
vice, depicted in Fig. 11 (c), was conducted over 10,000 cycles at a 
current density of 6 A/g, employing a voltage range of 0 – 1 V to 
demonstrate its practical application. Notably, the device exhibited an 
impressive capacitance retention of 90.77 % at the 5000th cycle and 
74.40 % at the 10000th cycle, establishing its stability and reliability for 
practical applications. Furthermore, the charge/discharge curves in the 
insert of Fig. 11 (c) indicate consistent performance throughout the 
cyclic stability test, with no discernible difference between the initial 
and final twenty cycles. The Ragone plot in Fig. 11 (d) demonstrates a 
power density of 500 W/kg and an energy density of 21.94 Wh/kg at a 
current density of 1 A/g. Moreover, at higher current densities of 5 A/g 
and 10 A/g, the Act_OFSCBC//Act_OFSCBC supercapacitor maintains 
energy densities of 14.17 Wh/kg and 6.11 Wh/kg, respectively, 
affirming exceptional performance for the novel biochar-based elec -
trode over a range of current densities. These achieved results are in 
good comparison to the literature as seen on Table 4 .
Following the completion of stability testing for 10,000 cycles, the 
Act_OFSCBC supercapacitor underwent analysis utilizing a scanning 
electron microscope (SEM) and X-ray diffractometer to assess any al -
terations in its morphology and structure. Examination of SEM micro -
graphs revealed no discernible variances in the sample's morphology 
pre- and post-stability test, as depicted in Fig. S4(a – c) and (d – f) corre -
spondingly. Furthermore, the XRD analysis in Fig. S5 indicated near 
identical positioning of the (002) and (100) planes to the pre-cycling test 
structure in Fig. 2 (d). These observations serve to substantiate the 
exceptional cycling stability exhibited by the Act_OFSCBC// 
Act_OFSCBC supercapacitor throughout the 10,000-cycle evaluation 
[ 43 ].

flower seed cover biomass, resulting in a biochar with distinctive nano- 
sheets, enriched functional groups, graphitic carbon, and an impressive 
surface area of 2538.31 m

/g due to KOH-activation. The biochar

This study utilized pyrolysis to develop biochar from a novel onion 
flower seed cover biomass, typically considered waste. The resulting 
biochar boasted a distinctive nano-sheet-like structure, enriched func -

outperformed the control sample (rice straw) in all the electrochemical 
tests performed. Therefore, this study provides significant insights into 
the engineering of innovative agricultural biomasses as high- 
performance supercapacitors for efficient energy storage. It also dem -
onstrates the potential of pyrolysis for managing agricultural waste and 
reducing carbon dioxide levels.

ABSTRACT
Excessive fossil fuel use has caused severe pollution and global warming, making the adoption of clean, efficient, 
and renewable energy essential. This study focuses on synthesizing the Ni@MCTAC nanocomposite, comprising 
multi-walled carbon nanotubes (MWCNTs), activated carbon from Conocarpus tree bark (AC-CTB), and Ni 
nanoparticles, using a straightforward ultrasonic technique. Structural and morphological analyses reveal Ni and 
MWCNTs attached to the AC-CTB surface in the Ni@MCTAC nanocomposite. The Ni@MCTAC nanocomposite 
(1034 m

� 1

electrode at 0.5 A g
� 1

exhibited an energy density of 19 Wh kg
� 1

� 1

g
� 1

cycles at bending angles of 45

◦

◦
. The fabricated ASC powered a blue LED for over 5 min, show -
casing its excellent performance. This highlights the potential of the Ni@MCTAC nanocomposite as a binder-free, 
flexible electrode for asymmetric supercapacitor.
1. Introduction
The increasing energy demand, and vastly depleting fossil fuels are 
the two main reasons to create the research interest towards clean, 
green, and renewable energy sources for energy production and storage. 
In the last few decades, fuel cells and batteries have played a major role 
in our earth's indispensable energy requirements but the two funda -
mental components of systems that continuously store and distribute 
energy are traditional capacitors and batteries. Batteries, on the other 
hand, provide a substantial amount of energy with low power density, 
whereas ordinary capacitors have no energy density but provide high 
power density [ 1 – 5 ]. As a result, attention to evolve the improved high- 
power, and high-energy density energy storage devices has been focused 
by many researchers [ 6 , 7 ].
Supercapacitors (SCs) are one kind of energy storage system that has 
captivated a lot of scientific interest today. Supercapacitors have two 
distinct methods of storing energy: electrical double-layer capacitance 
(EDLC) and pseudocapacitance. Carbonaceous materials with excess 
conductivity and high surface areas like activated carbon (AC), gra -
phene, and carbon nanotubes (CNTs) are known as EDLC electrode 
materials [ 8 , 9 ]. On the other side, metal oxides, carbides, nitrides, sel -
enides, and conducting polymers undergo reversible redox reactions 
which are pseudocapacitive electrode materials because of their abun -
dance in nature, cost-effectiveness, and extraordinary capacity to store
