In this work, we report for the first time according to our under -
standing the synthesis of a novel nanocomposite comprising nickel 
nanoparticles, multi-walled carbon nanotubes (MWCNTs), and activated 
carbon derived from Conocarpus tree bark (CTB-AC), highlighting a 
unique combination of materials. The use of biomass-derived activated 
carbon introduces a sustainable and cost-effective material, aligning 
with green chemistry principles and offering an eco-friendly alternative 
to conventional materials. A simple yet scalable ultrasonic-assisted 
method was employed to achieve a well-integrated structure, wherein 
CTB-based activated carbon enhances the surface area of MWCNTs, and 
Ni incorporation significantly boosts electrochemical performance. The 
resulting Ni@MWCNT/CTB-AC composite exhibited exceptional spe -
cific capacitance, rate capability, and cyclic stability, attributed to its 
unique structural synergy. Furthermore, the binder-free device fabri -
cated from this composite showcased excellent mechanical robustness 
and successfully powered a blue LED, demonstrating practical applica -
tion potential. This innovative approach introduces a new class of hybrid 
nanomaterials while advancing sustainable energy storage through the 
valorization of waste-derived biomass. By utilizing CTB, the work sup -
ports clean energy solutions and contributes to the global transition 
away from fossil fuels.

attributed to the Ni decoration on the AC-CTB surface, which indicates 
the formation of a crystalline structure. The XRD and SEM data provide 
strong support for the above findings.

4.2. Powering of blue LED using Ni@MCTAC//AC-CTB
The flexible devices are connected either in series or in parallel to 
satisfy the necessary energy/power constraint to assess the constructed 
Ni@MCTAC//AC-CTB's practical functionality. To demonstrate the 
adaptability of our ASC devices in both topologies, four devices were 
coupled in series and parallel ( Fig. 10 ). Surprisingly, compared to a 
single ASC device with an operating potential window of 0.8 V, the four 
serially connected devices generated a 3.2 V CV curve and a GCD po -
tential window with a comparable discharge duration. The CV results 
( Fig. 10 a and Fig. 10 b) and the GCD results ( Fig. 10 c and Fig. 10 d) of the 
Ni@MCTAC//AC-CTB fabricated electrodes in series and parallel con -
nections are demonstrated in the figures. Four devices could instantly 
power LEDs (blue) for longer than 5 min using the series connection 
( Fig. 10 e and Fig. 10 f). As a result, the Ni@MCTAC//AC-CTB asym -
metric hybrid flexible supercapacitor is likely to find an outlet in the 
green energy industry.
5. Conclusion
AC-CTB, MCTAC, and Ni@MCTAC were employed to create an 
innovative nanocomposite towards flexible asymmetric supercapacitor 
applications. Electrochemical, elemental, structural, and morphological 
characterizations were performed for the produced nanocomposite. The 
SEM image reveals that the AC-CTB structure is highly porous, enabling 
greater loading of MWCNTs and Ni nanoparticles, while also enhancing 
ion adsorption and desorption during charge – discharge cycles. In 1 M 
H
2
SO
4 
electrolyte, the supercapacitor's Ni@MCTAC working electrode 
delivers a superior specific capacitance of 513 F g
� 1 
at 0.5 A g
� 1 
and a 
specific capacitance retention of 89 %. The as-fabricated Ni@MCTAC|| 
AC-CTB asymmetric supercapacitor exhibits an elevated specific 
capacitance of 138 F g
� 1 
along with a capacitance retention of 88 % for 
more than 10,000 cycles. The fabricated ASC could power the blue LED 
for 5 min. Hence, these outstanding specific capacitance, cyclic stability, 
and straightforward synthesis ensure that the fabricated Ni@MCTAC 
nanocomposite might be a beneficial promising binder-free flexible 
electrode material for asymmetric supercapacitor applications.

ABSTRACT  
Biomass - derived carbon electrode material with a porous structure is widely used in supercapacitor applica -
tions, which can improve electron transfer and shorter ion diffusion pathways. In this work, the garlic peel 
biomass carbon (GPBC), NiMo
3
S
4
(NMS) and garlic peel biomass carbon decorated with NiMo
3
S
4 
(GPBC/NMS) 
composite were prepared through a in situ two-step hydrothermal method. The synthesized materials were 
characterized by X-ray diffraction (XRD) and field emission scanning electron microscopy (FE-SEM), energy 
dispersive x-ray spectroscopy (EDS), Transmission electron microscopy techniques (TEM), Raman spectroscopy 
and Brunauer-Emmett-Teller (BET) techniques were used to analyze the structure, morphology and specific 
surface areas and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS). The prepared bimetallic metal sulfide on a biomass - 
derived carbon namely the GPBC/NMS composite is used in supercapacitor application. The GPBC/NMS com -
posite electrode exhibits good cycle performance with high specific capacity of 304C/g at current density of 1 A/ 
g in a 3 M KOH electrolyte solution. The electrochemical performance of the GPBC/NMS//GPBC asymmetric 
supercapacitor device produces an excellent energy density 45.5 Wh kg
� 1 
at a power density of 1125 W kg
� 1 
in 
the 1.6 V operating potential window. The GPBC/NMS//GPBC also exhibits 93 % retention of its initial 
capacitance after the 10,000 GCD cycle performance. The above results demonstrate a new way of developing 
high performance electrode materials for energy storage applications.   
1. Introduction 
In today's world, the consumption of fossil energy for portable 
electronic devices, electronic vehicles, and other energy-consuming 
industrialization are increasing day by day and the demand of the en -
ergy causing environmental pollution and economic issues. [ 1 , 2 ]. With 
the increase in necessity for energy, it becomes necessary to store energy 
and use it efficiently. Advanced energy storage devices such as fuel 
batteries, supercapacitors and rechargeable batteries have been suc -
cessfully relieve environmental problems and energy shortage [ 3 , 4 ]. 
Among the advanced energy storage systems, Supercapacitors are the 
main energy storage system that has attracted more attention due to 
their long cycling stability, extremely low internal resistance, high 
power density capability, fast charge-discharge cycling, and longer life 
span [ 5 ]. The supercapacitor is mainly classified into three groups ac -
cording to the energy storage mechanism: Electrode double layer ca -
pacitors (EDLC), Pseudocapacitors, and Hybrid capacitors. In recent 
years, the combination of EDLC and pseudocapacitor in the hybrid 
capacitor has attracted attention due to its high performance, good 
cycling stability, and excellent specific capacitance [ 6 – 8 ]. 
The hybrid supercapacitor is largely dependent on the nature of 
Electrodes, electrolyte, separators and current collectors. The carbon 
based electrodes such as carbon nanotube (CNT), carbon nanofiber, 
graphene, activated carbon (AC), carbon aerogel, etc. are considered to 
be the ideal electrode materials in the supercapacitor because of their 
physiochemical properties such as high chemical stability, high specific 
surface area, excellent electrical conductivity, etc. [ 9 – 11 ]. In recent 
years, biomass-derived carbon materials synthesized from various

biomasses, including banana peel [ 12 ] corncob [ 13 ], rice husk [ 14 ], 
lotus stem [ 15 ], bamboo [ 16 ], pomelo peel [ 17 ], tobacco waste [ 18 ], 
pencil peel [ 19 ] and etc., have been used as carbon sources to prepare 
carbon materials for energy storage applications. Biomass-derived car -
bon materials have the advantages of a rich carbon content, high specific 
surface area, an enlarged pore structure, and excellent electrical con -
ductivity, making them suitable for use as electrode materials in 
supercapacitor applications [ 20 – 22 ]. Utilizing biomass waste as an 
electrode sources to create abundant electroactive sites carbon with 
enhanced EDLC supercapacitor performance due to their hierarchical 
meso/micro pores and presence of various heteroatoms. To develop 
hybrid super capacitor, the effective pseudo behavior nanomaterial's are 
composed with biomass derived carbon [ 23 ]. Hybridization of transition 
metal oxides on the surface of the carbon material is enhance the elec -
trochemical performance and makes synergistic effect that takes ad -
vantages in energy storage applications. To date, high-performance 
electrodes have undergone intensive exploration and exploitation to 
meet the aforementioned demands, such as metal oxides, metal sulfides, 
metal phosphides, and so on. Specifically, transition metal sulfides 
(TMSs) have received significant attention due to their superior con -
ductivity and remarkable electrochemical performance due to their 
pseudo capacitive ability [ 24 , 25 ]. Extensive research has been carried 
out to study the high theoretical specific capacity of binary transition 
metal sulfides and their use as supercapacitor electrode materials [ 26 ]. 
Furthermore, despite its attractive electrochemical properties, the TMS 
is exhibited low specific capacity. To overcome the problem, the new 
strategy method is used to increase the specific capacitance of TMS 
materials. Due to the high charge transfer resistance and low efficiency 
of the active material, the practical specific capacity of TMS is currently 
quite low in comparison to its theoretical value [ 27 ]. In the TMS ma -
terials, NiCo
2
S
4 
is mostly examined by supercapacitors because of their 
high theoretical capacitance, low cost, and easy synthesis process. Some 
reports on NiMo
3
S
4 
battery-type materials were investigated by super -
capacitor applications [ 28 , 29 ]. Research investigations required to find 
suitable composites along with TMS for enhanced electrochemical per -
formance and redox ability through synergistic effect [ 30 , 31 ]. 
In this work, the novel NiMo
3

enhance the conductivity of NiMo

(GPBC/NMS) through an in situ two-step hydrothermal process 
for energy storage applications. The GPBC was prepared by the hydro -
thermal method and activated by KOH with a developed pore structure 
to improve the conductive substrate of NMS, which could potentially 
enhance the electrochemical performance of the GPBC/NMS composite. 
In addition, the asymmetric supercapacitor assembled with GPBC/NMS 
for the positive electrode and GPBC for the negative electrode could 
produce excellent electrochemical performance. The strategy suggested 
here may inspire new possibility of sustainably producing biomass 
derived carbon materials for advanced energy storage.

material surface. As a result, the improved electrochemical performance 
arises from the synergetic effect due to the increases the active sites of 
GPBC by intercalation of NMS enhances the interface response with the 
electrode and electrolyte interface and improve the electrical conduc -

The electrochemical impedance spectroscopy analysis was carried out in 
a frequency range of 1 MHz to 0.1 Hz. Fig. 8 (a) shows the Nyquist plot of 
the prepared electrode materials, and their plots exhibit a semi-circle in 
the high frequency region and a straight line that is nearly parallel to the 
imaginary component. Fig. 8 a shows the GPBC/NMS electrode has 
semicircle in the high-frequency region is shorter than the NMS elec -
trode, which causes low resistance and high diffusion of ions to the 
electrode surface from the electrolyte. The GPBC/NMS composite has a 
lower semicircle than the NMS electrode, which indicates the GPBC/

tivity. Fig. 8 b shows the long-term cycling stability of the GPBC/NMS

electrolyte. After completing the 10,000 galvanostatic charge-discharge 
cycles, the composite electrode retained 90 % of its initial capacitance. 
These results show the GPBC/NMS has demonstrated excellent stability 
and good rate capability. 
4.1. Electrochemical properties of two electrode system 
The electrochemical superior performance of the GPBC/NMS com -
posite in three electrode configuration was investigated for real life 
application as redox feature electrode material to build an asymmetric 
supercapacitor device. In a two electrode configured systems, the GPBC/ 
NMS//GPBC was assembled using the GPBC/NMS as the positive elec -
trode, the GPBC as the negative electrode with 3 M KOH aqueous elec -
trolyte. We assembled the asymmetric two-electrode configuration 
based on a positive electrode of GPBC/NMS composite and a negative 
electrode of GPBC material in a 3 M KOH electrolyte. Fig. 9 a) shows the 
schematic illustration of the assembled asymmetric supercapacitor cell 
and the operating potential window has demonstrated by cyclic vol -
tammetry studies of GPBC/NMS composite and GPBC in a three- 
electrode system. The asymmetric supercapacitor device refers to the 
sum of positive and negative electrode potential. All the CV curves 
exhibit quasi rectangular shape which is demonstrating the EDLC 
behavior. Fig. 9 b) shows the GPBC/NMS composite and GPBC electrodes 
at a scan rate of 50 mV/s, and the corresponding potential windows are 
0 to 1.6 V and 0 to -1 V respectively. The working voltage range of 
GPBC/NMS//GPBC asymmetric device was 0 – 1.6 V. Fig. 9 c) shows the 
CV curves of an asymmetric device GPBC/NMS//GPBC at various po -
tential windows at 50 mV/s scan rate. All the CV curves of asymmetric 
device exists a combination of EDLC and pseudocapacitance character -
istics from GPBC and NMS electrode materials, which indicates rapid ion 
transfer behavior and good reversibility. Fig. 9 d) exhibits the asym -
metric device at various scan rates ranging from 10 to 50 mV/s in the 
0 – 1.6 V. Fig. 9 e) exhibits the GCD curves of GPBC/NMS//GPBC asym -
metric devices in different operating potential windows ranging from 
1.0 to 1.6 V at 1 A/g current density. Every GCD curves that displays a 
linear triangle shape indicates good electrochemical performance in the 
asymmetric capacitor. Fig. 9 f) shows the GCD curves of asymmetric 
device at different current densities ranging from 1 to 5 A/g in the po -
tential window of 0 – 1.6 V. Even with high current density applied, the 
GCD nonlinear curves maintain symmetrical shape without distortion 
due to faradic and non- faradic reactions of positive and negative elec -
trodes that can be carried out in supercapacitor cell, indicating that the 
GPBC/NMS//GPBC asymmetric device has good specific capacity and 
high reversibility performance. To estimate the performance of the 
asymmetric supercapacitor device, the energy and power density were 
very crucial parameters. Fig. 9 g) shows the ragone plot of the GPBC/ 
NMS//GPBC asymmetric device. The Ragone plot of high energy density 
at high power density confirms the ability of devices to charge and 
discharge with high specific capacitance. Fig. 9 g) shows the Ragone plot 
of an asymmetric device with an energy density of 45.5 Wh kg

5. Conclusion 
In conclusion, the GPBC was successfully prepared using waste garlic 
peel biomass raw material. The GPBC/NMS composite was synthesized 
by the facile hydrothermal method at 180 
◦
C for 12 h. The synthesized 
materials were characterized by various characterization techniques. In 
the three-electrode system, NMS was decorated on the GPBC surface of 
the GPBC/NMS composite to enhance the capacity performance, and it 
has a high capacity of 304 C/g at 1 A/g current density. Furthermore, an 
assembled asymmetric supercapacitor was fabricated with GPBC/NMS 
and GPBC as the positive and negative electrodes, respectively. The 
asymmetric supercapacitor device GPBC/NMS//GPBC exhibits a high 
energy density of 45.5 Wh kg
� 1 
with a power density of 1125 W kg
� 1 
at 
1 A/g current density, respectively. Moreover, the asymmetric device 
has excellent stability, as it is able to retain 93 % of its specific capacity 
even after 10,000 charging-discharging cycles. Therefore, the above 
results were demonstrated that the biomass-derived GPBC material as a 
conductive substrate to support the bimetallic sulfide NMS active ma -
terials will be a promising electrode for developing high-performance 
asymmetric supercapacitor applications.

Constructing nitrogen/sulfur co-doped hierarchical porous cellulose-based 
carbon derived from larch via regeneration by dissolution approach 
for supercapacitor 
Rongrong Si
a , 1
, Honggang Luo
b , 1
, Junwen Pu
a , * 
a
Beijing Key Laboratory of Lignocellulosic Chemistry, Beijing Forestry University, Beijing 100083, China 
b
State Key Laboratory of Biobased Materials & Green Papermaking, Qilu University of Technology (Shandong Academy of Sciences), Jinan, Shandong 250353, China   
ARTICLE INFO  
Keywords: 
Activation 
Doping 
Supercapacitor 
ABSTRACT  
The effective strategies to increase the energy density of carbon-based supercapacitors are increasing the specific 
surface area (SSA) and heteroatom doping, however the methods to achieve such outcomes are often time- 
consuming and complicated. Herein, a time-saving and facile method was adopted to fabricate hierarchical 
carbonized wood electrodes with both delignification and partly dissolution/regeneration through NaOH/thio -
urea solution followed by carbonization. The partial dissolution/regeneration treatment not only generates the 
interconnected network structures on the surface of the regenerated wood and improves the porosity, but also 
achieves the efficient co-doping of nitrogen/sulfur heteroatoms. A relatively excellent activation was achieved by 
dissolving for only 3 h, with a SSA of 1416.25 m
2
/g, which was 2.86 times higher than the SSA of the samples 
carbonized directly with delignified wood. Remarkably, the as prepared electrode exhibits superior areal (spe -
cific) capacitance of 6.11 F/cm
2 
(413.6 F/g, 1.0 mA/cm
2
) and durability (98.9%, 12,000 cycles, 50 mA/cm
2
). In 
addition, a symmetrical supercapacitor (SSC) assembled from carbonized regenerated wood has an excellent 
energy density of 1.15 mWh/cm
2 
(51.24 Wh/kg) at a power density of 699 mW/cm (31.11 W/kg). This facile 
doping and activation method may be able to provide a new concept for the carbon electrode preparation of bio- 
based materials.   
1. Introduction 
As one of the most widely used electrochemical energy storage de -
vices, supercapacitors (SCs) performing a crucial function in electro -
chemical storage and release of energy due to their potentially high 
electrochemical efficiency, long operating life, and certifiable safety ( Fu 
et al., 2021; Xu et al., 2022 ). The output performance of SCs is heavily 
relevant to the electrode substances. Carbon-based electrodes were 
regarded as promising electrode for SCs due to the presence of large 
specific surface area (SSA), adjustable pore size distribution and high 
electrical conductivity ( Wang et al., 2019b; Yang et al., 2022 ). Unfor -
tunately, the low energy density of carbon-based electrode is the major 
obstacle towards the flexible application due to the lack of structure 
optimization and control of surface properties. Therefore, finding a 
simple way to optimize the structure and control surface properties of 
carbon-based material electrodes can achieve energy density 
improvements. 
Lignocellulosic biomass-derived materials are encountering the most 
flourishing moment due to their versatile properties and wide potential 
applications( Shen and Sun, 2021 ). Controllable preparation of ligno -
cellulosic biomass-derived materials, development of new methods to 
prepare novel biomaterials from lignocellulose, and provision of envi -
ronmentally friendly, low-cost and easily scalable lignocellulosic func -
tional materials are essential to achieve carbon neutrality( Kang et al., 
2021 ). Woody biomass possesses a rich source, a wide variety, low cost, 
degradable, renewable, and a significant anisotropic and hierarchical 
structure, allowing it to be applied directly to SCs without the use of 
other conductive agents or adhesives ( Daotong et al., 2023 ). However, 
wood has a diversity of chemical components and structural complexity 
( Zhao et al., 2020 ). Due to the different distribution of the three major 
components including cellulose, hemicellulose and lignin ( Schubert 
et al., 2022 ), the uneven decomposition of the three components during

2
the direct carbonization of the natural wood leads to uneven conduc -
tivity and pore distribution in the thick cell walls, which results in still 
unsatisfactory electrochemical properties ( Wang et al., 2021c; Wang 
et al., 2021d; Zhang et al., 2019a ). Therefore, reducing the 
non-uniformity of conductivity and pore distribution due to the 
complexity of the wood itself is the valid methods to enhance the elec -
trode performance. In contrast to the classic bottom-up method of 
delignification in the paper and pulping industry, the top-down 
approach allows the embedded lignin to be removed from the wood 
cell wall structure while maintaining the natural anisotropic structure. 
The carbonization of wood after delignification will minimize the 
inhomogeneous pore structure produced by the complexity of the wood 
and facilitate the regulate the charge/ion transport pathway. 
The large SSA provides active sites that can retain electric charges. 
For instance, in our previous work, the delignified wood carbon elec -
trode obtained by controlling the carbonization temperature and the 
multi-stage carbonization process had a high SSA of 945.09 m
2
/g, this is 
significantly higher than the 357.25 m
2
/g of natural wood and 481.05 
m
2
/g for delignified obtained by one-stage carbonization, its capaci -
tance was 211.3 F/g (0.5 A/g), far exceeding the natural carbonized 
wood (20.6 F/g)( Luo et al., 2022a ). That is, the electrochemical per -
formance is improved by the electric double layer capacitances (EDLC) 
mechanism( He et al., 2022b ). Therefore, the activation of carbon pre -
cursors before or during the carbonization process is one of the effective 
means to increase the SSA. Wang et al. prepared carbonized wood 
through delignification followed by enzyme treatment, the pore gener -
ation was controlled by controlling the ratio and treatment time be -
tween cellulase and delignified wood. The obtained electrode had a high 
SSA (1418 m
2
/g), capacitance (328 F/g, 1 mA/cm
2
) and the assembled 
SSC can achieve areal/volumetric energy density of 0.21 mWh 
cm
� 2
/0.99 mWh cm
� 3 
and durability (86.58%, 15,000 cycles)( Wang 
et al., 2021c ). N, S could cause electron density imbalance and improve 
carbon surface activity due to the electronegativity difference between 
atoms( He et al., 2022a ; Wang et al., 2023 ). The surface functional 
groups could provide additional pseudo-capacitance via redox reaction, 
thus improving the weight capacitance( Lyu et al., 2023 ). Importantly, 
the introduction of heteroatoms into the carbon structure could enhance 
surface polarity and wettability could further overcome the limitations 
of carbon in structure, surface performance and electrochemical per -
formance ( Ma et al., 2020 ). However, the methods that can simulta -
neously achieve an increase in SSA and heteroatom doping were often 
complex, time-consuming and could not be obtained in one step. For 
example, Tang et al. first achieved the doping of N and S double atoms 
by soaking a mixture of delignified wood and trithiocyanuric acid so -
lution, then two high-temperature carbonizations in N
2 
and NH
3
, 
respectively, were performed to obtain larger SSA. The obtained wood 
carbon electrode had a high SSA (1438 m
2
/g), the specific capacitance 
(704 F/g, 0.2 A/g) and superior oxygen reduction reaction performance 
( Tang et al., 2018 ). Therefore, in order to boost the output performance 
of biomass-based carbon, we are very interested in a simple and versatile 
strategy that enables a combination of activated pore generation and 
regulation surface properties. 
Herein, an effective method was adopted to fabricate hierarchical 
carbonized wood electrodes with both delignification and partly disso -
lution/regeneration through NaOH/thiourea solution followed by 
carbonization. The delignification is to obtain a more uniform hierar -
chical structure, and the process of dissolution regeneration of the 
NaOH/thiourea reagent system is also a process of activation and het -
eroatom doping. A relatively high activation effect was achieved in three 
hours, and the SSA obtained after carbonization was 1416.25 m
2
/g, 
much higher than that of 494.89 m
2
/g for direct carbonization after 
delignification. In addition, the doping of N,S double heteroatoms in -
creases the surface wettability and improves the defects and graphiti -
zation degree of the carbon structure. Therefore, the structure of this 
regenerated wood makes it an outstanding substrate for multi- 
functionalities, which makes up for the defects of traditional 
activation and doping methods and opens new opportunities for the 
development of supercapacitors. 
2. Experiment sections 
Detailed preparation and electrochemical test methods were 
included in the Supporting Information . 
3. Result and discussion 
A schematic diagram is shown in Fig. 1 , where we describe the entire 
procedure of converting waste Larch (Natural wood, NW) to a carbon 
material through delignification, regeneration and thereafter carbon -
ization, followed by assembly into a symmetrical supercapacitor (SSC) 
device. First, delignification and bleaching methods were mentioned in 
our previous study (process I) to obtain delignified wood (TW)( Luo 
et al., 2022b ). After delignification, NaOH/thiourea solution was 
introduced to dissolve a portion of the wood cell wall. Regenerated TW-x 
(RTW-x) was obtained after regeneration and drying of the dissolved cell 
walls in ethanol, where the x represents the time of dissolution (process 
II). Specifically, NaOH can not only penetrate the microcrystals but also 
enter the microcrystals to destroy the cellulose molecules, thiourea as 
blockers can prevent the recombination of cellulose molecular chains, 
the synergistic effect enables cellulose to achieve activation and the 
introduction of N and S atoms. NaOH/thiourea solvent is an effective 
inorganic solvent for dissolving cellulose, and NaOH is considered to be 
a useful activator, so the activation and two-element doping can be 
achieved very skillfully by this method. It is worth noting that this 
method has the advantage of being rapid and safe compared to con -
ventional activation and doping methods. RTW-x was carbonized under 
inert gas (N
2
), also to gain conductive carbon wood with extensive 
surface area (Process III), and carbonized RTW-x (CRTW-x) was ob -
tained. This is expected to achieve excellent capacitive performance by 
regulating N/S content and improving porosity through partial dis -
solution/regeneration while preserving the wood microtubule structure. 
3.1. Characterization of RTW-x 
From the physical object displayed in Fig S1a and b, it can be seen 
that compared to NW, the color of TW becomes white due to the removal 
of a large amount of lignin. Particularly, given its outstanding lignin 
solubility, cellulose protection, and low energy consumption, formic 
acid has been used as a cooking agent for pulping to remove lignin from 
lignocellulosic feedstock ( Wang et al., 2019a ). In addition, the dual 
solvent system is formed by formic acid and water with the character -
istic of a high azeotropic point, which is 107. 6 º C at 101.3 kPa pressure, 
and easy recovery with distillation ( Luo et al., 2022b ). Additionally, 
deep eutectic solvent (DES) is an emerging candidate as compared to 
others due to its high efficiency, recoverability, biodegradability, and 
has a low cost of preparation ( Kesari et al., 2022 ; Sirvio et al., 2015 ). 
DES is expected to be an efficient solvent for obtaining delignified wood 
directly from wood by the "Top-down" method. After dis -
solution/regeneration, as shown in Fig. S1 c-f, it is noted that, the RTW-x 
changes into yellow. When the time was 1 – 3 h, the morphology of the 
dried RTW did not change significantly. When the dissolution time was 
longer than 3 h, however, RTW crumples after drying, which is detri -
mental to the establishment of wood-based hierarchical porous mate -
rials. Fig. 2 a. ( Fig S2a ) shows the scanning electron microscope (SEM) 
images of TW that presented a more closed block structure. Differently, 
after one hour of dissolution, RTW-1 exhibits a slight volume of pore 
structure ( Figs. 2 b and S2b ). As shown in Fig. 2 c, lots of pores and 
interwoven network appeared on the cell wall of RTW-2. RTW-3 shows 
the anisotropic multi-channel structure of the wood is preserved, and in 
the lumen with a nanofiber network is the result of regeneration 
( Fig. 2 d). The original channel structure of RTW-3 facilitates the for -
mation of interconnected layered porous structures in the subsequent

carbonization process. It is worth noting that, interconnected pore 
structures appear inside and on the surface of the cell wall ( Fig. 2 e-f). As 
compared to the chemical components of NW and TW displayed in 
Fig. S3 , after delignification, a substantial reduction in the relative lignin 
content occurred from 23.0% in NW to 1.7% in TW. However, the cel -
lulose content is improving, reducing the risk of inhomogeneous pores 
due to the complexity of the wood during the carbonization process. In 
this process, the density also decreased from 0.559 for NW to 0.32 g/cm
3 
for RTW-3 due to the creation of pores ( Fig. S4a ), while the porosity 
increased to 78.67% (RTW-3), which was higher than those of NW 
(62.73%) and TW (73.53%) ( Fig. S4b ). The generation of pores in the 
cell walls, the decrease in density and the increase in porosity all proved 
the superior activation effect of NaOH/thiourea, and the production of 
network structure in the lumen can effectively use the space. 
To clarify the effect of dissolution/regeneration treatments on the 
crystalline structure of delignified wood, X-ray Diffraction (XRD) was 
performed ( Fig. 2 g). By analyzing the diffraction angle of NW and TW 
(14.7
◦
, 16.6
◦
, 22.8
◦
, and 34.9
◦
) and amorphous cellulose (21.5
◦
) rep -
resents cellulose I ( French, 2014 ). This indicates that the delignification 
process would not change the crystal structure of the wood. The 
diffraction angle of RTWs has changed to (11.9
◦
, 20.2
◦
and 21.7
◦
) were 
confirmed cellulose II, which indicated that the dissolution process de -
stroys the crystalline structure ( Zhang et al., 2019b ). It is known from 
this phenomenon that the regeneration of wood from NaOH/thiourea 
solutions usually takes place in a non-ordered manner, in both amor -
phous and crystalline cellulose ( Yang et al., 2011 ). The crystallinity (CI) 
was calculated using Jade software, after delignification, the CI of TW 
was 69.80%, which was higher than that of NW at 59.26%. The CI for 
RTW-1, RTW-2 and RTW-3 were 59.00%, 41.75% and 40.08%, respec -
tively ( Fig. 2 h), which might be caused by the greater damage of cel -
lulose by NaOH/thiourea with increasing time. The FTIR spectra of the 
TW and RTW-x displayed in Fig S5 . This result indicates no change in the 
characteristic functional groups before and after regeneration, there is 
no chemical reaction did occur during the dissolution process reactions. 
The thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) curves of TW and RTW-x are 
presented in Fig S6 , RTW-x is less thermally stable than TW, due to the 
cellulose molecular chain were broken and less constrained, which is in 
accordance with the result of XRD. 
In natural wood, cellulose is the skeletal structure and lignin is the 
filler that provides strength to the wood. After delignification, the lignin 
is almost completely removed, which limiting the application, since its 
mechanical properties can be severely reduced. The dissolution/regen -
eration process can improve the mechanical properties of delignified 
wood, which can make it more widely available ( Tu et al., 2021 ; Ye 
et al., 2019 ). From Fig. 2 i, TW exhibited a poor tensile strength 
( σ b = 5.06 MPa) and elongation at break ( ε b = 9.14%), lower than that 
of the RTW-1 ( σ b = 11.07 MPa, ε b = 9.68%), RTW-2 ( σ b = 20.42 MPa, 
ε b = 16.22%) and RTW-3 ( σ b = 17.29 MPa, ε b = 10.34%). The 
increased mechanical strength broadens the application prospects of 
delignified wood. Regenerated wood can improve the porosity and 
mechanical strength of wood-based materials, providing a better plat -
form for the design of multifunctional materials. 
3.2. Characterization of CRTW-x 
Fig. 3 a, c show SEM images of the cross section of CNW and CTW.

After high-temperature carbonization, both CNW and CTW maintained 
the anisotropic structure of the wood without collapse. CNW showed 
regularly arranged and intact fibroblasts with thick cell walls. However, 
CTW showed more channels in cross section due to the large amount of 
lignin being shed. Fig. 3 b shows the longitudinal section of CNW with a 
smooth surface and no wrinkling under high temperature conditions. 
However, CTW shows folds and a few pores in the longitudinal section 
( Fig. 3 d). After performing one step of dissolution, the surface of the cell 
wall already appeared to be more different. There are some sheet-like 
network structures appeared on the surface of CRTW-1 ( Fig. 3 e), prob -
ably due to the reason that the one-hour dissolution occurs only on the 
surface of the cell wall. Fig. 3 f shows that the network structure of the 
longitudinal section of CRTW-2 is significantly increased, however, 
there is a more obvious separation between the network and the wood 
matrix. The CRTW-3 sample is portrayed in Fig. 3 g, the structure is well 
integrated without the appearance of sheet-like structures on the sur -
face. As shown in Fig. 3 h, high temperature carbonization did not 
collapse the cell walls of RTW and was still able to maintain the hier -
archical structure. Compared with CNW and CTW, which had a tighter 
structure, the cell wall of CRTW-3 clearly showed broader pores inside 
the cell wall ( Fig. 3 i). From Fig. 3 j, it can be clearly observed that 
amorphous grooved porous structures appear in the cell wall, which 
facilitates rapid ion transport. The water contact angle (WCA) shows 
that water droplets can penetrate the CRTW-3 electrode quickly and 
absorb water completely after only 60 ms, which is faster than any other 
samples, especially CNW and CTW ( Fig S7 ). Due to the introduction of 
N/S dual atoms through dissolution/regeneration and the creation of a 
surface porous structure, CRTW-x has a generally fast ion transport rate 
when used as an electrode and ensures a high diffusion rate ( Liu et al., 
2022 ). 
The appearance of this phenomenon indicates that NaOH/thiourea 
can show a clear activation effect in a short time, and has the charac -
teristics of simple operation and non-dangerous. From the Energy

4. Conclusion 
In summary, N/S heteroatom functionalized, structure-engineered 
and surface aera-boosted carbonized wood was fabricated through 
both delignification and partly dissolution/regeneration by NaOH/ 
thiourea followed by carbonization. At first, during the delignification 
process, the wood can still maintain the anisotropic structure and the 
complexity will be reduced to obtain a relatively homogeneous carbon 
precursor. And then, the partial dissolution regeneration of NaOH/ 
thiourea solution increased the porosity of the carbon precursor, a large 
number of interconnected pore structures were produced in the cell wall 
and nanofiber network in the lumen. In addition, high temperature 
carbonization did not destroy the anisotropic properties of the wood and 
still managed to maintain the hierarchical structure. The last reason is, 
in the process, doping of N, S atoms is introduced offer extra pseudo- 
capacitive properties. 
The hierarchical structure, amorphous network porous structure and 
the doping of N/S heteroatoms synergistically improve the wettability 
and electrochemical properties of the carbonized cellulose. The CRTW-3 
electrode exhibits superior areal (specific) capacitance of 6.11 F/cm
2 
(413.6 F/g, 1.0 mA/cm
2
) and durability (98.9%, 12,000 cycles, 50 mA/ 
cm
2
). In addition, a SSC assembled from carbonized regenerated wood 
has an excellent energy density of 1.15 mWh/cm
2 
(51.24 Wh/kg) at a 
power density of 699 mW/cm (31.11 W/kg). We believe that the high 
porosity and mechanical properties of the regenerated wood obtained in 
this work provide a suitable platform for the preparation of multifunc -
tional materials, and that the dissolution regeneration method is a 
simple, time-saving and safe way to obtain good activation and diatomic 
doping results.

ABSTRACT  
Porous carbon sheets exhibit a big open flat layer with large surface area, short ion transfer distance, which has 
attracted massive research as electrode materials for supercapacitors. Here, O, N, and P co-doped porous carbon 
sheets (ONPC) were developed by one-step activation way using sunflower straw as the carbon source,

ONPC-700 electrode exhibits a specific capacitance of 340 F g

� 1

zation with the capacitance retention rate of 100.5% after 10,000 cycles. More interestingly, the assembled 
symmetric supercapacitor (ONPC-700//ONPC-700) achieves an energy density of 22.0 Wh Kg

and superior 
electrochemical stabilization. The above excellent results indicate that this paper offers a feasible and simple 
strategy for preparing biomass-based heteroatom doped porous carbon sheets for supercapacitors.   
1. Introduction 
Supercapacitors with super high power density, speedy charge- 
discharge rate, and exceptional operation life have emerged widely 
concerned in recent years [1 – 5] . According to the energy storage 
mechanisms, supercapacitors can be classified into pseudocapacitors 
and electric double layer capacitors. Compared with pseudocapacitors, 
electric double-layer capacitors exhibit higher cycle life and better rate 
performance. Activated carbon is the preferred electrode material for 
the commercialization of supercapacitors because of its big specific 
surface area, cheap cost, and good electrochemical stabilization [6 – 9] . 
Nevertheless, activated carbon is usually mainly composed of micro -
pores, which faces long ion migration distance, high ion migration 
resistance, and poor conductivity [10 – 12] . As a result, the electro -
chemical performance of activated carbon is not satisfactory. 
Two-dimensional (2D) porous carbon sheets have attracted massive 
attention as electrode material for supercapacitors due to their great 
open smooth layer with big specific surface area, low ion migration 
distance, and short ion migration resistance [13 – 16] . Template syn -
thesis is an available method to produce 2D porous carbon sheets. For 
example, Wei et al. [17] prepared multi-mesoporous carbon nanosheets 
using Mg(OH)
2 
as the template and hydroxyquinoline-zinc complex as 
the carbon source. The synthesized carbon nanosheets exhibit a specific 
capacitance of 220 F g
� 1 
at 1 A g
� 1
. Although some results have been 
obtained, the template method requires synthesis and removal of tem -
plates, and the preparation process is tedious, time-consuming, and 
resource-consuming. 
Recently, the preparation of two-dimensional porous carbon sheets 
from biomass shows prominent development prospects due to its simple 
technology, cheap cost, and good electrochemical performance [18 – 21] . 
Wang et al. [22] developed porous carbon sheets (PCs) by carbonization 
treatment of corn straw, NaCl, and KCl in air atmosphere. The synthe -
sized PCs deliver a specific capacitance of 407 F g
� 1 
at 1 A g
� 1
. Du et al. 
[23] synthesized nitrogen-rich porous carbon sheets (N-PC) by acti -
vating carrots with Na
2
SiO
3
. The obtained materials deliver a specific 
capacitance of 268 F g
� 1 
at 1 A g
� 1
. In addition, doping heteroatoms can 
not only increase the electron transfer ability and provide additional 
pseudocapacitance, but also construct functional groups on the exterior 
of carbon materials to enhance the wettability [24 – 26] . On the other 
hand, since some heteroatoms can enter the carbon materials in a special 
configuration, the active sites are increased, which provides the possi -

Sunflower is widely planted in the world, and its straw has become 
the main waste and incineration object of farmland, which causes 
environmental pollution and waste of resources. Transforming biolog -
ical waste sunflower straw into high performance electrode materials for 
supercapacitors can not only effectively alleviate environmental prob -
lems, but also become a treasure to achieve efficient utilization of re -
sources. In this paper, O, N, and P co-doped porous carbon sheets were 
prepared by a one-step activation method using sunflower straw as the 
carbon source, NH

capacitance of 340 F g

symmetric supercapacitor delivers an energy density of 22.0 Wh Kg

N, P co-doped cellulose-based carbon aerogel: A dual-functional porous 
material for CO
2 
capture and supercapacitor
Jian Yu
a
, Jianfei Xiao
a
, Yuan Wang
a
, Tian C. Zhang
b
, Ji Li
a
, Ge He
a , *
, Shaojun Yuan
a , *
a
Low-carbon Technology & Chemical Reaction Engineering Lab, College of Chemical Engineering, Sichuan University, Chengdu 610065, China
b
Civil and Environmental Engineering Department, University of Nebraska-Lincoln, Omaha, NE 68182-0178, USA
ARTICLE INFO
Editor: Luo Guangsheng
Keywords:
Cellulose
Carbon aerogel
N, P co-doped
CO
2 
capture
Supercapacitor
ABSTRACT
Biomass-derived carbon aerogels have attracted considerable attention for applications in CO
2 
capture and 
supercapacitors (SCs). However, these carbon aerogel materials often suffer from an insufficient number of active 
sites. In this study, a novel N, P co-doped porous carbon aerogel with a hierarchical structure was synthesized 
using cellulose biomass as the raw material, a NaOH/urea system as the solvent and activator, and urea and urea 
phosphate as heteroatom dopants. Owing to the synergistic effects of heteroatom co-doping and the hierarchical 
pore structure, the optimal sample, NPCA-600 – 0.5, exhibited a large specific surface area of 582.9 m
2
/g and a 
high pore volume of 0.187 cm
3
/g. It demonstrated a CO
2 
adsorption capacity of 2.89 mmol/g (25 
◦
C, 1 bar), 
along with high CO
2
/N
2 
selectivity and excellent recyclability, retaining 91 % efficiency after 10 cycles. As a SC 
electrode, NPCA-600 – 0.5 achieved a high specific capacitance of 238 F/g at 1 A/g, maintaining 80 % of its initial 
capacitance after 5000 cycles at 10 A/g. This work not only provides a promising adsorbent and electrode 
material for CO
2 
capture and supercapacitors, but also offers valuable insights for the design of advanced carbon- 
based materials.
1. Introduction
As the global population grows and industrialization expands, the 
demand for energy has led to the consumption of vast amounts of fossil 
fuels, resulting in significant greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions [1,2] . 
This situation has triggered a severe energy crisis and exacerbated the 
greenhouse effect. Carbon dioxide, in particular, stands out as the pri -
mary GHG (75 % of total GHG emissions) responsible for climate change 
and accelerated global warming [3,4] . In view of the above problems, 
the development of efficient CO
2 
capture technologies and energy 
storage devices emerges as a potent approach to alleviate the energy 
crisis and mitigate climate change [5,6] .
Based on the capture process principles, several CO
2 
capture 
methods, including chemical absorption [7] , membrane separation [8] , 
and gas – solid adsorption [9] , have undergone extensive research and 
application. Of these, gas – solid adsorption technology has emerged as a 
compelling option, thanks to its high absorption rate, convenient 
regeneration system, energy efficiency, and environmental friendliness 
[10] . Porous carbons are highly regarded as promising CO
2 
gas – solid 
adsorption materials. Their high chemical and thermal stability, exten -
sive specific surface area, adjustable pore structure make them a top 
choice [11] . Furthermore, carbon materials usually possess a layered 
porous structure alongside a substantial specific surface area. Micro -
pores and small mesopores can enhance the storage of charge ions. 
While meso-macro pores provide mass transfer channels to facilitate the 
transport of charge ions in solution [12,13] . This configuration facili -
tates the efficient transfer of ions and electrons, as well as the accu -
mulation of charge, thereby rendering them an excellent candidate for 
energy storage materials [14 – 16] .
In recent years, carbon aerogel-type porous carbon, with its three- 
dimensional structure, high surface area, high electrical conductivity 
and stable physicochemical properties, has been identified as an 
emerging class of functional materials for CO
2 
capture and super -
capacitors [17 – 19] . Zhai et al. [20] prepared the starch-based carbon 
aerogel. When used as an electrode material for supercapacitors, it 
showed excellent electrochemical properties, reaching a specific 
capacitance of 211.5 F/g at 0.5 A/g. Ji et al. [21] prepared a biochar- 
silicon hybrid aerogel using carbon nanotubes and silicon as raw ma -
terials. The hybrid aerogel exhibited good CO
2 
adsorption performance, 
with a CO
2 
adsorption capacity of 2.74 mmol/g at 25 
◦
C and 1 bar. 
Moreover, carbon aerogel-type adsorbents and electrode materials 
derived from renewable biomass sources like cellulose [22] , chitosan

segments.text:
[23] , lignin [12] , and starch [20] have gained increasing attention. 
Cellulose is a macromolecular polysaccharide consisting of glucose 
molecules, and it is widely present in the cell walls of green plants and 
algae [24,25] . As a highly favored renewable biomass material, cellulose 
boasts remarkable attributes such as biodegradability, non-toxicity, 
lightness, and ease of chemical modification [4] . These properties 
collectively render cellulose an appealing feedstock for the production 
of biomass-derived carbon aerogel materials.
However, carbon aerogels ’ limited surface active sites result in low 
CO
2 
absorption capacity or low specific capacitance when used as ad -
sorbents or electrodes [26,27] . Previous research has indeed demon -
strated that doping carbon surfaces with heteroatoms significantly 
boosts CO
2 
capture and electrochemical performance [5,6,14] . N doping 
is the most commonly employed method to improve CO
2 
adsorption and 
discharge capacity by enhancing surface alkalinity and forming pseudo- 
capacitance [13,28] . N doping mainly occurs in the carbon skeleton in 
the form of pyridine-N (N-6), pyrrole-N (N-5), oxide-N (N-X) and gra -
phene (N-Q) [29] . Unlike N atoms, P atoms have a larger radius than 
carbon atoms, which enables them to create vacancy defects and alter 
the electronic structure within the carbon framework. This modification 
enhances the interaction between the adsorbent and CO
2 
molecules and 
provides additional pseudocapacitance [30,31] . Different from single- 
atom doped, co-doped multiple heteroatoms may amplify charge 
transport through the synergistic action of multiple impurity atoms and 
produce more efficient reaction sites [10,32] . Hence, the modification of 
carbon aerogel materials by utilizing the synergistic effect of co-doped 
heteroatoms is an effective approach.
Accordingly, the objective of this study is to develop a novel N, P co- 
doped cellulose-based carbon aerogels for CO
2 
capture and super -
capacitors. Cellulose was selected as the biomass precursor, and the 
NaOH/urea system was used as the pore-forming agent and cellulose 
solvent with urea as the nitrogen source and urea phosphate as the 
phosphorus and nitrogen source. The effects of carbonation temperature 
and heteroatom doping on CO
2 
adsorption and supercapacitor perfor -
mance were systematically determined by adjusting the mass ratios of 
urea phosphate to cellulose and the activation temperature. In addition, 
CO
2 
adsorption thermodynamics and kinetics, as well as CO
2 
cyclic 
adsorption properties and selectivity were systematically evaluated. 
Results indicate that the prepared N, P co-doped porous carbon aerogel 
(NPCA) exhibits a hierarchical porous structure, abundant surface- 
active sites, a good CO
2 
adsorption ability, high selectivity, good 
regeneration, and good capacitance performance.
2. Experimental Section
2.1. Materials
Cellulose (average particle size of 50 μ m) was purchased from 
Aladdin Industrial Co. (Shanghai, China). NaOH, urea, hydrochloric acid 
(HCl), N-methyl-2-pyrrolidone (NMP), polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF), 
and acetylene black were obtained from Kelong Chem. Co. (Chengdu, 
China). Urea phosphate was bought from Shanghai Macklin Biochemical 
Co. (Shanghai, China). KOH was purchased from Changliao Chem. Co. 
(Chengdu, China). All reagents were utilized in their original state 
without any further purification.
2.2. Preparation of N, P co-doped carbon aerogels from cellulose
A solution of NaOH (2.50 g), urea (3.83 g) and water (27.0 g) were 
precooled and then cellulose powder (3.83 g) was added. The solution 
was stirred magnetically for 1 h until cellulose was completely dissolved. 
Subsequently, a urea phosphate aqueous solution (10 mL, 0.025 � 0.1 g/ 
mL) was added dropwise and stirred for another 1 h. The gel was then 
frozen at � 25 
◦
C for one day and dried in a freeze-dryer for 2 days to 
obtain a cellulose aerogel precursor.
In order to prepare NPCA, the aforementioned precursor was then 
transferred to a tube furnace and heated under N
2 
protection for 2 h at 
600 
◦
C with a ramp rate of 5 
◦
C/min. Subsequently, the materials were 
washed thoroughly with 1 M HCl and a large volume of DI water until 
the pH of the filtrate became neutral. Finally, the cellulose-derived 
carbon aerogels were dried overnight at 80 
◦
C. The final carbon aero -
gels were labeled as NPCA-T-n, where T represents the activation tem -
perature ( = 500, 550, 600, 650, and 700 
◦
C), and n represents the urea 
phosphate/cellulose mass ratio ( = 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1). For comparison, a 
control carbon aerogel, designated as NPCA-600 – 0 (urea phosphate =
0), was also prepared at 600 
◦
C using a similar synthetic procedure. 
Fig. 1 presents a schematic representation of the synthesis of carbon 
aerogel.
2.3. Characterization
The crystalline structure of the materials was analyzed using X-ray 
diffraction spectroscopy on a DX-2007 X (Haoyuan Instruments Co., 
Dandong, China) with Cu-Ka radiation (k = 1.5418 Å) at room tem -
perature and 2 θ ranging from 10
◦
to 80
◦
. Raman spectra were measured 
with DXR Raman spectroscopy (Thermo-Fisher Scientific Inc. Waltham, 
MA, USA) to assess the degree of graphitization and surface defect with 
455 nm laser excitation at the range from 2200 to 800 cm
� 1
. Fourier 
transform infrared spectroscopy (FT-IR) spectra were characterized on a 
Spectrum Two infrared spectrometer (PerkinElmer Inc. Waltham, MA, 
USA) to identify surface functional groups. X-ray photoelectron spec -
troscopy (XPS) spectra were recorded with Axis Ultra DLD Kratos AXIS 
SUPRA Xray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS, Kratos Analytical Ltd, 
Wharfside, Manchester, UK) to ascertain the surface elemental compo -
sition and molecular structure of the samples. The pore structure of the 
materials was analyzed through the N
2 
adsorption – desorption test at 77 
K, using a specific area surface and pore size analyzer (ASAP 2460, 
Micromeritics, USA). The Brunner-Emmet-Teller (BET) and the density 
functional theory (DFT) model were employed to calculate the specific 
surface areas and the pore size distribution, respectively. Scanning 
Electron Microscopy (SEM) (JSM-7610F using 15 kV accelerating 
voltage) was used to study the morphology of the materials. Thermog -
ravimetric analysis (TGA) was conducted on a simultaneous thermal 
analyzer (NETZSCH STA 449 F3 Jupiter ® , NETZSCH Group, Deutsch -
land, Germany) to analyze the thermal stability of the as-prepared car -
bon aerosol samples.
2.4. Electrochemical measurements
These were firstly conducted in a three-electrode system, employing 
a modified Ni foam as the working electrode, Ag/AgCl, and Pt as the 
reference electrode and the counter electrode, respectively. The elec -
trode preparation process involved the incorporation of 80 % carbon 
aerogel, 10 % acetylene black as the conductive support, and 10 % 
polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) into an N-methyl pyrrolidone (NMP) 
solution under ultrasonic dispersion, thus producing a homogeneous 
ink. The resulting ink was then applied in a dropwise deposition manner 
onto the nickel foam in an area of 1 cm
2
. The modified Ni foam was then 
subjected to a drying process overnight in a vacuum oven at 60 
◦
C. The 
mass loading of the active materials in each electrode was set at 1.2 – 1.6 
mg. Cyclic voltammograms (CV) were obtained from different scanning 
rates (10 � 200 mV/s), while galvanostatic charge – discharge (GCD) 
tests were carried out at a current density between 1 and 20 A/g. 
Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) was conducted within a 
frequency range of 0.01 to 100 kHz, with a potential window of 5 mV. 
All the aforementioned measurements were conducted in 6 M KOH 
electrolyte solution using the CHI660E instrument (Shanghai, China). 
The specific capacitance (C) was calculated based on the discharge time,

3.1. Characterization of the materials
The surface functional groups of the NPCA-T-n samples were 
analyzed using FT-IR spectroscopy ( Fig. 2 ). The results indicated similar 
stretching vibrational peaks across all samples, except for NPCA-600 – 0. 
As illustrated in Fig. 2 a and 2b, the introduction of urea phosphate led to 
the emergence of a distinct peak at 1060 cm

broad peak centered around 3427 cm

hydroxyl groups [34] . Peaks at 2920 and 1255 cm

� 1 
repre -
sents the C = C/N – H bond [29,33] . These findings demonstrate suc -
cessful doping of N and P atoms into the prepared carbon aerogels.
In order to access the thermal stability of the prepared carbon aer -
ogels, the NPCA-600 – 0 and NPCA-600 – 0.5 samples were characterized 
by TGA. As illustrated in Fig. S1 , the two samples exhibit comparable 
thermogravimetric curves, and the weight loss rates of both are almost 
the same, indicating that the addition of urea phosphate has minimal 
impact on the thermal stability of the carbon aerogels. In addition, the

3.2. CO
2 
adsorption performance
An ideal adsorbent should exhibit several key characteristics: low 
cost, high CO
2 
adsorption capacity, excellent selectivity, reduced 
regeneration energy, and remarkable stability throughout numerous 
adsorption and desorption cycles [9] . To assess these attributes in the 
prepared carbon aerogels, an intelligent gravimetric adsorption analyzer 
was employed to measure CO
2 
adsorption in all samples under stan -
dardized conditions of 25 
◦
C and 1 bar. Fig. 6 a illustrates how the 
adsorption performance of materials varies with different urea phos -
phate ratios. Initially, as the urea phosphate ratio increases from 0 to 
0.5, the CO
2 
adsorption capacity of the materials rises. However, further 
increasing the urea phosphate content leads to a decrease in perfor -
mance. Similarly, Fig. 6 b reveals that CO
2 
adsorption follows the same 
trend with an increase in activation temperature. As shown in Table S3 , 
the sample NPCA-600 – 0.5 achieves the best CO
2 
adsorption perfor -
mance of 2.89 mmol/g, which is notably higher (25.6 %) than that of the 
control (NPCA-600 – 0, 2.3 mmol/g), primarily attributable to the 
beneficial effects of moderate phosphorus doping that enhances the 
porosity of the carbon material [29] . Furthermore, BET data reveals that 
NPCA-700 – 0.5 possesses the largest specific surface area, yet its CO
2 
adsorption performance is inferior to NPCA-600 – 0.5. This indicates that 
the relative content of heteroatoms may be the dominant factor in the 
CO
2 
adsorption of the materials. As shown in Table S2 , the content of N 
and P atoms in the materials decreased with increasing activation 
temperature, resulting in fewer active sites for CO
2 
adsorption. Addi -
tionally, the adsorption performance of the best samples was compared 
with currently reported porous carbon materials ( Table S6 ).
To further explore the adsorption mechanism of NPCA-600 – 0.5 for 
CO
2
, four isothermal adsorption models (Freundlich, Langmuir, Redlich- 
Peterson and Sips) were fitted to the experimental data of this optimal 
sample. The specific fitting equations are provided in the ESI (S 1.1), 
while the fitting results and related parameters are presented in Fig. 6 c 
and Table S4 . Previous research has demonstrated that the fitting 
parameter χ 
2 
serves as a metric for assessing the accuracy of the fit, with 
lower values indicating higher precision [44,45] . As observed in 
Table S4 , under identical conditions, the Freundlich model exhibits a 
lower χ
2 
value than that of the Langmuir model, suggesting that physical 
adsorption likely plays a dominant role in CO
2 
adsorption. Moreover, 
the Redlich-Peterson model yields the lowest χ
2 
value and the highest 
correlation coefficient R
2
; thus, this model is more in line with the 
adsorption characteristics of the material, indicating both physical and 
chemical adsorption occurring concurrently. Furthermore, Fig. 6 d 
shows that the adsorption capacities (in mmol CO
2
/g) of NPCA-600 – 0.5 
were 3.80 at 0 
◦
C, 3.40 at 10 
◦
C, and 2.89 at 25 
◦
C, suggesting that the 
adsorption process is exothermic.
As a crucial metric for evaluating the adsorption performance of a 
material, Q
st 
was calculated for NPCA-600 – 0.5 using the Clausius- 
Clapeyron equation ( ESI, S1.4 ) based on the adsorption data obtained 
at various temperatures. Fig. 6 e reveals that the slope derived from the 
fitting line corresponds to the ratio of the isothermal heat of adsorption 
(Q
st
) to the gas constant (R). Notably, all slopes are negative, unequiv -
ocally demonstrating that the adsorption of CO
2 
onto NPCA-600 – 0.5 is 
an exothermic process. The values of Q
st 
range from 24.8 to 32.1 KJ/mol 
( Fig. 6 f), suggesting that the adsorption process is primarily 
physisorption-dominated. The initially higher Q
st 
value signifies a strong 
interaction between the adsorbent and CO
2 
molecules [28,46] . How -
ever, as the adsorption amount gradually increases, the value of Q
st 
decreases, primarily attributed to the occupation of strong active sites by 
the adsorbed molecules [26] . Based on the aforementioned results, it is 
evident that the heat of adsorption for NPCA-600 – 0.5 is relatively low, 
signifying that the adsorption and regeneration processes of this mate -
rial are more readily achievable with low energy consumption. The 
favorable characteristic renders it a promising candidate for practical 
production applications.
The adsorption rate of CO
2 
molecules on the surface of NPCA- 
600 – 0.5 was assessed through kinetic experiments conducted at 25 
◦
C 
and 1 bar, as depicted in the respective Fig. 6 g. Notably, NPCA-600 – 0.5 
achieved maximum adsorption within 10 min, signifying its rapid CO
2 
adsorption kinetics. To further analyze the correlation between CO
2 
adsorption capacity and adsorption time, two kinetic models, Fick 
diffusion and Linear Driving Force (LDF) diffusion, were applied to fit 
the kinetic data. The detailed descriptions and formulas for these models 
are provided in the ESI (S 1.3). The fitted curves and corresponding 
parameters are presented in Fig. 6 g and Table S5 . Notably, the LDF 
model exhibited a relatively small χ
2 
value, indicating that the kinetic 
behavior of NPCA-600 – 0.5 aligns more closely with the LDF model. This 
also reflects that the overall adsorption process of NPCA-600 – 0.5 is 
primarily governed by the CO
2 
transfer rate [30] . The dynamic 
adsorption capacity of NPCA-600 – 0.5 was evaluated by adjusting the 
flowmeter ’ s flow rate to simulate dynamic pressure changes, thereby 
measuring the variation in CO
2 
adsorption over time. As depicted in 
Fig. 6 h, the CO
2 
adsorption by NPCA-600 – 0.5 increased in tandem with 
rising pressure, highlighting its excellent dynamic adsorption capacity 
for CO
2
. Notably, the dynamic cumulative adsorption amount of NPCA- 
600 – 0.5 closely approximates the static adsorption amount under 
identical temperature and pressure conditions.
The selectivity of the adsorbent for CO
2
/N
2 
is also a crucial criterion 
for evaluating its adsorption performance. The isothermal adsorption 
lines of CO
2 
and N
2 
single-component gases were measured under 
identical conditions (25 
◦
C, 1 bar) and fitted to the CO
2 
and N
2 
adsorption data using the Redlich-Peterson model and the Freundlich 
model, respectively. As illustrated in Fig. 6 i, the saturated adsorption of 
nitrogen was 0.25 mmol/g, which was considerably lower than the 
saturated adsorption of CO
2 
of 2.89 mmol/g. The initial slopes (Henry ’ s 
law) of the CO
2 
and N
2 
adsorption isotherms were utilized to calculate 
the CO
2
/N
2 
selectivity of 9.7 for NPCA-600 – 0.5 [47] , indicating NPCA- 
600 – 0.5 is favorable for CO
2 
adsorption. To further assess the practical 
usability of the NPCA-600 – 0.5 sample, dynamic breakthrough experi -
ments were conducted using a standard flue gas mixture with a CO
2 
to 
N
2 
volume ratio of 10:90 [46] , maintained at a gas pressure of 1 bar, and 
a continuous gas flow. As evident in the Fig. 6 j, N
2 
saturated and began 
to permeate after approximately 1 min, while CO
2 
gradually saturated 
and permeated after roughly 4 min. This difference in breakthrough 
time between CO
2 
and N
2 
demonstrates that NPCA-600 – 0.5 exhibits 
good CO
2
/N
2 
separation performance. Calculations based on the 
breakthrough curve revealed that the dynamic adsorption capacity of 
NPCA-600 – 0.5 is 0.982 mmol/g, closely resembling the static CO
2 
capture capacity observed during isothermal adsorption under the same 
partial pressure (1.01 mmol/g, 0.15 bar).
Fig. 6 k shows that NPCA-600 – 0.5 after 10 cycles of adsorption and 
desorption experiments still maintains a capacity retention rate of 91 %, 
signifying its excellent reusability. Additionally, isothermal desorption 
experiments on NPCA-600 – 0.5 revealed that as desorption progressed,

600 – 0.5 exhibits the largest CV curve area, indicating superior capaci -

density of 1 A/g, the GCD curve of NPCA-600 – 0.5 displays nearly perfect 
triangular symmetry, suggesting that its charge storage primarily relies 
on ion adsorption. The minimal voltage drop further indicates a low 
equivalent series resistance [18] . The longest discharge time observed 
for NPCA-600 – 0.5 confirms its highest specific capacitance, aligning 
with the findings from the CV curve. The specific capacitances of all 
materials ( Table S3 ) show that NPCA-600 – 0.5 stands out with the 
highest specific capacitance of 238 F/g, significantly surpassing the 194 
F/g recorded for NPCA-600 – 0, the sample without the addition of urea 
phosphate. The superior electrochemical performance of NPCA-600 – 0.5 
is likely due to the increased heteroatom content, specifically N-5 and N- 
6 configurations, introduced by the urea phosphate addition. This in -
crease in heteroatom forms enhances the redox reaction and subse -
quently boosts the pseudocapacitive activity of the electrode. A 
comparative performance analysis of NPCA-600 – 0.5 sample against the 
previously reported porous carbon materials, as outlined in Table S7 , 
reveals that it outperforms most of them, demonstrating its excellent 
potential as a supercapacitor electrode material.
The electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) analysis of the 
NPCAs electrodes provides insights into their resistance and ion trans -
port characteristics. In the low frequency region, the electrodes exhibit 
nearly vertical lines, suggesting excellent capacitive performance and 
ion diffusion efficiency. In the high frequency region, the intercept of the 
EIS curves on the real axis corresponds to the equivalent series resis -
tance, while the semicircle width reflects the charge transfer resistance 
of the material. Notably, all samples exhibited smaller intercepts and 
narrower semicircles, indicating a lower impedance for the NPCAs 
electrodes [14] ( Fig. 7 c and S 3a). The CV curves of NPCA-600 – 0.5 were 
evaluated at varying scan rates ranging from 10 to 200 mV/s within a 
voltage window of � 1 to 0 V ( Fig. 7 d). As the scan rate increased, the CV 
curves maintained a rectangular shape with minimal distortion, indi -
cating NPCA-600 – 0.5 ’ s swift ion transport capability [12,48] . Similarly, 
when the CV curves of the other samples were tested at different sweep 
speeds ( Fig. S4 ), they exhibited comparable shapes, indicating the 
presence of double-layer capacitance in all samples. The GCD curves of 
NPCA-600 – 0.5 and the remaining samples, at various current densities, 
are depicted in Fig. 7 e and Fig. S5 . All samples exhibited approximately 
symmetrical triangular shapes, demonstrating a typical double-layer 
capacitive behavior and remarkable Coulombic efficiency. The specific 
capacitance of NPCA ’ s electrodes at different current densities is shown 
in Fig. 7 f and S 3b. It is evident that NPCA-600 – 0.5 displays excellent 
rate capability, maintaining a specific capacitance of 122 F/g even at a 
high current density of 20 A/g.

600 – 0.5, when used as a supercapacitor electrode material, is primarily

NPCA-600 – 0.5 as an electrode material, cycling tests were conducted at 
a current density of 10 A/g. After enduring 5000 charge/discharge cy -
cles, NPCA-600 – 0.5 retained approximately 80 % of its initial capacity 
( Fig. 7 i), demonstrating its excellent cycling stability.
The practical potential of NPCA-600 – 0.5 was investigated by fabri -
cating a two-electrode symmetric electrochemical cell using two iden -
tical NPCA-600 – 0.5 electrodes in a 6 M KOH aqueous electrolyte. Fig. 8 a 
presents the CV curves of the NPCA-600 – 0.5//NPCA-600 – 0.5 cell at a 
scan rate of 40 mV/s for various voltage ranges. At a voltage window of 
1.2 V, the CV curve exhibits polarization, and upon increasing the 
voltage to 1.4 V, significant polarization occurs due to oxygen evolution. 
Therefore, an optimal voltage window of 0 � 1 V was determined. 
Within this voltage window, the GCD curves maintain symmetrical 
triangular shapes across varying current densities from 0.1 to 8 A/g 
( Fig. 8 b), indicating good electrochemical reversibility and rapid ion 
transport in the NPCA-600 – 0.5 electrode. Fig. 8 c shows that the CV 
curve remains largely undistorted as the scan rate increases from 10 to 
200 mV/s, demonstrating the NPCA-600 – 0.5 electrode material ’ s 
excellent capacitive response. The power density and energy density of 
the NPCA-600 – 0.5 sample were calculated and plotted on a Ragone 
chart ( Fig. 8 d). At a power density of 50 W/kg, the NPCA-600 – 0.5 cell 
exhibits a high energy density of 6.5 Wh/kg, outperforming several 
symmetric supercapacitors made from carbon materials previously re -
ported in the literature [50 – 54] . These tests highlight the promising 
potential of NPCA-600 – 0.5 for high-performance supercapacitor 
applications.
4. Conclusion
This study successfully demonstrated the preparation of N, P co- 
doped porous carbon aerogels from cellulose using a simple carboniza -
tion method with a NaOH/urea system. The optimized NPCA-600 – 0.5 
sample exhibited a notably large specific surface area (582.9 m
2
/g) and 
microporous volume (0.187 cm
3
/g), along with appropriate N (9.78 %) 
and P (0.14 %) doping levels. As a CO

600 – 0.5 exhibited a high specific capacitance (238 F/g at 1 A/g) and 
remarkable cycling stability. Notably, in a two-electrode symmetric 
device configuration, the NPCA-600 – 0.5 electrode achieved an energy 
density of 6.5 Wh/kg at a power density of 50 W/kg. This exceptional 
performance could be mainly attributed to synergistic effects of its hi -
erarchical porous structure and N, P co-doping. This study not only 
validates the dual-functional potential of N, P co-doped carbon aerogels 
as CO

valuable insights into the design of porous carbon materials.

Ni(OH)
2 
composite coffee grounds-derived biomass carbon for 
supercapacitor electrode materials
Yu-Cheng Chang
*
, Pei-Lin Fu , Shao-Ru Chang
Department of Materials Science and Engineering, Feng Chia University, Taichung, 40724, Taiwan
ARTICLE INFO
Keywords:
Supercapacitor
Coffee grounds
Biomass carbon
Ni(OH)
2
Microwave-assisted hydrothermal
ABSTRACT
This research investigated the electrochemical properties and cycling stability of coffee grounds-derived biomass 
carbon (CGBC) and Ni(OH)
2
-CGBC composite materials as supercapacitor electrodes. These materials were 
produced by transforming coffee grounds into biomass carbon through thermal annealing and then growing Ni 
(OH)
2 
nanosheets onto the CGBC using a microwave-assisted hydrothermal method. Optimal properties were 
achieved with 10 mM Ni(OH)
2 
precursors for enhancing electrochemical performance. Various analyses, 
including FESEM, XRD, FETEM, and XPS, confirmed the uniform incorporation and beneficial properties of Ni 
(OH)
2
-CGBC composite materials. Electrochemical tests under the 1 M KOH solution revealed significant im -
provements in specific capacitance and coulombic efficiency, maintaining good reversibility across different 
current densities. After 1000 charge-discharge cycles at 1 A/g, the capacitance retention rates were 64.8 % 
(CGBC) and 55.9 % (Ni(OH)
2
-CGBC), with stable coulombic efficiencies of 97.5 % and 96.8 %, respectively. 
These results suggest that Ni(OH)
2
-CGBC composite materials hold significant promise for long-term super -
capacitor applications.
1. Introduction
The finite resources of fossil fuels, continuous population growth, 
and technological advancements pose energy shortage challenges for 
humanity [ 1 , 2 ]. Therefore, renewable energy development has become 
the current energy trend [ 3 , 4 ]. However, the regional limitations of 
renewable energy and the issue of power storage present significant 
challenges in their application [ 5 ]. Hence, until a breakthrough in power 
generation technology occurs, energy storage devices play a critical role 
[ 6 ]. Supercapacitors combine the rapid charging and discharging ca -
pabilities of capacitors with the high energy storage capacity of batte -
ries. This allows them to deliver quick energy bursts and store significant 
power, making them suitable for various applications, from consumer 
electronics to industrial equipment. Their capacity to endure frequent 
charge cycles without considerable degradation makes them highly 
efficient and reliable in demanding situations [ 7 , 8 ]. It integrates the fast 
charge and discharge capabilities found in capacitors with the robust 
energy storage capacity of batteries, offering a unique solution that 
harnesses both technologies ’ strengths to deliver both rapid energy 
bursts and long-term power storage [ 9 , 10 ]. Supercapacitors offer several 
benefits compared to traditional options, including higher power 
density, fast charge and discharge rates, extended lifespan, excellent 
cycle stability, and low sensitivity to temperature changes [ 11 ]. These 
advantages make their application range extremely wide, encompassing 
energy supply, vehicle transportation, mobile communications, artificial 
intelligence, biosensing, medical equipment, and wearable devices 
[ 12 – 14 ].
Biomass carbon, a carbon-rich material similar to charcoal, is pro -
duced by thermally decomposing biological waste (such as food and 
agricultural residues) in a limited oxygen environment [ 15 – 19 ]. Owing 
to its physicochemical properties, including a large surface area, sig -
nificant pore volume, and unique functional groups, it holds great 
promise as an exceptional alternative to activated carbon for use as an 
adsorbent [ 20 – 24 ]. The effectiveness of biomass carbon production is 
determined by various carbonization and activation factors, such as the 
type of biomass, temperature, duration, and choice of activating agent 
[ 21 , 25 ]. The largest quantities of biomass, which are abundant and 
renewable globally, typically come from agricultural waste, forest resi -
dues, wood processing by-products, and energy crops [ 26 , 27 ].
Coffee is the second largest agricultural product after tea, making 
coffee grounds a noteworthy subject of study in food waste [ 28 – 30 ]. 
However, the electric double-layer capacitance provided by carbon
