meet the higher storage capacity required by current technology [ 31 ,
32 ]. Studies have demonstrated that transition metal compounds, which 
possess pseudocapacitive properties, can be effectively integrated into 
porous carbon, significantly boosting the electrochemical properties of 
electrode materials. This enhancement is attributed to the multiple 
reversible oxidation states of transition metals [ 33 – 36 ]. Among them, 
nickel is a widely used transition metal for creating supercapacitor 
cathode materials [ 37 ]. Due to its abundant availability on Earth, nickel 
has garnered significant attention in development and utilization, 
making it a crucial transition metal element [ 38 , 39 ]. Nickel-based 
transition metal compounds exist in several forms, including the 
well-known nickel oxide (NiO), nickel hydroxide (Ni(OH)
2
), and nickel 
sulfide [ 40 , 41 ]. NiO, with its cubic crystal structure, is a typical tran -
sition metal oxide whose oxygen content changes lattice constants, 
making it suitable as a p-type semiconductor [ 41 ]. Ni(OH)
2
, known for 
its high theoretical capacitance and stable electrochemical behavior due 
to its intricate 3D structure, exhibits poor rate performance, limiting its 
research applications [ 42 , 43 ]. However, studies suggest that downsizing 
the structure of Ni(OH)
2 
to the nanoscale significantly shortens the ion 
diffusion path and expands the reaction interface between the electrode 
and electrolyte, thereby markedly improving its rate performance [ 44 ,
45 ]. Therefore, the effective combination of biomass carbon derived 
from coffee grounds and Ni(OH)
2 
enhances electrochemical perfor -
mance and promotes efficient waste utilization.
This study synthesized Ni(OH)
2
-CGBC composite materials from 
coffee grounds using thermal annealing and microwave-assisted hy -
drothermal methods. The optimal Ni(OH)
2 
precursor concentration (10 
mM) yielded a structure with enhanced electrochemical performance 
suitable for supercapacitor electrodes. Electrochemical tests demon -
strated the Ni(OH)
2
-CGBC composite material ’ s excellent stability, 
reversibility, and high coulombic efficiency, indicating potential for 
long-term supercapacitor applications.
2. Experimental
2.1. Fabrication of coffee grounds-derived biomass carbon (CGBC)
The material is transferred into a tube furnace after grinding the 
coffee grounds into a fine powder. Under a nitrogen atmosphere, the 
powder is subjected to high-temperature carbonization at 650 
◦
C for 2 h. 
Once the process is complete and the product has cooled, coffee ground- 
derived biomass carbon (CGBC) is obtained.
2.2. Fabrication of Ni(OH)
2
-CGBC composite
The 0.01 g prepared CGBC (coffee ground-derived biomass carbon) is 
added to 40 mL of deionized water containing various concentrations of 
Ni(OH)
2 
precursors (nickel nitrate: urea = 1: 2). After thorough stirring 
to ensure a uniform mixture, the solution is placed into a Teflon-lined 
autoclave and transferred to a microwave reactor. The reaction condi -
tions are set at a temperature of 150 
◦
C, involving a heating period of 20 
min and a subsequent holding period of 30 min. Following the micro -
wave reaction, the resulting product is extracted through centrifugation, 
thoroughly washed, and dried. This meticulous process produces the Ni 
(OH)
2
-CGBC materials specifically tailored for electrode applications.
2.3. Electrochemical experiment
The synthesized Ni(OH)
2
-CGBC composite materials are blended 
with carbon black and polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) in a ratio of 8:1:1 
[ 46 ]. An appropriate 1-methyl-2-pyrrolidone (NMP) is added to create 
an electrode slurry. After ultrasonic treatment for 30 min, 75 μ L of the 
slurry is deposited onto a nickel foam that has been cleaned with 
acetone, ethanol, hydrochloric acid, and deionized water. The coated 
nickel foam is then placed in an oven and dried overnight at 50 
◦
C. 
Electrochemical testing is conducted using a Zahner Zennium electro -
chemical workstation. In this setup, each electrode is analyzed within a 
three-electrode electrochemical system: the sample is attached to the 
working electrode, a saturated calomel electrode (SCE) acts as the 
reference electrode, and a platinum sheet functions as the counter 
electrode. Various concentrations of potassium hydroxide (KOH) serve 
as the electrolyte.
2.4. Characterization
The synthesized Ni(OH)
2
-CGBC composite materials underwent a 
thorough analysis of their morphology, crystal structure, and physical 
properties utilizing various advanced characterization techniques. Sur -
face morphology was examined using field emission scanning electron 
microscopy (FESEM, Hitachi S-4800), which provides detailed visuali -
zation of the material surface. Field-emission transmission electron 
microscopy (JEOL 2100F) was used to observe the microstructure, 
crystal structure, and composition in depth. The crystal structure was 
elucidated with X-ray diffraction (XRD, Bruker D2 Phaser system), 
which identified the material ’ s crystallographic phases. The composite ’ s 
elemental composition and chemical states were analyzed using X-ray 
photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS, PHI 5000 VersaProbe). Furthermore, 
the Brunauer-Emmett-Teller (BET) method (Micromeritics ASAP 2020) 
was employed to quantify the surface area and porosity, offering crucial 
insights into the material ’ s adsorption properties.
3. Results and discussion
Fig. 1 depicts the synthesis of Ni(OH)
2
-CGBC from coffee grounds 
using thermal annealing and microwave-assisted hydrothermal 
methods. This preparation process can be divided into two stages: (1) 
Direct conversion of coffee grounds into biomass carbon through ther -
mal annealing. (2) Fabrication of Ni(OH)
2 
nanosheets onto the CGBC 
using microwave-assisted hydrothermal. First, coffee grounds are con -
verted into biomass carbon using a simple thermal annealing method 
under a reaction temperature of 650 
◦
C for 2 h. Second, Ni(OH)
2 
nanosheets are fabricated on the CGBC via a microwave-assisted hy -
drothermal method at 150 
◦
C for 30 min under the different concen -
trations of Ni(OH)
2 
precursors (nickel nitrate: urea = 1: 2).
FESEM analysis was performed to investigate the changes in surface 
morphology. Fig. 2 a and b depict the differences in surface morphology 
before and after carbonization. It can be observed that the surface 
changes from smooth and flat to rough, which increases the material ’ s 
surface area and the number of active sites. The FESEM analysis after 
incorporating Ni(OH)
2 
nanosheets under the different concentrations of 
Ni(OH)
2 
precursors is shown in Fig. 2 c – f. The surface morphology of Ni 
(OH)
2 
materials appears as stacked nanosheets. The Ni(OH)
2 
precursor 
concentrations significantly influence their structures. At a concentra -
tion of 5 mM Ni(OH)
2 
precursors ( Fig. 2 c), the nanosheet structure is 
very dense, which can hinder the penetration of the electrolyte and 
negatively impact electrochemical performance. The nanosheets 
become larger and less densely packed when the concentration is 
increased to 10 mM ( Fig. 2 d). However, at a concentration of 20 mM Ni 
(OH)
2 
precursors ( Fig. 2 e), the nanosheets grow excessively large and 
stack together, reducing the specific surface area and active sites, 
thereby diminishing electrochemical performance. At 30 mM Ni(OH)
2 
precursors ( Fig. 2 f), the nanosheets are large and begin to grow densely 
again. These observations indicate that the microwave-assisted hydro -
thermal synthesis of Ni(OH)
2 
on CGBC with a Ni(OH)
2 
precursor con -
centration of 10 mM produces a surface structure that closely matches 
the ideal properties of a supercapacitor electrode active material. This 
optimized structure may effectively enhance the electrochemical per -
formance of the active material.
The crystal structure of the synthesized materials was analyzed using 
X-ray diffraction (XRD). As shown in Fig. 3 a, the CGBC exhibits a 
noticeable broad peak around 2 θ values of 23

and 43

current density increases from 1 A/g to 5 A/g. The coulombic efficiency 
at these different current densities is 94.1 %, 92.8 %, 96.8 %, 97.6 %, 
and 97.3 %, respectively, demonstrating excellent coulombic efficiency. 
These results confirm that the Ni(OH)
2
-CGBC composite materials 
exhibit good electrochemical reversibility.
To elucidate the charge storage mechanism of the optimized Ni 
(OH)
2
-CGBC composite (10 mM Ni(OH)
2 
precursors) materials, a kinetic 
analysis was conducted based on its CV data. A strong linear relationship 
(R
2 
= 0.99) between the peak current (i
p
) and the square root of the scan 
rate ( ν
1/2
), shown in Fig. 10 a, initially suggested a process dominated by 
diffusion. This was confirmed by applying the power law, where the 
plots of log(i
p
) versus log( ν ) in Fig. 10 b yielded b-values of 0.56 and 
0.52. As these values are close to 0.5, they affirm that the energy storage 
is primarily a diffusion-controlled, battery-like mechanism [ 73 ]. To 
quantitatively separate the capacitive (k
1
ν ) and diffusion-controlled 
(k
2
ν
1/2
) contributions using the equation i(V) = k
1
ν + k
2
ν
1/2
, it was 
found that the diffusion process accounts for 95.3 % of the charge 
storage at 5 mV/s, as depicted in Fig. 10 c and d. This contribution de -
creases to 81.9 % as the scan rate increases to 100 mV/s, which is 
attributed to the insufficient time available for ion diffusion into the 
electrode bulk at higher rates, thereby making faster surface-capacitive 
processes more prominent [ 74 ].
To evaluate the cycle stability of the CGBC and Ni(OH)
2
-CGBC 
composite (10 mM Ni(OH)
2 
precursors) materials prepared as electrode 
materials for supercapacitors, a 1000-cycle charge-discharge test was 
conducted. As depicted in Fig. 11 , CGBC and Ni(OH)
2

materials gradually decrease specific capacitance during cycling at a 
current density of 1 A/g. This decline is primarily due to the redox 
processes involved in the charge-discharge cycles, which result in more 
pronounced material degradation over time. After 1000 cycles, the 
capacitance retention rates are 64.8 % (CGBC) and 55.9 % for Ni(OH)
2
- 
CGBC composite materials. Despite the significant impact on the energy 
storage performance of the electrode materials after prolonged cycling, 
the coulombic efficiency remains stable and even improves slightly. 
After 1000 cycles, the coulombic efficiency is 97.5 % (CGBC) and 96.8 % 
for Ni(OH)
2
-CGBC composite materials. This outcome illustrates that 
CGBC and Ni(OH)
2
-CGBC composite materials maintain good electro -
chemical reversibility even after extensive charge-discharge cycling, 
highlighting their potential for long-term applications in 
supercapacitors.

4. Conclusions
This study extensively evaluated the electrochemical performance 
and cycle stability of CGBC and Ni(OH)
2
-CGBC composite materials as 
supercapacitor electrodes. These syntheses converted coffee grounds 
into biomass carbon through thermal annealing and subsequently grew 
Ni(OH)
2 
nanosheets on CGBC using a microwave-assisted hydrothermal 
method. The optimal structure achieved with 10 mM Ni(OH)
2 
pre -
cursors demonstrated ideal properties for superior electrochemical 
performance. Several analyses, such as FESEM, XRD, FETEM, and XPS, 
verified the consistent integration and advantageous characteristics of 
Ni(OH)
2
-CGBC composite materials. Electrochemical tests under a 1 M 
KOH solution revealed enhanced performance and stability of the 
composite materials. The CV and GCD analyses indicated that incorpo -
rating Ni(OH)
2 
nanosheets significantly improved specific capacitance 
and coulombic efficiency, maintaining good reversibility across 
different current densities. Specific capacitance values ranged from 
137.07 to 45.98 F/g for current densities of 1 – 5 A/g with a retention rate 
of 33.4 % and coulombic efficiencies between 92.8 % and 97.6 %. A 
charge-discharge test conducted over 1000 cycles at 1 A/g demonstrated 
a gradual reduction in specific capacitance due to redox processes, with 
retention rates of 64.8 % for CGBC and 55.9 % for Ni(OH)
2
-CGBC, 
respectively. In addition, coulombic efficiency remained stable or 
slightly improved, reaching 97.5 % (CGBC) and 96.8 % (Ni(OH)
2
-CGBC) 
after 1000 cycles. These results indicate excellent electrochemical 
reversibility and stability, suggesting Ni(OH)
2
-CGBC composite mate -
rials are promising for long-term supercapacitor applications.

Valorizing palm date wastes for 
supercapacitor electrode synthesis 
and evaluation
Amany Mostafa1, Sodky H. Mohammed2, Nouby M. Ghazaly1 & Ahmed ElSheikh 1
Climate and energy issues continue to drive researchers to develop fossil-free energy technologies that 
are both sustainable and scalable. In this work, date seeds (DS) are used to produce activated carbon 
(DSAC), which is then used as a supercapacitor electrode. The synthesis method uses KOH activation 
coupled with argon-gas flow calcination at 950 °C. The produced DSAC has a high specific surface area 
of 1374 m2/g and a turbostratic microporous structure (pore size = 1.14 nm), in addition to oxygen-
containing functional groups (–C–O–, –OH). The DSAC electrochemical performance exhibits an electric 
double-layer capacitor (EDLC) with a minor pseudocapacitive contribution and delivers a 3-electrode 
specific capacitance of 1800 F/g at 4 A/g (estimated full-device specific capacitance is 450 F/g, energy, 
and power densities: 40 Wh/kg and 1440 W/kg, respectively). These numbers are remarkably higher 
than the current state-of-the-art carbon supercapacitor findings. Furthermore, it retains 83.3% of its 
initial discharge capacity after 2000 galvanostatic charge-discharge cycles at 10 A/g. Finally, the DSAC 
electrode performance is slightly enhanced with increasing the KOH concentration from 1 M to 3 M.
Keywords Biomass, Activated carbon, Supercapacitor, KOH activation
The climate change and energy supply crises continue to call for accelerated research and development efforts 
of sustainable energy technologies1. This is particularly true in electric mobility, where supercapacitors and Li-
ion batteries play a vital role. Supercapacitors or electrochemical capacitors are electrochemical cells comprised 
of two electrodes, a separator, and an electrolyte. Their inherent merits, which occasionally enable them to 
outperform Li-ion batteries, include fast charging and discharging, high power density, and long cycle life 2. 
There are two main mechanisms for storing electrical charge in supercapacitors: electric double-layer capacitors 
(EDLCs) and pseudocapacitors. The former adopts the electrostatic adsorption and desorption of electrolyte 
ions at the electrode-electrolyte interface, forming the double-layer configuration. The latter is achieved via a 
reversible redox charge-transfer reaction at the electrode-electrolyte interface. Occasionally, both mechanisms 
occur simultaneously in a single material, combining the advantages of both 3. Furthermore, supercapacitors 
could be classified based on their materials into metal oxide, polymer, and carbon-based. Unlike oxide and 
polymer-based supercapacitors, carbon-based supercapacitors have demonstrated stable performance in 
addition to their cost-effectiveness4.
Biomass-based electrodes have garnered considerable attention due to their inherent properties, such 
as raw material abundance, high surface area, chemical stability, high specific surface area, low weight, and 
interconnected porous structure5. Wood residues, coconut shells, apricot pits, agricultural wastes, and marine 
algae are some of the examples of biomass precursors that have been extensively studied in the preparation of 
porous activated carbons with well-developed micro/mesoporous structure that can be used in supercapacitor 
applications6–11. The chemical activation process can be used to produce hierarchical porous carbons with a 
large surface area and tunable pore structure using these lignocellulosic resources. Recent research work has 
shown that carbons produced by biomass have the potential to provide promising electrochemical properties 
when optimized activation conditions are used and thus can serve as sustainable alternatives to standard carbon 
materials. As an example, it has been reported that porous carbons obtained using many natural precursors as 
hydrogen storage and energy-related materials have been investigated in the past, thus showing the success of the 
chemical activation strategies in the development of pore structure and surface chemistry12,13.
A palm date tree (Phoenix dactylifera) generates 40 kg of waste from leaves, surface fibres surrounding the 
trunk, and fruit-bearing seeds per year 14. Palm dates are a crucial food whose total production reached 9.66 
million metric tons in 2024, with the Middle East countries (especially Egypt) as the top producers due to ideal

climate conditions. Thus, its consumption generates tremendous amounts of biowastes that are better valorized 
for energy storage and adsorption applications. For instance, date seeds have been hydrothermally and chemically 
treated for supercapacitor applications 4. They have given a microporous structure with a maximum specific 
capacitance of 179 F/g at 5 mV/s and retained 94% of their capacitance after 5500 cycles of galvanic charge 
and discharge. In another work 3, date-seed supercapacitors were applied to optimize ionic liquid electrolytes: 
BMIMPF6, HMIMTFS, and BMIMOTf. The supercapacitor with BMIMOTf has produced remarkable energy 
and power densities of 129.9 Wh/kg and 403.8 W/kg, respectively. Furthermore, its specific capacitance was 
103.9 F/g at 0.5 A/g and maintained 97.3% of its capacity after 5000 cycles. The authors claim that combining 
date seed electrodes with BMIMOTf demonstrates a significant development of eco-friendly supercapacitors. 
They also found that a mild temperature increase (up to 50 °C) would boost the electrochemical performance by 
enhancing the ionic conductivity. In a third work1, date seeds were activated by sodium oxalate (Na2C2O4) and 
provided a high-surface-area activated carbon (up to 1630 m 2/for the sample with a 1:4 ratio of DS/Na 2C2O4). 
This sample has produced a specific capacitance of 112 F/g at 0.5 A/g. In another study regarding the date-
seed-derived activated carbon2, the authors have mixed seeds of olive and date seeds, and later added sugar to 
the binary system, to produce H 3PO4-activated carbons. The ternary date-olive-sugar sample has achieved the 
highest specific capacitance of 528 F/g at 0.3 A/g with power and energy densities of 107 W/kg and 37 Wh/kg.
Recent studies confirmed that date-seed activated carbon (DSAC) is a promising and viable electrode 
substance in supercapacitors since it combines cost-effectiveness, environmental compatibility, large surface 
area, and porosity control. In a study of this type, a DSAC was assembled with Ni-doped α-Bi₂O₃ to form a 
hybrid electrode; the carbon part of the electrode provided electronic conductivity, increased ion-accessible 
surface area, and strengthened charge transportation, and the Ni-doped oxide part of the electrode provided 
pseudocapacitive redox properties. Accordingly, the Ni-doped α-Bi₂O₃ /DSAC composite exhibited a specific 
capacitance of 174 F/g at 5 mV/s, which is better than the oxide on its own and supports the positive synergy of 
electric double layer capacitance and faradaic charge storage 15. In another work DSAC was confirmed to give 
a parallel trend to a Zn 2O3/AC composite; their activation has significantly increased the BET surface area of 
1.6779 to 114.17 m2/g, promoted a porous nanosheet-like structure, reduced the charge transfer resistance, and 
provided a high specific capacitance of 281 F/g at 5 mV/s 16. In a different related study, discarded dates were 
transformed into porous carbon aerogels by hydrothermal pretreatment, freeze-drying, and KOH activation, 
which offered a three-dimensional heteroatom-rich porous structure with a specific surface area of 1348.87⁻¹ m 
2 g− 1 , the optimized material had a high capacitance of 769 F/g at 0.5 A/g, highlighting the high energy-storage 
capability of porous DSAC17.
Although date-seed-derived carbons have been previously reported for supercapacitor applications 14,18–21, 
most studies focus primarily on demonstrating feasibility rather than systematically optimizing activation 
conditions and correlating pore structure with electrochemical performance. In this work, emphasis is placed 
on tailoring the activation strategy and elucidating the structure–performance relationship to achieve enhanced 
capacitive behavior.
Experimental
Chemicals and methods
The raw material is date seed (DS) waste from households in Qena, Egypt. The chemicals used in this synthesis 
are KOH, HCl, poly(vinylidene fluoride) (PVDF) as a binder, and dimethylformamide (DMF) as a solvent, in 
addition to argon and nitrogen gases. The devices are a D8 Advance XRD diffractometer (Bruker, Germany), 
a Confocal Raman Microscope (WiTec, 300R alpha, Germany), an ST2 on NOV A touch 4LX equipment (SN 
17016062702), an FEI Quanta 250, Thermo Fisher Scientific (Czech Republic), a ATR-FTIR Bruker Alpha IFS-
125, a JEM-2100 (Japan), and a Quartz Kejia Tube furnace. For the evaluation of electrochemical capacitors, an 
Origalys OFG + 500 potentiostat/galvanostat (France) was used.
Synthesis of date seed activated carbon (DSAC)
Figure 1 exhibits the synthetic procedure of activated carbon synthesis from date seeds. Household DSs were 
collected, washed with tap water, and dried. Then, they were carbonized at 350 °C for 4 h in a muffle furnace in 
an air atmosphere. The pre-carbonization was designed to remove volatiles, promote initial carbon framework 
formation, and introduce some oxygen functionalities. Following, DSs were manually ground using a zirconia 
planetary ball mill at 400 rpm for 2 h, followed by 30-minute hot sonication (50 °C) to dissolve the carbon in 
distilled water. Thereafter, they were chemically activated using KOH, since it is a versatile method to activate

diverse biomass feedstocks22. The KOH: DS weight ratio was kept to 2 :1 to optimize and critically balance the 
yield and porous structure. For example, increasing the KOH decreases the yield but increases the pore volume 
and mesoporosity23–25. The reaction continued for 24 h at room temperature. Following, the solid material was 
collected by centrifuge running at 6000 rpm for 12 min. It was subsequently dried at 90 °C overnight. Then, 
they were activated at 950 °C under argon flow for 1.5 h. Although it reduces the yield due to extensive burn 
off, the 950 °C was chosen to promote the development of graphitic carbon structures, which enhance electrical 
conductivity, a desirable property for supercapacitor applications. For example, increasing the temperature 
from 800 °C to 1000 °C enhances the graphitic order 25–27. The argon flow was 350 sccm. The temperature was 
increased from room temperature to 950 °C within 30 min, corresponding to a relatively rapid heating ramp. 
Such a heating profile can influence the activation pathway by affecting volatile release, KOH etching kinetics, 
pore widening, and carbon framework contraction. The activated carbon powder was rinsed with 0.1 M HCL to 
neutralize the KOH, followed by a cold water-ethanol mixture bath washing. Subsequently, it was dried at 90 °C 
for 24 h. The DSAC yield following this method is 41%.
Physiochemical characterization
X-ray diffraction (XRD) data of the samples were collected with a D8 Advance with Davinci design (Bruker, 
Germany), using an X-ray source the Cu Kα radiation (wavelength λ = 1.5418 Å), at 40 kV and 40 mA, a 2θ range 
of 20–80°, a step size of 0.02°, and a time/step of 0.6 s. A Si zero-background sample holder operated by Diffrac 
was used. Raman spectroscopy was applied to study the structure of the produced carbon. A confocal Raman 
spectrometer equipped with a laser source of 532 nm was utilized to collect the spectra. N2 adsorption/desorption 
measurements, at 77.35°K, utilizing the St 2 on NOV A touch 4LX equipment to analyze the Brunauer-Emmett-
Teller (BET) surface area and porosity, were performed. Field emission scanning electron microscopy (FE-
SEM) and energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX) were performed using FEI Quanta 250, Thermo Fisher 
Scientific. The ATR-FTIR measurement was carried out by Fourier transformation infrared spectrophotometer 
model Bruker Alpha IFS-125 in the wavenumber range 400–4000  cm − 1, scan time = 32, resolution = 4.High-
resolution transmission microscopy (HRTEM) was performed utilizing JEOL JEM-2100. The suspension of the 
material was sonicated for 10 min on an ultrasonicator (Crest Ultrasonics Corp., USA). Then, a few drops were 
loaded onto a carbon-coated copper grid and left to dry.

Results and discussions
Physiochemical characterization
The DSAC yield for the current work is 41%, close to other reported yields in28 , 29. However, it is slightly lower, 
likely due to the 350 °C air precarbonation. The XRD pattern (Fig. 2. A) shows a broad hump around ~ 23–26° 
(2θ) corresponding to the (002) plane of turbostratic/amorphous carbon and a weak, broad peak around 44° 
associated with the (100) and (101) planes of disordered graphite-like domains. The broad diffraction peak 
observed at ~ 23–26° (2θ), corresponding to the (002) plane, was used to estimate the interlayer spacing (002) via 
Bragg’s law, yielding values in the range of ~ 0.34–0.38 nm. This spacing is slightly larger than that of crystalline 
graphite (~ 0.335 nm), indicating a turbostratic and disordered carbon structure with expanded interlayer 
distance. These diffraction features are characteristic of poorly ordered graphitic carbon and are consistent with 
the standard ICDD Powder Diffraction File (PDF) card No. 41-1487 for graphitic carbon. Similar patterns were 
obtained with other DSAC samples3,14,30,31. The absence of any other minor sharp or broad peaks signals the clean 
carbon production. The high intensity at low diffraction angles (< 30°) does not reflect structural information but

may be attributed to air scattering or sample holder fluorescence contributions. Figure 2C and D demonstrate 
the Nitrogen isotherm and pore size distribution of DSAC, respectively. The N₂ adsorption–desorption isotherm 
exhibits a hybrid type I/IV behavior, characterized by a sharp uptake at low relative pressures (P/P₀ < 0.1), 
indicating microporosity, along with a hysteresis loop at intermediate pressures corresponding to mesopores. 
This confirms that the DSAC possesses a hierarchical micro–mesoporous structure with moderate adsorption 
volume (~ 450 cc/g). The BET surface area of DSAC is 1374 m2/g, which is close to that of some reported DSAC 
samples1 and significantly higher than others2,3,5. This indicates the 950 °C calcination did not harm the carbon 
porous structure, unlike26. The Raman spectrum (Fig. 2. B) shows prominent D (~ 1350 cm −1 ) and G (~ 1580 
cm−1 ) bands with ID/IG ≈ 0.98, indicating highly disordered, defect-rich turbostratic carbon with small graphitic 
domains. The weak 2D band confirms poor graphitization, consistent with porous biomass-derived activated 
carbon, which is suitable for electrochemical applications. Similar results are reported in 28,30,31. The EDX (Fig. 
2. E) shows the elemental composition of DSAC. Typically, biomass-derived carbons after KOH activation 
contain: C (dominant framework of the material, O (surface functionalities of OH, COOH, C = O), residual 
KOH reaction K, and minor inorganics (Si, Ca, Mg) from natural biomass ash. DSAC is constituted mainly 
from C (77.7 at%), O (19.8 at%), and K (1.89 at%). The detected K content (~ 1.89 at%) is attributed to residual 
potassium species remaining after KOH activation. Despite acid washing, trace potassium may remain trapped 
within micropores or bound to surface functional groups. The absence of crystalline K-containing phases in 
XRD indicates that potassium exists in a highly dispersed form rather than as a distinct phase. The DS dense 
precursor structure allows KOH etching but resists deep intercalation, resulting in a cleaner surface. Figure 2. 
F shows the Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) spectrum of DSAC. The FTIR spectrum of DSAC 
shows a broad band at ~ 3400 cm⁻¹ corresponding to O–H stretching, indicating hydroxyl groups and adsorbed 
moisture, while weak peaks at ~ 2920–2850 cm −1  arise from aliphatic C–H vibrations. The band near ~ 1600 
cm−1  reflects aromatic C = C and/or C = O groups, confirming partially graphitized carbon. Peaks in the ~ 
1200–1000 cm⁻¹ region are attributed to C–O stretching (phenols/ethers), evidencing oxygen-containing surface 
functionalities. Overall, the spectrum indicates a defect-rich, oxygen-functionalized carbon structure suitable 
for pseudocapacitive behavior. Although EDX and FTIR analyses confirm the presence of oxygen-containing 
functional groups, XPS analysis would provide more detailed information regarding their chemical states and 
relative abundance, which will be considered in future work.
To analyze the DSAC surface topography and morphology, SEM and HRTEM analyses were performed 
(Fig. 3). The SEM images show irregular, fractured carbon particles with rough, etched surfaces (Fig. 3. A). At 
low magnification, angular particles and interparticle voids indicate macroporosity that aids mass transport. At 
higher magnification (Fig. 3. B), a sponge-like surface with pits and cavities reveals mesopores and pore openings. 
Although micropores are not directly visible, their presence is implied by activation. Overall, the material exhibits 
a hierarchical pore structure (macro–meso–micro), suitable for adsorption and electrochemical applications. 
The average pore size (~ 1.14 nm) indicates dominant microporosity, which is favorable for charge storage due to 
the increased surface area and effective ion confinement. Notably, the pore size is well matched with the hydrated 
ion size of KOH electrolyte (~ 0.3–0.4 nm), facilitating efficient ion adsorption within micropores. In addition, 
the presence of mesopores provides ion transport pathways and reduces diffusion resistance, particularly at 
high scan rates. This hierarchical micro–mesoporous structure enables a synergistic effect, leading to enhanced 
capacitance and rate performance. The TEM image (Fig. 3. C) shows thin, wrinkled, and turbostratic carbon

sheets aggregated into porous clusters, typical of activated carbons derived from biomass. The absence of well-
defined lattice fringes indicates a predominantly amorphous or poorly graphitized structure, with short-range 
ordering only. The SAED pattern displays a diffuse halo rather than sharp diffraction spots or rings, confirming 
the non-crystalline (amorphous) nature of the carbon framework. This structural disorder is consistent with high 
surface area and abundant microporosity, which are desirable for adsorption and electrochemical applications. 
Similar morphological and structural features were observed with other DSAC samples2,5.
Electrode evaluation
To evaluate the DSAC electrochemical performance, a three-electrode system was assembled and attached to 
an OFG + 500 potentiostat/galvanostat to run the cyclic voltammetry (CV), galvanostatic charge and discharge 
(GCD), and stability tests. The applied electrolytes are 1 M and 3 M KOH. All CV and GCD scans were performed 
four times to ensure reproducibility. Figure 4a exhibits the cyclic voltammograms of the DSAC electrode at 5, 10, 
20, 50, 100, and 200 mV/s. Quasi-rectangular voltammograms are observed for almost all scan rates up to 100 
mV/s, which signals the favorable capacitive performance of the produced DSAC. The absence of pronounced 
redox peaks suggests that the charge storage process is primarily dominated by electric double-layer capacitance 
(either at the electrode-electrolyte interface or inside the porous structure), although surface functional groups 
may contribute to additional pseudocapacitive behavior32. It is noteworthy that some minor broad humps appear 
with increasing the scan rate at 100 and 200 mV/s (Fig. 4A), which might be attributed to the oxygen-groups-
associated redox reactions.
Upon increasing the scan rate, however, there is a notable diversion from the rectangular shape, which 
could be attributed to the decreasing contact between the ions and the electrode. As confirmed by the EDX and 
FTIR analyses (Fig. 2E, F), the prepared carbon contains a significant amount of oxygen functionalities (e.g., 
–OH, C–O, and C = O groups). These groups are known to contribute to pseudocapacitive behavior in alkaline

the active material. Following 33, for practical device evaluation, the capacitance of a symmetric two-electrode

T o understand the charge storage kinetics, the Dunn method was applied7. The Dunn method is a standard 
and effective tool for elucidating charge-storage mechanisms in supercapacitor electrodes and guiding the design 
and optimization of materials to improve performance. Equation (8) was applied to estimate both the capacitive 
(surface-controlled) and diffusion-controlled contributions:

The 𝑘𝑘1𝑣𝑣 represents the capacitive (surface-controlled) current contribution, while the 𝑘𝑘2𝑣𝑣0.5 represents the 
diffusion-controlled contribution. The k1 and k2 coefficients are determined from the linear fit of the i/v0.5 
versus v0.5 plot, as illustrated in Fig.  5a. Following, the surface-controlled (capacitive) and diffusion-controlled 
contributions could be estimated at each scan rate, and that is plotted in Fig. 5b.
In contrast to another study 7, the diffusion-controlled contribution is dominating the charge-transfer of 
the current DSAC, which could be directly correlated to its interconnected porous structure, with micropores 
dominating it. But both works agree that increasing the scan rate decreases the diffusion-controlled contribution 
and increases the capacitive one. Figure 5c demonstrates that at 10 mV/s, only 10% of the specific capacitance is 
contributed by the surface capacitive interactions, while the remaining is contributed by the diffusion-controlled 
processes.
Figure 6a shows the stability testing of the DSAC electrode via a 2000-cycle GCD test at 10 A/g in 1 M KOH. 
It shows that the DSAC electrode retains 83.3% of its initial capacity after 2000 discharge cycles. The 10-A/g 
current density was chosen because lower currents would take a few days to charge/discharge < 2000 cycles, 
which proves the high capacity to store electric charges. The 17% loss of capacitive performance after 2000 cycles 
is relatively high compared to conventional > 90% capacity retention after 5000–10,000 GCD cycles, which calls 
for deeper investigation. Although the exact reasons for the capacity decay cannot be accurately identified, several 
insights could be drawn. First, the pseudocapacitive and the diffusion-controlled EDLC (inside the microporous 
channels) contributions are significant, as shown in Fig. 6. The pseudocapacitive contribution stems from the 
surface oxygen-functional groups (Fig. 2E, F). Unfortunately, the ion uptake into the electrode material during 
oxidation causes swelling and strain, generating internal stresses and forming cracks. Furthermore, the surface 
oxygen groups might experience degradation with repeated redox reactions. Such changes could reduce the 
available surface area and ion accessibility for further charge/discharge cycles34.
Alternatively, the applied PVDF binder strength of adhesion with the carbon matrix might have been 
weakened with the repeated GCD cycles. Other DSAC papers have found similar decays in the capacitive 
performance of the DSAC supercapacitor 7. In another study 28 that used banana peel activated with H 3PO4 to 
develop a Zn-ion hybrid supercapacitor, also 83% (initial capacity is 70 F/g) of the capacity was retained after 
50,000 cycles at 1 A/g.
To study the effect of increasing the KOH electrolyte concentration on the DSAC electrode performance, CV 
(Fig. 6b) and GCD tests in 3 M KOH were performed. Figure  6c exhibits the GCD of DSAC in KOH 1 M and 
3 M at 4 A/g, which demonstrates an increase in the capacity overall in the case of 3 M compared to 1 M KOH. 
The GCD results indicate that 3 M KOH exhibits longer charge–discharge times, suggesting higher capacitance 
due to increased ionic conductivity and higher utilized surface area in the KOH 3 M case.
To evaluate the performance novelty in this work, two parameters: specific surface area (m 2/g) and 
2-electrode specific capacitance (F/g), were chosen to compare the current material performance to previously-
published articles. In general, the electrochemical performance of the current DSAC electrode surpasses most 
of the published reports of biomass-derived activated carbon supercapacitor electrodes. Y et, to make the 
comparison reliable and meaningful, Refs1,3,5,15–17 were chosen to compare with since the same raw material and 
supercapacitor application are pursued, while the synthesis and experimental measurements are not identical. 
Figure 7 shows the comparison, and it demonstrates that the current DSAC electrode is one of the best in terms 
of its surface area and specific capacitance.
The comparison presented in Fig. 7 provides a visual assessment of the relationship between surface area 
and specific capacitance for date-seed-derived carbon materials reported in the literature. It is evident that 
capacitance is not solely governed by surface area; for example, some studies report high surface areas but 
relatively moderate capacitance1, indicating that not all surface area is electrochemically accessible. In contrast,

the higher capacitances obtained in studies15,16, and17 are attributed to the more desirable pore structures, better 
ion-transport pathways, and other pseudocapacitive contributions to capacitance by metal oxides in some 
studies. The high surface area and a turbostratic/defect-rich carbon structure in the current study indicate the 
existence of an established porous structure that supports efficient charge storage. In general, the findings prove 
that capacitance is more sensitive to the accessibility of the pore and structural characteristics rather than to the 
surface area.
The present DSAC demonstrates a favorable balance between surface area and electrochemical performance, 
suggesting that its hierarchical pore structure and surface functionalities enable efficient ion accessibility and 
charge storage. This highlights that pore accessibility and structural characteristics play a more critical role than 
surface area alone in determining electrochemical performance.
Conclusions
Date seeds were successfully valorized and upgraded to produce a high-surface-area and functionalized 
activated carbon (DSAC) that can be used to fabricate a hybrid supercapacitor electrode. The prepared DSAC 
has a turbostratic amorphous and hierarchical porous structure combining micro- and mesopores with 1374 
m2/g with functional oxygen groups. The electrochemical evaluation findings ensure that the DSAC has a hybrid 
EDLC-pseudocapacitive charge storage behavior with the pseudocapacitive contribution dominating. The 
3-electrode-calculated specific capacitance is remarkably 1800 F/g (450 F/g of the full device). at 4 A/g. Also, 
the DSAC material can retain 83.3% of its initial capacity after 2000 GCD cycles. Finally, the prepared DSAC 
material achieves a better performance in the 3 M KOH M concentration than the concentrated 1 M one.

Self-assembly fabrication of lignin-derived 
carbon with dual heteroatoms doping 
for high-performance supercapacitor
Zehong Chen1†, Haihong Lai1†, Hao Zhuo2, Yu Lin Zhong3, Linxin Zhong1* and Xinwen Peng1* 
Abstract 
Renewable and low-cost biomass is an ideal sustainable alternative to petroleum-based resources, but producing bio-
mass-based carbon electrode with high performances remains a challenge. Herein, we propose a facile self-assembly 
strategy to fabricate a biomass-derived N, S co-doping carbon electrode from lignosulfonate without any activation 
or template process. Taking advantage of the coordination between Fe ions and lignosulfonate, the resultant carbon 
exhibits a spherical structure with abundant graphitized nanosheets, leading to a high specific surface area with 
rational pore structure, which are beneficial to the electron/ion transport and storage. The high contents of doping N 
(8.47 wt%) and S (2.56 wt%) significantly boost the electrochemical performances. As a supercapacitor electrode, the 
carbon material displays high specific capacitance of 390 F  g−1 , excellent cycling stability and high energy density of 
14.7 W h  kg−1  at a power density of 450 W  kg−1 . This study provides a potential strategy for synthesizing cost-effective 
heteroatom-doped carbon materials from biomass with abundant functional groups and heteroatom sources, such 
as chitosan, collagen, and gelatin.
Keywords Biomass, Lignosulfonate, N, S co-doping, Self-assembly, Supercapacitor

Graphical Abstract
1 Introduction
Supercapacitors have been considered as a promis -
ing energy conversion technology because of their high 
power density, fast charge–discharge rate, and long-term 
durability [1, 2]. Among different electrodes, carbon 
material possessing high specific surface area, porous 
structure, and high physicochemical stability is a promis -
ing candidate for supercapacitors [3, 4]. To obtain high-
performance carbon electrodes, great efforts have been 
made to regulate the specific surface area, porous archi -
tecture, and heteroatom doping.
It has been widely reported that increasing the spe -
cific surface area can effectively enhance the superca -
pacitance performances [5 ]. Additionally, hierarchical 
porous structure with rational micropore/mesopore 
ratio also plays an important role in enhancing the 
supercapacitance performances of carbon electrodes, 
since abundant micropores can increase the accessi -
ble surface area for charge storage, while connected 
mesopores are beneficial for shortening ion transport 
distance and allowing high rate capability [6 , 7]. Fur -
thermore, doping heteroatoms into the carbon matrix 
is regarded as the most promising and versatile way to 
boost the electrochemical performances. For instance, 
nitrogen (N) doping can enhance the wettability, elec -
trical conductivity, structural quality, electrochemical 
active sites of carbon electrode and provide pseudo-
capacitance [8 , 9]. Sulfur (S) doping is supposed to 
improve electrical conductivity and specific capaci -
tance owing to the formation of an extended p-system 
with a filled valence band and the enhanced polariza -
tion [10, 11].
In addition to regulating the physicochemical prop -
erties, fabricating carbon materials in a sustainable 
and environmentally friendly way is quite imperative 
when considering the depletion of fossil resources and 
environmental problems. Biomass, as the most abun -
dant renewable carbon source, has attracted increas -
ing interest for energy application. Up to now, carbon 
materials for energy storage have been widely obtained 
from biomass resources, such as cellulose [12, 13], 
chitosan [14], glucose [15], straw [16], corn [17], and 
collagen-enriched biomass [18, 19]. For example, a 
multi-heteroatom doped porous carbon was efficiently

segments.text:
Page 3 of 13
Chen et al. Collagen and Leather            (2023) 5:15 
 
prepared via a controllable pyrolysis of fish scale with 
KOH [19]. The obtained carbon possessed ultrathin 
nanosheet structure, micropore-dominate poros -
ity and rich surface heteroatoms, which endowed the 
electrode with a high capacitance of 306  F   g− 1 at the 
current density of 1  A   g− 1. Though many high-per -
formance biomass-based carbon materials have been 
successfully fabricated, the synthetic strategies usually 
involve traditional activation or template processes. 
Traditional activation may introduce small micropo -
res, consume large amounts of chemical agents, and 
even corrode equipment, while template method is 
complicated and high-cost [20, 21]. Thus, more sus -
tainable and cost-effective approaches should be con -
sidered when fabricating biomass-derived carbon 
materials.
Lignin, as the third most abundant renewable 
resource, accounts for 20–30% in plants and has a 
high carbon content (45–60 wt%) [22]. About 70 mil -
lion tons of lignin is generated annually as a residual 
product of paper-making industries, but only ~ 5% 
is utilized for value-added applications [23]. Thus, 
using lignin as a precursor for synthesizing advanced 
carbon materials can provide economic and envi -
ronmental benefits. Particularly, lignosulfonate, a 
derivative of lignin produced from sulfite pulping or 
sulfonation of lignin, contains abundant functional 
groups (e.g., sulfonate and phenolic hydroxyl groups), 
which makes it soluble in water and easily coordi -
nate with other components, allowing for structural 
adjustments [24, 25]. Furthermore, the sulfonate 
group is an intrinsic S source for S self-doping in the 
carbon framework [26].
Herein, we propose an economic and simple strat -
egy to synthesize a carbon material (Fe-SN 6C@900) 
with dual heteroatoms (N and S) doping from ligno -
sulfonate without activation or template process. The 
coordination between Fe ions and lignosulfonate via 
hydrothermal treatment results in Fe–lignosulfonate 
(Fe–LS) complex with spherical shape, while the high-
temperature carbonization with melamine produces 
abundant graphitized nanosheets. The resultant car -
bon Fe-SN 6C@900 displays large specific surface area 
and rational pore structure, which are favorable for 
electron transport, ion storage and improving elec -
trical conductivity. The high contents of doping N 
(8.47  wt%) and S (2.56  wt%) can improve the surface 
wettability, afford additional pseudo-capacitance, and 
finally boost the electrochemical performances. Thus, 
Fe-SN6C@900 reveals excellent supercapacitance per -
formances with high specific capacitance of 390 F   g− 1, 
superior cycling stability, and high energy density of 
14.7 W h  kg− 1.
2  Materials and methods
2.1  Materials
Lignosulphonate (LS) was purchased from Shanghai 
Aladdin Industrial Corporation (China). Ferric chlo -
ride hexahydrate  (FeCl3·6H2O), copper chloride dihy -
drate  (CuCl2·2H2O), melamine, ammonium chloride 
 (NH4Cl), urea, sulfuric acid  (H2SO4), and sodium sul -
fate  (Na2SO4) were analytical grade and used without 
purification.
2.2  Preparation of Fe–Lignosulphonate (Fe–LS)
1.67  g  FeCl3·6H2O was dissolved in 10  mL water and 
stirred for 20 min. 1.00 g LS was added into the  FeCl3 
solution with stirring for 1  h. The mixture was trans -
ferred into a Teflon autoclave reactor for hydrothermal 
treatment at 180 °C for 4 h. After hydrothermal treat -
ment, the obtained product was thoroughly washed 
with water and recovered by filtration. The dried prod -
uct was denoted as Fe– LS. Control sample without the 
addition of  FeCl3 was conducted for comparison, which 
was denoted as HT– LS.
2.3  Preparation of Fe‑SNXC@T
To synthesize Fe-SN XC@T ( X represents the mass ratio 
of melamine to Fe–LS, and T represents the carboni -
zation temperature), Fe–LS was mixed with a certain 
amount of melamine (the mass ratios of melamine 
to Fe–LS were 2:1, 4:1, 6:1, and 8:1) and grinded for 
20  min. The mixture was heated to a targeted tem -
perature (800, 900 or 1000 °C) for 2 h at a heating rate 
of 5  °C   min− 1 in a  N2-filled tube furnace. The control 
sample Fe-SC@900 was obtained by direct carbonizing 
Fe–LS without melamine. HT– LS was mixed with mel -
amine and carbonized in the same condition for syn -
thesizing  SN6C@900. Cu-SN 6C@900 was synthesized 
using a similar procedure of Fe-SN 6C@900 by replacing 
 FeCl3·6H2O with  CuCl2·2H2O. Fe-SN6C@900-A and Fe-
SN6C@900-U were fabricated using a similar procedure 
of Fe-SN6C@900 by replacing melamine with  NH4Cl or 
urea, respectively.
2.4  Characterizations
Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images were 
carried out on a scanning electron microscope (FE-
SEM Merlin, Zeiss) at an acceleration voltage of 5 kV. 
The dimension and internal structures of samples 
were characterized by a transmission electron micros -
copy combined with high-resolution imaging feature 
(TEM, JEM-2100F) operating at 200 kV. Fourier trans -
form Infrared (FT-IR) data were recorded on a Fou -
rier transform IR spectrometer (VERTEX 70, Bruker 
Corp., Germany). Element analysis was carried out on

chemical composition and structure of samples were 
determined by X-ray photoelectron spectrum (XPS, 
Thermo Scientific ESCALAB 250Xi spectrometer) with 
an exciting source of Al Kα (1286.6 eV). X-ray diffrac -
tion (XRD) spectra were recorded using a Bruker D8

Raman spectrometer (LabRAM ARAMIS-Horiba Jobin 
Yvon) with a 532 nm excitation.  N2 adsorption–desorp -

3  Results and discussion
3.1  Physicochemical structures
Figure  1 illustrates the fabrication of Fe-SN XC@T (X 
represents the mass ratio of melamine to Fe–LS, and T 
represents the carbonization temperature) through the 
assembly of metal ions and lignosulfonate and followed 
by a subsequent heat treatment with melamine. First, Fe 
ions were coordinated with hydrophilic groups (e.g., sul -
fonate and phenolic hydroxyl groups) in lignosulfonate to 
form Fe–LS complex. Then, by carbonizing the mixture 
of Fe–LS and melamine, Fe-SN XC@T with successful N, 
S co-doping was synthesized. Moreover, owing to the 
abundance of lignosulfonate and the cost-effective strat -
egy, Fe-SNXC@T can be fabricated in a kilogram-level 
(Additional file 1: Fig. S1), suggesting its potential indus -
trial application.
The intrinsic S source in lignosulfonate was confirmed 
by elemental analysis, and is determined to be 5.90 wt% 
(Additional file  1: Table  S1). In the Fourier transform 
Infrared (FT-IR) spectrum of lignosulfonate, the absorp -
tion band at 1043   cm−1 is related to the S–O vibration 
in sulfonate groups, while the band at 525   cm−1  is attrib-
uted to the C–S vibration (Additional file  1: Fig. S2a) 
[27]. With the addition of  FeCl3, lignosulfonate and Fe 
composite without hydrothermal treatment (named as 
Fe–LS-without HT) exhibits a new Fe–O absorption 
band at 596   cm−1, verifying the coordination between 
Fe and lignosulfonate [27]. As shown in SEM images, 
Fe–LS-without HT is compact and lumpy without visible 
pore (Additional file  1: Fig. S3a), and HT–LS obtained

also irregular and lumpy (Additional file  1: Fig. S3b). In 
contrast, Fe–LS complex is composed of loosely packed 
carbon nanoparticles (Additional file  1: Fig. S3c and d), 
indicating that the hydrothermal treatment with the 
presence of Fe can affect the structure. To further inves -
tigate the influence of the Fe coordination on structure, 
FT-IR spectra of LS, HT–LS and Fe–LS complex were 
carried out (Additional file  1: Fig. S2b). As compared 
with LS, the adsorption bands of HT–LS exhibit neg -
ligible change, indicating that the original structure of 
lignosulfonate is retained at 180  °C, since the cleavage 
of aryl–ether bond cannot occur at a low temperature. 
However, in the FT-IR spectrum of Fe–LS, the C–O–C 
absorption band at 1115   cm−1  disappears, implying the 
breakage of C–O bond, probably owing to destabiliza -
tion of C–O–C bond induced by metal complexation 
and formation of free radicals through electron trans -
fer between aromatic structure with metal cations [28]. 
Meanwhile, the presence of S in Fe–LS can be detected 
by scanning electron microscopy with energy dispersive 
X-ray spectroscopy (SEM–EDX), and the composition of 
the elements is presented in Additional file 1: Fig. S4. The 
X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) survey spec -
trum of Fe–LS also demonstrates the presence of C, O, 
and S (Additional file  1: Fig. S5a). The high-resolution C 
1s spectrum reveals the existence of four peaks at 284.4, 
285.2, 286.2, and 288.5 eV, corresponding to C–C, C–O, 
C–S, and C=O groups, respectively (Additional file 1: Fig. 
S5b) [29]. For the high-resolution S 2p spectrum (Addi -
tional file  1: Fig. S5c), the peaks appearing at 163.5 and 
164.7 eV correspond to S 2p3/2 and S 2p1/2 of thiophene S 
(C–S–C), while the peaks at 167.8 and 169.1 eV represent 
the oxidized S (–SOX–) [10, 29].
Fe–LS and HT–LS were mixed with melamine and 
then carbonized to obtain N, S co-doping carbons Fe-
SNXC@T and  SN6C@900, respectively. As shown in 
Fig.  2a,  SN6C@900 displays a compact structure with -
out visible pores, which is similar to that of HT–LS. Fe-
SN6C@900 retains the same particle-packed structure 
to Fe–LS (Fig.  2b and c). Interestingly, some nanosheets 
are detected around the particles, which are supposed 
to facilitate the ion/electron transport [30]. Fe-SC@900 
without melamine, however, reveals a particle-packed 
structure without any nanosheet (Fig.  2d), suggesting 
that the cooperation of melamine and Fe–LS can induce 
the formation of carbon nanosheets. The morphologies 
of Fe-SN6C@T obtained at 800 and 1000  °C are shown 
in Fig.  2e and f. Fe-SN 6C@800 displays a similar archi -
tecture to Fe-SN 6C@900, while Fe-SN 6C@1000 reveals 
more collapsed particles due to the severe carboniza -
tion at a higher temperature. In addition, SEM images

observed via the high-resolution TEM, which are favora -
ble for the mass transfer. The high-resolution TEM also 
indicates a partial graphitization structure with disor -
dered carbon and some graphitic lattice fringes, which 
can enhance the conductivity of carbon (Fig.  2i) [32]. 
Specifically, the electrical conductivity of Fe-SN 6C@900 
is detected to be up to 46.8 S  m−1, which can facilitate the 
electron transport and thus enhance the electrochemical 
performances.
The Raman spectra of Fe-SN 6C@T display two broad 
peaks at 1335 and 1585   cm−1 , corresponding to the 
disordered (D) and graphitic (G) bands, respectively 
(Fig. 3a). The intensity ratios of D band to G band (I D/IG) 
for Fe-SN6C@800, 900, and 1000 are 0.96, 0.88, and 0.84, 
respectively, suggesting that a higher carbonization tem -
perature will promote the graphitization [33]. Addition -
ally, the ID/IG of Fe-SN6C@900 (0.88) is lower than that of 
 SN6C@900 (1.02), indicating that the addition of Fe can 
enhance the graphitization degree (Additional file  1: Fig. 
S9). The XRD spectra of Fe-SN 6C@T reveal two broad 
and low-density peaks at 2θ = 24.3 and 43.6°, attributed to 
the (002) and (100) graphitic planes, respectively, further 
confirming the partial graphitization (Fig. 3b) [34].
The  N2 adsorption–desorption isotherms of Fe-
SN6C@T,  SN6C@900, and Fe-SC@900 are displayed 
in Fig.  3c and Additional file  1: Fig. S10. As shown in 
Fig.  3c, all samples reveal combining isotherms of type 
I and IV, demonstrating the co-existence of micropores 
and mesopores [35, 36]. The BET (Brunauer–Emmett–
Teller) specific surface areas  (SBET) calculated from  N2 
adsorption–desorption isotherms are summarized in 
Additional file  1: Fig. S10b and Table S2. In comparison 
to  SN6C@900 (91   m2  g−1 ) and Fe-SC@900 (338   m2  g−1 ), 
Fe-SN6C@900 displays a much higher  SBET (542   m2  g−1 ), 
owing to the loosely particle-packed structure and gra -
phitized nanosheets with numerous pores (as indicated 
by SEM and TEM analyses). The  SBET of Fe-SN 6C@900 
(542   m2   g−1 ) is higher than that of Fe-SN 6C@800 
(359   m2  g −1 ), suggesting that a higher carbonization 
temperature will increase specific surface area. Particu -
larly, Fe-SN6C@1000 displays a relatively lower  SBET of 
392  m2  g−1  as compared with Fe-SN 6C@900, which may 
result from the partial collapse structure at the severe 
carbonization temperature. The pore size distribution 
curves are shown in Fig.  3d.  SN4C@900 exhibits the 
least micropores and mesopores, and Fe-SC@900 pos -
sesses numerous micropores less than 0.5 nm. However,

Fe-SN6C@900 exhibits a porous structure with abundant 
pores ranging from 0.8 to 2.2 nm (peak value at ~ 1.2 nm), 
which is believed to be the rational porous structure for 
electrochemical applications [37, 38].
To further investigate the chemical composition and 
surface chemistry of the as-prepared carbons, elemen -
tal analysis and XPS measurement were carried out. As 
shown in Additional file  1: Table S1, all Fe-SNXC@T dis-
play high N content (6.07–12.82 wt%) and relatively low 
self-doping S content (0.43–2.33 wt%). Obviously, as the 
carbonization temperature increases, the N content of 
Fe-SN6C@T decreases gradually, indicating a severer 
decomposition of nitrogen at high temperature. Mean -
while, the N content of Fe-SN XC@900 gradually rises 
(6.07–9.23 wt%) by increasing melamine. Particularly, Fe-
SN6C@900 displays a higher N content (8.47  wt%) than 
 SN6C@900 (4.81  wt%), possibly indicating that as com -
pared with the irregular and lumpy structure of HT-LS, 
the particle structure of Fe–LS is beneficial to the nitro -
gen fixation.
The XPS spectra of the samples are displayed in Fig.  4, 
Additional file  1: Figs. S11 and S12. In the low-resolu -
tion spectra of Fe-SN 6C@T and  SN6C@900, C, N, and 
O are detected (Fig.  4a), demonstrating the successful 
doping of nitrogen. The high-resolution N 1s  spectra 
of Fe-SN6C@T (Fig.  4b, e and f) and  SN6C@900 (Addi -
tional file  1: Fig. S11) show that four kinds of N species 
have been doped into the carbon framework. The four 
peaks at 398.2, 399.4, 400.9, and 402.5 eV are attributed 
to pyridinic-N, pyrrolic-N, graphitic-N, and oxidized-
N atoms, respectively [29, 39]. Among these four kinds 
of N species, pyridinic and pyrrolic-N are believed to 
provide pseudo-capacitance, while graphitic-N may 
enhance the conductivity [9 , 40]. The relative concen -
trations of N species (Additional file  1: Table S3) show 
that with the increase of carbonization temperature, the 
concentration of graphitic-N rises gradually, indicating 
a higher graphitization degree. In the high-resolution 
S 2p  spectra of Fe-SN 6C@900 (Fig.  4c) and Fe-SC@900 
(Fig. 4d), two peaks at 163.9 and 165.4 eV are consistent 
with S 2p 3/2 and S 2p 1/2 of thiophene S (C–S–C), which 
are supposed to give a positive charge to C atoms and 
thus increase storage capability. The peak at 168.3  eV 
corresponds to oxidized S (–SO x–), which is antici -
pated to produce pseudo-capacitance [10, 41]. Fur -
thermore, N and S located at the carbon network are 
reported to improve the wettability and thus increase 
the accessibility of electroactive surface area [8 , 42]. As 
shown in Additional file  1: Fig. S13, the contact angles 
of Fe-SN 6C@900 and Fe-SC@900 are 60.5° and 97.4°, 
respectively, indicating that N doping can effectively 
improve the wettability, and thus facilitate the electro -
lyte ion diffusion.

3.2  Electrochemical performances
The as-prepared carbon materials with heteroatoms 
(N and S) co-doping can be utilized as electrodes for 
supercapacitors. The performances of the samples 
in a three-electrode system are displayed in Fig.  5. 
The cyclic voltammetry (CV) curve of Fe-SN 6C@900 
reveals a rectangular-like shape with a small hump, 
indicating the existence of both electrical double layer 
capacitance and pseudo-capacitance (Fig.  5a). The 
pseudo-capacitance contribution may result from the 
reversible electro-chemical reactions of nitrogen and 
sulfur functionalities [8 , 43]. The capacitance calculated 
from CV curve of Fe-SN 6C@900 is 470 F   g− 1, which is 
remarkably higher than those of  SN6C@900 (144 F   g− 1), 
Fe-SC@900 (155  F   g− 1), and Fe-SN 6C@900-without 
HT (209 F   g− 1, Additional file  1: Fig. S14). Meanwhile, 
N doping carbons with high performances can be also 
fabricated by replacing melamine with other nitrogen 
sources (e.g.,  NH4Cl or urea). As shown in Additional 
file  1: Fig. S15, the capacitances calculated from CV 
curves of Fe-SN 6C@900-A (using  NH4Cl as nitrogen 
source) and Fe-SN 6C@900-U (using urea as nitrogen 
source) are 458 and 369  F   g− 1, respectively, which are 
comparable to that of Fe-SN 6C@900 (470  F   g− 1). Fur -
thermore, by replacing Fe with Cu, the resultant car -
bon Cu-SN 6C@900 also exhibits a high capacitance 
of 370  F   g− 1, indicating that such synthetic strategy 
can be extended to other metals (Additional file  1: 
Fig. S16). The excellent supercapacitance perfor -
mance of Fe-SN 6C@900 may derive from the high  SBET 
(542  m2  g− 1) with rational porous structure, more dop -
ing heteroatoms (8.47  wt% for N and 2.56  wt% for S), 
and high concentrations of active N species (35.34% 
for pyridinic-N, 23.67% for pyrrolic-N, and 31.80% for 
graphitic-N), as shown in Additional file  1: Tables S1, 
S2 and S3. The pyridinic and pyrrolic-N are believed to

Particularly, the carbonizing temperature has a sig -
nificant influence on physicochemical properties, which 
may result in regulable electrochemical performances. 
The capacitance performances of Fe-SN 6C@T fabri -
cated from different temperatures were investigated, 
and the results are shown in Fig.  5b, c, and Additional 
file  1: Figs. S17, S18 and S19. In the CV curves, all Fe-
SN6C@T show a quasi-rectangular shape, and the GCD 
curves exhibit a quasi-triangle shape with a small dis -
tortion, indicating the presence of pseudo-capacitance 
resulting from the heteroatoms doping [44]. The specific 
capacitances at 1 A  g− 1 for Fe-SN6C@800, Fe-SN6C@900, 
and Fe-SN6C@1000 are 244, 304, and 285 F   g− 1, respec-
tively (Fig. 5e). The highest capacitance of Fe-SN 6C@900 
ascribes to the relatively higher  SBET, graphitic degree, 
and heteroatom content, as certified in Fig.  3 and 
Additional file  1: Tables S1, S2 and S3. Meanwhile, the 
Nyquist plots of Fe-SN 6C@T are shown in Additional 
file  1: Fig. S19. In the low-frequency region, a steep 
capacitive spike is observed, suggesting an ideal capaci -
tance behavior [45]. The real axis intercepts representing 
the equivalent series resistances of Fe-SN 6C@900 (3.6 Ω) 
and Fe-SN6C@1000 (5.2  Ω) are significantly lower than 
that of Fe-SN6C@800, indicating that Fe-SN 6C@900 and 
Fe-SN6C@1000 have a higher conductivity [46].
Since the N content plays an important role in the 
capacitance performances, the electrochemical prop -
erties of Fe-SN XC@900 prepared from different mela -
mine contents were investigated, as shown in Fig.  5d 
and Additional file  1: Figs. S20, S21 and S22. Notice -
ably, Fe-SN 6C@900 (304  F   g− 1) possesses a higher 
specific capacitance than Fe-SN 2C@900 (170  F   g− 1),

Fe-SN4C@900 (263  F   g− 1), and Fe-SN 8C@900 
(233 F   g− 1) (Fig.  5e), which can be explained by its suit -
able N content and higher concentration of electro -
chemically active N species, as indicated by Additional 
file  1: Fig. S12, Tables S1 and S3. The Nyquist plots 
show that Fe-SN 2C@900, Fe-SN4C@900, Fe-SN6C@900, 
and Fe-SN 8C@900 possess low equivalent series resist -
ances of 4.4, 5.2, 3.6, and 5.0 Ω, respectively, suggesting 
their high conductivity (Additional file 1 : Fig. S22).
The CV curves at various scan rates and GCD curves 
at different current densities of Fe-SN 6C@900 are dis -
played in Fig.  5f and g. Remarkably, the CV curve of 
Fe-SN6C@900 remains a rectangular-like shape even at 
a scan rate of 200  mV   s−1  (Fig.  5f), and the capacitance 
retention (from 5 to 200  mV   s−1) is high up to 77.3% 
(Fig.  5h), suggesting a superior rate capability [47]. 
Additionally, the GCD curves of Fe-SN 6C@900 reveal 
quasi-symmetrical triangular shapes at various current 
densities, demonstrating an outstanding electrochemi -
cal reversibility and columbic efficiency (Fig.  5g). The 
corresponding capacitance of Fe-SN6C@900 is as high as 
390 F  g−1  at 0.5 A   g−1 and remains 228 F   g−1  at 10 A   g−1 
(Fig.  5h). The specific capacitance of Fe-SN 6C@900 
(390 F  g−1  at 0.5 A  g−1) outperforms those of many other 
biomass-derived carbon materials, including activated 
carbons, heteroatoms-doping carbons, carbon nano -
spheres, and so on (Additional file  1: Table S4) [48–57]. 
Furthermore, the stability of Fe-SN 6C@900 was con -
ducted by repeated GCD test at 5  A   g−1 . Fe-SN6C@900 
displays an outstanding durability with a capacitance 
retention of ~ 102%, and the slightly increasing capaci -
tance possibly ascribes to the enhance of the ion acces -
sibility after the long-term cycling (Fig.  5i) [58]. The CV 
curves of Fe-SN 6C@900 at the first and last cycles show 
no visible change, further certifying its electrochemical 
stability (the inset of Fig. 5i).
The two-electrode symmetric capacitance behavior 
of Fe-SN 6C@900 was conducted in 1  M  Na2SO4 solu -
tion. The CV curve is almost rectangular in the potential 
window of 0–1.6 V (Fig.  6a). The symmetric capacitance 
behavior of Fe-SN 6C@900 was investigated at the volt -
age range of 0–1.6 V. The CV curves at various scan rates 
remain a rectangular shape without distinct distortion 
(Fig. 6b). Furthermore, the GCD curves at different cur -
rent densities display symmetric triangle shapes, again 
indicating a superior electrochemical reversibility and 
high columbic efficiency (Fig.  6c). The specific capaci -
tance at 0.5  A   g−1 is 165  F   g−1  (Fig.  6d), and maintains 
111 F   g−1 at 10 A   g−1 . Additionally, Fe-SN6C@900-based 
symmetric supercapacitor reveals an energy density of 
14.7  W  h  kg−1 at the power density of 450  W   kg−1  and 
remains 12.2 W h   kg−1 at 4500 W   kg−1 , which are com -
parable to those of many other biomass-derived carbons,

4  Conclusion
We propose a promising approach for synthesizing car -
bon materials (Fe-SN XC@T) from lignosulfonate via 
self-assembly of Fe ions and lignosulfonate and followed 
by a thermal treatment with melamine. As compared 
with samples achieved at 800 or 1000 °C, Fe-SN 6C@900 
exhibits relatively higher  SBET, graphitic degree, and 
heteroatom content, resulting in the highest capaci -
tance. Meanwhile, the capacitance of Fe-SN 6C@900 
reaches the summit among various samples with dif -
ferent melamin contents, since Fe-SN 2C@900 with less 
melamine content shows a small amount of N doping, 
while Fe-SN 8C@900 with excessive melamine reveals a 
self-packed structure. Therefore, owing to the spheri -
cal structure with graphitized nanosheets, high specific 
surface area with rational pores, and successful N and S 
co-doping, the optimal carbon material (Fe-SN 6C@900) 
exhibits excellent supercapacitance performances with 
high specific capacitance (390 F   g−1), high energy density 
(14.7  W  h  kg−1 ), and outstanding durability. Consider -
ing the facile strategy and high electrochemical perfor -
mances, this research offers a valuable approach for the 
conversion of biomass (such as chitosan, collagen, and 
gelatin) into renewable carbon materials for energy-
related applications.

Main manuscript 
Green Production of Hookah Tobacco Waste-Derived Porous Carbon and Its Capacitive 
Performance 
 
 
 
 
Abstract 
 
Carbon materials generated from biomass garner significant interest for supercapacitor applications 
owing to their elevated specific capacitance, affordability, environmental sustainability, and the 
availability of natural precursors. In this work, oxygen -rich porous carbons are fabricated using 
sodium thiosulfate (Na₂S₂O₃)—a less toxic activating agent compared to conventional chemicals. The 
structural and textural characteristics of the resulting carbons are strongly influenced by the synthesis 
parameters. Among the prepared samples , HTWB -0.5-900 exhibits a well -developed hierarchical 
network consisting of micro -, meso -, and macropores and possesses a high surface area of 1018.74 
m²/g, features that enhance ion transport and increase the accessibility of electrocatalytically active 
sites. When applied as a supercapacitor electrode, the HTWB -0.5-900 material, obtained at 900 °C 
using a Na₂S₂O₃/HTWB mass ratio of 0.5/1, delivers the highest specific capacitance of 175 F/g at 0.5 
A/g in 1 M KOH. Furthermore, this electrode exhibits exceptional cycling stability, maintaining its 
initial capacitance after 10,000 charge -discharge cycles, even at a current density of 10 A/g. Overall, 
the findings highlight the potential of converting hookah tobacco waste into efficient and sustainable 
electrode materials for high-performance supercapacitors. 
 
Keywords: Sodium thiosulfate activating, hookah tobacco waste, supercapacitor, biochar, chemical 
activating 
 
1. Introduction 
 
In recent years, an increasing number of researchers have concentrated on transforming biomass 
and biomass waste into high -value goods [1]. Statistics show that China, the world's largest producer 
of tobacco, produces an estimated 1.20x10 6 tons of waste tobacco annually  [2]. Originating in North 
and South America, tobacco is a plant with broad leaves that is farmed for use in  waterpipes. These 
days, it has spread around the globe, and the dried leaves are known as tobacco [3]. A common form of

segments.path: D:\机器学习-超级电容器\新增文献整理_20261020\originals\ADD_058.pdf
segments.text:
3 
 
tobacco known as the hookah first became popular over four hundred years ago. Over a quarter of the 
populace in the eastern Mediterranean is thought to smoke hookah  [4–6]. The name, shape, and size of 
the hookah (e.g., waterpipe, shisha, hubble -bubble, nargileh, and argileh)  vary depending on the 
location [4,5]. The chemical compositions of the smoke produced by cigarettes and hookahs are 
somewhat similar. Both of them include a variety of poisonous substances, including volatile organic 
chemicals, radionuclides, metals, volatile aldehydes, ultrafine particles, and polycyclic aromatic 
hydrocarbons (PAHs), as well as particulate matter, tar, carbon monoxide, nicotine, and volatile 
organic compounds  [7–9]. As the use of hookah increases day by day, useless waste is created. 
Therefore, it is important in practice to learn how to recover hookah tobacco waste with high value and 
high efficiency. The ideal alternative for this is to produce activated carbon from hookah tobacco  
waste. The a ctivated carbon materials have been created using a variety of biomass or biological 
wastes, including Moringa oleifera [10], pea pods [11], date palm fiber [12], mango leaves [13], Pisum 
Sativum peels [14], prickly pear seed  [15], waste cooked rice  [16], cocoa leaves [17], mandarin peels 
[18], pitaya fruit peel [19], Water Hyacinth [20]. 
It is important to note that porous activated carbon is the best type of electrode for 
supercapacitors. Porous carbon generated from biomass may acquire unique microstructures from its 
antecedents, which serve as active locations for numerous  ion transport channels and energy storage.  
The two most significant factors that would have an impact on the electrochemical properties of 
carbon materials are their high specific surface area and hierarchical porous structure  [21]. There may 
be enough active places for charge storage with a large specific surface area. The appropriate pore 
structure can enhance the area of the electrode -electrolyte interface and facilitate the ingress of 
electrolyte ions, hence augmenting capacitance  [22]. Previous research indicates that the majority of 
porous carbons were synthesized by a two -step procedure  [23–25]. Pre-carbonization was the first 
step, followed by pyrolysis or activation. There have been numerous studies done in the past that have 
favored low-temperature pyrolysis before carbonization. Hydrothermal carbonization (HTC) has a 
significant impact on the synthesis of hydrocarbons and has the ability to add oxygen -rich substituents 
to carbon-based materials [26]. Hydrothermal carbonization technology is also an economical, simple, 
and efficient  technique [27]. The preparation process is one of the most often employed 
thermochemical conversion procedures for biomass carbon -based materials, attributable to two 
advantages. The efficiency of the ensuing activation process is improved by hydrothermal 
carbonization and chemical activation, which lowers the overall cost of manufacturing. The final 
material's microstructural properties are enhanced by the two-step procedure, too.

segments.path: D:\机器学习-超级电容器\新增文献整理_20261020\originals\ADD_058.pdf
segments.text:
4 
 
The main factors influencing the capacitive characteristics of carbon materials are the 
appropriate pore size distribution and specific surface area.  The specific surface area of carbon 
compounds is often increased through chemical activation and physical activation. Due to its low 
temperature, low cost, high yield, and quick activation period to create  porous structures, chemical 
activation has garnered interest.  Commonly used activators are H2SO4 [28], ZnCl2 [29], KOH [30], 
NaOH [31], etc. 
However, the use of chemical activation is becoming progressively problematic because of the 
significant corrosiveness and toxicity associated with this approach. In addition to these concerns, 
chemical activation often results in low production yields, thereby constraining its potential for large -
scale industrial deployment  [32]. Consequently, extensive efforts continue to focus on developing 
alternative synthesis routes that employ inexpensive, sustainable carbon precursors together with 
benign, non-corrosive activating agents. 
Recent studies have introduced comparatively benign activating agents —such as sodium 
thiosulfate [33], potassium bicarbonate  [34], and potassium carbonate  [35]—for the preparation of 
porous carbons. In particular, Sevilla and co -workers [36,37] explored environmentally friendly routes 
for producing porous carbons from diverse biomass -derived precursors, such as sucrose,  gelatin, and 
glucose. In their approach, aqueous sodium thiosulfate served as the activating agent, while potassium 
chloride functioned as the reaction medium. This synthesis route is considered green and sustainable, 
as it relies solely on environmentally safe materials such as Na₂S₂O₃, KCl, water, and biomass. The 
resulting carbons exhibited high BET surface areas (reaching ~2600 m² /g) and delivered specific 
capacitances of approximately 200 F /g in aqueous electrolytes. A further significant finding of their 
work is that sodium thiosulfate enables the incorporation of sulfur functionalities into the carbon 
matrix through a self-doping mechanism. 
In this study, sodium thiosulfate is employed as a benign activating agent to produce porous 
carbon from hookah tobacco waste (HTW). To our knowledge, porous carbon synthesized from HTW 
using Na 2S2O3 as the pore -forming species has not been previously documented. During activation, 
Na2S2O3 decomposes at high temperatures to yield sodium sulfate, a highly reactive species that plays 
a key role in generating pores within the carbon framework. The resulting sample, HTW B-0.5-900, 
exhibits a sponge -like morphology with a large specific surface area of 1018.74 m² /g and a well -
developed hierarchical pore structure. Notably, the fabricated electrode material demonstrates 
enhanced electrochemical performance, attributed to shortened ion -diffusion paths, rapid charge 
transport through the porous network, and an expanded interfacial area accessible to electrolyte ions.

2. Experimental section 
2.1. Chemicals and reagents 
The hookah tobacco waste (HTW) used in this study was collected from the Taksim hookah cafe 
in the Osmaniye region, Türkiye. Sodium thiosulfate (Na₂S₂O₃, 99% purity), potassium chloride (KCl, 
99% purity), and hydrochloric acid (HCl, 37% purity) were purchased from Interlab (Türkiye). N-
methyl-2-pyrrolidone (NMP) (99% purity) and poly(vinylidene fluoride) (PVDF) were obtained from 
Sigma-Aldrich. Nickel foam was purchased from Teknotip (distributor for MTI Corporation). 
Deionized water (DI) was used for all hydrothermal carbonization (HTC) treatments. All chemical 
reagents were of analytical grade and utilized as received without additional purification.  
 
2.2 Preparation of porous carbon from hookah tobacco waste (HTWB) 
Porous carbon was synthesized through a multistep procedure. Initially, hookah tobacco waste  
(HTW) was thoroughly rinsed with distilled water to remove surface contaminants, followed by drying 
at 105 °C and grinding to a particle size below 200 mesh. Subsequently, 10 g of the ground material 
and 80 mL of distilled water were loaded into a 150 mL PPL -lined stainless-steel autoclave. 
Hydrothermal carbonization (HTC) was conducted at 180 °C for 4 hours, followed by natural cooling 
of the reactor to ambient temperature. The resulting solid was filtered, washed, and dried at 110 °C for 
24 h to obtain the preliminary biochar. 
To eliminate inorganic impurities, the biochar was treated with 3.0 M HCl for 45 min under 
continuous stirring, filtered, and sequentially washed with distilled water three times (45 min each). 
The purified biochar (HTWB) was then dried again at 110 °C for 24 h. 
The method employed in this study utilizes comparatively less hazardous activating agents, 
namely sodium thiosulfate and KCl. In contrast, traditional activation processes typically rely on more 
corrosive and aggressive chemicals such as KOH or ZnCl₂ to generate porous carbon [38–40]. 
For the activation step, HTWB was blended with Na₂S₂O₃ and KCl at mass ratios of 1/0.5/3 and 
1/1/3, maintaining a total mass of 2.0 g. The mixtures were placed in a quartz boat and activated in a 
tubular furnace under a continuous N₂ flow. Thermal activation was carried out at 700, 800, and 900 
°C for 60 min with a heating rate of 10 °C min⁻¹ to produce porous carbon materials. Based on the 
Na₂S₂O₃ / biochar ratio and activation temperature, the resulting samples were designated as HTWB -
0.5-700, HTWB -0.5-800, HTWB -0.5-900, HTWB -1-700, HTWB -1-800, and HTWB -1-900. The 
synthesis of hookah tobacco waste-derived porous carbons is illustrated schematically in Fig. 1.
