3. Materials and Methods
3.1. Synthesis of Nanoporous Activated Biochar
The raw materials, goose feathers and waste pine sawdust, were collected from
discarded badminton and a furniture factory in China (Henan, Kaifeng), respectively.
Figure 8 details the synthesis of nanoporous biochar samples. First, the waste pine sawdust
and badminton feathers were dried in an oven at 80 ◦C for 12 h to a constant weight. The
dried raw materials were then ground further in the crusher and passed through an 80-
mesh sieve. To accurately adjust the effect of heavy metals throughout the experiment, the
Cu-contaminated plants used in the reactions were synthesized using appropriate amounts
of Cu and crushed pine sawdust according to reported methods [ 59–61]. The desired
amounts of crushed pine sawdust and CuSO4·5H2O (Aladdin Industrial Corporation in
Shanghai, China) were mixed in a beaker and stirred vigorously at 500 rpm for 6 h. The
resulting mixtures (0, 25, 50 mg Cu/g biomass) and crushed badminton feathers were
utilized together in the first step Co-HTC reaction. Then, 150 mL of ultrapure water

3.3. Electrochemical Measurements
3.3.1. Electrode Preparation
For the three-electrode system, 8 mg porous carbon simples, 1mg acetylene black, and
1 mg polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) binder (Aladdin Industrial Corporation, Shanghai,
China) were mixed at a specific mass ratio of 8:1:1. The mixture was dispersed in anhydrous
ethanol, serving as an emulsion-breaking agent, and thoroughly ground using a mortar
and pestle to ensure homogeneity. The resulting composite, once uniformly ground, was
then coated onto the square area (measuring 1.0 × 1.0 cm) of a nickel foam (AR, Tianjin
Kemio Chemical Reagent Co., Ltd., Tianjin, China) sheet (measuring 1.0 × 2.0 cm). Finally,
1 × 1.5 cm nickel foam was used to cover the electrode material and the whole electrode
slice pressed into a thin sheet under moderate pressure (10–20 MPa). For the two-electrode
system, while maintaining the same method for the synthesis of the electrode slice, a
polypropylene diaphragm was chosen for the construction of the symmetrical capacitors.
3.3.2. Electrochemical Performance Measurements
The electrochemical evaluations encompassed cyclic voltammetry (CV), galvanostatic
charge–discharge (GCD), and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) reactions and
cycling stability tests at room temperature, executed on an electrochemical workstation
(CHI760E Chenhua, Shanghai, China). In the three-electrode setup, Pt and HgO/Hg served
as the counter and reference electrodes, respectively, with 6 M KOH as the electrolyte. For
the two-electrode configuration, a simulated double-layer capacitor was assembled with
two identical 1.0 × 1.0 cm carbon electrodes separated by a polypropylene diaphragm,
also utilizing 6 M KOH. EIS measurements were conducted at frequencies spanning from
0.1 Hz to 100 kHz, with an amplitude of 5 mV .

4. Conclusions
Herein, the present work demonstrated an easy and value-added utilization strategy
for sports waste by co-HTC and pyrolysis activation. M-3-25 reached an ultrahigh specific
capacitance of 587.14 F g−1 at 1 A g−1 and, after 10,000 cycles, its retention rate was high as
91.39% at a current density of 10 A g−1. In addition, the symmetrical supercapacitor M-3-
25//M-3-25 also exhibited an excellent energy density of 42.16 W h kg−1 when the power
density was 398.17 W kg −1 in the 6 M KOH electrolyte, which indicated an exceptional
overall supercapacitor performance. Remarkably, compared with biochar from a single
feedstock and typical biochar-based supercapacitors on the market (the energy/power
density is usually 1–10 Wh/kg/<10,000 W/kg), when incorporating discarded badminton
feathers as auxiliary materials into the hydrothermal carbonization process of pine saw-
dust, the obtained nanoporous biochar after pyrolysis activation displayed a superior
porous structure and electrochemistry performance. Given the obstacles to managing
huge amounts of sports waste, this work delivers a promising strategy for optimization
of the resource utilization of sports waste, which offers an environmentally friendly and
sustainable pathway that enables concurrent disposal of multiple solid waste biomass and
synthesis of functional biochar-based electrode materials.

segments.text: 1. Introduction With the swift advancements in global science and technology coupled with the accelerated pace of industrialization, a substantial quantity of sports and daily necessities have been manufactured to cater to the demands of individuals for sports training and for work or day-to-day life [ 1 , 2 , 3 ]. However, the lack of proper measures for effective resource utilization has led to waste of recyclable resources, the occupation and pollution of land resources, and the destruction of ecological balance [ 4 , 5 , 6 ]. The recently concluded Paris Olympic Games garnered extensive attention towards solid waste management and associated environmental challenges [ 7 ]. The Olympic Games leverage a significant amount of infrastructure that utilizes waste plastic, cardboard, wood, and other materials as environmental protection measures, largely reducing carbon emissions and minimizing environmental pollution [ 8 ]. Globally, 2.01 billion tons of waste is generated annually and by 2050 this is estimated to hit 3.4 billion tons. Lignocellulosic biomass comprises almost 63% of the total waste mass [ 9 ]. Materials with high resource recovery value derived from used sporting goods waste and infrastructures, such as badminton feathers, wood, pine sawdust, etc., are still not effectively recycled. Due to the high global demand for wood and the widespread distribution of the wood processing industry, the amount of discarded pine sawdust is considerable [ 10 , 11 ]. Failure to devise an effective strategy for managing this sporting goods waste not only undermines the objective of green and sustainable development but also constitutes an additional waste of resources and energy. Since the industrial revolution, the excessive consumption of fossil fuels, including coal, oil, and natural gas, has triggered global environmental problems, encompassing an energy crisis and global warming, which has stimulated the exploration of new alternative energy sources [ 12 , 13 , 14 ]. Supercapacitors (SCs) with fast charging speed, long cycle life, high energy density and power density, and geared towards green environmental protection, provide a promising method for the rapid storage of renewable energy and show a wide range of applications in new energy power generation systems, consumer electronics, automotive transportation and other fields [ 15 , 16 , 17 ]. Feathers from poultry used in badminton, such as goose feathers, chicken feathers, duck feathers, etc., have an extremely high nitrogen content [ 18 ]. Doping them into biochar as an exogenous nitrogen element can not only omit the chemical nitrogen doping steps, but also increase the content of heteroatoms in biochar, enrich its pore structure and surface active sites, and improve its stability [ 19 , 20 , 21 , 22 ]. How to utilize discarded sports equipment, specifically badminton shuttlecocks, as a potential recyclable resource and to compound it as an auxiliary material into the preparation process for biochar, proposing reasonable resource utilization measures, and producing excellent nitrogen-rich electrode materials, is a project full of hope and challenge. Based on the need to improve the performance of supercapacitors, the doping of nitrogen, oxygen, and other heteroatoms in biochar is regarded as an effective method to effectively enhance the performance of carbon-based supercapacitors [ 23 , 24 ]. For example, Geng et al. [ 25 ] used  Spirulina platensis  as the carbon and nitrogen source to prepare porous carbon, which showed abundant heteroatomic oxygen (13.78%) and nitrogen (2.55%) and had an exceptional capacitance of 348 F g −1 . Yu et al. [ 26 ] synthesized P-doped hierarchical porous carbon by using  Typha orientalis  leaves with high phosphorus content, possessing a large specific surface area (SSA) of 1975 m 2  g −1  and a high specific capacitance of 324 F g −1  provided by P self-doping. Samage et al. [ 27 ] researched N, O, and Fe self-doped electro-active carbon material for zinc-ion hybrid capacitor derived Solanum melongena, which delivered an excellent specific capacitance of 313.08 F/g. However, most reports have only concentrated on how to dope more heteroatoms to enhance the electrochemical performance of supercapacitors, ignoring the importance of circular stability and sustainability and not proposing a promising approach for addressing the large amount of solid waste with potential for recycling. Although the doping of elements such as nitrogen and oxygen can induce pseudo-capacitance effects, it simultaneously introduces irreversible redox reactions [ 28 , 29 ]. While these reactions may initially elevate the total specific capacitance by augmenting pseudo-capacitance, their irreversible nature leads to the gradual diminution of pseudo-capacitance over numerous constant current charge–discharge cycles, ultimately resulting in capacitance degradation [ 30 , 31 ]. Therefore, apart from pursuing the high specific capacitance of biochar, how to endow it with circular stability, sustainability, and as an effective measure to deal with the recycling potential of sports solid waste is also worth noting.  To fill this gap, we propose a promising strategy for sports waste disposal by using co-hydrothermal carbonization, simultaneously resolving the problem of the issue of sports waste and enhancing the electrochemical performance of supercapacitors. Nanoporous biochar was prepared by incorporating discarded badminton feathers as auxiliary materials into the hydrothermal carbonization process of pine sawdust containing heavy metals. To gain a deeper understanding of the effects of the raw material ratio and reaction conditions, morphological characteristics, pore size distribution, elemental analysis, and phase analysis of the as-synthesized hydro-char and porous carbon materials were investigated. Furthermore, the electrochemical properties of the samples were also explored. In addition to providing a promising countermeasure against the resource waste from sports, this study also helps to expand our current understanding of the co-HTC of different forms of biomass to more easily prepare high-performance electrochemical energy storage materials.

segments.text: 2. Results and Discussion 2.1. Physical and Chemical Characterization of Nanoporous Activated Biochar Material In order to investigate the morphological structure of the prepared carbon materials, the surface morphological structure of the most representative nanoporous carbon and hydro-char samples was observed by SEM, revealing the influence of raw material ratio and reaction conditions on the surface texture of carbon materials ( Figure 1 ). In  Figure 1 a, the inactivated hydro-char M-25 shows a pyknotic structure with a rough surface and no pore size, which affects its application in the field of electrochemistry. Activated carbon material M-2-25 ( Figure 1 b) has a porous structure with a variety of pore shapes, but the distribution of these pores is not uniform enough, indicating that the degree of activation is not complete. At a higher activation ratio, a more developed pore structure of M-3-25 was observed ( Figure 1 c). This pore structure was more evenly distributed on the “honeycomb-like” porous carbon, compared to other samples. The developed pore structure and the addition of heavy metal elements can adjust the electrochemical activity and specific surface area of the electrode material, optimizing the electrochemical performance [ 32 , 33 ]. Energy dispersive spectral analysis (EDS) was carried out on M-3-25 ( Figure S1 ,  Supplementary Materials ). The results of element spectra showed that the distribution of C, N, O, and Cu elements was uniform, indicating that the nitrogen and heavy metal elements were successfully doped into the nanoporous biochar in the process of sample preparation. With the increase of Cu content in the sample, there are obvious granular sediments in some pores of M-3-50, which occupy the pore structure of nanoporous carbon ( Figure 1 d). A clogged pore can lead to a decrease in specific surface area and active sites, the blockage of ion transport, and a decrease in electrochemical stability. The M-4-25 ( Figure S2 ) showed a collapsed pore structure, the relatively poor pore structure indicating that too high an activation ratio is not conducive to the development of the pore structure. Compared with pine sawdust not compounded with goose feather, the sample with moderate heavy metal content after composite (M-3-25) has the best morphology and best developed pore structure, which has great potential for electrochemical application. The specific surface area and pore structure distribution of activated carbon samples were analyzed by the N 2  absorption–desorption method. All samples showed a combination of types I and IV isotherms ( Figure 2 a), and hysteresis loops were relatively insignificant, possibly because pore size distribution in the material was relatively uniform and microporous [ 34 , 35 ], which is consistent with the results in  Table 1 . At low relative pressure (P/P 0  < 0.05), the isotherms exhibited a sharp increase in adsorption capacity, indicating the presence of abundant micropores. However, at high relative pressure (P/P 0  > 0.4), the adsorption and desorption processes are not completely reversible, and there is a weak hysteresis effect, which is shown as an H4 hysteresis loop with a certain mesoporous structure. All the samples had abundant hierarchical microporous (under 2 nm) and mesoporous (2–50 nm) structures ( Figure 2 b). The high specific surface microporous area increases the contact area between the electrode and the electrolyte, improving the charge transport and the electrochemical reaction rate. At the same time, the mesopore provides enough space for the ion transport in the material, which means that the prepared carbon material can be used as an excellent ion transport channel and improve electrochemical performance [ 36 , 37 ]. The rise in specific surface area of PS-3-0 and M-3-0 (1327.36 and 2309.43 m 2 /g) is due to feather biomass, as an additional auxiliary material, having a high protein and nitrogen content. During pyrolysis, these elements form volatile nitrogen compounds that deposit in pores, enhancing pore size distribution and complexity [ 38 ]. For M-2-25 and M-4-25, the increase in the proportion of activators enables more KOH to participate in the pyrolysis reaction and produce more H 2 , CO 2 , etc., which contributes to the generation of micropores and mesopores. Nevertheless, at excessive KOH, the carbon skeleton of M-4-25 may be destroyed by KOH erosion, and the pore structure collapses to form a blockage, which cannot effectively improve electrochemical performance. In addition, we found that, with the increase of Cu content in the sample, the specific surface of M-3-0, M-3-25, and M-3-50 continued to decline, (2309.43, 25.1.08, 1555.15 m 2  g −1 ). This is because, when the dose of copper is small, the uniform distribution of copper particles has little influence on the pore channels. At the same time, the catalytic action of copper particles may promote the graphitization of carbon materials, and at the same time produce gases, leaving micropores in the carbon materials. When the dose of copper increases, more copper particles block the pore structure on the surface of the carbon material, resulting in a decrease in the specific surface area [ 39 , 40 ]. Overall, the activated carbon materials have a high specific surface area and abundant pore structure. Activation ratio and heavy metal content can affect the structural properties of nanoporous carbon, and then affect its electrochemical performance. The performance of the activated carbon electrode material was well regulated by adjusting the two reaction conditions. The elemental composition and yield of hydro-char and activated carbon obtained from the raw materials after hydrothermal conversion and pyrolytic activation are shown in  Table 2 .  Figure 3 a shows the Van Krevelen diagram. After HTC, the O/C of Pine Sawdust decreased from 0.75 to 0.38, indicating that dehydration and decarboxylation reactions occurred during HTC [ 41 ]. The H/C of hydro-chars showed a declining trend with the addition of goose feather in co-HTC, while the O/C showed a fluctuating trend. In the subsequent process of high temperature pyrolysis activation, hydrogen and oxygen elements in biological carbon are gradually removed, resulting in a decrease in the ratio of H/C and O/C in activated carbon, and an increase in the degree of aromatization. The improvement in the degree of aromatization of biochar makes the carbon atoms in biochar more closely arranged, forming a more perfect conductive network, stronger electron supply capacity, and higher chemical stability, which helps to improve the electrochemical performance of carbon materials [ 42 , 43 , 44 ]. Figure 3 b shows the Raman spectrum of the samples. The peaks around 1367 and 1605 cm −1  correspond to the D and G bands, respectively. The D band corresponds to the disordered carbon structure, while the G band is related to the graphitic carbon of the as-prepared sample. The intensity ratio of D to G peaks (I D /I G ) of the M-3-0 and PS-3-0 are 0.95 and 0.87, indicating that the Co-HTC of feathers with high nitrogen content contributes to the increase of disordered carbon [ 45 ]. The I D /I G  ratios of M-3-0 and M-3-25 were 0.95 and 1.02, respectively, showing that a moderate amount of Cu can increase the graphitization degree of the samples, thus enhancing the specific surface area and electrochemical performance of the electrode material. The crystallinity and phase purity of the prepared electrode material were analyzed by powder X-ray diffraction (XRD). The peaks in  Figure 3 c show the XRD patterns of the samples, in which the peaks of Cu 2 O (PDF#05-0667) and Cu (PDF#04-0836) are associated with the cubic phase structure [ 46 ]. By comparing the XRD pattern of the M-3-25 with the above standard PDF card, the peak is found at 2θ values 43.3° and 50.5°, attributed to the (111) and (200) planes, respectively, which proves the formation of Cu. Similarly, the peak at 2θ values 36.5° and 42.1° are attributed to the (111) plane, demonstrating the formation of Cu 2 O. Meanwhile, for M-3-0 and PS-3-0, no heavy metals were detected. The wide peaks in the 2θ range of 15–25° are correlated with the nanoporous structure of the material. The chemical and electronic states, and elemental composition, of nanoporous biochar samples M-3-25, M-3-0, and PS-3-0 were analyzed by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS). The full-scan XPS spectra in  Figure 4 a revealed that M-3-25 contains Cu (Cu 2p), O (O 1s), C (1s), etc. Deconvoluting the high-resolution spectra was performed by Gaussian fitting method.  Figure 4 b shows the existence of deoxygenated carbon (C-C) at 284.80 eV, oxygenated carbon (C-O, 285.50 eV), and (C=O, 288.81 eV) [ 46 , 47 ]. The O1s signal of M-3-25 is shown in  Figure 4 c, and the O 1s spectra are deconvoluted into two oxygen-based components: O-C (531.50 eV) and O=C (533.71 eV) [ 48 , 49 ]. The oxygen-containing groups increase the force between biochar and aqueous electrolytes and improve the wettability and interfacial stability of carbon materials [ 50 , 51 ].  Figure 4 d shows the high-resolution Cu 2p spectrum of M-3-25. The two peaks at binding energies of 933.97 and 952.97 eV are ascribed to Cu +  of Cu 2 O. Similarly, the other two peaks at binding energies of 935.51 and 955.17 eV are ascribed to Cu 2+  of CuO [ 47 , 52 ]. Moreover, the noticeable satellite peaks at 944.71 eV are related to CuO, and the peaks at 963.12 eV are related to Cu 2 O [ 53 ]. The XPS analysis of samples further supports the XRD results and confirm the successful synthesis of incorporated nanoporous biochar electrode materials. 2.2. Electrochemical Performance of Three Electrodes To explore the charge storage behavior of the prepared samples in supercapacitors, cyclic voltammetry (CV), galvanostatic charge–discharge (GCD) tests, and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) were first performed on a three-electrode system and a two-electrode system in a 6M KOH electrolyte solution. The GCD curves of five samples at a current density of 1 A g −1  are presented in  Figure 5 a. All GCD curves exhibited an almost isosceles triangular shape, indicating excellent charge–discharge characteristics and electrochemical reversibility. For samples containing heavy metals, we found that the GCD curve would bend slightly during the charge and discharge process, especially on the samples of M-3-25 and M-3-50, while this was not the case for other samples. This is because the presence of heavy metals may change the microstructure of electrode materials, such as specific surface area and pore structure, and participate in the electrochemical reaction as an active site, thus affecting the efficiency and path of the electrochemical reaction, resulting in the bending of the GCD curve [ 54 ].  Figure 5 b shows the GCD curves of M-3-25 at different current densities. All GCD curves maintained relative symmetry, revealing great electrochemical reversibility, the stability of electrode materials, and the effective transfer of ions at the electrode–electrolyte interface. At the scan rate of 20 mV s  −1 , different samples showed different CV curve shapes  Figure 5 c. Notably, M-3-50 exhibited the largest CV integral area and the longest charge–discharge time ( Figure 5 a,c), confirming the highest charge storage capacity. However, elevated heavy metal content in the M-3-50 altered its carbon structure, changing parameters like grain size, surface area, and pore size, resulting in the distortion of the GCD curve, leading to excessive fluctuations and unstable charge–discharge cycles. To sum up, M-3-25 exhibited less fluctuation, more stability, and better overall performance in the electrochemistry test, possessing excellent asymmetric rectangular shapes, and indicating a fast electrochemical reaction and the behavior of dominant EDLCs. The CV curves of M-3-25 at scan rates (5–200 mV s −1 ) are shown in  Figure 5 d. The CV curve maintained approximately a rectangular shape at low scan rates (5–10 mV s −1 ), indicating its quick ion transport capability. With the increase in scanning rate, the CV curve shows a tendency to distort because, at a high scanning rate, ion diffusion is limited, resulting in uneven electrode surface charge and CV curve deformation [ 55 , 56 ]. The specific capacitance at different current densities (0.5–20 A g −1 ) was calculated according to the discharge curve and equation (1).  Figure 5 e shows the specific capacitance of M-3-25 at different current densities. Apparently, M-3-25 exhibits ultrahigh specific capacitance (581.74 F g −1 ) at a current density of 1 A g −1 , indicating its phenomenal charge storage capacity. The cyclic stability of M-3-25 was tested at 10 A g −1  ( Figure 5 f). The capacitance of M-3-25 could still be maintained at 91.39% after 10,000 cycles, demonstrating its excellent cyclic performance. EIS measurements of three samples were studied to evaluate electrochemical performance. The equivalent circuit diagram is shown in  Figure S3 , where R s  denotes the equivalent series and R ct  represents the charge transfer resistances. Notably, within the low-frequency spectrum, a trendline with an inclination was observed, which corresponds to the Warburg impedance (W). The Warburg impedance is intimately linked to the diffusion coefficient of the charge-carrying substance within the solution [ 57 ]. The Nyquist plots in  Figure 6  show approximately vertical lines in the low-frequency region, revealing their excellent EDLC behavior [ 58 ]. Specifically, M-3-25 exhibited significantly reduced R s  (0.805 U) and R ct  (0.077 U), indicative of its low internal resistance and superior conductivity. This diminished internal resistance further minimized thermal losses, potentially extending the operational lifespan of M-3-25. 2.3. Electrochemical Performance of Two Electrodes To further evaluate the performance of M-3-25, we assembled a symmetric supercapacitor M-3-25//M-3-25 using 6 M KOH as the electrolyte. The CV test was performed in the voltage window of 0-1.8 V at a scan rate of 20 mV s −1  ( Figure 7 a) to test the rate performance of the symmetric supercapacitor. The emergence of the anode current in the CV curve upon increasing the voltage window to 1.3 V suggested the stable operation of the symmetric supercapacitor within the voltage range of 0–1.3 V. As depicted in  Figure 7 b, the CV curves exhibited a well-maintained rectangular shape across varying scan rates, thereby validating the superior capacitive properties of prepared nanoporous carbon materials [ 56 ]. Additionally, the GCD curves and the specific capacitance at different current densities ( Figure 7 c,d and Equation (2)) revealed an isosceles triangular profile at different current densities, indicative of the symmetric supercapacitor’s excellent rate capability and rapid reversibility during charging and discharging. Notably, the specific capacitance of the symmetric supercapacitor attained a peak value of 630.6 F g −1  at a current density of 1 A g −1 , underscoring its remarkable charge storage capability. To assess the comprehensive performance of the M-3-25//M-3-25 configuration, we derived the relationship between energy density and power density from the GCD curves, through Equations (3) and (4), respectively, as illustrated in  Figure 7 e. It is worth noting that the energy density achieved a peak value of 42.16 W h kg −1  at a power density of 398.17 W kg −1 , and it maintained a commendable value of 12.75 W h kg −1  even at a significantly higher power density of 6463.30 W kg −1 . Overall, the two-electrode system of the M-3-25 possesses high capacity, excellent cycle stability, and superior rate performance.  Table 3  lists the performances of some recently reported biomass electrode materials in the literature, among which the M-3–25 demonstrates significant advantages, which exhibit outstanding physicochemical structure, exceptional electrochemical characteristics, and promising applications of the investigated biochar electrode materials.

3. Materials and Methods 3.1. Synthesis of Nanoporous Activated Biochar The raw materials, goose feathers and waste pine sawdust, were collected from discarded badminton and a furniture factory in China (Henan, Kaifeng), respectively.  Figure 8  details the synthesis of nanoporous biochar samples. First, the waste pine sawdust and badminton feathers were dried in an oven at 80 °C for 12 h to a constant weight. The dried raw materials were then ground further in the crusher and passed through an 80-mesh sieve. To accurately adjust the effect of heavy metals throughout the experiment, the Cu-contaminated plants used in the reactions were synthesized using appropriate amounts of Cu and crushed pine sawdust according to reported methods [ 59 , 60 , 61 ]. The desired amounts of crushed pine sawdust and CuSO 4 ·5H 2 O (Aladdin Industrial Corporation in Shanghai, China) were mixed in a beaker and stirred vigorously at 500 rpm for 6 h. The resulting mixtures (0, 25, 50 mg Cu/g biomass) and crushed badminton feathers were utilized together in the first step Co-HTC reaction. Then, 150 mL of ultrapure water and the desired amounts of Cu-contaminated plants (composed of 7.5 g of pine sawdust and the desired amount of Cu) and 7.5g badminton feathers were loaded into a 250 mL autoclave and heated up to 240 °C for 120 min. After the reactor had cooled down to room temperature, the HTC products were filtered with deionized water three times and poured into a culture dish, which was then dried to a constant weight at 80 °C for 12 h for further experiments. The dried solid HTC products were named PS-X and M-Y (pine sawdust and mixture), where X and Y represent the Cu content (mg) per gram in pine sawdust (X or Y = 0, 25, 50). Using KOH (AR, Tianjin Kemio Chemical Reagent Co., Ltd., Tianjin, China) as the activator, the prepared hydro-char was mixed with KOH at weight ratios of 1: Z (Z = 2, 3, or 4) in a mortar and ground into the powder. The mixture was then placed in a nickel crucible and subjected to activation in a nitrogen atmosphere (25 mL min −1 ). The temperature was increased at a heating rate of 10 °C min −1  to 700 °C and held for 1 h. Then, the sample was naturally cooled to room temperature in a tubular furnace (CHY-1200, Henan Chengyi Equipment Technology Co., Ltd., Zhengzhou, China) under a nitrogen atmosphere. The activated sample was filtered three times with 0.1 M hydrochloric acid and deionized water three times until neutralized. The washed sample was dried in a culture dish at 80 °C to a constant weight. The activated samples were named PS-Z-Y and M-Z-Y, where Z represents the weight ratio of KOH (Z = 2, 3, or 4), and Y represents the Cu content (mg) per gram in pine sawdust (Y = 0, 25, 50). All experiments were conducted three times to ensure reproducibility. 3.2. Materials Characterization The morphological structure of the samples was examined utilizing a field emission scanning electron microscope (SEM, ZEISS Gemini SEM 500, Oberkochen, Germany), and energy diffraction spectroscopy (EDS) was used to investigate the elemental composition. The specific surface area of the nanoporous biochar was analyzed employing the multipoint Brunauer–Emmett–Teller (BET, V-Sorb 2800P, Gold APP Instruments, Xi’an, China) method. The total pore volume (Vt) was calculated based on nitrogen adsorption measurements at a relative pressure of 0.99. The pore size distribution was determined using the Barrett–Joyner–Halenda method. The elemental contents of carbon (C), hydrogen (H), and nitrogen (N) in the samples were analyzed with an elemental analyzer (Elementar Vario EL cube, Frankfurt, Germany). The surface elemental composition and chemical groups of the nanoporous biochar samples were exhaustively characterized via X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS, AXIS SUPRA + , SHIMADZU, Buckinghamshire, UK). The crystal structure was systematically investigated using an X-ray diffractometer (D8-ADVANCE, Bruker, Dresden, Germany). Furthermore, Raman spectroscopic analysis was performed with a laser micro-Raman spectrometer (Renishaw, Wotton-under-Edge, UK). 3.3. Electrochemical Measurements 3.3.1. Electrode Preparation For the three-electrode system, 8 mg porous carbon simples, 1mg acetylene black, and 1 mg polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) binder (Aladdin Industrial Corporation, Shanghai, China) were mixed at a specific mass ratio of 8:1:1. The mixture was dispersed in anhydrous ethanol, serving as an emulsion-breaking agent, and thoroughly ground using a mortar and pestle to ensure homogeneity. The resulting composite, once uniformly ground, was then coated onto the square area (measuring 1.0 × 1.0 cm) of a nickel foam (AR, Tianjin Kemio Chemical Reagent Co., Ltd., Tianjin, China) sheet (measuring 1.0 × 2.0 cm). Finally, 1 × 1.5 cm nickel foam was used to cover the electrode material and the whole electrode slice pressed into a thin sheet under moderate pressure (10–20 MPa). For the two-electrode system, while maintaining the same method for the synthesis of the electrode slice, a polypropylene diaphragm was chosen for the construction of the symmetrical capacitors. 3.3.2. Electrochemical Performance Measurements The electrochemical evaluations encompassed cyclic voltammetry (CV), galvanostatic charge–discharge (GCD), and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) reactions and cycling stability tests at room temperature, executed on an electrochemical workstation (CHI760E Chenhua, Shanghai, China). In the three-electrode setup, Pt and HgO/Hg served as the counter and reference electrodes, respectively, with 6 M KOH as the electrolyte. For the two-electrode configuration, a simulated double-layer capacitor was assembled with two identical 1.0 × 1.0 cm carbon electrodes separated by a polypropylene diaphragm, also utilizing 6 M KOH. segments.text: 3.1. Synthesis of Nanoporous Activated Biochar The raw materials, goose feathers and waste pine sawdust, were collected from discarded badminton and a furniture factory in China (Henan, Kaifeng), respectively.  Figure 8  details the synthesis of nanoporous biochar samples. First, the waste pine sawdust and badminton feathers were dried in an oven at 80 °C for 12 h to a constant weight. The dried raw materials were then ground further in the crusher and passed through an 80-mesh sieve. To accurately adjust the effect of heavy metals throughout the experiment, the Cu-contaminated plants used in the reactions were synthesized using appropriate amounts of Cu and crushed pine sawdust according to reported methods [ 59 , 60 , 61 ]. The desired amounts of crushed pine sawdust and CuSO 4 ·5H 2 O (Aladdin Industrial Corporation in Shanghai, China) were mixed in a beaker and stirred vigorously at 500 rpm for 6 h. The resulting mixtures (0, 25, 50 mg Cu/g biomass) and crushed badminton feathers were utilized together in the first step Co-HTC reaction. Then, 150 mL of ultrapure water and the desired amounts of Cu-contaminated plants (composed of 7.5 g of pine sawdust and the desired amount of Cu) and 7.5g badminton feathers were loaded into a 250 mL autoclave and heated up to 240 °C for 120 min. After the reactor had cooled down to room temperature, the HTC products were filtered with deionized water three times and poured into a culture dish, which was then dried to a constant weight at 80 °C for 12 h for further experiments. The dried solid HTC products were named PS-X and M-Y (pine sawdust and mixture), where X and Y represent the Cu content (mg) per gram in pine sawdust (X or Y = 0, 25, 50). Using KOH (AR, Tianjin Kemio Chemical Reagent Co., Ltd., Tianjin, China) as the activator, the prepared hydro-char was mixed with KOH at weight ratios of 1: Z (Z = 2, 3, or 4) in a mortar and ground into the powder. The mixture was then placed in a nickel crucible and subjected to activation in a nitrogen atmosphere (25 mL min −1 ). The temperature was increased at a heating rate of 10 °C min −1  to 700 °C and held for 1 h. Then, the sample was naturally cooled to room temperature in a tubular furnace (CHY-1200, Henan Chengyi Equipment Technology Co., Ltd., Zhengzhou, China) under a nitrogen atmosphere. The activated sample was filtered three times with 0.1 M hydrochloric acid and deionized water three times until neutralized. The washed sample was dried in a culture dish at 80 °C to a constant weight. The activated samples were named PS-Z-Y and M-Z-Y, where Z represents the weight ratio of KOH (Z = 2, 3, or 4), and Y represents the Cu content (mg) per gram in pine sawdust (Y = 0, 25, 50). All experiments were conducted three times to ensure reproducibility.

Materials Characterization The morphological structure of the samples was examined utilizing a field emission scanning electron microscope (SEM, ZEISS Gemini SEM 500, Oberkochen, Germany), and energy diffraction spectroscopy (EDS) was used to investigate the elemental composition. The crystal structure was systematically investigated using an X-ray diffractometer (D8-ADVANCE, Bruker, Dresden, Germany). Furthermore, Raman spectroscopic analysis was performed with a laser micro-Raman spectrometer (Renishaw, Wotton-under-Edge, UK).

segments.text: 4. Conclusions Herein, the present work demonstrated an easy and value-added utilization strategy for sports waste by co-HTC and pyrolysis activation. M-3-25 reached an ultrahigh specific capacitance of 587.14 F g −1  at 1 A g −1  and, after 10,000 cycles, its retention rate was high as 91.39% at a current density of 10 A g −1 . In addition, the symmetrical supercapacitor M-3-25//M-3-25 also exhibited an excellent energy density of 42.16 W h kg −1  when the power density was 398.17 W kg −1  in the 6 M KOH electrolyte, which indicated an exceptional overall supercapacitor performance. Remarkably, compared with biochar from a single feedstock and typical biochar-based supercapacitors on the market (the energy/power density is usually 1–10 Wh/kg/<10,000 W/kg), when incorporating discarded badminton feathers as auxiliary materials into the hydrothermal carbonization process of pine sawdust, the obtained nanoporous biochar after pyrolysis activation displayed a superior porous structure and electrochemistry performance. Given the obstacles to managing huge amounts of sports waste, this work delivers a promising strategy for optimization of the resource utilization of sports waste, which offers an environmentally friendly and sustainable pathway that enables concurrent disposal of multiple solid waste biomass and synthesis of functional biochar-based electrode materials.

NaOH-Activated Bamboo Carbon with Hierarchical Porosity for High-
Performance Electrochemical Capacitors 
 
E. C. Udochukwu1,2*, O. E. Onyelucheya1, A. C. Orga1,3 and I. S. Ike1, 3 
Department of Chemical Engineering, Federal University of Technology, Owerri, Nigeria1 
Department of Chemical Engineering, Federal University Otuoke, Bayelsa2 
African Centre of Excellence in Future Energies and Electrochemical Systems (ACE-FUELS), Federal University of Technology, 
Owerri, Nigeria3 
Corresponding Author*: udochukwuec@fuotuoke.edu.ng 
 
1. Introduction 
The global shift toward sustainable energy systems necessitates the development of advanced 
energy storage technologies capable of mitigating the intermittent nature of renewable energy 
sources such as solar and wind [1], [2] . Electrochemical capacitors (ECs), commonly known as 
supercapacitors, have gained significant attention as promising candidates in this transition due to 
their high-power density, fast charge–discharge rates, and excellent cycle stability [3]. Compared to 
conventional batteries, ECs offer superior operational safety and reliability; however, their relatively 
low energy density continues to constrain their widespread adoption in large -scale ap plications, 
including electric vehicles and grid-level energy storage systems. 
Article information  Abstract 
 
Article History 
Received 08 October 2025 
Revised   27 October 2025 
Accepted 18 November 2025 
Available online 02 December 2025 
 This work reports the development of an electrode material derived from 
bamboo stem via NaOH activation, integrating hierarchical porosity, and 
surface functionalization for electrochemical capacitor applications. The 
synthesized carbon exhibits a flaky, fibrous morphology with micro –
mesoporous networks as confirmed by SEM, and a predominantly 
amorphous structure with short -range graphitic ordering from XRD. 
Elemental analysis via EDS reveals a high ca rbon content (94.65%) and 
nitrogen content (3.4%), which enhances charge storage and electrical 
conductivity. BET and BJH analyses indicate a high surface area (865 –
1147 m²/g), a pore volume of 0.552 cm³/g, and an average pore diameter 
of 2.43 nm, favourab le for ion diffusion and electrolyte access. 
Electrochemical testing demonstrates a high specific capacitance of 833 
F/g at 0.5 A/g, attributed to combined electric double -layer capacitance 
and pseudocapacitive contributions from oxygen- and nitrogen-containing 
functional groups, as evidenced by FTIR and CV (b = 0.787; 21% 
diffusion-controlled contribution). Electrochemical impedance 
spectroscopy shows a low equivalent series resistance of 0.2 Ω, while 
charge–discharge cycling confirms excellent stability w ith 94% 
capacitance retention after 5000 cycles. The CV and GCD further confirm 
its potency for efficient charge transport and high energy storage 
performance. These findings highlight the potential of bamboo -derived 
activated carbon as a sustainable and c ost-effective electrode material. 
However, the overall energy and power densities remain constrained by 
the narrow voltage window of the aqueous electrolyte and the limited 
cycling evaluation, indicating the need for further study with other 
electrolytes with higher voltage window and long-term testing. 
 
 
Keywords: 
Electrochemical energy storage, Extra 
capacitance from surface reactions, 
NaOH treatment, Nitrogen-doped 
carbon, Porous structures

7(4) 2025 pp. 184-203 
185 
 
 
ECc store energy through two primary mechanisms: electrical double -layer capacitance (EDLC) 
[4], wh ich involves non -faradaic ion adsorption at the electrode/electrolyte interface, and 
pseudocapacitance, which results from faradaic redox reactions associated with surface functional 
groups or transition metal compounds [5], [6]. The overall performance of ECs is largely dependent 
on the intrinsic properties of the electrode material, particularly its specific surface area, pore 
structure, electrical conductivity, and surface chemistry [7]. Among various c andidates, carbon-
based materials have emerged as the dominant class for supercapacitor electrodes, owing to their 
high surface area, tunable porosity, low density, and excellent chemical stability [8]. However, 
conventional activated carbons are often derived from fossil -based or synthetic precursors, raising 
environmental and economic concerns that conflict with the broader goals of sustainability and 
carbon neutrality [9]. 
 
In response, there has been a growing inter est in biomass -derived carbons as eco -friendly 
alternatives that align with circular economy principles [10]. Biomass precursors, including coconut 
shells, rice husks, sawdust, and corn stalks, have demonstrated promising performance when 
properly activated and functionalized [11]. Among these, bamboo has emerged as a particularly 
attractive candidate due to its fast growth rate (up to 1 m/day in some species), abundant availability 
in tropical and subtropical regions, and favourable lignocellulosic composition [12]. Rich in 
cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin, bamboo biomass provides a carbon-rich framework suitable for 
conversion into porous carbon structures. Its naturally hierarchical vascular architecture further aids 
the deve lopment of interconnected micro -, meso -, and macropores essential for efficient ion 
transport and charge accumulation [13]. 
 
Despite its potential, the use of bamboo-derived carbon in supercapacitors remains underexplored, 
particularly in the context of tailored chemical activation and heteroatom doping. Previous studies 
have reported specific capacitance values ranging from 150 to 400 F/g using physical activation or 
simple pyrolysis [14], which are lower than those achieved with advanced processing techniques. 
One key challenge lies in engineering a pore structure that optimally balan ces micropores (for 
increased surface area and energy density) with mesopores (to facilitate ion diffusion and power 
delivery) [15]. Additionally, improving the surface chemistry through nitrogen and oxygen doping 
can introduce faradaic red ox-active sites, thereby enhancing pseudocapacitive behaviour and total 
capacitance [16]. 
 
Chemical activation using alkali hydroxides, especially NaOH and KOH, has been shown to 
significantly enhance porosity and surface area of carbon materials. NaOH, in particular, reacts 
effectively with carbonaceous precursors to form pore -generating gases and salts, yielding well -
developed hierarchical pore systems [17]. When combined with thermal treatment under inert 
atmosphere, NaOH activation can produce highly porous carbon with tailore d textural and 
electrochemical properties. The incorporation of nitrogen -containing functional groups during 
carbonization or activation, particularly species such as pyridinic-N and pyrrolic-N has been widely 
associated with enhanced electrochemical performance, including increased capacitance, improved 
wettability, and higher electrical conductivity [18]. 
 
This study reports the synthesis of NaOH-activated carbon derived from bamboo waste, specifically 
sourced from discarded scaffold material. The objective was to address the performance limitations 
typically observed in conventional biomass-derived carbons for electrochemical energy storage. The 
precursor underwent controlled pyrolysis  followed by chemical activatio n to induce hierarchical 
porosity. The resulting material was thoroughly characterized using scanning electron microscopy 
(SEM), Brunauer –Emmett–Teller (BET) surface area analysis, Fourier -transform infrared

spectroscopy (FTIR), X-ray diffraction (XRD), en ergy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS), and 
Raman spectroscopy, to investigate its morphology, surface chemistry, and structural features [19]. 
 
Electrochemical performance was assessed through cyclic voltammetry (CV), galvanostatic charge–
discharge (GCD), and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) [20]. The as-prepared carbon 
exhibited a high specific capacitance of 833 F/g, an ultra -low internal resistance of 0.2 Ω, and 
excellent cycling stability with 94% capacitance retention over 5000 cycles. The goal of this study 
is to explore bamboo stem biomass as a potential green, low-cost supercapacitor electrode material. 
 
While the bamboo -derived carbon electrode exhibited a high specific capacitance of 833 F/g, the 
overall energy and power densities remained modest due to the use of an aqueous 6 M KOH 
electrolyte, which inherently limits the operating voltage to 1.0 V. Future studies will explore 
organic or gel-polymer electrolytes to expand the voltage window and unlock higher energy outputs. 
 
2.  Materials and Methods 
 
2.1 Materials 
Dry bamboo stems were sourced locally from a building site as waste materials from a  local 
scaffold. The stems were thoroughly washed with deionized water to remove surface impurities, dirt, 
and residual biomass contaminants. Analytical -grade NaOH were obtained from African University 
of Science and Technology (AUST) Laboratory and used without further purification. Analytical -
grade Hydrochloric Acid (HCl) was used to wash the activated carbon to neutralize residual NaOH.  
 
2.2 Preparation of Bamboo Stem-Derived Activated Carbon 
The cleaned and dried bamboo stems were then ground using a milling machine into fine powder. 
Then sieved using an electric sieve for a uniform particle size of 100 µm to increase surface area for 
subsequent carbonization. 
 
2.2.1  Carbonization 
The powdered bamboo was placed in a ceramic crucible with a lid and heated in a tubular furnace 
under a nitrogen atmosphere to prevent oxidation.  Carbonization was carried out at a t emperature of 
500 °C for 2 hours, with a heating rate of 10 °C/min. This step decomposed the cellulose, 
hemicellulose, and lignin in the bamboo, resulting in a preliminary carbon-rich material. 
 
2.2.2 Chemical Activation 
 After cooling to room temperature, the carbonized bamboo powder was mixed with NaOH at a weight 
ratio of 1:3 (carbonized material: NaOH) in deionized water to create a uniform paste. The mixture 
was stirred thoroughly and then dried in an oven at 110°C for 12 hours to remove any excess wat er. 
The dried sample was subsequently subjected to a second heat treatment in a tubular furnace under a 
nitrogen atmosphere, this time at a higher activation temperature of 800 °C for 1 hour, with a 
controlled heating rate of 5 °C/min. During this step, th e NaOH interacted with the carbon matrix, 
effectively promoting the development of a porous structure and significantly increasing the surface 
area of the material. 
 
2.2.3  Washing and Neutralization 
After activation, the carbon material was carefully remo ved from the furnace and washed multiple 
times with 0.1 M hydrochloric acid to neutralize any residual NaOH and eliminate potential metallic 
impurities. This was followed by thorough rinsing with deionized water until the filtrate reached a 
neutral pH of 7 , ensuring the complete removal of acid and by -products. The cleaned material was 
then oven-dried at 105 °C for 12 hours and subsequently ground into a fine powder, yielding the final 
bamboo-derived activated carbon.

2.3  Characterization of Bamboo Stem-Derived Activated Carbon 
2.3.1 Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM) 
The surface morphology of the activated carbon was analysed using a scanning electron microscope 
(SEM, JEOL JSM -7100F) to assess the formation of pores, variations in pore size distribution, a nd 
the overall surface texture. This provided visual insight into the material's porous architecture 
resulting from the activation process. 
 
2.3.2 Surface Area and Porosity (BET Analysis) 
The Brunauer–Emmett–Teller (BET) method was employed to measure the specific surface area of 
the activated carbon using a nitrogen adsorption -desorption isotherm at 77 K. Pore size distribution 
and total pore volume were determined by the Barrett –Joyner–Halenda (BJH) method, focusing on 
mesopore and micropore distribution. 
 
2.3.3 Surface Functional Groups (FTIR) 
Fourier-Transform Infrared Spectroscopy (FTIR) was conducted to identify the surface functional 
groups present on the activated carbon, as these can play a key role in influencing its electrochemical 
behaviour. The spectra were collected over a wavenumber range of 4000 to 500 cm⁻¹, allowing for 
the detection of various oxygen - and nitrogen-containing groups introduced during activation and 
doping. 
 
2.4 Electrochemical Characterization 
2.4.1 Electrode Preparation 
The bamboo-derived activated carbon was combined with conductive carbon black and 
polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) binder in a weight ratio of 8:1:1 to prepare the electrode material. 
This composition ensured good electrical conductivity and mechanical stability  for subsequent 
electrochemical testing. N -methyl-2-pyrrolidone (NMP) was used as a solvent to create a 
homogeneous slurry, which was then coated onto a cleaned nickel foam current collector and dried at 
80°C for 12 hours. The coated electrodes were pressed to ensure uniform thickness and good contact 
between materials. 
 
2.4.2 Electrochemical Testing 
2.4.1.1 Cyclic Voltammetry (CV) 
CV was performed in a 3-electrode setup using the electrode made from the bamboo-based activated 
carbon infused on nickel foam as current collector, a platinum counter electrode, an  Ag/AgCl 
reference electrode, and a 6 M KOH electrolyte. The potential window was set between 0 to 1.0 V 
(vs. Ag/AgCl) with scan rates ranging from 5 to 100 mV/s to investigate the specific capacitance and

2.4.1.3  Electrochemical Impedance Spectroscopy (EIS) 
Electrochemical Impedance Spectroscopy (EIS) was performed over a frequency range of 0.01 Hz to 
100 kHz to assess internal resistance, ion transport behaviour, and overall electrical conductivity. The 
resulting data were presented as Nyquist plots, which are commonly used to interpret EIS results. For 
the bamboo -derived activat ed carbon, the Nyquist plot provided key insights into the electrode's 
equivalent series resistance (ESR) and ion diffusion characteristics. These findings reflect the 
material's ability to support efficient charge transfer and ion movement, both of which are critical for 
high-performance supercapacitor applications. 
 
3. Results and Discussion 
 
3.1 Surface Area and Porosity Analysis (BET and BJH) 
The textural properties of the bamboo -derived activated carbon were investigated using nitrogen 
adsorption–desorption isotherms at 77 K. Analyses based on the Brunauer –Emmett–Teller (BET) 
method (Figure 1a) and the Barrett –Joyner–Halenda (BJH) model (Figure 1b) provided detailed 
information on the material’s surface area, pore volume, and pore size distribution, key  factors that 
directly influence ion transport and charge storage performance in electrochemical capacitors [21].

3.2 Morphology Analysis (SEM and EDS) 
3.2.1 Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM) Analysis 
The surface morphology of the NaOH -activated bamboo -derived carbon was examined using 
Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM), with images shown in Figure 2a - d at various magnifications. 
The SEM micrographs reveal a highly porous, flaky structure, ch aracterized by interconnected 
networks of micro-, meso-, and macropores. This hierarchical pore architecture is a key feature for 
effective electrochemical capacitor electrodes, as it facilitates both rapid ion transport and efficient 
charge storage [26]. 
 
At lower magnifications (500×–1000×), the surface appears rough and irregular, with large cavities 
and fractured textures resulting from the intense chemical etching during NaOH activation at 800 °C. 
These larger macropores, likely formed through the removal of vola tile components and structural 
decomposition of lignocellulosic biomass, serve as ion -buffering reservoirs that shorten diffusion 
paths between the electrolyte and internal pores. 
 
At higher magnifications (1500× –2000×), the carbon material exhibits micro -sheeted domains and 
fibrous textures, with clear evidence of mesoporous channels and micropore openings. These smaller 
pores significantly increase the specific surface area (BET: 865 –1147 m²/g) and enable double-layer 
formation and fast electrolyte accessibility. The porous walls and fractured surfaces also expose more 
active sites for faradaic reactions, consistent with the pseudocapacitive behaviour observed in CV and 
FTIR analyses. The flaky morphology observed is a typical indicator of layered carbon a ssemblies 
with interconnected pore systems, suggesting good mechanical integrity and electron percolation 
pathways. This contributes to the excellent rate capability and low internal resistance (EIS: 0.2 Ω) 
demonstrated by the electrode.

3.4 Raman Spectroscopy Analysis 
Raman spectroscopy was employed to investigate the structural ordering and degree of graphitization 
in the bamboo -derived activated carbon [29]. As shown in Figure 4, the spectrum displays two 
prominent peaks: the D -band located around 1350 cm⁻¹ and the G -band around 1580 cm⁻¹. The D -
band corresponds to the presence of disordered carbon structures or structural defects associated with 
sp³-hybridized carbon atoms [30], while the G -band arises from the E2g vibrational mode of sp² -
hybridized graphitic carbon domains [31], [32]. 
 
The intensity ratio of the D to G bands (ID/IG) is a widely used metric to evaluate the level of disorder 
and the extent of graphitic structure in carbon -based material s. In this study, the ID/IG ratio was 
calculated to be 0.89, indicating a moderately disordered carbon matrix with the presence of short -

A moderate ID/IG ratio such as this is advantageous for supercapacitor applications. The presence of 
graphitic domains enhances electrical conductivity, while the disordered regions and associated

3.5  X-ray Diffraction (XRD) Analysis 
X-ray diffraction (XRD) was used to investigate the crystallographic structure and degree of 
graphitization of the bamboo -derived activated carbon. The XRD pattern, shown in Figure 5a & b, 
displays a broad diffraction peak centred at approximately 23° (2θ) , which corresponds to the (002) 
plane of turbostratic carbon structures [35]. This broad peak is characteristic of amorphous or 
disordered carbon, commonly observed in biomass-derived carbons subjected to chemical activation. 
The low-intensity and broad nature of the (002) peak indic ates the presence of short-range graphitic 
domains without significant long -range ordering. This structural disorder is beneficial for 
electrochemical applications, as it provides abundant defect sites that can enhance ion accessibility 
and facilitate faradaic reactions. The absence of sharp, well-defined peaks associated with crystalline 
graphite (typically at ~26.5°) confirms that the carbon structure remains largely amorphous, even after 
high-temperature activation at 800 °C under nitrogen atmosphere. 
 
In addition to the dominant amorphous carbon peak, several minor crystalline reflections were 
observed. Weak peaks around 28° –34° (2θ) may be attributed to residual inorganic salts, including 
NaCl (halite) and SiO₂ (silicon oxide), which are likely remnants  from the NaOH activation or 
inherent to the bamboo precursor’s mineral content. Trace peaks related to osumilite and other silicate 
phases were also detected, consistent with prior reports on biomass-derived carbons containing natural 
mineral impurities. 
 
Importantly, the lack of heavy metal oxide residues (e.g., Fe, Ti, Ca) indicates the effectiveness of the 
post-activation washing and purification steps. This contributes to the material’s electrochemical 
stability and minimizes parasitic reactions during cycling. While high crystallinity is often associated 
with better electrical conductivity, the combination of amorphous domains and short -range ordering

activation methods.  Collectively, the comparison underscores a trade -off between maximizing 
specific capacitance and ensuring long -term cycling stability, with material selection and activation 
strategy being decisive factors. Nitrogen -doped bamboo-derived carbons clearly push the limits of 
capacitance, while more conventional precursors such as ginseng and walnut shells offer superior 
cycle life. This suggests that future research should emphasize integrating heteroatom doping or 
hierarchical porosity with processing routes that sustain stability over extended operation, thereby 
bridging the gap between high energy density and device reliability.

3.8  Charge Storage Mechanism and Role of Surface Functionalities 
The superior electrochemical performance observed in the bamboo -derived activated carbon is 
attributed to a hybrid charge storage mechanism, involving both electric double -layer capacitance 
(EDLC) and pseudocapacitance. The EDLC behaviour originates from the physical a dsorption of 
electrolyte ions at the electrode –electrolyte interface, primarily supported by the material's high 
specific surface area (865–1147 m²/g) and hierarchical micro–mesoporous structure, which facilitates 
ion transport and rapid charge–discharge cycles. In addition to EDLC, pseudocapacitive contributions 
play a significant role in enhancing the overall capacitance. These arise from faradaic redox reactions 
involving heteroatoms, notably oxygen and nitrogen-containing functional groups, introduced during 
the NaOH activation and pyrolysis steps. Evidence from FTIR analysis confirms the presence of C=O 
(carbonyl), C–O–C (ether), and O–H (hydroxyl) groups, while EDS and elemental mapping reveal a 
nitrogen content of 3.4 %, mainly as pyridinic-N, pyrrolic-N, and quaternary-N configurations. 
 
These surface functionalities facilitate reversible redox reactions at the electrode surface, contributing 
to pseudocapacitance through the following mechanisms: 
i Oxygen functional groups, particularly carbonyl and hyd roxyl groups, engage in surface 
faradaic reactions such as equation (4): 
> 𝐶 = 𝑂 + 𝐻+ + 𝑒− ↔> 𝐶 − 𝑂𝐻          (4) 
which can reversibly store charge at the carbon/electrolyte interface. 
ii Nitrogen functional groups enhance capacitance in multiple ways: 
▪ Pyridinic-N and pyrrolic -N can act as redox -active centres, contributing directly to 
faradaic reactions. 
▪ Quaternary-N improves electrical conductivity by enhancing the delocalization of π -
electrons within the carbon matrix, facilitating faster electron transport. 
▪ It also enhances wettability, allowing better electrolyte infiltration into the pore network. 
The hybrid behaviour is supported by the CV scan rate analysis, where the b -value of 0.787 and 
diffusion-controlled contribution of 21% indicate mixed charge storage behaviour. This synergy 
between EDLC and pseudocapacitance results in the high specific capacitance (833 F/g at 0.5 A/g) 
and excellent rate capability and cycling stability.

4. Conclusion 
 
In this study, a sustainable and high-performance electrode material was successfully developed from 
bamboo stem biomass using NaOH chemical activation. The resulting carbon featured a hierarchical 
pore structure and a high surface area (BET: 865 m²/g; BJH: 1147 m²/g), along with surface 
functionalities rich in oxygen and nitrogen-containing groups—all of which contributed to its strong 
electrochemical performance. 
 
Detailed structural and morphological analyses showed that the carbon had a flaky, fibrous texture 
with a well -connected network of micro -, meso -, and macropores. This interconnected pore 
architecture plays a crucial role in facilitating efficient ion transport and enabling rapid charge –
discharge behaviour, making the material highly suitable for supercapacitor applications.

FTIR, Raman, and XRD characterizations confirmed the presence of defect -rich amorphous carbon 
domains, redox-active surface groups, and partial graphitic ordering. These features enabled a hybrid 
charge storage mechanism, combining electric double-layer capacitance and pseudocapacitance. 
Electrochemical evaluation demonstrated a remarkably high specific capacitance of 833 F/g at 0.5 
A/g, excellent rate capability, and 94% capacitance  retention after 5000 cycles, highlighting the 
material’s robust stability and energy storage potential. The low equivalent series resistance (0.2 Ω) 
further validated the material’s high conductivity and fast ion diffusion pathways. Compared with 
other recently reported biomass-derived carbons, the bamboo-derived electrode material outperforms 
in terms of both capacitance and sustainability. 
 
This work demonstrates that bamboo stem, an abundant and renewable biomass resource, can serve 
as an effective prec ursor for producing activated carbon with tunable porosity and functional 
chemistry. The green synthesis route, combined with scalable processing, positions this material as a 
promising candidate for next-generation eco-friendly supercapacitor devices. 
Although the bamboo-derived activated carbon demonstrated high specific capacitance and excellent 
short-term cycling stability, the study is limited by the narrow aqueous voltage window and absence 
of long-term or large-scale evaluation. Future work will focu s on optimizing the activation process  
and expanding the voltage window through alternative electrolytes.

30Abstract
31In this study, gold nanoparticles (AuNPs) are deposited onto rice straw-derived activated 
32carbon via ultrasound-assisted irradiation and conventional magnetic stirring to enhance 
33electrochemical performance.  A control experiment demonstrates that ultrasonic irradiation 
34alone introduces structural disorder without improving capacitive behavior, confirming that 
35performance enhancements originate specifically from the incorporated AuNPs.  Transmission 
36electron microscopy reveals that ultrasound-assisted deposition yields uniformly dispersed 
37nanosized AuNPs across the carbon surface, whereas magnetic stirring produces significant 
38particle agglomeration.  X-ray diffraction and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy confirm the 
39formation of crystalline, zero-valent Au⁰ nanoparticles, with the high specific surface area (2180 
40m² g⁻¹) and microporous structure of the carbon support well preserved following Au 
41incorporation.  The optimized electrode, ACAu-20-60-ul, delivers a specific capacitance of 387 
42F g⁻¹ at 0.5 A g⁻¹ in a three-electrode configuration, representing a 66% enhancement over 
43pristine AC700 (233 F g⁻¹).  In a symmetric two-electrode device, ACAu-20-60-ul achieves a 
44maximum energy density of 22.2 Wh kg⁻¹ at 500 W kg⁻¹, retains 96.5% capacitance after 5000 
45charge–discharge cycles.  These findings establish ultrasound-assisted AuNPs deposition as an 
46effective and scalable strategy for developing high-performance, eco-friendly supercapacitor 
47electrodes from biomass-derived activated carbon.
48
49Keywords: Soluble, Activated carbon, Supercapacitor, Ultrasound irradiation, Gold nanoparticle

541. Introduction
55The rapid depletion of fossil fuel resources and the increase in environmental concerns 
56associated with greenhouse gas emissions have stimulated extensive research on sustainable and 
57efficient energy storage systems [1].  In recent years, electrochemical energy storage devices 
58have attracted considerable attention due to their capability to store and deliver electrical energy 
59efficiently [2, 3].  Among various energy storage technologies, supercapacitors have emerged as 
60promising candidates because of their high-power density, rapid charge–discharge capability, 
61and long cycle life [4].  These advantages make supercapacitors particularly attractive for 
62applications in portable electronics, hybrid electric vehicles, and renewable energy systems.  
63However, despite these benefits, supercapacitors still suffer from relatively low energy density 
64compared with conventional batteries, which limits their broader practical applications [5, 6].  
65Therefore, significant research efforts have been devoted to improving the electrochemical 
66performance of supercapacitors through the development of advanced electrode materials [7, 8].
67Recently, carbon materials including graphene [9], carbon nanotubes [10], carbon aerogel 
68[11], and activated carbon [12] have been comprehensively researched to produce high 
69performance supercapacitor electrode.  Among these carbon materials, activated carbon has been 
70widely used as an electrode material in supercapacitors due to its high specific surface area, 
71excellent chemical stability, and relatively low cost [7, 13].  The porous structure of activated 
72carbon provides abundant active sites for electrolyte ion adsorption, which is essential for 
73efficient charge storage in electric double-layer capacitors (EDLCs) [14].  Agricultural waste has 
74been recognized as promising precursor for producing activated carbon [15, 16].  Despite the

79properties of activated carbon, including heteroatom doping, surface functionalization, and the

88composite of graphene quantum dots and AuNPs exhibited a high specific capacitance of 480 F

98nanoparticles and carbon substrates remains an important challenge.
99Ultrasound irradiation has emerged as a promising technique for the synthesis and 
100modification of nanomaterials [28].  Tiong et al. reviewed ultrasonic wave propagation and 
101discussed that acoustic cavitation occurred at localized high temperatures and pressures, which 
102could significantly enhance mass transfer and chemical reactions in the system [29].  These 
103unique effects can promote the nucleation and uniform dispersion of nanoparticles on substrate 
104surfaces.  Recently, Tanaka et al. applied ultrasound irradiation in deposition of AuNPs on 
105cathode material for Li ion batteries [30].  Compared with conventional magnetic stirring 
106methods, ultrasound irradiation can facilitate better dispersion of metal precursors and promote 
107more uniform nucleation of nanoparticles on the carbon surface, which are beneficial for 
108improving electrochemical performance.
109In this study, activated carbon derived from rice straw soluble was successfully 
110synthesized and utilized as a carbon support for AuNPs decoration.  Gold nanoparticles were 
111deposited onto the activated carbon surface using an ultrasound irradiation method at a frequency 
112of 200 kHz.  The structural and morphological characteristics of the prepared materials were 
113systematically investigated using various characterization techniques. Furthermore, the 
114electrochemical performance of the electrodes was evaluated using cyclic voltammetry, 
115galvanostatic charge–discharge, and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy to assess their 
116potential application in supercapacitors.

1222. Experimental section
1232.1 Materials
124Rice straw (RS) obtained from Nakhon Ratchasima province, Thailand, was employed as 
125the biomass precursor throughout this investigation.  Prior to utilization, the as-received RS was 
126subjected to mechanical size reduction through cutting operations to achieve a particle size of 
127less than 100 µm.  Potassium hydroxide (KOH, Kemaus) served as the chemical activating agent 
128for the fabrication of porous carbon materials.  The decoration of activated carbon with gold 
129nanoparticles was accomplished using HAu(III)Cl₄·4H₂O (99.9%, Wako) as the Au precursor 
130source.  All chemical reagents were of analytical purity and were utilized directly without any 
131further purification steps.
132
1332.2 Preparation of activated carbon
134The soluble fraction was obtained via solvent extraction performed at 350 °C using a 
135petroleum-based solvent (A-150) as the extraction medium, following a procedure described in 
136detail elsewhere [31].  The resulting soluble fraction was then carbonized at 700 °C for 1 h 
137under a nitrogen atmosphere at a heating rate of 10 °C min⁻¹. The char obtained was 
138subsequently activated with potassium hydroxide (KOH) at a carbon-to-KOH mass ratio of 1:3 at 
139700 °C for 1 h under nitrogen flow at the same heating rate.  After activation, the products were 
140washed sequentially with 0.1 M HCl solution and deionized water until neutral pH was reached, 
141ensuring complete removal of residual inorganic impurities.  The resulting samples were dried at 
142110 °C for 24 h. The activated carbon product thus prepared was designated as AC700.

1442.3 Synthesis of Au decorated activated carbon
145Gold precursor solutions were prepared by dissolving hydrogen tetrachloroaurate (III) 
146tetrahydrate (HAuCl₄·4H₂O) at varying loadings (5, 10, 20, and 30 mg) in a binary solvent 
147system comprising 2 mL of 2-propanol and 100 mL of deionized (DI) water, where 2-propanol 
148was first added to facilitate precursor dissolution and improve dispersion prior to the addition of 
149DI water.  Separately, 0.5 g of AC700 was pre-wetted with 2 mL of ethanol to enhance surface 
150wettability and promote uniform interfacial contact with the Au precursor solution.  The prepared 
151gold solution was then added into the carbon suspension, and the combined mixture was 
152subsequently degassed by purging with argon gas for 30 min to remove dissolved oxygen and 
153prevent unwanted oxidation reactions from occurring during the deposition process.  For 
154ultrasound-assisted deposition, the suspension was irradiated using a high-frequency ultrasonic 
155processor (KAIJO, Quava Mini) operating at 200 kHz and 100 W for durations of 20, 60, and 
156120 min.  For comparative purposes, a conventional magnetic stirring approach was also 
157employed, in which the mixture was agitated at 300 rpm at room temperature for 60 min.  
158Following deposition, the samples were vacuum-filtered, washed thoroughly with DI water to 
159remove residual ionic species, and dried at 110 °C overnight.  The dried samples were then 
160subjected to sequential thermal treatment: pyrolysis at 700 °C for 1 h under nitrogen atmosphere 
161(heating rate: 10 °C min⁻¹), followed by oxidation at 300 °C for 30 min in air at the same heating 
162rate.  The resulting Au-decorated activated carbon samples were designated as ACAu-X-Y-Z, 
163where X denoted the Au precursor loading (mg), Y represented the treatment duration (min), and 
164Z indicated the deposition method ("ul" for ultrasonic irradiation and "st" for magnetic stirring).  
165The ultrasound treated activated carbons without Au loading were designated as AC-0-X-ul,

1692.4 Surface characterization of carbon materials
170The microstructural features and morphological characteristics of the as-prepared 
171samples were examined by transmission electron microscopy (TEM, JEOL JEM-2100 Plus). 
172Bulk elemental composition (C, H, and N contents) was quantified using a CHN elemental 
173analyzer (J-Science Lab, CHN JM10).  Crystal structure characterization was conducted by X-
174ray diffraction (XRD, Bruker D2 Phaser) utilizing Cu Kα radiation (λ = 1.5418 Å) at an 
175accelerating voltage of 40 kV and a tube current of 100 mA.  The extent of structural disorder 
176and graphitic character of the carbon materials were probed by Raman spectroscopy employing a 
177micro-Raman spectrometer (Horiba, Xplora™ Plus) with a 514 nm argon ion laser as the 
178excitation source.  Textural characteristics, encompassing specific surface area and pore size 
179distribution, were determined from nitrogen adsorption–desorption isotherms acquired at 77 K 
180on a volumetric surface area analyzer (BEL Japan, BELSORP-mini II).  The specific surface 
181area was computed by applying the Brunauer–Emmett–Teller (BET) model, whereas pore size 
182distribution was extracted from the adsorption branch of the isotherm.  Surface elemental 
183composition and chemical bonding states were investigated by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy 
184(XPS, Kratos Axis Supra-8, Shimadzu).  The Au content of the decorated samples was 
185quantitatively assessed by inductively coupled plasma atomic emission spectroscopy (ICP-AES,

293direct structural modification of the carbon framework, but rather its capacity to facilitate

6974. Conclusions
698AuNPs were successfully deposited onto rice straw-derived activated carbon via 
699ultrasound-assisted irradiation and conventional magnetic stirring.  A control experiment 
700confirmed that ultrasonic irradiation alone introduces structural disorder without improving 
701electrochemical performance, establishing that the enhancements originate specifically from the 
702incorporated AuNPs.  TEM analysis revealed that ultrasonic deposition yielded uniformly 
703dispersed nanosized AuNPs, whereas stirring resulted in significant agglomeration.  XRD and 
704XPS verified the formation of crystalline, zero-valent Au⁰ nanoparticles, with the high surface 
705area and microporous structure well preserved following Au incorporation.  The optimized 
706sample, ACAu-20-60-ul, achieved a specific capacitance of 387 F g⁻¹ (~66% enhancement over 
707AC700), a maximum energy density of 22.2 Wh kg⁻¹, a capacitance retention of 96.5% after 
7085000 cycles with a coulombic efficiency of 98.9%, and a reduced charge transfer resistance of 
7090.8 Ω.  These results indicate that ultrasound-assisted deposition is an effective strategy for 
710fabricating high-performance supercapacitor electrodes from biomass-derived activated carbon.

Preparation of Carbon Electrode Material with a Large
Speciﬁc Surface Area and Multiscale Pore Structure from
Biowaste Kochia for Symmetrical Supercapacitor
Kai Fan, Xiping Lei,* Junzhan Zhang,* Ting Yu, Haonan Chen, and Jing Liu
1. Introduction
Recently, the excessive consumption of fossil fuel energy and the
deterioration of the living environment have attracted strong
attention, prompting the scientiﬁc community to turn to research
on renewable green energy such as wind energy, solar energy,
and hydropower, but they all have a common shortcoming that
is intermittent and dif ﬁcult to satisfy today ’s world with increas-
ing demand for energy. [1–3] And with the continuous expansion
of the electric vehicle market, people have increased the demand
for environmentally friendly, renewable resources with the high
power density and high energy density. [4,5] Therefore, to solve
this problem, it is necessary to study sustainable energy produc-
tion and storage technology.
Among various energy storage devices, supercapacitors, as a
very ideal energy storage device have a higher power density than
batteries,[6] a higher energy density than
traditional capacitors, [7] fast charging
speed,[8] and excellent cycle performance, [9]
have been studied. Among them, electrode
materials play a vital role in the capacitance
performance of supercapacitors. Electrode
materials that are currently being studied
extensively include carbon materials, con-
ductive polymers, and metal oxides. [10–12]
Carbon-based materials with electric
double-layer capacitance behavior, such
as activated carbon, have a rich pore struc-
ture, large speci ﬁc surface, and good cycle
stability.[13–15] They have the conditions for
the preparation of excellent electrode mate-
rials and have attracted attention. However,
traditional activated carbon is produced
from coal and its derivatives, which is
non-renewable and its high cost limits its
development. In contrast, to comply with
the global advocacy of the circular economy
and the effective reuse of resources, waste
biomass can be used as the main raw mate-
rial for the preparation of activated carbon. [2] Among them,
plants with high carbon content, speci ﬁc structure and composi-
tion, and renewable nature can be the preferred biomass carbon
source. Through the high-temperature carbonization process,
the lignocellulose in the original plant skeleton is removed to
form a carbon skeleton and a porous structure.[16] However, most
plant-based carbon materials have the disadvantages of low spe-
ciﬁc capacitance, inconspicuous pore structure, and small spe-
ciﬁc surface area (SSA) through simple high-temperature
pyrolysis.[17] Activators such as potassium hydroxide, [18] sodium
hydroxide,[19] and phosphoric acid [20] have been studied to opti-
mize them. The use of chemical activators can ameliorate the
porous structure of different morphologies and optimize the
SSA.[21–23] The improved pore structure will signi ﬁcantly accel-
erate the transport rate of electrolyte ions and have more active
sites. Some studies have developed activated carbon for superca-
pacitor electrode materials by directly carbonizing waste plants.
Yifu Zhang prepared biomass activated carbon by directly car-
bonizing kelp, bamboo leaves, and waste rice husks, not only
achieved waste recycling and reuse to prepare new energy carbon
materials with excellent pore structure but also used carbon
materials with excellent pore structure as a substrate to prepare
composite materials with higher speciﬁc capacitance.[24–27] Other
studies have used a combination of carbonization and KOH acti-
vation, such as Zhanglin Liu used lignocellulose-rich waste

Kochia that is used as Chinese herbal medicine is always abandoned as a
biowaste after extracting useful components. However, the richness of ligno-
cellulose and the natural tubular structure make it a potential source of biomass
carbon. After high-temperature pyrolysis at 800 °C and further etching by proper
activation conditions, a graded porous structured carbon-based supercapacitor
electrode material (KAC-5) can be obtained. The electrode material is prepared in
a 1:5 carbon-to-base ratio, possessing a speci ﬁc surface area of 1441.30 m 2 g/C0 1,
and a graded macro-meso-micro structure that is rich in micropores. The
capacitance retention retains at 90.31% even after 10 000 cycles in 6 M KOH
electrolyte and exhibits outstanding capacitance performance with a speci ﬁc
capacitance of 284 F g /C0 1 at a current density of 1 A g /C0 1. The symmetrical
supercapacitor is assembled with KAC-5 and also has good cycling stability in 6 M
KOH aqueous electrolyte, reaching 88.83% after 10 000 cycles with an energy
density of 12.3 Wh kg /C0 1 at a power density of 300 W kg /C0 1. Based on the above,
sustainable preparation of energy storage material from waste biomass for high
capacitance and stable biomass-based supercapacitors has been achieved.
