segments.text:
wheat straw to prepare biomass activated carbon with a very high
SSA, other biomass include tree leaves, bagasse, feather ﬁnger
grass ﬂower, and Miscanthus grass. [28–32]
This article uses the biomass waste collected from the tradi-
tional Chinese herbal medicine Kochia as the raw material. A
large number of Kochia is directly discarded, which leads to a
waste of resources. The lignin, cellulose, and hemicellulose in
the plant are pyrolyzed under high temperatures to retain the
pore structure and the volatile components are discharged to
make the natural tube bundle structure in the original plant more
obvious and stable. Use different proportions of KOH for chem-
ical activation to further optimize the pore structure. The micro-
pore and mesopore structure are fully etched on the original
tube-like macroporous wall to obtain a biomass-activated carbon
electrode material with a hierarchical pore structure, promoting
the storage and rapid transportation of a large number of elec-
trolyte ions, and the increased SSA provides more active sites.
So far, there are only a few reports of using Kochia as electrode
material for supercapacitors. This study explored the in ﬂuence
on the electrochemical performance of electrode materials by
changing the ratio of activators. The electrode material samples
exhibit excellent electrochemical performance, high surface area,
and effective ion diffusion characteristics. We have also explored
the assembly and application of electrode material with electro-
lytes, which is expected to go further in the application of
supercapacitors.
2. Results and Discussion
Figure 1 is a schematic representation of the entire experimental
process including the activation mechanism. The Kochia was car-
bonized at 800 °C making the lignocellulose pyrolysis open mac-
ropores to obtain KC-800. Then chemically etched with different
proportions of KOH and KAC-n was obtained. Usually, KOH is
completely decomposed at 600 °C. During this period, potassium
compounds as a chemical activator with carbon undergo redox
reactions to etch the carbon skeleton. [23,33] The process had
H2O and CO 2 generated for further physical activation.
During the activation process, the potassium ions are effectively
embedded in the lattice of the carbon matrix causing lattice
expansion, which cannot be recovered and therefore results in
a large SSA and high porosity. [34] Finally, a symmetric superca-
pacitor was assembled using KAC-5 as the electrode material
with optimal performance. The experimental section shows
the detailed preparation process.
According to the FESEM image of Kochia in Figure 2 a, the
powder was found to be composed of ﬁbrous lignocellulose
and had a very rough surface with no visible pore structure.
In contrast to it, Figure 2b,c shows the optimal sample that
was ﬁrst carbonized and then activated by KOH because of
the pyrolytic volatilization of lignocellulose, the originally blocked
plant tube structure is exposed, the tubes with macropores at
both ends are completely opened with pore size distribution
in the range of 5-10 μm, and opening tube structure increases
the SSA of the entire material. The exposed macropores can
be used as channels for rapid electrolyte transfer [35] and facilitate
KOH etching of the internal duct walls to form more micropores
and mesopores, thus providing a large number of active sites. [36]
To further investigate the etching of the KAC-5 surface after
KOH treatment, TEM analysis was carried out, and the results
could be seen in Figure 2d. The red circles show some of the
micropores and the mesopores formed by the interconnection
of the etched micropores, and there are a large number of more
evenly distributed micropores and some mesopores on the sur-
face, this is the result of etching the surface of the material by
KOH activation and etching through the macropores into the
tube structure. Figure 2e,f shows the C and O elemental
mapping images of KOH-5, respectively. After the activation
treatment, the surface is composed of only C and O elements,
which indicates that KAC-5 can only be used as an electrode
material for a carbon-based double-layer supercapacitor, but
the presence of some oxygen increases the surface wettability
of the electrode material and provides some pseudo capacitance,
which facilitates the higher electrochemical performance of
supercapacitors in aqueous electrolytes. [31]

segments.text:
To explore the composition of Kochia, the FT-IR spectrum of
Kochia is shown in Figure 2g. The absorption peaks of lignin,
cellulose, and hemicellulose are obvious. The characteristic
absorption peak of lignin occurring at 830 cm /C0 1 is ascribed to
C-H out-of-plane stretching. The peaks at 1624 cm /C0 1 indicate
aromatic skeletal vibrations. Moreover, the peaks centered at
2926 and 3357 cm /C0 1 can be attributed to the C ─H and O ─H
stretching vibration, respectively. [37] The absorption peaks of cel-
lulose can be found at 895, 1038, 1157, and 1375 cm /C0 1, which
correspond to ring vibration, C ─O stretching vibration of gluco-
sidic bond, C ─O asymmetric stretching vibration, and C ─H
bending vibration, respectively. [38] As for hemicelluloses, the
peaks at 1240 and 1733 cm /C0 1 indicate the C ─O asymmetric
vibrations and C =O stretching vibrations of acetyl. [39,40] The
results show that Kochia is composed of lignocellulose. Lignin
in most plant cells acts as a binder to wrap around cellulose
as a skeleton, and hemicellulose acts as a ﬁller to form a stable
structure similar to reinforced concrete in cells. [41,42] Therefore,
lignocellulose can be decomposed to form porous carbon
through high-temperature pyrolysis, and chemical activation
can greatly change the structure of this biomass. The above
conditions indicate that rationally optimizing the components
of Kochia has certain signi ﬁcance for the preparation of target
carbon materials.
To select a suitable carbonization temperature, the TGA curve
of the above sample is observed in Figure 2h. It is mainly divided
into three stages: ﬁrst, continuous decomposition of free water in
the temperature range of 100 °C with about 6.7% of weight loss;
the most obvious decline is the second stage of lignocellulose
decomposition process with 71.9% of weight loss: hemicellulose
is ﬁrst decomposed in the range of 220 to 315 °C, followed by
cellulose in the range of 315 to 400 °C and lignin is completely
decomposed at 550 °C. [43] In addition, the third stage was rela-
tively stable with a weight loss of 21.4% from 550 to 900 °C.
To determine the carbonation temperature, galvanostatic
charge/discharge tests at a current density of 1 A g /C0 1 were car-
ried out on KC-600, KC-700, KC-800, and KC-900, and the high-
est speci ﬁc capacitance of 184 F g /C0 1 with a current density of
1Ag /C0 1 was obtained at the temperature of 800 °C, as shown
in Figure S1, Supporting Information. Therefore, 800 °C was
selected as the carbonization temperature.
To further investigate the role of KOH as an activator, N 2
adsorption/desorption isotherms were used to test KAC-5.
Figure 2i shows a type I isotherm with a large increase in the
relative pressure P/P 0 < 0.1, indicating that KOH activation
forms a large number of micropores; [25,44] the existence of hys-
teresis loops and good overlap of the isotherms prove that the
pore size distribution of mesopores is very narrow. The inset

segments.text:
of Figure 2i shows the pore size distribution, which is mainly in
the range of 1 –7 nm. From Table 1 , the large SSA of KAC-5
reaches 1441.30 m2 g/C0 1. This result is higher than the previously
reported SSA of most biomass carbon electrode materials, the
comparison results are shown in Figure S2, Supporting
Information. The microporosity reaches 82.28% with an average
pore size of 1.6632 nm, which is also the reason for the large
number of micropores that can be seen in TEM images. A small
number of mesopores can be used as a channel to store and
transmit electrolytes, while a large number of micropores pro-
vide active sites and increase the SSA and contribute to the
improvement of electrochemical performance. [24,45]
As shown in Figure 3 a from XRD determination, two broad
diffraction peaks at a 2 θ value of approximately 15° and 23° were
observed and ascribed to the diffraction peaks of cellulose and
hemicellulose in Kochia. [46] Diffraction peaks of around 23°
and 43° can be seen in the curves of KC, KAC-4, KAC-5, and
KAC-6, corresponding to the (002) and (100) crystal planes of gra-
phitic carbon, respectively. [47] Compared to KC, the (002) crystal-
line plane of the activated samples is all shifted to the left.
Previous studies have demonstrated the redox reaction between
KOH and carbon during activation to form potassium-containing
compounds as well as the production of gas such as CO 2 further
physical activation affects the extent of defects and produces
more active sites, while the metal potassium ions expand the
space of the atomic carbon layer, inﬂuencing the degree of graph-
itization.[23] Accordingly, further structural information can also
be obtained from the Raman spectra measured in Figure 3b, in
which the independent peaks at 1340 cm /C0 1 (D-band) and
1580 cm/C0 1 (G-band) corresponded to the disordered form of car-
bon materials and graphitic lattice vibrations, respectively. [48]
Assessment of the degree of disorder in carbon materials by
the intensity ratio of the D-band to the G-band. The ID/IG values
for KC, KAC-4, KAC-5, and KAC-6 were 0.96, 0.98, 0.99, and
1.00, indicating an increase in defect density after activation.
The abundant disordered and defective carbon in KAC-n was
beneﬁcial to the improvement of surface area and the number
of activated sites for reactions and promoted ion diffusion and
transportation, and these were all positive for the capacitive per-
formance of carbon materials. [45]
XPS analysis was performed to determine the surface elemen-
tal composition and content of KAC-5. The presence of C and O
can be obtained from Figure 3c. Element C accounted for 91.75%
of the total and the element O accounted for 8.25%. The C 1 s
spectrum of KAC-5 can be ﬁtted into four peaks in Figure 3d,
corresponding to the C ─C (284.8 eV), C ─O (286.4 eV), C = O
(287.9 eV), and O ─C = O (288.9 eV). [49,50] Similarly, in
Figure 3e, the O 1 s spectrum could be ﬁtted with three major
peaks at 530.8, 532.1, and 533.3 eV, representing C = O, C ─O,
and O─C─O, respectively.[27,32,51] Surface wettability of electrode
materials can be improved by the presence of these oxygen-
containing functional groups, as also evidenced by the contact
angle test shown in Figure 3f. A drop of water was transiently
absorbed within 1 s of contacting the porous carbon material,
and the measured contact angle was 58.25°, indicating that
KAC-5 has good hydrophilicity, which is conducive to full contact
between electrolyte and electrode material as a way to generate
more electrochemical reactions. [49]
Due to the porous structure and high SSA of the prepared
samples, performances of KC, KAC-4, KAC-5 and KAC-6 were
ﬁrst evaluated using 6.0 M KOH as the electrolyte in a three-
electrode system. Figure 4a compares the CV curves of this acti-
vated carbon at a scan rate of 50 mV s /C0 1. These curves are almost
always rectangular in shape and are typical of double-layer capaci-
tors.[2,44,52] After activation by KOH, compared to KC, the CV
curves of the others have bulges in the lower potential region
around /C0 0.5 V, which is caused by the oxygen content on the
surface leading to the formation of pseudo-capacitance. The
effect of KOH activation is re ﬂected, KAC-4, KAC-5, and KAC-
6 are accompanied by redox peaks due to the pseudo-capacitance
provided by the presence of oxygen after activation, which makes
the area surrounded by CV curve larger and the electrochemical
performance is better than KC. Compared to the other three
materials, KAC-5 has the largest integral area of the CV curve,
indicating its highest speci ﬁc capacitance. [44,47,53] This result is
also reﬂected in the charge/discharge curves in Figure 4b, where
KAC-5 has the longest discharge time at a current density of
1Ag /C0 1. The symmetrical GCD curves demonstrate the excellent
capacitive performance and high coulomb ef ﬁciency of all four
materials,[10,19] and this suggests that the appropriate carbon-
base ratio is also particularly important for electrochemical per-
formance. According to Equation (1), the speci ﬁc capacitances of
KC, KAC-4, KAC-5, and KAC-6 are 184, 256, 284, and 239 F g /C0 1,
respectively. KAC-5 exhibits the highest speci ﬁc capacitance and
higher than previously reported biomass carbon electrode mate-
rials as shown in Table S1, Supporting Information. Compared
with KC, the surface of activated KAC-5 contains certain oxygen
elements and is more abundant in microporous structure and
mesoporous structure, which will increase the contact area
between the electrode material and the electrolyte, so that the
active site increases, which are particularly important for porous
carbon materials, and re ﬂect a difference of 100 F g /C0 1 before and
after activation in terms of speci ﬁc capacitance. A comparative
multiplier performance graph is made to test the performance
of the material at high current densities, as shown in
Figure S3, Supporting Information. The speci ﬁc capacitance
was further calculated from Equation (1) for current densities
from 0.5 to 10 A g /C0 1. The maximum speci ﬁc capacitance of
the KAC-5 reaches 288 F g /C0 1 (0.5 A g/C0 1), even at high current
densities of 10 A g /C0 1, and KAC-5 still maintains a speci ﬁc capac-
itance of 227 F g /C0 1 with a capacitance retention rate of 78.8%.
Based on the Nyquist diagram of the samples in Figure 4c, in
the low-frequency region, the straight lines of all three activated
specimens are nearly perpendicular to the real axis, [45] in contrast
to KC, which has a small slope, and the diffuse resistance of
the activated specimens becomes smaller. The intercept of the
high-frequency region with the x-axis indicates the intrinsic

KAC-4, KAC-5, and KAC-6, respectively, and the intrinsic
resistance (ESR) are all very close. In addition, the interfacial
charge transfer resistances ( Rct) were 0.055, 0.05, 0.039, and
0.041 Ω. In summary, KAC-5 had the lowest resistance, which
was attributed to the increased SSA due to chemical activation,
which facilitated the transport of electrolyte ions in the electrode
material, and the presence of oxygen-containing functional
groups, which improved the wettability of the surface of the
electrode material, resulting in such excellent impedance perfor-
mance. The above electrochemical analysis showed that KAC-5
has the best electrochemical performance, which proves the spe-
ciﬁc capacitance of KC is further enhanced followed by chemical
activation and that the appropriate carbon-to-alkali ratio is
equally important, as excessive KOH will transitionally
etch the original carbon skeleton, collapsing the skeleton and
impeding the transport of electrolyte ions, reducing the SSA
and the number of active sites, making the electrochemical
performance poor. [5,45,52]
A more comprehensive electrochemical analysis of the
optimum sample KAC-5 was carried out. Figure 4d shows the
CV curves at rates from 5 to 200 mV s /C0 1. The overall rectangular

utilization of the electrode material, so the speci ﬁc capacitance
decreases as the current density increases. [55] As shown in
Figure 4f, after 10 000 charge/discharge cycles, the speci ﬁc
capacitance of the KAC-5 electrode still maintains 90.31% of
the original capacitance, which has good stability.
In order to detect the practical use, KAC-5 was used as the
active substance, CR2032 button cell as the case, and 6 M
KOH electrolyte to assemble a miniature symmetrical superca-
pacitor for practical use. As shown in Figure 5 a, the anode
current does not increase signi ﬁcantly at 1.2 V and the CV curve
maintains its rectangular-like shape, while at 1.4 V the anode cur-
rent increases rapidly, indicating that the symmetrical
supercapacitor can cycle reversibly within a voltage window of
1.2 V. The increase in anode current after a potential of 1.2 V
indicates that the water molecules in the electrolyte start to
decompose rapidly, which is detrimental to electrochemical sta-
bility.[33,56] The CV test was carried out at different sweep speeds
by selecting a voltage window of 0 to 1.2 V, as shown in Figure 5b.
As the sweep speed goes from low to high, the curve stays well
rectangular like, indicating good performance. [57] Figure 5c
shows the charge/discharge test at different current densities.
According to Equation (2), the speci ﬁc capacitance is calculated
to be 61.7 F g /C0 1 at a current density of 0.5 A g /C0 1 and still kept
41.7 F g/C0 1 at a high current of 10 A g /C0 1, with a capacitance

charges and discharges, the capacitor still retains 88.83% of its
original capacity, exhibiting good durability. Figure 5e shows the
power density versus energy density graph and comparison with
other studies.[28,58–64] From the results, the energy density of the
miniature symmetrical supercapacitor with 6 M KOH aqueous as
the electrolyte can reach 12.3 Wh kg /C0 1 when the power density is
300 W kg/C0 1 and still reach 8.3 Wh kg /C0 1 when the power density
is as high as 6000 W kg /C0 1. Figure 5f shows that using three
supercapacitors connected in series as a small bulb power source
to easily light tricolor LED bulbs. These above results demon-
strated that the prepared biomass activated carbon KAC-5 could
be used as excellent electrode materials for supercapacitors.
3. Conclusions
Kochia was ﬁrst used as a precursor in the preparation of
activated carbon material for supercapacitors in this work. The
results showed that the SSA of the electrode material was
increased by opening the natural tube structure originally con-
tained in the plant through the carbonation process, and then
further modulating the pore size distribution to create a multi-
scale pore structure by KOH activation to increase the active sites
and SSA. Its electrochemical performance as an electrode mate-
rial for supercapacitors was superior to that of other previously
reported biomass carbon materials. By adjusting the appropriate
carbon-to-base ratio, KAC-5 has a rich microporous structure
occupying 82.28% of the pore volume, with a SSA of
1441.30 m2 g/C0 1. In the three-electrode system, the maximum
speciﬁc capacitance of KAC-5 reaches 284 F g/C0 1 when the current
density is 1 A g/C0 1, and the capacitance retention for 10 000 cycles
is 90.31%. The energy density of the symmetrical supercapacitor
assembled with KAC-5 as the active material can reach
12.3 Wh kg/C0 1 when the power density is 300 W kg /C0 1. All these
excellent properties are derived from its natural tubular structure
and its rich lignocellulose. This study provides a sustainable
method for the preparation of supercapacitor electrode material
from biomass waste.
4. Experimental Section
Materials: The following materials, Kochia (Deyang, Sichuan Province,
China). potassium hydroxide (KOH, Macklin, AR), hydrochloric acid (HCl,
AR), acetylene black (AB, ECP600JD, LION Ketjenblack), polyvinylidene
ﬂuoride (PVDF, Arkema), and ethanol (C 2H6O, AR), were purchased.
Deionized water was employed directly without further treatment.
Preparation of Activated Carbon : The purchased Kochia was ultrasoni-
cated with absolute ethanol ﬁrst to remove surface impurities, then rinsed
with deionized water, and then placed in an oven for thorough drying.
These dried sticks were crushed and grounded through a 35-mesh sieve.
Then the Kochia powder was kept in a tube furnace at 800 °C for 2 h at a
heating rate of 5 °C min/C0 1,N 2 was used as the protective gas. The samples
were thoroughly washed with deionized water and dried in an oven,
recorded as Kochia carbon (KC). KC and KOH were mixed according to
a mass ratio of 1:5 and a suspension is prepared, and dried it in a
75 °C oven for 12 h. The mixture after drying was activated in a tube fur-
nace at 600 °C under an N 2 atmosphere for 2 h at a heating rate of
5 °C min/C0 1. The product ’s excess KOH and soluble salts were removed
with 1M hydrochloric acid and then washed with deionized water for
neutrality. The resulting carbon material was recorded as Kochia activated
carbon (KAC). For comparison, three different carbon-to-base ratios
(1:4, 1:5, 1:6) were prepared, respectively, as KAC-4, KAC-5, and KAC-6.
Characterization: The powder X-ray diffractometer was performed with
an X-ray diffraction instrument to characterize the crystal structure of sam-
ples (XRD, Bruker D8). Raman spectrometer was used to characterize the
degree of defects and graphitization. (LabRAM HR Evolution). The micro-
scopic morphology of samples was carried out by ﬁeld-emission scanning
electron microscope (FESEM, GeminiSEM500). The distribution of ele-
ments in the samples was determined through energy-dispersive spectros-
copy (EDS, GeminiSEM500). Transmission electron microscopy (TEM,
Talos F200X) was performed to observe the microstructures of the
obtained products. The SSA and pore size distribution of the analyzed
samples were tested by using a nitrogen adsorption meter (BET,
Micromeritics APSP 2460). X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy was per-
formed to analyze chemical composition (XPS, ESCALAB 250 electron
spectrometer). The Fourier transform infrared was used to characterize
the type of functional group of the raw material (FTIR, ISQ 7000
Nicolet iS50 TGA/DSC3).
Electrochemical Performance : The prepared carbon material, polyvinyli-
dene ﬂuoride, and acetylene black were thoroughly mixed in a mass ratio of
8:1:1 to form a slurry, the slurry was coated on the foamed nickel with a
size of 1 cm /C2 1 cm and dried at 75 °C after 1 h, and they were pressed at
10 MPa for 1 min. The three-electrode system was assembled with pressed
electrode sheets as working electrodes, and the Hg/HgO electrode was
used as the reference electrode and the platinum sheet as the counter
electrode. The single-electrode sheet active material load of the three-
electrode system was 3 mg cm /C0 2, with 6 M KOH as the electrolyte.
CHI605E electrochemical workstation for cyclic voltammetry (CV) tests
was recorded from /C0 1.0 to 0 V at a scan rate of 5, 10, 20, 50,
100 mV s/C0 1, and galvanostatic charge –discharge (GCD) tests were
recorded from /C0 1.0 to 0 V at a current density of 1,2,3,5,10 A g /C0 1.
Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) tests in the frequency
range 0.01 HZ –100 kHz with an amplitude of 5 mV were performed on
a CHI660E electrochemical workstation.
In electrochemical tests, the speci ﬁc capacitances ( Cm,F g /C0 1) were

Facile Synthesis of Colocasia esculenta Peels- Derived 
Activated Carbon for High- Performance Supercapacitor

Keywords: activated carbon | Colocasia esculenta  peels | electrochemical energy storage | high-  energy density | supercapacitor
ABSTRACT
Biomass and biowaste resources can be used to create self-  doped carbon with a distinctive microstructure. Using an economical 
and environmentally friendly method to create heteroatom- doped carbon electrode materials with excellent electrochemical per-
formance has attracted much attention in the energy storage industry. A novel facile two- step, low- cost, and eco- friendly synthesis 
method for Colocasia esculenta peels has been developed to manufacture activated carbon (CEPAC) and used as an electrode 
material for supercapacitor application. The CEPAC 1:1 displayed a high specific surface area of 910 m2/g with oxygen- heteroatom 
polar sites in the carbon network. A specific capacitance of 525.3 F/g was recorded in the three- electrode system using a 3 M KOH 
solution. The assembled symmetric cell delivered an impressive specific capacitance of 98.7 F/g at 1 A/g while maintaining 98.4% 
of the initially recorded capacitance after 10 000 charge– discharge cycles. These results present a promising low-  cost and simple 
processing route for synthesizing electrode materials with superior surface properties for high- performance supercapacitors.
1   |   Introduction
Considering the recent fast-  growing demand for energy supply 
to meet the sustainable development goals, fast-  depleting fossil 
fuel energy sources pose a major concern. Industrialization and 
civilization are the critical aspects of sustainable development 
that need an enormous energy supply. Fossil fuel energy re -
serves are linearly declining because of the relatively long time 
required for mineralization [1]. With this, there is a need to find 
other alternative energy sources to augment the existing fossil 
fuel. Renewable energy technologies have been in the system for 
a while to complement fossil resources [ 2]. These new energy 
supply technologies are clean and environmentally friendly and 
may be affordable. To outwit the present energy demand crisis in 
the world, energy conversion and storage systems are required 
to harness clean and environmentally stable renewable energy 
sources. Among the fast-  growing and promising energy stor -
age and conversion systems that have attracted, the attention of 
modern researchers are supercapacitors [ 3– 5], fuel cells [ 6, 7], 
rechargeable batteries [8], and metal– air batteries [9, 10].
One of the significant drivers of the new energy storage and 
conversion systems is their pristine electrode materials, 
such as carbon-  based hybrids [ 11], especially carbon-  based

trodes are inherently costly and produce relatively low yields. 
Constant optimization of the energy storage precursor mate -
rials has led to a renewed interest in the utilization of car -
bon from biomass sources that are environmentally friendly 
[14, 15 ]. These alternative carbon precursors use green syn -
thesis approaches such as hydrothermal [ 16, 17 ], pyrolysis 
[18], and electrospinning [ 19].
Recent evidence suggests that biomass-  derived carbon precur -
sors are the key to harvesting renewable energy in enormous 
quantities, which represents a major milestone in the domain of 
energy technology [20]. Biomass- derived carbon electrodes pos -
sess a wide range of advantages over their counterparts obtained 
from petroleum coke such as heteroatoms self-  doping onto the 
precursor substrate, large specific surface area (SSA), low cost 
of precursor production, and high specific pore volume [ 21– 23]. 
Hence, biomass-  derived carbon electrodes may offer a solu -
tion to the drawback of low energy density of supercapacitors 
[24, 25 ]. Electrode materials synthesized from biomass waste 
reportedly offer high specific capacitance due to the large SSA, 
sufficient defect sites, and micro/mesopores [26]. Also, there are 
abundant oxygen-  containing functional groups that enhance 
electrode conductivity. Biomass-  derived carbon is reported to 
contain heteroatoms such as potassium, phosphorus, nitrogen, 
and oxygen [26, 27].
Although extensive research has been carried out on waste 
biomass materials, some waste biomass materials remain un -
explored. Due to this, large quantities of biomass are rendered 
annually as waste which even becomes an environmental pol -
lutant. It is, therefore, logical to convert the ever-  increasing 
natural biomass wastes into electrode materials for energy 
storage applications. The carbon derived from biomass sources 
possesses unprecedented properties and has found applications 
in wearable electronics [ 28, 29] and fast energy storage systems 
[30, 31]. More recently, researchers have shown keen interest in 
plant biomass sources as these are in high abundance [ 14, 32]. 
Plant biomass that have been studied over the years includes 
coconut shells [33], basswood [ 3], leaves [34], stems [35], starch 
[36, 37], bean shell [38], peanut shell [39], miscanthus grass [40], 
lotus leaves [41], and cauliflower [42].
Supercapacitors (SCs) are one of the outstanding sought-  after 
essential energy storage devices that are considered by the re -
search and development (R&D) community for fast energy stor -
age in most of the recent electronic devices such as wearable 
electronics and cell phones [43]. Research on the supercapacitor 
subject has been mostly restricted to the electrode materials and 
their derivatives. Due to this, the electrode materials usually 
define the purpose of the supercapacitors, which can either be 
electrical double-  layer capacitors (EDLCs) or pseudocapaci -
tors, the two principal charge storage mechanisms presented 
by the different types of electrode materials. There has been a 
lot of interesting ongoing research seeking to improve the elec -
trode properties to maximize the performance of the electrode 
materials.
Biowaste-  based carbons have been utilized as promising 
EDLC electrodes over the years. The synthesis methods that 
have been adopted for activated carbon production are usu -
ally expensive and require advanced instrumentation. It is 
necessary to adopt a simple, cheap, and eco-  friendly approach 
to produce carbons with superior properties. In this work, a 
novel facile two-  stage activation protocol was employed to 
synthesize activated carbon (AC) from biowaste precursor 
(Colocasia esculenta  peels [CEPs]) using KOH as the activa -
tion agent. The AC derived from this precursor (CEPAC) was 
employed as an electroactive material in EDLC energy storage 
applications. This precursor is abundant locally and contains 
inherent heteroatoms, which may be beneficial for electro -
chemical energy storage applications; hence, exploiting its 
benefits is necessary. The use of the precursor not only cre -
ates electroactive material but also helps to revive the useful -
ness of the biowaste and creates a circular economy for the 
local people. Two different activation ratios (carbon:KOH; 1:1 
and 1:0.5) were used. The as-  synthesized AC was tested as an 
electrode material in 3 and 6 M KOH solutions of three-  and 
two-  electrode systems, respectively. The CEPAC 1:1 displayed 
a high SSA of 910 m2/g with numerous mesopores. The as -
sembled cell delivered a high specific capacitance with stable 
capacitance retention during cycling. These results present a 
promising low-  cost, facile, and environmentally friendly pro -
cessing route for synthesizing electrode materials with supe -
rior surface properties for high-  performance supercapacitors.
2   |   Materials and Experimental Method
2.1   |   Materials
The Colocasia esculenta  corm samples were obtained from the 
Ejisu market in the Ashanti region of Ghana. Analytical grades 
of chemicals were used in this study. A nickel foam current col -
lector of dimensions (300 × 300 mm2 area and 1.2 mm thickness) 
and density of 0.45 g/cm3 with corresponding 95% porosity was 
purchased from Merck & Co, Kenilworth, New Jersey. The car -
bon cloth (15 mm diameter and 0.2 mm thickness) was purchase 
from Fisher Scientific. Potassium hydroxide (KOH, 95% pu -
rity) and hydrochloric acid (HCl, 35.5% purity) were purchased 
from Danniemma Medichem Venture Gh Limited. The polyvi -
nylidene fluoride (PVDF) was procured from Zhejiang Fluorine 
Chemical New Co, China. Dimethyl formamide (DMF, 99% pu -
rity) was purchased from VWR Chemicals, France.
2.2   |   Experimental Methods
2.2.1   |   Sample Preparation and Precarbonization
The fresh C. esculenta  corm samples were initially washed with 
tap water in a bowl to get rid of mud and debris. The samples 
were subsequently air-  dried for 24 h, after which the corms 
were peeled and chopped into smaller pieces using a knife. The 
CEPs were sun-  dried until there was no significant change in 
sample weight, followed by oven drying at 105°C for 24 h. After 
progressively drying, the samples became crispy and were eas -
ily crushed using mortar and pestle. Fifty grams of the crushed 
samples were loaded into a crucible and precarbonized at a tem-
perature of 250°C for 3 h in a muffle furnace at a heating rate of 
5°C/min.

2.2.2   |   Synthesis of AC From CEPs
For the activation of the precarbonized CEPs, potassium hy -
droxide was utilized as the activation agent. Two activation 
ratios of 1:1 and 1:0.5 (CEP:KOH) were used to synthesize the 
ACs. For the 1:1 ratio, 5 g (2.5 g for the 1:0.5 ratio) of pulverized 
KOH was mixed with 5 g of the precarbonized CEP and homog -
enized in an evaporation dish. The homogenized mixture of the 
precarbonized CEP and KOH was transferred into a porcelain 
crucible and then covered with a lid. The sample in the porcelain 
crucible was embedded in a bigger crucible; this is a slight mod -
ification of the work reported by Yeboah [ 44]. Prior to this, the 
bigger crucible was initially filled with green sand to the brim 
to prevent easy access to oxygen molecules, which can signifi -
cantly reduce the yield. This was done to create an inert con -
dition for the activation process. The sample was activated in a 
muffle furnace at a temperature of 750°C for 2 h at a heating rate 
of 5°C/min. After the activation process, the samples were thor -
oughly washed with 0.1 M HCl to ensure a neutral pH. After acid 
washing, the mixture was filtered using Whatman filter paper 
(Grade 1, 240 mm ∅), and the residue was oven-  dried at 105°C 
for 24 h to obtain the AC. The CEPs-  derived ACs were denoted 
as CEPAC 1:1 and CEPAC 1:0.5. Figure  1 shows the facile two- 
stage schematic preparation process for the CEPAC samples.
2.2.3   |   Fabrication of Electrode Materials 
and Supercapacitor Cell
The working electrodes for the electrochemical analysis were 
fabricated using a binder-  to- AC ratio of 1:9. For the electrode 
preparation, 10 wt.% of PVDF was mixed with 90 wt.% of the AC 
in a petri dish. Four drops of N, N-  dimethyl formamide were 
added to the mixture and ground to form a slurry which was 
then coated on a nickel foam current collector of dimensions 
(1 × 4 cm). The mass of the active material deposited on the cur -
rent collector was approximately 3 mg. The working electrode 
was oven-  dried for 24 h at a temperature of 105°C. After 24 h 
of drying, the electrodes were then cooled to room temperature 
before the electrochemical studies in a three-  electrode setup. 
A symmetric two-  electrode SC cell was also assembled in coin 
cells (2032 CR stainless steel) using carbon clothes as the current 
collector and 6 M KOH electrolyte solution.
2.2.4   |   Electrochemical Measurement
The electrochemical performance of the synthesized acti -
vated carbon electrodes was investigated using a Corrtest 
Electrochemical Workstation (Model CS350) in the three- 
electrode setup and Parstat MC Workstation (AMETEK, 
Princeton Applied Research) for the two-  electrode system. 
Electrochemical tests such as cyclic voltammetry (CV), elec -
trochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS), and galvanostatic 
charge–  discharge (GCD) were performed in a three-  electrode 
system using Ag/AgCl reference electrode and graphite as the 
counter electrode. The working electrode used in the three- 
electrode system for the electrochemical analysis was the 
fabricated AC electrodes. All the electrochemical tests were 
performed in 3 and 6 M KOH electrolytes, respectively, at a po -
tential window of 1.2 V (−1.2–  0 V) at room temperature (25°C). 
The CV tests were carried out at scan rates ranging from 5 to 
100 mV/s, while the current density used for the GCD investi -
gation ranged from 1 to 3 A/g. The EIS test was performed at 
5 mV amplitude and in a frequency range of 10 MHz to 100 kHz.

where Δ t is the discharge time (s), I  is the current (A) of the 
discharge cycle, m  is the mass of an active material deposited 
on the current collector (g), and Δ V is the potential window 
(V).
2.3   |   Material Characterization
The surface morphology of the synthesized AC was investigated 
with a Tescan Solaris FIB-  SEM (Tescan Orsay Holding, Brno, 
Czech Republic) using ultra-  high- resolution scan mode with 
both secondary (SE) backscattered (BSE) detectors. The textural 
properties and SSA of the AC materials were studied using nitro-
gen adsorption techniques with surface and pore size analyzer 
Quantachrome Instruments NOVAtouch LX2. Phase composi -
tion identification and crystallinity of the synthesized AC mate -
rial was carried out using the Bruker D8 Advance Diffractometer 
(Bruker, MA, USA) with Cu Kα1 radiation ( λ = 1.54 Å) attach-
ment. Furthermore, Raman spectra of the carbonaceous materi -
als were collected at room temperature using a DXR2xi Raman 
Imaging Microscope (Thermo Fisher Scientific, MA, USA) with 
a 532- nm line Ar- ion laser excitation source.
3   |   Results and Discussion
3.1   |   Structural Characterization
Microstructural images of CEPAC 1:0.5 and CEPAC 1:1 are 
presented in Figure  2a,f, respectively. Although both CEPAC 
samples were prepared from the same source/precursor, the 
difference in the porous network is likely due to the activation 
protocols used.
CEPAC 1:0.5 exhibited uniformly distributed macropores as can 
be seen from Figure  2a. On the contrary, CEPAC 1:1 showed a 
cluster of mesopores interconnected with a continuous carbon 
structure as shown in Figure  2f. The morphology of CEPAC 1:1 
suggests that using equal portions of the precursor and KOH for 
activation offers electrodes with desired mesoporous structures, 
unlike in the case of CEPAC 1:0.5. During the activation pro -
cess, small and low-  volume pores are activated which increases 
the surface area of the carbonaceous materials available for ad -
sorption. It is clear from the SEM images that small and low- 
volume pores were effectively activated with the activation ratio 
of 1:1. Aside from the morphological differences, the presence of 
carbon and impurity elements in the CEPAC samples are shown 
in the energy-  dispersive x-  ray spectroscopy (EDS) elemental 
maps in Figure 2c–  e,h,i.
Using equal amounts of precursor and KOH, no traces of im -
purity elements such as Si were found in CEPAC 1:1. In addi -
tion to the main constituent carbon (C), only traces of oxygen 
were noticed in the elemental maps as provided in Figure  2g– i. 
However, substantial amounts of Si and O were found in CEPAC 
1:0.5 as presented in Figure  2b– e. Phase composition analysis 
via x- ray diffraction provided results which agreed well with the 
EDS maps. The diffraction pattern presented in Figure  3a for 
CEPAC 1:1 showed the characteristic peaks of AC for reflections 
from (002) and (101) planes at peaks position 24° and 42°, re -
spectively. In Figure  3b, the presence of quartz (SiO 2) is seen in 
addition to the main graphitic carbon phase. These diffraction 
patterns confirm the results provided in the EDS maps and sug -
gest a possible removal of impurities using an equal amount of 
precursor and KOH.
The highly sensitive Raman scattering revealed the typical 
peaks of graphitic carbon as shown in Figure  3c,d. Raman shifts 
at 1347 and 1583 cm−1 which correspond to the D (“disorder”) 
and G (“graphite”) of highly amorphous graphite carbon [ 45] 
were observed for both CEPAC samples. The R - values for both 
CEPAC samples were estimated using the ratio of the peak in -
tensity of the D-  band (ID) to the G-  band (IG). This dimension -
less parameter is widely used to distinguish between carbon 
types (diamond or graphitic) as well as a basis for understand -
ing the structure of the carbonaceous material (crystalline or 
amorphous). According to existing literature, a high R-  value 
symbolizes a high disorder and, thus, a lower crystallinity. The 
estimated ID/IG ratios of the CEPAC samples are provided in 
Figure  3c,d and suggest somewhat amorphous carbonaceous 
material. The higher values obtained in this work also suggest 
more disorderliness/defects in the prepared samples [ 46– 50], 
which is beneficial for energy storage capabilities.
At a temperature of 77 K, nitrogen adsorption was assessed em -
ploying a high-  speed surface area analyzer, the Quantachrome 
Instruments NOVAtouch LX2. Prior to the measurements, the 
samples were subjected to degassing within a dynamic vacuum 
for a minimum of 120 min at 180°C, with a gradual tempera -
ture increase of 10°C per minute. The SSA was derived from the 
nitrogen adsorption data within the range of relative pressure 
(P/P0) from 0.05 to 0.30, utilizing the Brunauer–  Emmett– Teller 
(BET) methodology. To determine the distribution of pore sizes 
within the CEPAC 1:1 and CEPAC 1:0.5 samples, the Barrett– 
Joyner– Halenda (BJH) approach was applied to the relative 
pressure range (P/P0) from 0.35 to 0.98. Notably, the analysis ex-
clusively considered the desorption phase of the isotherm.
For the CEPAC 1:1 and CEPAC 1:0.5 samples, Figure 4a,d shows 
the BET isotherm plot in linear coordinates, and Figure  4b,e 
shows the corresponding pore size distribution of the same. 
The CEPAC 1:0.5 displayed a remarkable SSA of roughly 
265 m2/g, whereas the estimated SSA of the CEPAC 1:1 was 
around 910 m2/g. The findings show that the CEPAC 1:1 had 
a pore radius (Dv[r]) of 1.8 nm, a pore surface area of 71 m2/g, 
and a pore volume of 0.08 cc/g. The CEPAC 1:0.5 exhibited a 
slightly lower pore radius (Dv[r]) of 1.9 nm, a slightly larger pore 
surface area of 102 m2/g, and a slightly greater pore volume of 
0.21 cc/g. These numbers show that the SSA of the CEPAC 1:1 
was significantly higher than that of the CEPAC 1:0.5. These 
results can be attributed to the KOH activation in higher quan -
tities in CEPAC 1:1, thereby, creating a larger surface area. The 
high SSA can contribute to an enhanced specific capacitance, 
rate capabilities, energy density, and cycling stability of the su -
percapacitor device. The obtained pore volume could also fa -
cilitate ionic movement, leading to improved electrochemical 
performance. The adsorption–  desorption N 2 isotherm of the 
CEPAC 1:1 sample exhibited a Type IV isotherm, indicating a 
mesoporous structure as shown in Figure  4c. Conversely, the 
CEPAC 1:0.5 sample (see Figure  4f) is indicative of a Type III 
behavior, suggesting a macroporous structure characterized by 
weak interactions.

3.2   |   Electrochemical Performance of the EDLC 
Electrode
Based on the structural characterization, the as-  synthesized AC 
materials possessed high SSA and numerous mesopores, making 
it a suitable electrode material for supercapacitor applications. A 
three- electrode system was designed in 3 M KOH and 6 M KOH 
electrolyte solutions and used to investigate the electrochemical 
capacitive performance of the carbon materials. Analysis of CV, 
GCD, EIS, and cyclic stability tests were conducted to ascertain 
the electrochemical performance of the samples.
3.2.1   |   CV Analysis
The electrochemical performance of the electrode materials in 
the three-  electrode system was analyzed and the results dis -
cussed. Figure  5a,b shows the CV curves of the as-  synthesized 
CEPAC 1:1 in 3 M KOH and 6 M KOH, respectively, at differ -
ent scan rates and a wide potential window of 1.2 V, with a 
quasi- rectangular or isosceles shape which is a feature of 
EDLCs. The CV comparative analyses displayed higher vol -
umetric current, resulting in a higher specific capacitance at 
lower electrolyte concentration (3 M KOH). This result can 
be attributed to the direct effect of the potassium ions (K +) at 
the AC interface since there is enough time for ion migration. 
Such behaviors are evident, especially with decreasing scan 
rate (at 5 mV/s). The presence of oxygen heteroatom, which 
serves as some form of pseudocapacitive element [ 46, 51], also 
contributed to the improved performance as a result of higher 
redox reaction as shown in Figure  5c. Using a scan rate of 
5 mV/s, a specific capacitance of 472 and 307 F/g was recorded 
in 3 M KOH and 6 M KOH electrolyte solution, respectively. 
As the concentration of the electrolyte increases, there exists 
much competition of the ions during migration into the porous 
interiors of the AC, thereby decreasing the volumetric current 
(hence, lowering specific capacitance), as shown in Figure  5d. 
The lower capacitance recorded in higher electrolyte concen -
trations can also be attributed to the disruption of the active 
sites of the AC by the highly concentrated potassium ions. 
These results are shown in Table  1. To understand the effect 
of the activator on the sample during activation, the quantity 
of KOH was reduced by 50%. The sample was labeled CEPAC 
1:0.5. Figure  5e,f shows the CV results of the electrode materi -
als tested in 3 and 6 M KOH, respectively, at different scan rates 
(using −1.2–  0 V potential window). From the figures, similar

3.2.2   |   Galvanostatic Charge–  Discharge Analysis

electrode materials (CEPAC 1:1) were charged and discharged

that there are no deviations from the linearity of the charging 
regime with no visible IR drop during discharging. These linear 
and symmetric profiles of the GCD curves are typical of EDLCs. 
This gives rise to high columbic efficiency of the electrode mate-
rials. The specific capacitance increases as the current densities 
decrease. This is because enough time is allowed for ions to

3.2.3   |   EIS Analysis
The Nyquist plot of the as- synthesized electrode materials tested in 
both solutions is presented in Figure  6g. The results describe the 
interfacial kinetics between the electrode and electrolyte. The plots 
show a semicircle and almost vertical line in the high-  and low- 
frequency regions, respectively. Table 3 shows the EIS equivalent 
circuit analysis results obtained from fitting using Figure 6h. The 
equivalent circuit analysis results revealed circuit components, in-
cluding electrical double- layer capacitance (Cdl), charger transfer 
resistance (Rct), solution resistance of the bulk electrolyte (Rs), and 
Warburg frequency parameter (Wo). The presence of the Warburg 
frequency parameter indicates that the electrode reaction kinetics 
were present in the supercapacitor system studied. From Table 3, it 
can be observed that the electrochemical performances of the two 
different AC samples, denoted as CEPAC 1:1 and CEPAC 1:0.5, 
were different when tested in 3 and 6 M KOH electrolytes, respec-
tively. Comparatively, it can be observed that CEPAC 1:1 in 3 M 
KOH exhibited relatively higher electrical properties than CEPAC 
1:0.5 samples in 3 and 6 M KOH, respectively.
CEPAC 1:1 in 3 M KOH showed circuit properties such as C dl 
of 984.62 μF, Rs of 0.830 Ω, and R ct of 0.368 Ω. Due to the rela -
tively low solution and charge transfer resistances observed in 
the 3 M KOH electrolyte, it is more likely that efficient charge 
conduction or diffusion probably occurred in the electrolyte. 
Also, CEPAC 1:1 shows Wo of 1.481 and 1.018 Ω/s ½ in 3 and 6 M 
KOH electrolytes, respectively. The Warburg frequency parame-
ter was favored in the 3 M KOH electrolyte as shown in Table 3 .
Again, it can be observed from Table  3 that there was an ap -
preciable change in C dl values of CEPAC 1:0.5 from 513.14 to 
196.02 μF for the 3 and 6 M KOH electrolyte medium, respec -
tively. This significant change can be attributed to the relatively 
high solution resistance of 13.872 Ω observed in the 6 M KOH 
electrolyte. Moreover, comparing the CEPAC 1:0.5 samples in 
both 3 and 6 M KOH, similar trends were observed with electro -
lytes having lower concentrations.
The results presented in Table  3 revealed possible circuit com -
ponents that can be associated with an ideal supercapacitor 
system. It was observed that electrolyte composition and elec -
trode material greatly influenced the electrical properties of 
the circuit elements of the supercapacitor system studied. One 
of the most significant factors that measure how well a super -
capacitor cell can store charges is its electrical double capac -
itance value. From Table  3, it can be seen that the activation 
ratio plays a vital role in the electrical double-  layer storage 
mechanism. CEPAC 1:1 sample exhibited the highest electri -
cal double- layer capacitance ( Cdl) as compared to CEPAC 1:0.5. 
Looking at the electrical double-  layer capacitance values, sev -
eral inferences could be drawn. It can be seen that CEPAC 
1:1 sample was more porous, indicating that using KOH of the 
same amount as the carbon material creates more mesopores 
for accommodating more charges, which is in agreement with 
the SEM and BET results. Another point worthy to note is the 
concentration of the electrolyte used. Usually, the activation 
agent creates pores that are similar to their ionic sizes, and 
since the activation agent is the same as the electrolyte, ionic 
diffusion could occur with ease.
However, increasing electrolyte concentration leads to a reduc -
tion in the Cdl values, and this might be due to the disruption 
of the pore networks by the highly concentrated electrolyte.

shown in Figure  7a,b. The device delivered an impressive spe -
cific capacitance of 98.7 F/g and energy and power density of 
13.7 Wh/kg and 500.5 W/kg, respectively, at 1 A/g. The device 
also offered low charge transfer resistance even after cycling, 
delivering a real capacitance of 0.17 F as shown in Figure  7c,d. 
The lower charge transfer resistance after cycling can be at -
tributed to the variation in the internal structure and features 
of the electrode–  electrolyte interface during cycling which can 
alter the transport of ions. After 10 000 charge–  discharge cycles, 
the assembled cell maintained 98.4% of the initial recorded ca -
pacitance and a Coulombic efficiency of 100% (see Figure  7e), 
suggesting that the CEPAC 1:1 can be used for practical super -
capacitor applications. These results outperform previously re -
ported data on biowaste-  derived AC (see Table  4) and suggest 
that the facile synthesis used for this work is a more efficient and 
viable option for supercapacitor applications.
4   |   Conclusion
By using a simple, low-  cost, and environmentally friendly two- 
stage facile activation process, a sustainable biowaste-  derived 
carbon with numerous mesoporous textures was synthesized 
from CEPs. The as-  synthesized AC was used as an electrode 
material for electrochemical supercapacitor application. A 
specific capacitance of 525.3 F/g was recorded at 1 A/g in the 
three- electrode system using 3 M KOH solution, and the elec -
trode maintained 96.6% of this capacitance after 3000 charging 
and discharging. The assembled symmetric SC cell delivered 
an impressive specific capacitance, energy, and power densities 
of 98.7 F/g, 13.7 Wh/kg, and 500.5 W/kg, respectively, at 1 A/g. 
The device, after 10 000 charge–  discharge cycles, maintained 
98.4% of the initial recorded capacitance, suggesting that the 
CEPAC 1:1 can be used for a practical supercapacitor. With a 
focus on utilizing available and reasonably low-  cost biowaste 
with superior qualities as precursors for possible energy storage 
applications, the current work aims to increase the green and 
sustainable synthesis approach.

Porous Carbon Electrode from Starch Soluble for Realizing
High-Performance Supercapacitor
Jv Zhang,
[a]
Mingxing Jiao,
[a]
Ziyi Geng,
[a]
Yaofeng Liu,
[a]
Zheng Cui,
[a]
Siyu Xu,
[a]
Zhuo Li,
[a]
Xin Zhang,
[a]
Shaoheng Cheng,*
[a]
Qiliang Wang,*
[a]
and Hongdong Li*
[a]
Organic potassium salts are the promising green activators for
synthesizing porous carbon materials for energy storage. Here-
in, we report the synthesis of hierarchical porous carbon
material derived from the mixture of soluble starch and
ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid dipotassium salt dihydrate
(EDTA-2K) via carbonization and activation strategy. The sample
is used as supercapacitors electrode, which exhibits superior
mass specific capacitance (307.3 F g
 1
at 1 A g
 1
), good rate
performance (255.0 F g
 1
at 10 A g
 1
), and excellent stability
(retaining 83 % after 15000 cycles). This enhanced electrode
performance is mainly due to the high specific surface area, the
heteroatom co-doping providing pseudo-capacitance and the
improved electronic conductivity. In addition, the asymmetric
supercapacitor device shows a high energy density of
15 Wh kg
 1
at the power density of 800 W kg
 1
and capacitance
retention of 90 % after 12000 cycles.
1. Introduction
With the urgent demand for efficient energy storage technolo-
gies, supercapacitors have attracted widespread attention for
their excellent stability, high charging and discharging effi-
ciency, and ultra-high power density.
[1,2]
Currently, porous
carbon materials are widely used as electrode materials for
supercapacitors due to their low cost, large specific surface
area, high electrical conductivity, and adjustable pore
structure.
[3,4]
In general, different pore sizes play different roles,
where micropores (< 2 nm) contribute to ion storage, meso-
pores (2–50 nm) help to accelerate ion diffusion, and macro-
pores (> 50 nm) shorten the ion transport path.
[5,6]
Thus, adjust-
ing the pores size to a proper ratio can effectively improve the
performance of supercapacitors.
The preparation of porous carbon usually needs the proper
carbon source as the precursor. Starch (corn starch,
[7]
soluble
starch,
[8]
cassava starch,
[9]
etc.) has been widely used as a source
of porous carbon due to its advantages of oxygen enrichment,
low cost, and degradability. However, due to the inferior pore
structure and low specific surface area, activation is usually
required for obtaining porous carbon materials.
[10,11]
Chemical
activation is a preferred method to obtain high-performance
porous carbon materials compared with physical activation.
[12]
Furthermore, some activators can introduce heteroatoms, which
will further improve the capacitance performance.
[13,14]
However,
the most used chemical activators of KOH,
[13]
ZnCl
2
,
[15]
K
2
CO
3
,
[16]
and KHCO
3
[5]
are highly corrosive, and their high consumption
leads to serious pollution.
[17,18]
Therefore, the development of
green and efficient chemical activators has become a research
hotspot.
[19]
At present, organic potassium salts (OPSs) of
potassium citrate, potassium alginate, ethylenediaminetetra-
acetic acid dipotassium salt dihydrate (EDTA-2K) and potassium
oxalate have been explored to be activators. OPSs is less
corrosive to facilities, and less dosage is required.
[20]
In addition,
the carbon matrix will limit the growth of inorganic intermedi-
ates, resulting in forming porous carbon materials with high
specific surface area and large specific capacitance.
[20,21]
How-
ever, it has not been explored for the design of soluble starch
and EDTA-2k composite materials for supercapacitors electrode.
In this study, with the soluble starch as a carbon source and
EDTA-2K as the activator, we successfully prepared N  O co-
doped porous carbon (NOPC) electrode by a one-step carbon-
ization method. The electrode exhibits a high mass specific
capacitance (307.3 F g
 1
, 1 A g
 1
) and high cycling stability
(83 %, 10 A g
 1
, 15000 cycles). In addition, we assembled
asymmetric supercapacitors with the NOPC product as the
positive electrode and activated carbon as the negative
electrode. After 12000 charge/discharge cycles, the device has
90 % capacitance retention and 95 % Coulombic efficiency,
showing excellent cycling stability.
Experimental Section
Materials
The following chemicals used: soluble starch, ethylenediaminetetra-
acetic acid EDTA-2K, and activated carbon were purchased from
Aladdin Industrial Corporation (Shanghai, China). Hydrochloric acid
(HCl, 36–38 %) was supplied by Nanjing Chemical Reagent Co., Ltd.
Potassium hydroxide (KOH) was available from Sinopharm Co., Ltd.
All reagents were analytical reagent grade and used as received
without further treatment. The nickel foam was obtained from Love
Blue Sky High-Tech Materials Co., Ltd.

Materials Synthesis
The nickel foam was ultrasonically cleaned in acetone, 3 M HCl
solution, deionized water, and ethanol for 15 min, respectively.
Then the nickel foam was dried at 60 ° C for 12 h. EDTA-2K was
ground into a uniform mixture with soluble starch in various mass
ratios (1, 2, 4 and 8). The mixture was calcined at 500 ° C with a
heating rate of 5 ° C/min for 4 h under Argon (Ar) atmosphere. After
thermal treatment, the product was soaked in 1 M HCl solution to
remove impurities and then cleaned with deionized water until the
pH of the washing solution was neutral. The precipitate was dried
at 60 ° C for 12 h. As prepared porous carbon was denoted NOPC-x,
where x was the mass ratio of EDTA-2K to soluble starch (x = 1, 2, 4
and 8).
Characterization
The elements, morphologies, and crystalline structures were
investigated by scanning electron microscopy (SEM, FEI Magellan
400) equipped with energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS), trans-
mission electron microscopy (TEM, JEM-2200FS, JEOL), X-ray photo-
electron spectroscopy (XPS, ESCALAB-MKII) and X-ray diffraction
(XRD, Smart Lab, Rigaku). The specific surface area was tested
through the Multi-point Brunauer-Emmett-Teller (BET) method. The
pore size distribution (PSD) of the samples were calculated by
modeled by employing the regularization method according to
Density Functional Theory (DFT).
[22,23]
The Raman spectra was
recorded by Renishaw in a Via system excited by the 532 nm Ar
+
laser.
To prepare the porous carbon electrode, the mixture contained the
prepared NOPC (80 wt%), acetylene black (15 wt%), and polytetra-
fluoroethylene (PTFE, 5 wt%), which were pressed on a nickel foam
(1×1 cm
2
) and dried at 60 ° C for 12 h. The mass loading of the active
material was about 1.3 mg, and the thickness of electrode was
about 10 μm. For the three-electrode tests, the NOPCs electrode,
saturated calomel electrode, and Pt foil were used as the working,
reference, and counter electrodes, respectively. The performance
was evaluated by electrochemical characterization methods using a
2 M KOH solution as the electrolyte including cyclic voltammetry
(CV), galvanostatic charge-discharge (GCD), and electrochemical
impedance spectroscopy (EIS). All measurements were character-
ized by a CHI760E electrochemical workstation (Shang-hai Chenhua
Inc., China).
Asymmetric supercapacitors device was assembled with NOPC-4 as
the positive electrode, activated carbon as the negative electrode,
cellulose paper as the separator, and 2 M KOH as the electrolyte.

2. Results and Discussion
2.1. Morphology and Structure
As shown in Figure S1, the soluble starch used in the experi-
ment mainly contains C and O elements. It exhibits high yield
of carbonaceous product after carbonization, thus soluble
starch is a promising precursor to produce oxygen rich porous
carbon materials. The SEM images in Figures 1a and b and S2
present the morphology of samples activated by different
amounts of EDTA-2K, and the hierarchical porous structure can
be observed. For the NOPC-1 sample, the pores are not well
developed (Figure S2a), since a small amount of activators are
not enough to create pores. As the activator increases, more
pores can be created as observed. When the EDTA-2K is
increased to a certain amount (mass ratio of 4), the stage of
pores is well developed (Figure 1a and b). With further addition
of EDTA-2K to mass ratio of 8, the collapse of porous structure
results in stackable fragment structure (Figure S2c). The EDS of
the NOPC-4 sample in Figure 1c shows that C, N and O
elements are uniformly distributed on the sample surface. The
abundant N and O play an important role in improving the
capacity, which has been reported in literature.
[24–27]
TEM images
show a disordered carbon (Figure 1d and e), and the inset
image in Figure 1e shows the diffused concentric diffraction
rings in the selected area electron diffraction (SAED) pattern,
which denotes the amorphous feature of the sample.
[28,29]
The XRD patterns of the samples are shown in Figure 2a. All
the XRD patterns show a broad diffraction peak at about 24 °
and a weak peak at about 43 ° , corresponding to the (002) and
(100) planes of disordered carbon, respectively.
[30,31]
This obser-
vation confirms the amorphous feature of the synthesized
NOPC samples, which closely matches the TEM and SAED
results in Figure 1d and e. The Raman spectra in Figure 2b show
that two characteristic peaks centered at 1350 cm
 1
and
1588 cm
 1
are D band and G band.
[32]
The D band reflects the
defect of disorder caused by the sp
3
-hybridization carbon, and
the G band refers to the in-plane vibration of sp
2
-hybridized
carbon atoms.
[24,33]
The intensity ratio of the D band to G band
(I
D
/I
G
) is used to evaluate the degree of carbon disorder.
[21,34]
Specifically, the I
D
/I
G
values of NOPC-1, NOPC-2, NOPC-4, and
NOPC-8 are 0.87, 0.93, 0.94 and 0.97, respectively, which also
suggests that NOPC sample possesses a high degree of
amorphousness.
The pore structure and surface area of samples were
investigated by N
2
adsorption-desorption isotherms in Fig-
ure S3. With a steep rise at the low relative pressure in adsorbed
volumes, NOPC samples mainly display type-I nitrogen adsorp-
tion/desorption isotherms (Figure S3a), which denotes plentiful
micropores.
[35]
With the further increase of the pressure, the
adsorption capacity increases slowly to a steady state, indicat-
ing the presence of mesopores.
[36]
The specific surface areas of
NOPC-1, NOPC-2, NOPC-4, and NOPC-8 are 284.7, 305.3, 285.7

microscopic interpretation of gas adsorption in micro and
mesopores on a molecular level. Gas adsorption-equipment
manufacturers have commercialized the DFT model to interpret
experimental data and calculate PSD from adsorption
isotherms.
[22,37]
The pore size distribution curves in Figure S3b
are consistent with the results of the nitrogen adsorption/
desorption curves. There are two pore distributions, which are
in the range of 0.78–2 nm and 2.0–3.5 nm. Apparently, the two
ranges provide significant evidence for the rich micro/meso-
porous structure of NOPC, which effectively enhances its
performance as a capacitor.
[38]
Since the carbonaceous material
prepared in this work is powder, which needs to be coated on
the substrate surface with binder and conductive agent for
electrode preparation. However, the use of binders may block
part of the pores for the porous electrodes, increases the
diffusion resistance of electrolyte ions, and leads to the
decrease of the capacitance. Thus, PTFE is chosen as the binder,
which is better in performance than other binders for super-
capacitors electrode preparation.
[39]
Thus, the reduced PSD is
minimum to maintain the performance of electrode.
XPS technique was employed to determine the surface
elemental composition of the NOPC samples, as shown in
Figure 3a. The C, O, and N elements are found in the NOPC
samples, and N and O elements should be originated from
EDTA-2k and starch in the precursor. In comparison with the
XPS spectra of NOPC-x (x = 1, 2, 8) in Figure S4 and Table S2,
the contents of O and N in NOPC-4 (O = 16.58 % and N = 6.33 %)
are higher than those of others. In the XPS spectrum of C 1s,
the four peaks at 284.8 eV, 285.3 eV, 286.5 eV and 288.9 eV are
attributed to C = C, C  N, C  O and C = O, respectively (Fig-
ure 3b).
[3,36,40]
As shown in Figure 3c, the peaks at 531.2 eV,
532.4 eV, 533.1 eV and 534.2 eV correspond to COOR, C  OH,
O  C and O = C, respectively.
[36,41]
The O = C plays an active role in
Faraday reactions during charge/discharge process.
[42]
The other
oxygen-containing functional groups can optimize the surface
wettability and electronic conductivity, which benefits the
improvement of pseudo-capacitance.
[43,44]
The N 1s spectrum in
Figure 3d exhibits four peaks at 399.0 eV, 400.3 eV, 401.0 eV,
and 401.9 eV, corresponding to pyridinic-N, pyrrolic-N, graphite-
N and oxidized-N.
[11,36]
The presence of pyridinic-N and pyrrolic-
N can produce additional pseudo-capacitance by providing
additional free or delocalized electrons to the electron-deficient
carbon atoms, and graphite-N and oxidized-N increase the
electron transfer ability and enhance the conductivity of the
electrode material.
[42,45,46]

0–0.5 V and a scanning rate of 100 mV s
 1
. The CV curves show
a pair of obvious oxidation/reduction peaks, which indicates

[47]
The CV curve

samples, indicating that it has better capacitance properties.
GCD curves in Figure 4b show that the NOPC-4 sample exhibits
the longest discharge time. Mass specific capacitance of NOPC-
x at different current densities was calculated from GCD curves
and presented in Figure 4c. As the current density increases, the
mass specific capacitance decreases gradually, which is a
common phenomenon for pseudocapacitive electrodes.

With
the current density of 1 A g

, the mass specific capacitance

Although NOPC-4 shows a smaller specific surface area
compared to those of NOPC-2 and NOPC-8 samples, NOPC-4
exhibits the best capacitance performance. The synergies from
high surface area, large heteroatom content and hierarchical
porous structures can significantly improve capacitance per-
formance. Meanwhile, NOPC-4 maintains 255.0 F g
 1
even at the
current density of 10 A g
 1
, which indicates that the sample
exhibits excellent rate performance. The EIS of NOPC-x sample
is presented in Figure 4d. The Nyquist plot shows that in the
high-frequency region, the four samples exhibit similar equiv-
alent series resistances value of approximately 0.8 Ω. In the low-
frequency region, NOPC-4 is more parallel to the vertical axis,
indicating that its internal resistance is smaller, and it has good
capacitance behavior.
[49–51]
Therefore, NOPC-4 displays better
capacitance performance than NOPC-2 and NOPC-8.
Figure 5a shows the CV curve of NOPC-4 at the scan rate
from 10–100 mV s
 1
. At different scanning rates, the shape of CV
curves remains similar, indicating that the sample has excellent
charge conductivity and rate properties. The GCD curves of
NOPC-4 at different current densities are shown in Figure 5b. A
symmetrical nature indicates a high reversibility of the sample
with a high Coulombic efficiency.

[52]
Figure S5a shows a side-by-side CV curves of
activated carbon and NOPC-4 from three electrode system at
100 mV s
 1
to reasonably estimate the appropriate potential
window for the asymmetric supercapacitor. The potential differ-
ence between activated carbon and NOPC-4 is about 1.6 V. In
addition, CV curves of NOPC-4//activated carbon are obtained
at different potential windows ranging from 0–1.0 V to 0–1.6 V
in Figure S5b. With the increase of the potential window, the
curves maintain a good shape, and no polarization reaction
occurs in the potential window of 0–1.6 V. Thus, 0–1.6 V is
selected as the working potential window of the device. The
electrochemical performance of the device is shown in Figure 6.
Figure 6a shows the CV curve with the scan rate of 10–
100 mV s
 1
and the potential window of 0–1.6 V. The trend of
CV shape is neither rectangular nor humpy depicting the
combination of both materials.
[53]
The slightly disordered
rectangular shape of the CV curves denotes the coexistence of
electric double-layer capacitor and faradaic pseudocapacitance.
In addition, the redox peaks in CV curves suggest the
occurrence of redox reaction, as observed in previous works,
[54]
which is caused by heteroatom doping into the carbon frame-
work. With the increasing scanning rate, almost no deformation
of CV curve is found, indicating the good reversibility of the
asymmetric supercapacitor device. In Figure 6b, a symmetric
shape is observed in the GCD curves at different current
densities, illustrating good charge-discharge performance. At
the current density of 1 A g
 1
, the mass specific capacitance of
the device is maximum (42.7 F g
 1
). The cycle stability of the
assembled device was evaluated by 12000 cycles at the high
current density of 5 A g
 1
. As shown in Figure 6c, the capaci-
tance retention rate of the NOPC-4//activated carbon asymmet-
ric supercapacitor device is about 90 %, and the Coulombic
efficiency is 95 %, indicating good cyclic stability. As presented
in the Ragone diagram in Figure 6d, when the maximum energy
density is 15.16 Wh kg
 1
, the power density is 800 W kg

, when
the maximum power density is 8000 W kg
 1
, the energy density
remains at 2.86 Wh kg
 1
. Obviously, as the current density
increases, the energy density is suppressed. It is worth noting

),

3. Conclusion
In summary, we successfully prepared hierarchical porous
carbon materials by carbonizing the mixture of soluble starch
and EDTA-2K. The obtained sample displays the best capaci-
tance performance by optimizing the ratio of the material.
Taking into account high specific surface area, heteroatom
content and proper micro/mesopores, the NOPC-4 electrode
exhibits the best electrochemical performance with high mass
specific capacitance (307.3 F g
 1
, 1 A g
 1
) and high cycling
stability (83 %, 10 A g
 1
, 15000 cycles). The assembled asymmet-
ric supercapacitor shows a mass specific capacitance of
42.7 F g
 1
at a current density of 1 A g
 1
, and an energy density
of 15.16 Wh kg
 1
at a power density of 800 W kg
 1
. It also shows
excellent cycle stability (90 %, 12000 cycles). This work denotes
that EDTA-2K is a green and efficient activator for the synthesis
of porous carbon materials. It provides a scalable approach to
produce simple, low-cost, and environmentally friendly super-
capacitor materials.

RESEARCH ARTICLE
Tailoring Porosity and Surface Functionality in Activated 
Carbon via Synergistic Ultrasonic and Microwave Activation 
for Energy Storage Applications 
Ayten Ateş1 Zaid Rossi2 
1 Faculty of Engineering, Department of Chemical Engineering, Sivas Cumhuriyet University, Sivas, Türkiye 2 Materials, Systems and Energy Engineering 
Laboratory (MaSEEL) -UAE/U04FSTTg- Faculty of Sciences and Techniques of Tangier, Abdelmalek Essaâdi University, Tétouan, Morocco 
Correspondence: Ayten Ateş( ates@cumhuriyet.edu.tr) 
Received: 8 November 2025 Revised: 12 January 2026 Accepted: 16 February 2026 
Keywords: acid activation | activated carbon | hazelnut shell | supercapacitor | ultrasonic activation 
ABSTRACT 
Hazelnut shell–derived activated carbons were synthesized via phosphoric acid chemical activation and subsequently modified 
using microwave (MW) and ultrasonic (US) treatments to tailor their physicochemical and electrochemical properties for 
supercapacitor applications. Structural and spectroscopic analyses confirmed the formation of turbostratic carbon frameworks 
with partial graphitic ordering and abundant surface functional groups. Elemental analysis revealed that microwave treatment 
induced pronounced surface oxidation, whereas ultrasonic treatment preserved high carbon content while introducing moderate 
oxygen functionalities. Thermal analysis demonstrated superior thermal stability for the ultrasound-assisted activated carbon. 
Electrochemical performance was evaluated in a three-electrode system using 3 M KOH electrolyte. Cyclic voltammetry revealed 
dominant electrical double-layer capacitive behavior with minor pseudocapacitive contributions, particularly for the ultrasound- 
treated sample. Among all electrodes, ACA-US exhibited the largest CV area, highest current response, and superior specific 
capacitance, attributed to its exceptionally high BET surface area (2138 m2 g− 1 ) and well-developed microporosity. Galvanostatic 
charge–discharge measurements confirmed excellent reversibility and rate capability, with ACA-US delivering the longest 
discharge times and highest capacitance over a wide current density range. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy revealed 
reduced charge transfer resistance and improved ion diffusion kinetics for ACA-US. Furthermore, the optimized electrode 
retained ∼ 85% of its initial capacitance after 2000 cycles, indicating excellent long-term stability. These results demonstrate that 
ultrasonic post-treatment is an effective strategy for producing high-performance biomass-derived activated carbons for advanced 
supercapacitor applications. 
1 Introduction 
The rising global energy demand, diminishing fossil fuel reserves, 
and growing environmental concerns due to climate change 
have collectively driven a rapid shift toward renewable energy 
sources such as solar and wind. This transition not only supports 
efforts to reduce greenhouse gas emissions but also promotes the 
development of cleaner transportation technologies, including 
electric and hybrid vehicles. Nevertheless, the intermittent and 
variable nature of renewable energy generation highlights the 
urgent need for efficient and reliable energy storage systems. 
In this context, batteries and electrochemical capacitors have 
emerged as two of the most commonly utilized technologies for 
storing electrical energy. While batteries offer high energy densi- 
ties, electrochemical capacitors—particularly  supercapacitors—
are capable of delivering significantly higher power densities
