(up to 10 kW kg− 1 ) and exhibit rapid charge–discharge capability, 
albeit with lower energy densities ( ∼ 5 Wh kg− 1 ) [ 1, 2 ]. 
Supercapacitors have gained significant attention as advanced 
energy storage systems, offering a balance between traditional 
capacitors and batteries. Their ability to deliver high power 
density, sustain rapid charge/discharge cycles, provide extended 
operational lifespans, and maintain cost-effectiveness makes 
them highly suitable for various demanding applications. These 
attribute render them suitable for various sectors, including 
portable electronics, hybrid electric vehicles, and grid stabi- 
lization. Despite these advantages, further advancements in 
materials science and a deeper understanding of charge storage 
mechanisms—particularly  at the electrochemical interface—are  
essential to meet the growing demands of next-generation energy 
systems [ 1, 2 ]. 
A critical factor influencing the performance of supercapacitors 
is the selection of electrode material. Extensive research has 
focused on developing novel electrode materials with optimized 
structure and surface chemistry. Common classes of materials 
include carbon-based materials (e.g., activated carbon, carbon 
nanotubes), transition metal oxides (e.g., NiO, MnO2 , RuO2 ), and 
conducting polymers [ 3 ]. Among them, carbon-based materials 
have garnered considerable interest due to their high electrical 
conductivity, chemical stability, tunable porosity, and low cost. 
In particular, activated carbon ( AC ), known for its high surface 
area and well-developed pore structure, has been extensively 
investigated. The performance of AC is strongly influenced by the 
type of precursor used and the activation method applied [ 4, 5 ]. 
Most commercial activated carbons are derived from fossil-based 
precursors, which are costly and environmentally unsustain- 
able. This limitation has spurred research into biomass-derived 
carbons, offering advantages such as renewability, low cost, 
and reduced environmental impact [ 2 ]. Various agricultural and 
agro-industrial wastes, including rice husks, sugarcane bagasse, 
apricot shells, palm kernel shells, and coffee residues, have 
been successfully converted into porous carbon materials for use 
in electric double-layer capacitors ( EDLCs ) [ 6 ]. These biomass 
wastes are often discarded or underutilized, yet they possess 
inherent porosity and carbon-rich content, making them suitable 
candidates for high-performance electrode materials. 
The physicochemical properties of biomass-derived carbon can 
be significantly enhanced through physical and chemical modifi- 
cation methods [ 7, 8 ]. Among chemical agents, acids (e.g., H3 PO4 , 
HNO3 ), bases (e.g., KOH, NaOH), and oxidants (e.g., H2 O2 , 
KMnO4 ) have been widely employed to improve surface area 
and pore development [ 9, 10 ]. H3 PO4 and KOH are among the 
most commonly studied activating agents due to their efficiency 
in tailoring surface structure and functionality [ 9, 11 , 12 ]. In 
particular, phosphoric acid (H3 PO4 ) is one of the most effective 
chemical activating agents for directing the structural evolution 
and pore morphology of biomass-derived activated carbon [ 13 ]. 
Owing to its strong affinity for oxygen-containing functional 
groups, H3 PO4 readily diffuses into lignocellulosic matrices and 
catalyzes a sequence of temperature-dependent transformations 
that control pore formation and carbon framework stability [ 14, 
15 ]. During the initial heating stage ( ≤ 200◦C), the acid promotes 
hydrolytic cleavage of glycosidic and ether bonds within cellulose 
and hemicellulose, while simultaneously inducing dehydration 
reactions that limit tar formation. At this stage, H3 PO4 under- 
goes condensation to generate polyphosphate species, which 
chemically bridge adjacent biopolymer chains and reinforce the 
precursor structure against thermal collapse [ 16, 17 ]. 
As pyrolysis proceeds to intermediate temperatures (200–400◦C), 
extensive depolymerization and dehydration of the organic 
matrix occur, leading to progressive aromatization of the carbon 
backbone. The presence of phosphate and polyphosphate link- 
ages moderates the rate of carbon consumption and preserves the 
integrity of the developing pore network, while the continuous 
evolution of volatile species initiates the formation of primary 
micropores [ 18–20 ]. This controlled activation pathway results 
in higher carbon yield and more uniform pore distribution 
compared with nonphosphoric activators [ 21 ]. 
At elevated temperatures (400◦C–700◦C), thermally unstable 
phosphate species decompose into phosphorus oxides, such 
as pyrophosphates and P2 O5 , which act as strong dehydrating 
and mild oxidizing agents within the carbon matrix [ 22, 23 ]. 
Simultaneously, the release of gaseous products (H2 O, CO, and 
CO2 ) expands previously formed micropores and generates inter- 
connected mesoporous channels, producing a hierarchical pore 
structure favorable for ion transport [ 23 ]. 
Further heating to very high temperatures ( ≥ 700◦C–900◦C) 
may intensify pore enlargement through carbon–oxide redox 
reactions; however, excessive thermal exposure can diminish 
surface functional groups and partially degrade pore walls, which 
may adversely affect electrochemical performance [ 24 ]. Overall, 
H3 PO4 activation uniquely integrates dehydration-driven cross- 
linking, controlled volatilization, and phosphate-mediated pore 
expansion, enabling precise regulation of pore size distribu- 
tion and surface chemistry. In addition, residual phosphorus- 
containing functionalities enhance electrolyte wettability and 
introduce faradaic contributions, rendering phosphoric-acid- 
activated carbons highly suitable for high-performance superca- 
pacitor electrodes [ 25 ]. 
Furthermore, combining chemical activation with alternative 
energy sources such as microwave irradiation and ultrasonic 
treatment has shown promise in improving activation efficiency 
and material performance. Microwave-assisted activation enables 
rapid and uniform heating, which can significantly shorten 
processing time and improve energy efficiency compared to 
conventional thermal methods. On the other hand, ultrasonic 
treatment generates localized cavitation and turbulence in the 
reaction medium, enhancing the penetration of activating agents 
and promoting the formation of a more accessible porous struc- 
ture [ 26 ]. Notably, the synergistic use of acid treatment, ultrasonic 
pretreatment, and microwave irradiation has been reported to 
significantly modify the surface chemistry and structural features 
of biochar [ 10 ]. 
Although phosphoric acid-activated biomass-derived carbons as 
well as microwave- and ultrasound-assisted activation techniques 
have been individually investigated, their combined and sys- 
tematic comparison within a unified activation strategy remains 
largely unexplored, particularly for hazelnut shell–based carbon 
materials. Addressing this gap, the present study proposes a

hybrid activation approach that integrates ultrasonic pretreat- 
ment, phosphoric acid chemical activation, and microwave- 
assisted heating for the first-time using hazelnut shells as a 
sustainable and locally abundant precursor. 
The originality of this work resides in the direct and controlled 
comparison of three activation pathways—conventional  chemi- 
cal activation (ACA), microwave-assisted activation (ACA-MW), 
and ultrasound-assisted activation (ACA-US)—prepared  under 
identical chemical impregnation and carbonization conditions. 
This design enables a clear assessment of how different physical 
activation routes influence pore development, surface chemistry, 
and structural stability following phosphoric acid activation, and 
how these features translate into electrochemical charge storage 
behavior in both alkaline and neutral electrolytes. 
Experimentally, hazelnut shells were impregnated with H3 PO4 
at a biomass-to-acid ratio of 1:3 and carbonized at 700◦C for 
2 h under an inert atmosphere, followed by microwave or ultra- 
sonic treatment where applicable. The resulting materials were 
comprehensively characterized using proximate and ultimate 
analyses, Raman spectroscopy, FTIR, XRD, TGA, SEM, and EDS 
to elucidate their physicochemical and morphological properties. 
Their electrochemical performance was subsequently evaluated 
to assess their suitability as supercapacitor electrodes. 
Overall, this integrated activation strategy provides new mech- 
anistic insights into synergistic chemical–physical activation 
effects and demonstrates a cost-effective and scalable route 
for converting an underutilized agricultural waste into high- 
performance carbon electrodes for energy storage applications. 
2 Results and Discussions 
2.1 Elemental Composition 
Elemental analysis results of the activated carbon samples are 
shown in Table 1 . The results revealed notable variations in car- 
bon, oxygen, hydrogen, nitrogen, and sulfur content as a function 
of the applied modification method. The pristine activated carbon 
( ACA ) exhibited a high carbon content (79.60 wt.%) and relatively 
low oxygen content (17.8 wt.%), indicative of a predominantly 
graphitic structure with limited oxygenated surface functionali- 
ties. This composition reflects a low degree of surface oxidation 
and a hydrophobic character. 
Microwave-assisted activated carbon( ACA-MW ) resulted in a pro- 
nounced decrease in carbon content (66.40 wt.%) alongside a sig- 
nificant increase in oxygen content (30.14 wt.%). These changes 
suggest the occurrence of oxidative processes facilitated by 
microwave irradiation, likely involving the formation of oxygen- 
containing functional groups such as hydroxyls, carbonyls, and 
carboxylic acids [ 27 ]. The elevated hydrogen content in ACA- 
MW (2.80 wt.%) further supports the presence of increased 
hydroxylation and/or chemisorbed water molecules [ 28 ]. 
In contrast, ultrasound-assisted activated carbon(ACA-US) main- 
tained a relatively high carbon content (77.50 wt.%) while 
inducing a moderate increase in oxygen content (20.33 wt.%) com- 
pared to ACA . This suggests that ultrasonic treatment promotes 
limited surface oxidation, likely via localized cavitation-induced 
reactions that introduce mild surface defects and oxygenated 
sites without severely disrupting the carbon matrix. The slightly 
reduced hydrogen (2.17 wt.%) and nitrogen (0.36 wt.%) contents in 
ACA-US imply minimal structural degradation or incorporation 
of heteroatoms. 
Sulphur was detectable only in ACA (0.29 wt.%) and ACA-MW 
(0.27 wt.%), while it was below detection limits in ACA-US, 
which may be due to sulphur volatilization or desorption during 
ultrasonic processing. 
2.2 XRD Results of Activated Carbon Samples 
Figure 1a illustrates the XRD patterns of the activated carbon 
samples. The diffraction patterns of all activated samples exhibit 
two broad reflections centered at approximately 2 θ≈ 23-24◦and 
43◦, equivalent to the (002) and (101) planes, respectively. All 
samples show a broad diffraction peak in the 2 θrange of around 
23-24◦irrespective of the activation conditions, suggesting the 
graphitization and carbonization of the biomass [ 29 ]. 
The diffraction feature observed near 43◦, attributed to the (101) 
plane, is associated with in-plane ordering of sp2 carbon atoms 
[ 30 ]. Changes in the intensity and sharpness of this peak reflect 
modifications in electrical conductivity and structural coherence 
of the carbon matrix [ 30 ]. A moderate enhancement of this peak 
is often linked to improved electron transport pathways, which is 
beneficial for electrochemical energy storage applications such as 
supercapacitors. 
2.3 Thermal Behavior of Activated Carbon 
Samples 
The thermal stability of the activated carbon samples was 
evaluated by thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) and derivative 
thermogravimetry (DTG), as illustrated in Figure 2b,c . The TGA 
profiles indicate a gradual mass loss for all samples depending 
on the applied activation and modification conditions. The total 
weight losses were determined as 17.1%, 24.0%, and 13.3% for 
ACA, ACA-MW, and ACA-US, respectively. Among the samples,

higher moisture adsorption capacity. 
The initial weight loss occurring between 30◦C and 110◦C 
corresponds to the removal of physically adsorbed moisture 
and volatile components. In this temperature range, ACA- 
MW showed the highest mass loss (5.3%), followed by ACA 
(2.9%) and ACA-US (1.4%), indicating differences in surface 
hydrophilicity and pore accessibility. The subsequent continuous 
mass loss observed from 110◦C to 800◦C is associated with 
the thermal decomposition of oxygen-containing surface func- 
tional groups and partial degradation of the carbon framework 
[ 31 ]. 
Notably, ACA-US displayed the lowest overall mass loss across 
the entire temperature range (30◦C–800◦C), which may be 
related to enhanced carbonization, dehydration, and structural 
stabilization induced by ultrasonication treatment. The DTG 
curves further support these observations, showing a distinct low- 
temperature peak (30◦C–110◦C) for all samples, corresponding 
to rapid desorption of moisture and volatile species. A broad 
DTG peak in the range of 110–275◦C is attributed to structural 
rearrangement and decomposition of residual organic matter, 
possibly accompanied by further carbonization or mild oxidation 
processes [ 31 ]. In contrast, ACA-MW exhibits a more pronounced 
and broadened peak in this region, suggesting that microwave 
modification delays dehydration, carbonization, and functional 
group elimination. At higher temperatures (275◦C–800◦C), the 
gradual and controlled decrease in DTG intensity reflects the step- 
wise decomposition of the activated carbon structure, indicating 
thermal instability of the carbon matrix [ 32 ].

segments.text:
2.4 Spectroscopic Characterization 
2.4.1 FTIR Spectroscopy 
The surface chemical composition of the activated carbon sam- 
ples was evaluated using FTIR spectroscopy (Figure 1d ). The 
FTIR spectra confirm the presence of multiple oxygen-containing 
surface functionalities, indicating that carbonization was not 
fully completed and that heteroatoms were retained on the carbon 
framework. A broad absorption band centered at approximately 
3402 cm− 1 is assigned to O ─H stretching vibrations, while 
the peak at 1564 cm− 1 corresponds to aromatic C ═ C skeletal 
vibrations. The band observed at 1165 cm− 1 is associated with C ─O 
and C ─C stretching modes originating from cellulose-derived 
or ether-like structures [ 33, 34 ]. Consistent with the TG–DTG 
results, the relative intensity of hydroxyl-related bands is higher 
for ACA-MW and ACA-US compared to ACA, reflecting their 
increased moisture affinity and surface polarity. 
Additional spectral features include a low-frequency band at 495 
cm− 1 , which is characteristic of phosphate-related vibrations and 
confirms the incorporation of phosphorus species through H3 PO4 
chemical activation [ 35 ]. The presence of C ─H deformation 
bands at 889 cm− 1 suggests partial preservation of aliphatic 
moieties [ 36 ], whereas the absorption at 2358 cm− 1 is attributed 
to CO2 -related vibrations, likely arising from surface carbonate 
species formed via oxidation or exposure to ambient air during 
post-treatment [ 37 ]. 
The coexistence of these oxygen- and phosphorus-containing 
groups correlates well with the thermal degradation behavior 
observed in TG–DTG profiles. The initial mass loss below 110◦C 
is consistent with the removal of physically adsorbed moisture 
associated with hydroxyl-rich surfaces, while the gradual weight 
loss at elevated temperatures is attributed to the decomposition 
of labile functional groups and progressive structural rearrange- 
ment of the carbon matrix. In particular, ACA-US exhibits a lower 
overall mass loss, suggesting enhanced thermal stability despite 
its relatively high surface oxygen content. 
2.4.2 Raman Spectroscopy 
Raman spectroscopy was employed to assess the structural order- 
ing and degree of graphitization of the activated carbon samples 
(Figure 2 ). All spectra display two characteristic bands: the D 
band located near 1350 cm− 1 , which arises from lattice defects and 
disordered carbon structures, and the G band centered around 
1580 cm− 1 , corresponding to the in-plane vibration of sp2 -bonded 
carbon atoms within graphitic domains [ 38–40 ]. Variations in 
both band positions and intensity ratios reflect changes in the 
carbon microstructure induced by activation and post-treatment 
processes. 
The intensity ratio of the D to G bands ( ID /IG ) is commonly 
used as an indicator of defect density and structural disorder. 
The pristine activated carbon (ACA) exhibits an ID /IG value of 
approximately 0.90, indicative of a predominantly amorphous 
carbon framework. Following microwave (MW) and ultrasonica- 
tion (US) treatments, this ratio slightly increases to 0.92 for both 
ACA-MW and ACA-US, suggesting the introduction of additional 
interplanar defects and edge sites within the carbon matrix as a 
result of combined chemical and physical activation. 
Despite the increase in defect density, the evolution of the 
Raman features implies a partial reorganization of amorphous 
carbon into more ordered graphitic domains. This structural 
transformation is consistent with the XRD results, which reveal 
the development of turbostratic or short-range graphitic ordering 
in ACA-MW and ACA-US samples. The coexistence of graphitic 
regions and defect-rich sites leads to the formation of a well- 
developed porous carbon architecture. 
From an electrochemical perspective, the relatively high defect- 
to-graphitization ratio is advantageous, as defects and edge 
sites serve as active centers for electrolyte ion adsorption and 
facilitate enhanced electrode–electrolyte interactions. Moreover, 
the presence of sp2 -hybridized conductive domains improves 
charge transport pathways, thereby accelerating charge transfer 
kinetics and supporting surface redox reactions. Consequently, 
the Raman analysis confirms that the combined activation strate- 
gies effectively tailor the carbon structure to achieve a balance 
between electrical conductivity and electrochemically active 
sites. 
2.5 Morphological Characteristics of the 
Activated Carbon Samples 
2.5.1 SEM 
Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) was utilized to examine the 
surface structures of the activated carbon samples, with selected 
images displayed in Figure 3 to illustrate their morphological 
features. The SEM image of the ACA sample shows a highly 
porous and fragmented surface, which is typical of phosphoric 
acid activation. Phosphoric acid acts as a dehydrating agent, 
promoting bond cleavage and facilitating the formation of cross- 
linked structures during pyrolysis. As a result, a developed 
network of mesopores and macropores is evident. The acid 
also assists in the retention of oxygenated functional groups, 
contributing to the rough, layered surface texture often observed 
in such materials. Similar surface features have been reported 
in the literature for H3 PO4 -activated lignocellulosic carbons 
[ 28, 41 ]. 
The ACA-MW sample, which underwent microwave-assisted 
treatment, reveals a significantly altered morphology with 
enhanced pore opening and more extensive surface fissures. 
Microwave heating provides rapid and volumetric energy input, 
causing local hot spots and accelerating the release of volatile 
matter. This effect leads to the expansion and deepening of 
pre-existing pores, producing a more open structure. Several 
studies have confirmed that microwave-assisted phosphoric acid 
activation improves both porosity and surface area compared to 
conventional heating [ 42 ]. The SEM image of the ACA-US sample 
demonstrates a cleaner and more ordered surface morphology, 
with better-defined pore boundaries and fewer surface residues. 
Ultrasonic treatment introduces high-frequency acoustic cavita- 
tion, which helps remove trapped by products and opens partially 
blocked pores [ 43 ]. This post-treatment also aids in exfoliating 
layered structures, resulting in improved pore accessibility and

surface cleanliness. Such observations are consistent with prior 
reports on the use of ultrasonication to enhance the surface 
properties of biochar and activated carbon [ 44, 45 ]. 
In summary, the SEM analysis shows that H3 PO4 activation cre- 
ates a highly porous carbon matrix, while subsequent microwave 
and ultrasonic treatments further enhance the morphological 
features. These modifications can significantly improve the mate- 
rial’s suitability for supercapacitor applications by tailoring its 
textural properties. 
2.5.2 N2 Adsorption–Desorption Isotherms and Pore 
Properties of Activated Carbon Samples 
Figure 4 illustrates the nitrogen adsorption–desorption isotherms 
together with the corresponding pore size distributions of the 
activated carbon materials. All samples exhibit isotherms that can 
be classified as type IV, accompanied by pronounced hysteresis 
loops, indicating the predominance of mesoporous structures. 
The presence of hysteresis loops in the relative pressure (P/P0 ) 
range of 0.4–0.95 corresponds to the H3-type hysteresis according 
to the IUPAC classification [ 46, 47 ]. This behavior is typically 
associated with slit-shaped pores, which are commonly formed 
by aggregates of plate-like particles, microcracks, layered pore 
networks, and wedge-shaped voids. Such textural characteristics 
are consistent with the average pore diameters listed in Table 1 , 
ranging from 26.5 to 28.3 Å, confirming the dominance of 
mesopores. 
Among the investigated samples, ACA-US exhibits the highest 
nitrogen uptake over the entire relative pressure range, resulting 
in the largest BET surface area (2138 m2 g− 1 ) and a compara- 
tively high micropore volume (0.31 cm3 g− 1 ). This enhancement 
can be attributed to the ultrasonic treatment, which promotes 
the opening of previously blocked pores and facilitates the 
development of accessible micro- and mesoporous networks. 
Similar improvements in porosity and surface area induced by 
ultrasound-assisted modification have been reported for activated 
carbon materials in earlier studies [ 48 ]. 
In contrast, the microwave-assisted acid-activated sample shows 
a lower adsorption capacity and a narrower hysteresis loop, 
indicating a less developed pore structure. When evaluated 
together with the XRD, Raman, TGA-DTG, FTIR, and elemental 
composition analyses, this behavior can be linked to the effects of 
microwave treatment, which may induce relatively lower degrees 
of effective carbonization and dehydration, while promoting 
rapid depolymerization, deoxygenation, and partial structural 
collapse. XRD results suggest a reduced development of tur- 
bostratic carbon domains, while Raman analysis reveals changes 
in the disorder degree of the carbon framework. Furthermore, 
FTIR spectra and TGA-DTA results indicate a increase in surface 
oxygen-containing functional groups, supporting the notion that 
excessive or rapid microwave-induced reactions may limit pore 
stabilization. Consequently, the combined structural and chemi- 
cal evidence confirms that ultrasonic activation is more effective 
than microwave treatment in preserving pore integrity and 
enhancing the accessible surface area of the activated carbons.

The evolution of specific surface area and pore structure observed 
in this study is consistent with previous reports on phosphoric 
acid–activated biomass-derived carbons. Megherbi et al. [ 49 ] 
reported the preparation of activated carbon from MC-leaves 
biomass via phosphoric acid–assisted heat treatment, achieving 
a high specific surface area of 1237 m2 g− 1 . Comparable results 
were obtained for bamboo-derived activated carbons, where 
microwave-assisted phosphoric acid activation led to a rapid 
activation process, a carbon yield of 48%, and a surface area of 
1432 m2 g− 1 [ 50 ]. In addition, Özpınar et al. [ 34 ] synthesized 
magnetic activated carbon from hazelnut shell waste using a 
single-step chemical activation and magnetization approach, 
reporting a BET surface area of 1363 m2 g− 1 along with a high 
micropore volume of 0.52 cm3 g− 1 . These literature findings 
quantitatively support the results of the present study, in which 
optimized activation conditions produced activated carbons with 
high surface area, well-developed mesoporosity, and abundant 
accessible active sites, rendering them promising candidates for 
electrochemical energy storage applications. 
2.6 Electrochemical Properties of the Activated 
Carbon Electrodes 
The physicochemical characterization confirms that the 
hazelnut-derived activated carbons possess structural and 
textural features suitable for electrochemical energy-storage 
applications. To evaluate their electrochemical performance, 
cyclic voltammetry (CV) measurements were first performed, 
as shown in Figure 5 . The electrochemical behavior of the 
activated carbon electrodes was examined in a three-electrode 
configuration using Hg/HgO as the reference electrode, a Pt 
wire as the counter electrode, and 3 M KOH as the aqueous 
electrolyte, within a potential window of − 1.2 to − 0.2 V. 
Figure 5a–c displays the CV responses of the activated carbon 
electrodes at scan rates ranging from 5 to 200 mV s− 1 . All samples 
exhibit nearly rectangular CV profiles, indicating dominant 
capacitive behavior. At lower scan rates, the quasi-rectangular 
shape (see Figure 5d ) is characteristic of electrical double-layer 
capacitance, where charge storage occurs via electrostatic adsorp- 
tion of electrolyte ions at the electrode–electrolyte interface [ 51, 
52 ]. As the scan rate increases, slight distortions from the ideal 
rectangular shape become apparent, which can be attributed to 
limited ion diffusion and increased mass transport resistance 
within the porous carbon framework. Additionally, minor devi- 
ations from ideal capacitive behavior suggest the contribution of 
surface-related faradaic reactions, likely associated with oxygen- 
containing functional groups present on the carbon surface [ 53 ]. 
Figure 5d compares the CV curves of all electrodes at a scan rate 
of 5 mV/s. Among the samples, the ACA-US electrode encloses 
the largest CV area and exhibits the highest current density, 
indicating superior charge storage performance relative to ACA 
and ACA-MW. 
The enhanced electrochemical activity of ACA-US is primarily 
attributed to its higher carbon content, exceptionally large BET 
specific surface area (2138 m2 g− 1 ), and substantial micropore 
volume, which collectively facilitate efficient ion adsorption and 
charge accumulation. The specific capacitance values calculated 
from the CV curves are summarized in Table 2 . Consistent with 
the CV analysis, ACA-US delivers the highest capacitance along 
with improved electrochemical stability. 
The electrochemical performance of the activated carbon elec- 
trodes was further investigated by galvanostatic charge–discharge 
(GCD) measurements, as illustrated in Figure 6 . In this technique, 
the electrodes were charged and discharged under constant 
current conditions to evaluate their capacitive behavior and 
rate capability. Figure 6a–c presents representative GCD pro- 
files of ACA, ACA-MW, and ACA-US electrodes recorded at 
different applied current densities. All samples exhibit nearly 
symmetric and linear charge–discharge curves, indicating good 
electrochemical reversibility and dominant capacitive behavior. 
As the applied current density increases, a gradual decrease in 
the charge–discharge time is observed for all electrodes. This 
behavior is attributed to the reduced time available for electrolyte 
ions to access and adsorb onto the internal pore surfaces at higher 
current densities. 
A comparative analysis of the GCD curves for all samples at 
the same current density is shown in Figure 6d . The discharge 
durations follow the order ACA-US > ACA > ACA-MW, which 
is consistent with the trends observed in the cyclic voltammetry 
results. The longer discharge time of ACA-US indicates a higher 
charge storage capability as seein in Table 2 .

kinetics, which can be attributed to its higher carbon content, 
well-developed porosity, and larger specific surface area. These 
structural features facilitate rapid ion diffusion and efficient 
utilization of electroactive sites during fast charge–discharge 
processes. 
Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) was employed 
to further elucidate the charge transport behavior and resistive 
characteristics of the activated carbon electrodes. The Nyquist 
plots recorded in the frequency range from 105 to 1 Hz are 
shown in Figure 7b . The ACA-US sample exhibited a steeper 
slope in the high-frequency region near the imaginary axis, 
indicative of more ideal capacitive behavior and lower internal 
resistance. At lower frequencies, a deviation from ideal verticality 
was observed, reflecting diffusion-controlled processes within the 
porous structure. In contrast, ACA-MW displayed a relatively 
sharper slope in the low-frequency region, while ACA showed 
the least pronounced capacitive response across both frequency 
domains. These differences are closely related to variations in 
pore size distribution and specific surface area (Table 1 ), as 
well as the presence of surface functional groups that enhance 
electrode–electrolyte wettability and reduce interfacial contact 
resistance. 
Quantitative EIS parameters were extracted by fitting the exper- 
imental data using the equivalent circuit model shown in 
Figure 7c , which exhibited good agreement with the measured 
spectra. The fitted parameters are summarized in Table 3 . The 
solution resistance (Rs), representing the combined resistance 
of the electrolyte and electrode–electrolyte interface, was deter- 
mined to be 202.5 Ωf o r ACA, 144.8 Ωf o r ACA-MW, and 
157.2 Ωf o r ACA-US. The reduced Rs values for the microwave- 
and ultrasound-assisted samples indicate improved electrical 
conductivity and more efficient ion transport compared to the 
conventionally activated carbon. Furthermore, the charge trans- 
fer resistance (Rct) was significantly lower for ACA-US (262.6 
Ω) than for ACA and ACA-MW, confirming facilitated electron 
transfer at the electrode surface. This improvement is consistent 
with the highly porous architecture and increased accessible 
surface area of ACA-US, which promote faster redox reactions 
and enhanced capacitive behavior. 
The low-frequency region of the Nyquist plots reveals the War- 
burg impedance (Wd), associated with ion diffusion within the 
electrode pores. A greater deviation of the Warburg tail from the 
ideal 45◦line was observed for ACA and ACA-MW, suggesting 
a more pronounced capacitive contribution and diffusion limita- 
tions [ 54, 55 ]. In comparison, ACA-US exhibited a more favorable 
diffusion response, supporting its superior rate capability. 
The long-term electrochemical stability of the optimized elec- 
trode was assessed through cycling tests, as depicted in Figure 7d .

2.7 Effect of Electrolyte Type and Concentration 
on Electrochemical Performance 
The electrochemical response of activated carbon electrodes is 
highly sensitive to both the chemical nature and concentra- 
tion of the electrolyte, as these parameters directly govern ion 
transport, electrode wetting, and charge storage mechanisms. 
The specific capacitance values of ACA, ACA-MW, and ACA- 
US electrodes obtained in alkaline (3 M and 6 M KOH) and 
neutral (0.5 M Na2 SO4 ) electrolytes at different scan rates are 
summarized in Table 2 . Among all investigated samples, ACA- 
US exhibits the most pronounced capacitive behavior across all 
electrolytes, demonstrating its superior structural and surface 
characteristics. 
In alkaline media, particularly 3 M KOH, the ACA-US electrode 
delivers the highest electrochemical performance, reaching a 
maximum specific capacitance of 175.4 F g− 1 at a scan rate 
of 5 mV s− 1 . This outstanding performance can be primarily 
attributed to the small hydrated radius and high ionic mobility 
of OH− ions, which enable rapid penetration into the porous 
carbon framework and promote efficient charge accumulation

at the electrode–electrolyte interface. Consistent with previous 
reports, KOH-based electrolytes provide favorable electrochemi- 
cal kinetics by minimizing ion diffusion resistance and enhancing 
electrical conductivity, thereby leading to higher capacitance 
values and improved rate capability [ 56, 57 ]. 
Even at elevated scan rates up to 200 mV s− 1 , ACA-US retains a 
relatively high capacitance of 122.2 F g− 1 in 3 M KOH, indicating 
excellent rate performance. This behavior reflects the synergistic 
effect of an optimized hierarchical pore structure and suitable 
surface functionality, which together facilitate fast ion diffusion 
and maintain effective electrochemical accessibility under rapid 
charge–discharge conditions. 
In contrast, the neutral electrolyte (0.5 M Na2 SO4 ) results in 
significantly lower capacitance values for all electrodes. The 
ACA-US sample achieves a maximum capacitance of only 51.3 F 
g− 1 at 5 mV s− 1 in this medium. This diminished performance 
is consistent with literature findings [ 57, 58 ] and is mainly 
associated with the larger hydrated radii and lower ionic mobility 
of Na+ and SO4 
2 − ions. Moreover, the divalent nature and 
strong hydration shell of SO4 
2 − anions restrict their diffusion 
into narrow micropores, limiting effective charge storage and 
reducing overall capacitance. 
Although increasing the electrolyte concentration to 6 M KOH 
is expected to enhance ionic conductivity, the ACA-US elec- 
trode exhibits slightly lower capacitance values in this medium 
compared to 3 M KOH at similar scan rates. For instance, at 
20 mV s− 1 , the capacitance decreases from 164.2 F g− 1 in 3 M 
KOH to 115.8 F g− 1 in 6 M KOH. This seemingly contradictory 
trend can be explained by the increased viscosity of highly 
concentrated alkaline solutions, which hinders ion diffusion 
and reduces electrolyte penetration into the porous electrode 
structure. Additionally, excessive OH− concentration may pro- 
mote parasitic surface reactions, such as partial carbon oxidation 
and the formation of oxygen-containing functional groups (e.g., 
carboxyl and lactone species), as reported by Zhang et al. [ 59 ]. 
These processes can adversely affect electrochemical stability and 
lead to a gradual decline in capacitance. 
Despite these effects, the capacitance retention of ACA-US with 
increasing scan rate remains relatively stable in KOH electrolytes, 
further confirming the beneficial role of its well-developed meso- 
porous network and favorable surface chemistry. Such structural 
features help mitigate diffusion limitations and support efficient 
charge storage under high-rate operation, in agreement with 
earlier studies. 
Overall, the results clearly demonstrate that electrolyte selection 
plays a crucial role in determining the electrochemical per- 
formance of activated carbon electrodes. Alkaline electrolytes, 
particularly 3 M KOH, provide an optimal balance between ionic 
conductivity and diffusion dynamics, yielding superior capaci- 
tance and rate capability. In contrast, neutral electrolytes such 
as Na2 SO4 impose intrinsic limitations due to their unfavorable 
ionic properties. These findings underscore the necessity of 
simultaneously optimizing carbon pore architecture and elec- 
trolyte composition to achieve high-performance supercapacitor 
systems. 
The electrochemical performance of the ACA-US electrode was 
further evaluated through a detailed comparison with previously 
reported biomass-derived activated carbons, as summarized in 
Table 4 . Although the reported materials exhibit a wide range 
of specific surface areas, pore volumes, activation strategies, 
and testing conditions, meaningful trends can be extracted by 
correlating these parameters with their capacitive behaviors. 
Activated carbons produced via KOH activation, such as those 
derived from corn straws [ 60 ] and chestnut shells [ 61 ], typically 
show exceptionally high specific surface areas exceeding 1300 
m2 g− 1 and deliver high specific capacitances, reaching up to 
327 F g− 1 in 6 M KOH at low current densities. However, 
these materials often rely on aggressive chemical activation 
and elevated alkali consumption, which may raise concerns

H3 PO4 -activated carbons exhibit moderate surface areas but still 
achieve competitive electrochemical performance, highlighting 
the importance of pore accessibility and surface chemistry in 
addition to total surface area. For instance, H3 PO4 -activated 
carbons derived from citrus bergamia peels [ 62 ] and Prunus 
persica stones [ 63 ] display specific capacitances close to 290–
300 F g− 1 , despite having surface areas below 800 m2 g− 1 . This 
behavior can be attributed to the presence of abundant oxygen- 
containing functional groups introduced by phosphoric acid 
activation, which enhance electrolyte wettability and contribute 
to pseudocapacitive effects. Conversely, some H3 PO4 -activated 
materials with relatively low surface areas and pore volumes, 
such as Zanthoxylum armatum seed-based carbons [ 64 ], exhibit 
comparatively limited capacitance, indicating that an optimal 
balance between pore structure and surface functionality is 
required. 
In the case of hazelnut shell-derived carbons [ 34 ], previously 
reported H3 PO4 -activated samples show a specific capacitance 
of 247.8 F g− 1 in 6 M KOH at 0.75 A g− 1 , associated with a 
surface area of 1363 m2 g− 1 . The ACA-US electrode developed in 
this work demonstrates a distinct structural advantage, achieving 
a substantially higher surface area (2138 m2 g− 1 ) and total 
pore volume (2.21 cm3 g− 1 ) through the combined effect of 
phosphoric acid activation and ultrasonication. This hierarchical 
pore architecture facilitates efficient ion diffusion and electrolyte 
penetration, leading to a high specific capacitance of 189.7 F g− 1 
at 1 A g− 1 in 3 M KOH. 
Although the capacitance of ACA-US is slightly lower than 
some high-performing KOH-activated carbons tested at lower 
current densities, its performance remains highly competitive 
when considering the milder activation conditions, sustainable 
biomass precursor, and relatively higher testing current density. 
These results clearly demonstrate that ultrasonication-assisted 
H3 PO4 activation plays a crucial role in tailoring pore connectivity 
and enhancing electrochemical accessibility, thereby enabling 
ACA-US to function as a promising electrode material for high- 
performance supercapacitors. 
3 Conclusion 
In this work, hazelnut shell–derived activated carbons were 
successfully synthesized via phosphoric acid chemical activa- 
tion followed by microwave and ultrasonic post-treatments, and 
their structural, thermal, and electrochemical properties were 
comprehensively evaluated. Physicochemical characterization 
confirmed that both post-treatment methods significantly mod- 
ified the carbon framework and surface chemistry. Microwave 
treatment promoted extensive surface oxidation and increased 
oxygen functionality, whereas ultrasonic treatment preserved a 
high degree of carbonization while inducing controlled surface 
functionalization through cavitation-driven reactions. 
XRD and Raman analyses revealed turbostratic carbon structures 
with short-range graphitic ordering and defect-rich domains in 
all samples, providing a favorable balance between electrical 
conductivity and electrochemically active sites. Thermal analy- 
sis demonstrated that the ultrasound-assisted activated carbon 
exhibited the lowest overall mass loss and enhanced thermal 
stability, reflecting improved dehydration, carbonization, and 
structural stabilization. 
Electrochemical investigations clearly demonstrated the superi- 
ority of the ultrasound-treated activated carbon. Cyclic voltam- 
metry confirmed dominant electrical double-layer capacitance 
with minor pseudocapacitive contributions arising from surface 
oxygen functionalities. The ACA-US electrode delivered the 
highest specific capacitance, excellent rate capability, and highly 
reversible charge–discharge behavior, as confirmed by GCD 
measurements. Ragone plots revealed that ACA-US achieved 
significantly higher energy densities across a broad power density 
range compared to pristine and microwave-treated samples, high- 
lighting its fast charge–discharge kinetics and efficient utilization 
of active sites. 
Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy further confirmed 
improved charge transport properties for ACA-US, including 
reduced charge transfer resistance and enhanced ion diffusion 
within the porous network. The electrode also exhibited excellent 
cycling durability, retaining approximately 85% of its initial 
capacitance after 2000 cycles at high current density, indicating 
robust structural integrity during prolonged operation. 
Overall, this study demonstrates that ultrasonic post-treatment is 
a highly effective strategy for optimizing biomass-derived acti- 
vated carbons by simultaneously enhancing porosity, electrical 
conductivity, and electrochemical stability. The resulting mate- 
rial exhibits outstanding energy storage performance, making 
it a promising and sustainable electrode candidate for next- 
generation supercapacitors. 
4 Experimental Section 
4.1 Materials and Chemicals 
Hazelnut shells (HS) were selected as the biomass precursor for 
biochar synthesis. The shells were obtained from the Çavuşlar 
region of Ordu, Turkey. Prior to use, the HS were mechanically 
ground into a fine powder using a milling device. The resulting 
material was then sieved to obtain particles in the 250–355 µm 
size range. Phosphoric acid (H3 PO4 ), purchased from Merck 
(Darmstadt, Germany), was used as received without further 
purification. 
4.2 Preparation of Activated Carbon 
Three different activated carbons were employed to obtain 
functionalized biochar samples, as described below: 
4.2.1 Activated Carbon Prepared by Acid Activation 
Hazelnut shell powder was impregnated with phosphoric acid 
(H3 PO4 ) using a biomass-to-acid weight ratio of 1:3 and stirred at 
room temperature for 24 h to ensure homogeneous contact. The 
resulting mixture was dried overnight at 80◦C and subsequently 
pyrolyzed in a tubular furnace (Protherm) at 700◦C for 2 h under

rate of 10◦C min− 1 . The obtained activated carbon sample was 
labeled ACA . 
4.2.2 Activated Carbon Prepared by Acid and 
Microwave Activation Pretreatment 
The acid-treated biomass was then subjected to microwave 
irradiation using a closed-vessel digestion system (CEM Mars 6) 
operated at 900 W power and 2.45 GHz frequency for 30 s. Despite 
the short exposure time, microwave irradiation provides rapid 
volumetric heating through direct interaction with polar species 
and the carbon matrix, generating localized high-temperature 
regions that promote dehydration, bond cleavage, and initial pore 
formation. This non-equilibrium heating mechanism enhances 
the penetration and reactivity of phosphoric acid within the 
biomass structure, thereby improving activation efficiency while 
minimizing processing time and energy consumption. Following 
the microwave-assisted pretreatment, the material was pyrolyzed 
at 700◦C under a continuous nitrogen flow to obtain the final 
activated carbon product. The resulting sample was denoted as 
ACA-MW. 
Activated carbon prepared by acid activation and ultrasonic 
pretreatment: In this route, the H3 PO4 impregnated HS powder 
was treated in an ultrasonic bath (40 kHz , 200 W ) for 60 min 
at ambient temperature. Following ultrasonication, the sample 
was dried and subsequently carbonized under the same thermal 
conditions as described above. The sample was denoted as 
ACA-US . 
4.3 Characterization of Activated Carbon 
Materials 
The elemental composition ( C , H , N , and S ) of the activated 
carbon samples ( ACA , ACA-MW , and ACA-US ) was measured 
using an elemental analyzer ( Thermo Scientific Flash 2000/ MAS 
200R ). The oxygen ( O ) content was determined via mass balance, 
based on the differences between the measured elements. Ele- 
mental analysis results represent the average of two independent 
measurements to ensure accuracy. 
The crystalline structure of the samples was examined by X-ray 
diffraction (XRD) using a PANalytical Empyrean diffractometer. 
Measurements were carried out employing Cu K αradiation 
under an operating current of 40 mA and an accelerating voltage 
of 5 kV. Diffraction patterns were collected over a 2 θrange of 10–
90◦with a fixed incident angle of 4◦. The step size was set to 0.013◦
for powder samples to ensure adequate resolution. 
Thermal decomposition of the activated carbo samples was 
analyzed using a PerkinElmer Diamond TG/DTA system 
(PerkinElmer, Waltham, MA, USA). Measurements were 
performed under nitrogen flow (100 mL min− 1 ) from room 
temperature to 800◦C at a heating rate of 10◦C min− 1 . 
Surface functional groups were identified using Fourier Trans- 
form Infrared ( FT-IR ) spectroscopy ( Bruker Tensor II ). For the 
FT-IR analysis, each sample was mixed with potassium bromide 
( KBr ) at a 2:100 sample to KBr weight ratio. Measurements were 
taken across the wavenumber range of 400–4000 cm− 1 , with a 
pure KBr pellet used to obtain the background spectrum. 
Raman measurements were conducted at room temperature 
using a Senterra II from Bruker . The spectra were recorded 
between 800 cm− 1 and 1800 cm− 1 , employing a laser excitation 
wavelength of 532 nm and a laser power of 5 mW. 
The morphology and surface features of the biochar samples 
were determined using a field-emission scanning electron micro- 
scope ( FE-SEM , TESCON Mira III XMU ), equipped with Energy 
Dispersive X-ray Spectroscopy ( EDS , Oxford Inst. INCA ). This 
analysis provided insight into the surface texture and elemental 
composition. 
The porosity and surface area of the samples were assessed 
using the Brunauer–Emmett–Teller (BET) technique. A gas sorp- 
tion analyzer (AUTOSORB 1C, Quantachrome Corp., USA) was 
employed to determine key parameters, including the specific 
surface area (SBET), total pore volume, and average pore diameter, 
offering comprehensive insights into the adsorption behavior of 
the materials. 
4.4 Electrochemical Tests 
Electrochemical characterization, including cyclic voltammetry 
(CV), galvanostatic charge–discharge (GCD), and electrochemi- 
cal impedance spectroscopy (EIS), was performed using a Gamry 
Instruments Potentiostat/Galvanostat/ZRA. All measurements 
were conducted in a three-electrode configuration. The working 
electrode was prepared by drop-casting the active material onto 
a glassy carbon electrode (GCE). A platinum wire served as the 
counter electrode. For alkaline electrolytes (3 M and 6 M KOH), 
a Hg/HgO electrode was used as the reference electrode, whereas 
an Ag/AgCl electrode was employed in the neutral 0.5 M Na2 SO4 
electrolyte. 
The working electrodes were fabricated from the activated carbon 
samples by dispersing 2 mg of active material with 10 µL of Nafion 
binder in 2 mL of ethanol. The mixture was ultrasonicated for 
30 min to obtain a homogeneous ink, which was subsequently 
drop-cast onto the GCE and dried at 60◦C for 12 h. 
CV and GCD measurements were carried out within a potential 
window of − 1.2 to − 0.2 V versus the reference electrode. CV 
curves were recorded at scan rates ranging from 5 to 200 mV s− 1 , 
while GCD tests were performed at current densities of 1, 2, 5, and 
10 A g− 1 . Electrochemical measurements were conducted in three 
different electrolytes: 3 M KOH, 6 M KOH, and 0.5 M Na2 SO4 .

Abstract
Hierarchical porous carbon aerogels were synthesized from liqueed wood via physical and chemical
activation. The morphology and structure of the KOH treated carbon aerogel (K-LWCA) and steam treated
carbon (H-LWCA) were systematically investigated by SEM, N2 adsorption, FTIR, XRD and XPS, and the
electrochemical properties were evaluated based on cyclic voltammetry, galvanostatic charge-discharge
and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy. The H-LWCA and K-LWCA had the high reached specic
surface area (1996 and 1780 cm2 g− 1, respectively) and developed hierarchical porous structures.
Compared with H-LWCA, K-LWCA showed the higher specic capacitance, better rate performance and
superior cyclic stability due to more defects and hydrophilic functional groups. As expected, the K-LWCA
exhibited the optimal mass-specic capacitance of 201.47 F g− 1 at 0.5 A g− 1, and achieved ideal
capacitance retention of 70.15% at 20 A g− 1 as well as exceptional cycling stability of 94.11% retention
after 5000 cycles. Moreover, the button symmetric supercapacitor device assembled based on K-LWCA
demonstrated a specic capacitance of 117.78 F g− 1 at 0.5A g− 1 and presented an energy density of 9.2
Wh kg− 1 at a power density of 375W kg− 1. Accordingly, this work provides a novel approach for the
preparation of biomass-derived carbon aerogel electrode materials in practical supercapacitor
applications.
1. Introduction
Recently, the signicant reduction of fossil fuels and higher greenhouse gases emissions have led to an
increase in the demand for sustainable energy. And supercapacitors have been used extensively in elds
such as electric vehicles, portable electronic devices (Zhong et al. 2022; Zhang et al. 2022). Owing to
faster charging, greater cycling stability and higher power density, supercapacitors are easier to achieve
high-performance compared with conventional capacitors (Zhang et al. 2019; Poonam et al. 2019). As an
important component of supercapacitors, electrode materials take on a critical role in the overall
performance of supercapacitors (Cheng et al. 2020). According to the different energy storage
mechanisms, the electrode materials are classied into electric double-layer capacitor electrode materials
(EDLCs) dominated by carbon materials (Benoy et al. 2022), and pseudo-capacitive electrode materials
such as transition metal compounds (Zhao et al. 2017), conductive polymers (Wong et al. 2022), etc.
Particularly, carbon-based materials are the most extensively studied active materials for EDLCs because
of its large specic surface area, chemical stability, low cost, and open porosity to electrolyte ions (Liu et
al. 2017).
Hitherto, carbon materials, such as carbon spheres (Li et al. 2019; Xu et al. 2018), carbon bers (Ma et al.
2018; He et al. 2016), carbon nanotubes (De Silva et al. 2021; Pal and Subhedar 2023), graphene (Ajravat
et al. 2022; Tian et al. 2019), carbon aerogel (Lv et al. 2023; Zu et al. 2016), and activated carbon (Huang
et al. 2021; Sun et al. 2016), are most widely used for supercapacitors. Compared with other carbon
materials, carbon aerogels have greater advantages as the electrical material of supercapacitors because
of the adjustable and graded pore structures, which meets the different needs of electrolyte ion

segments.text:
Page 3/21
adsorption, transport and as an ion buffer layer, thereby enhancing the overall electrochemical
performance. However, unactivated carbon aerogels generally can’t supply adsorption sites to electrolyte
ions for its low specic surface area. Meanwhile, hydrophilic functional groups are mostly removed
during carbonization process, thus causing the carbon aerogel highly hydrophobic. As a result, it's
unfavorable for the penetration and diffusion of electrolyte and increased the contact resistance between
pores and electrolyte ions, lead to a low capacitance nally. Therefore, carbon aerogels can be activated
to regulate its pore structure for increasing its specic surface area and improving its wettability.
There are two activation methods for carbon aerogels including physical and chemical activation. During
physical activation, steam (Maldonado-Hódar et al. 2004) and CO2 (Zu et al. 2016) are used as gas-phase
oxidants to react with the carbon atoms in the carbon skeleton at high temperature, which forms a
developed porous structure (Li et al. 2019). And chemical activation takes place in a series of complex
reactions with the carbon skeleton by chemical corrosion of acid and alkali salt reagents such as KOH
(Cai et al. 2019), K2CO3 (Li et al. 2017), HNO3 (Lee et al. 2015), H3PO4 (Li et al. 2019) and ZnCl2 (Yu et al.
2016), etc. Meanwhile, the resulting gases (such as H2O, CO2, H2, and CO) in activation process can
continue to etch carbon skeleton, which further increases the number of microporous (Luo et al. 2022).
The activation method greatly effects the pore structure and the surface chemistry of carbon aerogels.
Generally, the physical activation process is deemed as green and simple and can produce larger
microporous. But the activation temperature and time of physical activation are higher than those of
chemical activation, causing a higher energy consumption and cost (Zhang et al. 2021). However,
chemical activation (KOH activation) leads to a higher specic surface area, more uniform microporous
size and more abundant surface functional groups. Unfortunately, chemical activators cause certain
corrosion to equipment, which require complicated cleaning and desalting process (ElKhatat and Al-
Muhtaseb 2011). With this in mind, it is of vital importance to choose a reasonable activation method for
the synthesis of carbon electrode materials with outstanding electrochemical performance.
In this paper, hierarchical porous carbon aerogels derived from liqueed wood (LWCA) were synthesized
via sol-gel and carbonization, followed by steam and KOH activation respectively. And the effects of
various activation methods on microscopic morphology, chemical structure and electrochemical
properties of LWCA were investigated. As expected, etching the carbon skeleton with steam and KOH
afforded substantial enhancement in hydrophily and specic surface area, leading to sucient effective
active sites for the absorption of electrolyte ions. Therefore, as-prepared samples showed satisfactory
electrochemical properties of 201.42 F g− 1 and 111.18 F g− 1 for the KOH treated carbon aerogel (K-
LWCA) and steam treated carbon (H-LWCA), respectively. Moreover, the K-LWCA was also tested as an
electrode material of symmetric supercapacitors, with an energy density up to 9.2 Wh kg− 1 at a power
density of 375 Wkg− 1, further demonstrating its potential in practical applications such as energy storage
devices.
2. Materials And Methods

2.1 Preparation of aerogel from liqueed wood (LWA)
Typically, 20 g China r powder (0.2Dp0.8mm) and 120 g phenol (AR) were added to a three-necked
ask, then 9.6 g phosphoric acid (H3PO4, AR) was added and stirred for 2.5 h at 160 ℃  in a bath of oil to
obtain the liqueed wood (Ma and Zhao 2010). And 5 g of liqueed wood was collected in 3 mL
anhydrous ethanol, thereafter, 0.35 g hexamethylenetetramine (HMTA, AR) was added and stirred until
fully dissolved. Subsequently, 3 mL formaldehyde (AR) was added into the system and transferred to a
closed glass ask after 30 min ultrasound. And the glass ask was placed a water bath at 85 ℃  for 24 h
to form wet liqueed wood gel. The wet gel was then immersed in anhydrous ethanol to replace the
solvent (immersed for 72 h, replaced anhydrous ethanol daily) and follow by pre-frozen at -20 ℃  for 6 h
and freeze-drying at -50 ℃  for 24 h to synthetize LWA.
2.2 Preparation of K-LWCA
The unactivated carbon aerogels were prepared by carbonizing LWA at 800 ℃  for 2 h under N2
atmosphere with a heating rate of 5°C min− 1. The obtained pre-carbonized carbon aerogels were
pulverized and fully mixed with varying mass ratios of KOH before being placed to a porcelain boat for 12
h at room temperature. The activated samples were washed several times with 10% HCl and deionized
water till the pH was neutral, and then dried for 12 h in an oven at 60 ℃  to produce KOH activated carbon
aerogel (K-LWCA). According to the carbon alkali mass ratio (1:1, 1:2, 1:3, 1:4, 1:5), the products were
named K-LWCA1, K-LWCA2, K-LWCA3, K-LWCA4 and K-LWCA5, respectively.
2.3 Preparation of H-LWCA
The LWA was placed in a tube furnace, and the temperature was raised from room temperature to 800 ℃
at a rate of 5 ℃  min− 1 under an N2 protective atmosphere held for 1 h before injecting steam (5g min− 1)
into the tube furnace through the steam generator for 1 h water-steam activation. Following that, the
acquired sample was washed with deionized water and anhydrous ethanol several times before drying in
an oven at 60 ℃  for 12 h, named H-LWCA.
2.4 Characterization
The microscopic morphology of all samples was observed using scanning electron microscopy (SEM,
JSM-IT300LV). The chemical structure was characterized by Fourier infrared spectroscopy. The crystal
structure and chemical composition were analyzed by X-ray diffractometer. Nitrogen adsorption
desorption experiment was performed on a specic surface analyzer, while and the specic surface area
and distribution of pore sizes were determined using BET model and density functional theory. For
elemental analysis, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) tests were done on a Thermo Scientic K-
Alpha utilizing Al K α  rays.
2.5 Electrochemical measurements

3. Results And Discussion
Figure 1 shows the synthesis process of LWCA. Through the catalysis and cross-linking of HMTA,
liqueed wood containing various phenolic mixtures were cross-linked with formaldehyde to form a three-
dimensional gel network. Anhydrous ethanol with low surface tension was used to replace the aqueous
solvent in the gel, ensuring that the liqueed wood aerogel with a relatively complete three-dimensional
network structure after freeze-drying process. In order to obtain LWCA, the LWA was pre-carbonized to
remove small molecules and volatile substances, which promoted the formation of conjugated sp2 hybrid
carbon atoms and improved the specic surface area and conductivity of the material. Subsequently,
LWCA was activated by KOH and steam respectively. And the total reaction formula for KOH activation
was as follows:
4KOH + C →  K2CO3 + K2O + H2
Considering the decomposition of KOH at high temperatures and the reducing nature of carbon, it was
generally believed that KOH activation also included the reactions between the reduction of K in the
compound to free metallic K, the oxidation of carbon to CO2, carbonated, and various other reactive
intermediates: (Wang and Kaskel 2012)
2KOH →  K2O + H2O
C + H2O →  CO + H2
CO + H2O →  CO2 + H2
CO2 + K2O →  K2CO3
K2CO3 + 2C →  2K + 3CO
In KOH activation, the KOH distributed on the surface of LWCA rstly reacted with the carbon framework
in situ by redox reactions, etching uniformly distributed microporous on its surface and continuing the
reaction as an interface. When the temperature was above the boiling point of potassium (about 760°C),
part of the potassium vapor evaporates out with nitrogen, while another part of the vapor of potassium
and the generated salts penetrated between the graphite layers. In the latter case, the carbon lattice would
swell, and then left a large number of pores after the potassium was removed by washing (Romanos et
al. 2012).

Steam activation relied mainly on the reaction between C and steam for pore formation: H2O + C → CO + 
H2
As the activation proceeded, the carbon skeleton was continuously consumed, which may result in the
removal of adjacent pore walls and an increase in pore volume, and a decrease in specic surface area.
Figure 2 depicted the SEM images of LWCA under various activation conditions. It could be seen that the
K-LWCA3 possessed advanced pore structure, thinner pore wall, smaller particle size (Fig.2a-c).
Meanwhile, there were some etching marks appeared on the surface of K-LWCA. KOH was able to
penetrate into the interior of the carbon aerogel at high temperatures when reacting with the carbon
aerogel for chemical etching. At this time, some C atoms and other atoms such as N and H were
eliminated, and the generated salt was removed in subsequent washing (Bhatnagar et al. 2013), thus
formed a wealth of micropores on the etched sites. This would greatly increase the specic surface area
of the material and the contact area between materials and electrolyte ions, and offered more active sites.
Consequently, KOH activation was conducive to rapid charging and discharging of the material and
improving the specic capacitance. When the carbon alkali ratio was 1:4, some adjacent pores of the
carbon aerogel collapsed and created larger pores (Fig.2d). Meanwhile, it was also found from Fig.2e that
more impurities were observed on the surface of K-LWCA as carbon alkali ratio increase, and the pore
network of K-LWCA became undeveloped. In comparison to K-LWCA, H-LWCA had larger pore diameter,
thicker pore wall and smoother surface (Fig.2f), which was attributed to activation reaction between
steam and LWCA which was prot to etch external carbon atoms and emerge new pores after the initial
pores expansion.

distribution of samples. As displayed in Fig. 3a, both K-LWCA3 and H-LWCA exhibited a typical behavior
of type I isotherms with a sharp rise at the relative pressures close to zero, suggesting that the materials
were rich in micropore (77.4% and 73.5%, respectively), which indicated a more abundant pore volume
from the higher total adsorption of H-LWCA. Meanwhile, both of K-LWCA and H-LWCA had a small
hysteresis loop, manifesting the existence of meso- or macropores structure in sample. The mesoporous

rate of K-LWCA was 22.6%, slightly lower than that of H-LWCA (27.6%), implying that KOH activation only
formed new micropores without changing the original mesopore and macropore structures. Micropores
could be used for energy storage while mesopores could facilitate electrons and ions transfer at the
surface (Dong et al. 2020), thus both KOH and steam activated carbon aerogels are suitable as
supercapacitor electrode materials. The pore size distribution diagram was represented in Fig. 3b, K-
LWCA3 as well as H-LWCA were predominantly micropores less than 2 nm in size and concentrated
between 0.5 to 3 nm. According to the data in Table 1, the specic surface area of K-LWCA was 1780 m2
g− 1, slightly lower than of H-LWCA at 1996 m2 g− 1, which was consistent with their N2 adsorption
amounts. Additionally, the pore volume of K-LWCA were less than those of H-LWCA, which correspond to
the pore structure observed in the SEM images.
To characterize the chemical structure of LWCA with various activation treatments, FTIR spectra were
collected. As illustrated in Fig. 4a, all of the LWCAs with various activation treatments showed a broad
absorption peak at around 3440 cm− 1 ascribe to the stretching vibration of O-H in alcohol or phenol,
which indicated that LWCAs were hydrophilic and advantageous for improving the wettability. The small
peak between 1450–1650 cm− 1 corresponding to the vibration of C = C in the aromatic ring. Notably the
C-O stretching vibration peak intensity of H-LWCA at 1000 ~ 1260 cm− 1 was lower than those of K-
LWCA3, demonstrating that there were relatively fewer oxygen-containing functional groups in H-LWCA.
Furthermore, there could be seen numerous small peaks assigned to vibration of C-H in the FTIR
spectrum of K-LWCA, indicating that novel C-H bonds were generated as a result of chemical activation.
Besides, since the microstructure of LWCA was developed during activation and affected by the graphite
crystallite (Ma et al. 2014), XRD was performed to estimate the crystallinity for further grasping the
architectural of samples, and the corresponding results as displayed in Fig. 4b. It could be seen that two
broad characteristic diffraction peaks located at 23.5° and 43.8° were located in H-LWCA, corresponding
to the (002) and (101) planes of graphite, indicating the amorphous graphite structure of H-LWCA (Bai et
al. 2016). Compared with H-LWCA, the graphite (100) crystal plane at 43.5° weakened and the peak width
increased for K-LWCA3, whereas the (002) crystal plane at 23.8° nearly disappeared, indicating a lower
degree of graphitization and crystallinity. Meanwhile, more defects and functional groups were
introduced on the skeleton of K-LWCA. Since there were a series of complex reactions between KOH and
carbon aerogel skeleton occurred during the high temperature activation process and continuously
consumed graphite grains (Zhang et al. 2022). Consequently, the original framework structure of carbon
aerogel was partially altered and its disorder degree had enhanced. The defects and functional groups
were benecial to enhance the wettability of the material and the adsorption of electrolyte ions, thus
improving its electrochemical performance.
The surface element chemical states of K-LWCA3 and H-LWCA were characterized by XPS, and the results
were displayed in Fig. 5. Clearly, there were four typical peaks corresponding to C1s, O1s, N1s and P 2p at
285 eV, 532 eV, 401 eV and 133 eV in the wide scan XPS spectra, indicating that LWCA contain carbon,
oxygen, nitrogen and phosphorus species. Specically, the C1s spectrum of K-LWCA3 exhibited three
different characteristic peaks at 284.8 eV, 286.0 eV and 289.5 eV, corresponding to C-C, C-N/C-O and C = O

functional groups. Among, the C-C peak was the most abundant, indicating that K-LWCA3 contains
numerous carbon atoms. And the C-N peak was attributed to the C in the aromatic ring and the N in the
amide group, indicating that the nitrogen atom had substituted for a portion of the carbon atom. Also,
there were carbonyl and carboxyl (C = O) peaks because of the carboxylic acid produced by the LWCA
isomerization during the temperature carbonization and activation as well as the unbroken amide bonds
remained in the ring in the system. In addition, H-LWCA had a characteristic peak at 286.8 eV
corresponding to the epoxy structure (C-O), which originated from the condensation of aromatic
hydrocarbons. The N1s spectrum (Fig. 5a) was tted with various nitrogen-containing functional groups,
including pyridinic N (N-6, 398.9 eV), pyrrolic N (N-5, 400.3 eV), quaternary N (N-Q, 401.5 eV) and N-oxide
(N-X, 403.2 eV) (Sun et al. 2022). And the N-6 peak was usually found in amines due to the replacement
of part of the carbon within the carbon network by the nitrogen atom, while the appearance of N-5 was
owing to the aromatic nitriles produced during the homolytic process (Boudou et al. 2006). N-5 and N-6
were able to generate extra free electrons or delocalized electrons for the conductive process, while N-Q
could enhanced the electrical conductivity of the material through the electron transfer from graphite
(Wang and Ma 2021). Thus, doping of N atoms endowed the carbon aerogel with a great number of
defects and active sites to a certain extent. Similarly, the binding energy of the O 1s peak was found to be
at 532.1 eV and 533.3 eV, ascribing to -O- (C-OH/C-O-C) and C = O. And the binding energies of P 2p peaks
were 132.6 eV and 134.3 eV, which allotted to P-C and P-O bonds, respectively. The existence of P-C peaks
showed that there are phosphate bridges in the system, phosphate-like structures, for instance, which was
of advantage to maintain the carbon skeleton structure and produced pores during the activation
process. According to the elements content (C, O, N and P) listed in the wide scan XPS spectra, the atomic
contents in oxygen, nitrogen and phosphorus of K-LWCA3 were higher than H-LWCA. This was because
some complex reactions had occurred between KOH and the carbon skeleton, increasing the content of
hydrophilic elements, which also conrmed that KOH activation was performed via chemical etching.
The CV curves of the LWCA with varied activation were presented in Fig. 6a. It could be observed that all
samples displayed near-rectangular shapes at 5mV s− 1, exhibiting good symmetry and reversibility along
with the absence of redox peaks, which demonstrated the ideal double-layer capacitance behavior (Lai et
al. 2016). From the CV graph of K-LWCA3 at 5 to 100 mV s− 1 scanning rates in Fig. 6b, it took longer for
K-LWCA3 to reach the current plateau when the scan rate increased, and K-LWCA3 still kept a good
rectangular-like shape well even at 100 mV s− 1, which indicated an outstanding rate performance. And
the GCD curves of samples with different activation conditions at 0.5 A g− 1 were reected in Fig. 6c. all
GCD curves of LWCA were all close to the ideal isosceles triangle shape, indicating that LWCA had the
good reversibility and less energy loss in the process of the charging and discharging. The K-LWCA had a
signicantly longer discharge time than unactivated LWCA, and the longest discharge time at a carbon
alkali ratio of 1:3, indicating that the activation effect of the carbon alkali ratio was more appropriate at
this time, which was coincidence with the SEM results. The specic capacitance of samples was
calculated from the GCD curves as mirrored in Fig. 6g. Clearly, the specic capacitance of K-LWCA
increased and then decreased as the KOH content increased. And the K-LWCA3 obtained a remarkable
specic capacitance value of 201 F g− 1, apparently exceeding the specic capacitance of LWCA (62 F g−

1) and H-LWCA (111 F g− 1). The KOH activation was benecial to improve the specic capacitance of
carbon aerogels, and the effect was better than that of steam activation. The voltage decreases
increasing the applied current density, but the GCD graph of K-LWCA3 at various current densities in
Fig. 6d still maintained a good inverted triangle shape, indicating the excellent high-current charging and
discharging capability of K-LWCA3. The specic capacitance of K-LWCA3 and H-LWCA at various current
densities revealed that even at 20 A g− 1, the K-LWCA3 still possessed a specic capacitance of 141 F g− 1
and a capacitance retention rate of 70.15%, which was better than that of H-LWCA at 64.17%, indicating
that K-LWCA3 had superior rate performance to H-LWCA.
To further evaluate the transport behavior of electrolyte ions in the LWCAs with different activation
treatments, the EIS was tested in a frequency range from 0.01 Hz to 100 kHz (Fig. 6e). It could be seen
that all samples exhibited semicircular arcs reecting the interfacial charge transfer resistance in the
high-frequency region (He et al. 2015). Among them, H-LWCA had the smallest semicircular diameter,
indicating that it possessed the smallest interfacial resistance and ion migration resistance, ascribing to
the abundant pore structure and larger average pore size of H-LWCA which facilitates rapid electron
transfer. Besides, the intersection point of the curve and the real axis was the resistance value of the
equivalent series resistance (Rs) of the electrode material (Gao et al. 2014). It showed that the Rs of K-
LWCA3 was 1.03 Ω , slightly larger than 0.75 Ω  of H-LWCA, which was owing to the introduction of more
defects and functional groups into the carbon skeleton during KOH activation. In the low-frequency
region, the EIS graph was a almost vertical line, demonstrating excellent rapid charging and discharging
behavior, which was attributed to the interoperable pore structure facilitating rapid charge transfer(Geng
et al. 2016).
Furthermore, the long cycle performance of K-LWCA3 and H-LWCA were obtained via GCD test at 10 A g− 1
for 5000 cycles, and the results as given in Fig. 6f. After 5000 cycles, the capacitance retention of K-
LWCA3 and H-LWCA were 94.11% and 81.3%, respectively, indicating that both K-LWCA3 and H-LWCA had
excellent cycling performance as supercapacitor electrode materials. In particular, K-LWCA3 exhibited a
higher capacitance retention, because its interconnected hierarchical porous structure can shorten the ion
diffusion path and meet the various requirements of ion diffusion and transport, which resulted in higher
capacitance retention. Besides, the low equivalent resistance of K-LWCA3 facilitated the diffusion of
electrolyte ions, while the high carbon content enhanced its cycling performance.
To further explore the feasibility and practicality of K-LWCA3 as an electrode material, it was assembled
into a symmetrical supercapacitor device. Similar to its CV curve in the three-electrode system, the CV
curves of symmetrical supercapacitor device at various scan rates exhibited in Fig. 7a. It maintained a
rectangular-like shape even at 100 mV s− 1, which demonstrated typical electrical double layer capacitor
behavior and remarkable rate performance. Figure 7b showed the GCD curves of symmetrical
supercapacitor device from 0.5 to 10 A g− 1, which retained a symmetrical triangular shape, indicating
good charge/discharge reversibility. As displayed in Fig. 7c, the specic capacitance of symmetrical

supercapacitor device exhibited 117.78 F g− 1, and maintained 87.55 F g− 1 at 5 A g− 1 (retention rate
74.33%), which was owing to its outstanding electrical conductivity.
The Ragone plots of K-LWCA3 symmetrical supercapacitor device were displayed in Fig. 7d. The K-
LWCA3 symmetrical supercapacitor device delivered an energy density up to 9.2 Wh kg− 1 at a power
density of 375 W kg− 1, and an energy density as high as 6.11 Wh kg− 1 at a maximum power density of
7498 W kg− 1. And it can be found that the energy density of our device is superior to that of most
previously reported similar devices (Wei et al. 2016; Gong et al. 2017; Ma et al. 2015; Thillaikkarasi et al.
2022; Li et al. 2021; Li et al. 2022; Devarajan and Arumugam 2022; Wei et al. 2021; Awitdrus et al. 2022;
Qin et al. 2021). Remarkably, benetting from excellent rate performance of K-LWCA3, the energy density
of the device was not considerably inuenced by the power density, even though it varied over a wide
range, exhibiting huge potential application prospects in the eld of energy storage.
Conclusion
In summary, the KOH treated carbon aerogel (K-LWCA) and steam treated carbon (H-LWCA) were
synthesized by sol-gel and carbonization-activation. The activation methods had a substantial inuence
on the microstructure and electrochemical properties of the LWCA. K-LWCA appeared higher specic
capacitance, better rate performance and superior cyclic stability. Particularly, in the three-electrode
system, K-LWCA exhibited a high specic capacitance of 201.47 F g− 1 at a current density of 0.5A g− 1
and an excellent rate capability of 70.15% retention at 20A g− 1 as well as nearly 94.11% retention at 10A
g− 1 after 5,000 charge-discharge cycles. After being assembled into a symmetrical supercapacitor, the
energy density of K-LWCA at 0.5A g− 1 current density was up to 9.2Wh kg− 1, corresponding to a power
density of 375W kg− 1, and the energy density still reached 6.11Wh kg− 1 at a high power density of
7498W kg− 1. Therefore, K-LWCA is a promising alternative electrode material for supercapacitors.
