ARTICLE INFO
Keywords:
Cesium acetate
Lignin
Template method
Nitrogen doping
ABSTRACT
This experiment developed a high-performance lignin-based porous carbon electrode material prepared via the 
cesium acetate template method. Its abundant pore structure and high capacitance demonstrate significant po -
tential for high-performance supercapacitors. The cesium acetate used in this material serves not only as a 
templating agent but also functions as an activating agent, capable of catalyzing multiple reactions while 
inducing greater distortion in the carbon network to achieve a higher specific surface area. Due to the "cesium 
effect," the prepared porous carbon electrode material (LCC-3) exhibits a high specific surface area (3423.15 m
2 
g
 1
) and pore volume (2.6842 cm
3 
g
 1
), with a specific capacitance of 396 F g
 1 
(0.5 A g
 1
) in a three-electrode 
system. Subsequent heteroatom doping experiments further validated the feasibility of nitrogen doping in 
enhancing electrochemical performance. The sodium lignosulfonate used in this study offers sustainability 
benefits by combining lignin with cesium acetate to produce an environmentally friendly, high-performance 
supercapacitor electrode, thereby advancing sustainable energy storage technologies.
1. Introduction
With the rapid development of the new energy industry, demand for 
high-performance, environmentally friendly energy storage devices is 
growing. Against this backdrop, supercapacitors have become a research 
hotspot due to their superior characteristics, including high energy 
density and fast charging/discharging rates. The two types of super -
capacitors, electric double-layer capacitors and pseudocapacitors, differ 
significantly in their energy-storage mechanisms. In electric double- 
layer capacitors, charge storage relies on ion adsorption and desorp -
tion at the surfaces and interfaces or within the internal pores of elec -
trode materials. The energy storage mechanism of pseudocapacitors 
involves reversible redox or Faraday reactions between electrodes and 
electrolytes. The electrochemical energy storage process of pseudoca -
pacitors can extend to the interior of electrode materials, enabling 
higher capacitance per unit area and energy density. However, this 
mechanism results in slower energy storage and release rates in 
pseudocapacitors, often accompanied by volume expansion of electrode 
materials, which adversely affects power density and cycling stability. 
Although pseudocapacitors offer high energy density, enhancing their 
energy storage and release rates while minimizing structural damage 
remains a critical challenge ( Krishnan et al., 2026 ).
As a critical component that determines the performance of super -
capacitor electrode materials, electrode materials are also a primary 
focus of research. Currently, the electrode materials used for super -
capacitors are mostly derived from non-renewable, unsustainable coal 
or fossil petroleum sources ( Dissanayake and Kularatna-Abeywardana, 
2024; Divya and Rajalakshmi, 2020; Libretti et al., 2024; Rana et al., 
2020 ). Consequently, it is necessary to develop a range of renewable and 
sustainable precursors for the preparation of supercapacitors. Porous 
carbon materials are promising electrode materials for supercapacitors 
due to their abundant pore structure and high specific surface area. 
Lignin, a natural organic compound widely present in agricultural 
waste, offers advantages as a supercapacitor electrode material owing to

its three-dimensional aromatic hydrocarbon structure and layered 
characteristics ( Farma et al., 2023; Li et al., 2023a, 2023c ). Porous 
carbon materials derived from lignin exhibit high specific surface area, 
good thermal stability, and chemical stability. Its high carbon content 
and functional groups (such as benzyl, phenolic, hydroxyl, etc.) not only 
provide numerous active sites, but also enhance charge storage capacity 
and electronic conductivity through redox reactions and π - π coupling, 
making it an effective electrode material with high specific capacitance, 
high power density, and long cycle life ( Qiu et al., 2023; Sima et al., 
2024; Wang et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2020; Yi et al., 2025 ). In addition, 
lignin, as one of the main components of agricultural waste, has the 
characteristics of low cost and wide availability, which can meet the 
needs of large-scale production, reduce environmental pollution, and 
promote resource utilization ( Zhang et al., 2024a ). However, the direct 
use of lignin in agricultural waste as an electrode material for super -
capacitors presents limitations in terms of electrochemical performance, 
and the use of chemical reagents may cause secondary pollution. 
Therefore, given the selection of green, environmentally friendly 
chemical reagents, improving the electrochemical performance of 
electrode materials remains a current research priority. The template 
method is a widely used method for preparing porous carbon materials, 
readily yielding materials with high specific surface area and enabling 
control over the pore structure. The critical aspect of the template 
method is selecting appropriate template agents in combination with 
carbon precursors for carbonization. During this process, the template 
agents occupy space and leave a rich pore structure in the carbon ma -
terial after acid washing ( Muddasar et al., 2024; Zhu et al., 2024 ). 
However, the template method alone cannot yield carbon materials with 
excellent electrochemical performance; activation agents must be used. 
In previous experiments, researchers employed the dual-mode plate 
method (MgO/F127) to prepare lignin-based porous carbon materials. 
The specific capacitance of the resulting mesoporous carbon was 
186.3 F g
 1 
( Song et al., 2017 ), but after KOH activation, it reached 
350.1 F g
 1 
( Fu et al., 2024 ). The existence of a substance that can serve 
as both a template and an activator would greatly improve the efficiency 
of preparing porous carbon electrode materials.
In this experiment, cesium acetate was used as both a template and 
an activator for lignin-based porous carbon materials. This approach 
enabled both favorable electrochemical performance and increased 
preparation efficiency. Cesium acetate can catalyze various reactions, 
such as C-H activation, C-C coupling, and macrocyclization, all of which 
involve thermal condensation of molecular precursors to form carbo -
naceous materials. The larger size of cesium ions results in weaker 
binding forces with anions in the reaction medium, thereby enhancing 
their activity. Cs atoms are larger than K atoms, leading to greater 
distortion of the carbon network and higher SSA. Cesium ions can 
effectively interact with oxygen-containing functional groups in organic 
compounds, promoting their elimination and forming covalent net -
works. For example, cesium ions can effectively catalyze dehydration 
and decarboxylation, accelerate condensation reactions, and activate 
carbonyl to generate enol anions, thereby promoting substitution, 
addition, or macrocyclic reactions ( Banerjee and Kanan, 2018; De Lar -
ramendi et al., 2022; Mayeux et al., 2014; Xu et al., 2014, 2022 ). 
Research has found that the ethylene ketone produced by the pyrolysis 
of cesium acetate may also serve as a carbon precursor, which rapidly 
polymerizes, crosslinks, and condenses into a carbon skeleton at high 
temperatures. Cesium salts promote dehydroaromatization and stabilize 
carbon intermediates during this process. In addition, the activation 
process of Cs compounds can be carried out at lower temperatures ( ≈
600 ℃ ), while K or Na compounds ( > 800 ℃ ), owing to the lower 
melting point and decomposition temperature of Cs compounds. 
Therefore, Cs oxides and metals can be generated at lower temperatures 
and act as effective activators. As the carbonization temperature in -
creases, the mass retention rate of cesium acetate stabilizes at 800
◦
C. It 
exhibits a high specific surface area and a combination of microporous 
and mesoporous structure, forming a highly extended conjugated carbon 
framework. These structures enhance its electrical conductivity and 
energy storage capacity. At the same time, the addition of lignin as the 
main carbon source in this experiment increased the utilization rate of 
cesium. The inorganic cesium salt produced by in-situ pyrolysis is in 
close contact with carbon-based substances as an in-situ template to 
promote the formation of pore structure. At higher temperatures, the 
decomposition, melting, and volatilization of the cesium salt further 
promote the formation of more open microporous and mesoporous 
structures, thereby increasing the specific surface area and optimizing 
the pore structure ( Li et al., 2024 ). Although the specific surface area of 
reported cesium acetate-templated porous carbon has reached as high as 
2936 m² g
 1
, its electrochemical performance still exhibits certain 
limitations (less than 313 F g
 1 
at 0.1 A g
 1
, and this electrode material 
demonstrates low capacitance retention at high current densities 
(90 F g
 1 
at 10 A g
 1
), which is lower than the value observed at low 
current densities)( Li et al., 2023b ). In this experiment, lignin-based 
porous carbon materials (LCC) were prepared using cesium acetate as 
both a template and an activator. To illustrate the synergistic effect 
between cesium acetate and lignin during carbonization, we also con -
ducted comparative experiments using cesium metal salts and acetates 
to prepare additional porous carbon materials (LC-X). Based on the 
electrochemical performance and pore structure already achieved, 
additional nitrogen-doping experiments were conducted to further 
assess the feasibility of heteroatom doping for performance enhance -
ment. This led to the preparation of nitrogen-doped porous carbon 
materials (LCNC) with high specific surface areas, which exhibited 
improved electrochemical performance compared to those prepared 
with the same mass ratio using templates.

2.2. Synthesis of porous carbon LC-X
To control for variables, different salt templates were added at a 
fixed lignin-to-salt template mass ratio of 1:3, and the LCC  3 was the 
same as in 2.1. The selected salt templates (ST) were potassium acetate, 
sodium acetate, cesium carbonate, potassium carbonate, and sodium 
carbonate. The electrode materials prepared were named LC-KAc, LC- 
NaAc, LC-CsCc, LC-KCc, and LC-NaCc, respectively. As shown in Table 2 , 
the LC-to-Salt template mass ratio was kept constant at 1:3 across all 
samples.
2.3. Synthesis of porous carbon LCNC
The pretreated lignin was mixed with cesium acetate at a 1:1 ratio 
and ground. The mixed sample was placed in a porcelain boat and 
spread evenly. After carbonization was completed, the resulting product 
was ground. The ground product was then mixed with urea and ground 
again. The mass ratios of lignin to urea and cesium acetate were 1:0.5, 
1:1, 1:2, and 1:3, respectively. A control group was also established. The 
control group was directly mixed with pretreated lignin, urea, and 
carbonized. The mass ratio of lignin to urea was 1:1 (LNC) to evaluate 
the role of Cs metal in this doping experiment and its impact on elec -
trochemical performance, as shown in Table 3 . After mixing, the samples 
were placed flat in a porcelain boat and then placed in a tube furnace. 
The temperature was raised to 400 ℃ at a rate of 2 ℃ min
 1 
and held for 
2 h for carbonization and nitrogen-doping diffusion treatment. After 
carbonization, the resulting product was ground, washed with 1 M HCl, 
and then washed with deionized water to remove impurities and HCl. 
Finally, the obtained product was dried overnight in an 80 ℃ blast 
drying oven. The resulting samples were named LCNC  0.5, LCNC  1, 
LCNC  2, and LCNC  3, respectively.
2.4. Morphological characterization
Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and Raman spectroscopy were 
used to characterize the morphology and structure of the synthesized 
materials. Characterization of the phases of porous carbon materials 
using an Aeris type X-ray diffractometer (XRD); X-ray photoelectron 
spectroscopy (XPS, Axis Ultra, Kratos Analytical Ltd) was used to mea -
sure the elemental content and valence states of samples; Fourier 
transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) measurement was performed 
using potassium bromide method with Horiba FT  720 spectropho -
tometer; The specific surface area (SSA) was analyzed using the Bru -
nauer – Emmett – Teller (BET) method, and the pore size distribution was 
calculated using the Barret Joyner Halenda (BJH) model based on 
desorption data.

2.5. Electrochemical analysis
All electrochemical tests in this paper were conducted using the 
Shanghai Chenhua CHI660E electrochemical workstation at room 
temperature. 
(1) Preparation of electrode sheets 
The carbon material, conductive carbon black (Super P), and 
polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) were mixed at a mass ratio of 
8:1:1. An appropriate amount of N-methyl  2-pyrrolidone (NMP) 
was then added, and the mixture was ground until the slurry 
became smooth, uniform, and particle-free. The slurry should be 
thick but not dry, and thin but not dripping. The carbon cloth was 
then cut into approximately 1 cm × 1 cm pieces. Before coating, 
the carbon cloth was weighed, and the slurry was then applied to 
it. Afterward, the carbon cloth was then dried in a vacuum oven 
at 60 
◦
C for 12 h. The dried carbon cloth was weighed to calculate 
the mass loading of the carbon material. The mass loading was 
controlled to be approximately 1 – 2 mg.
(2) A three-electrode system was composed of a platinum electrode 
as the counter electrode, mercury/mercury oxide as the reference 
electrode, and 6 M KOH electrolyte. Cyclic voltammetry (CV), 
galvanostatic charge/discharge (GCD), and electrochemical 
impedance spectroscopy (EIS) tests were performed in the voltage 
range of  1 – 0 V.
(3) Electrochemical performance evaluation parameters In this sec -
tion, the mass-to-capacitance ratio is calculated based on the GCD 
curve. The calculation formula for the three-electrode system is as 
follows:
C = I × Δ t / m × Δ V ( Du et al., 2025 )                                                     
Among them, I (A) ， Δ t (s) ， m (g) ， Δ (V) represent discharge cur -
rent, discharge time, mass of carbon material loaded on a single elec -
trode, and potential window, respectively.

3. Results and discussion
3.1. Structural and morphological analysis
The morphology of the prepared samples was observed using scan -
ning electron microscopy. The SEM images of LCC porous carbon under 
different cesium acetate ratios are shown in the figure. In LC (the sample 
prepared without cesium acetate as a template), as shown in Fig. 2 (a), 
the surface is relatively flat with some pores visible. This is because the 
ammonia solution provides alkaline conditions during pretreatment, 
allowing hydrogen peroxide to act as an oxidizing agent ( Novia et al., 
2022 ). The primary objective of this method is to efficiently degrade 
and modify lignin, breaking down its complex, stable three-dimensional 
network and converting it into low-molecular-weight intermediates rich 
in oxygen- and nitrogen-containing functional groups, which exhibit 
higher reactivity ( Lin et al., 2002; Zhao et al., 2020 ). As the proportion 
of cesium acetate increases, as shown in Fig. 2 (b, c), pores gradually 
appear in the material, accompanied by thin sheet-like structures. As the 
proportion of cesium acetate continues to increase, honeycomb-like 
structures appear in the carbon material, as shown in Fig. 2 (d). The 
appearance of honeycomb-like structures in porous carbon materials 
further increases the material's porosity and specific surface area, 
thereby promoting ion adsorption and transfer ( Liu, 2025 ). A further 
increase in the proportion of cesium acetate leads to the collapse of pores 
in the material, and the layered structure becomes more apparent. This 
may be due to the accumulation of cesium acetate. From the SEM 
morphology of the material, it can be inferred that the pore structure and 
specific surface area of the LCC  3 material are the most developed.
As shown in Fig. 3 , under identical treatment conditions, AOLs 
derived from different salt templates exhibit significant differences in 
surface morphology and pore structure. Fig. 3 (a) presents the porous 
carbon prepared with a cesium acetate template. This sample exhibits an 
obvious honeycomb-like structure, which enhances porosity and specific 
surface area and facilitates ion adsorption and migration. Fig. 3 (b) 
shows the sample obtained using a cesium carbonate template. It also 
forms a honeycomb framework with a well-defined layered structure. In 
comparison, Fig. 3 (c, d) correspond to carbon materials templated by 
potassium carbonate and potassium acetate, respectively. The honey -
comb structure disappears, and a layered morphology becomes domi -
nant. For samples prepared with sodium carbonate and sodium acetate 
( Fig. 3 (e, f)), no obvious pores are observed, and the material surfaces 
are relatively smooth. Table 4 and Figure S1 also confirm the above 
analysis, showing that LCC  3 has the highest specific surface area 
(3423.15 m² g
 1
) and the highest pore volume (2.6842 cm³ g
 1
).
To investigate the specific surface area and pore-size distribution of 
porous carbon materials templated with cesium acetate, nitrogen 
adsorption and desorption isotherms were measured for each sample. As 
shown in Fig. 4 (a), the isotherms of LCC  2, LCC  3, and LCC  4 exhibit 
similar isotherm shapes, while the nitrogen adsorption capacity of LC is 
significantly lower than that of the other three. For LCC  3, in the low- 
pressure region (P/P
0 
< 0.1), the adsorption capacity rises rapidly at 
extremely low pressures, forming a steep initial segment, indicating the 
presence of micropores ( < 2 nm) in the material. The activation ratio of 
LCC  3 increases micropore volume more effectively (see Table S1 ). 
Micro pores can be quickly filled under low pressure due to their strong 
adsorption potential, which is consistent with the typical characteristics 
of Type I isotherms. At (P/P
0
= 0.1 – 0.8), the adsorption capacity slowly 
increases, with the curve showing a steady upward trend and a hyster -
esis loop. The steady increase indicates the presence of mesopores 
(2 – 50 nm), but the quantity is relatively small ( Stankiewicz et al., 2026; 
Zhang and Nie, 2026 ). From the aperture distribution image in Fig. 4 (b), 
there is a very sharp and high-intensity peak in the region where the 
aperture is less than 2 nm. This indicates that the material contains very 
abundant micropores. These pores are the direct cause of the sharp in -
crease in nitrogen adsorption capacity at low pressures (P/P
0
< 0.1). 
They are typical features of lignin after activation treatment, providing a 
huge specific surface area. Table 4 shows that, following treatment with 
a cesium acetate template, the specific surface area of the LC samples

may occur (decreasing specific surface area and pore volume), thereby 
negatively impacting the performance of the supercapacitor. These re -
sults indicate that the presence of cesium acetate successfully activates 
lignin-based carbon materials, which are predominantly microporous 
and contain a small amount of mesopores. It has a highly concentrated 
distribution of micropores, which is the main source of its high specific 
surface area.
At the same time, the presence of a small number of mesopores forms 
a hierarchical porous structure. The structural composition of the ma -
terial was analyzed by X-ray diffraction and Raman spectroscopy. Fig. 4
(c) shows the XRD curves of LC and LCC-X materials. Materials doped 
with cesium acetate exhibit sharp peaks at around 43.5
◦
, corresponding 
to the diffraction plane of amorphous carbon (100) ( Guan et al., 2025 ). 
The diffraction peaks of the pure lignin material, AOL, are not suffi -
ciently clear. The structure of the composite material was further 
detected using Raman spectroscopy. As shown in Fig. 4 (d), each sample 
exhibits two peaks at approximately 1312 cm

and 1580 cm
 1
, corre -
sponding to the D band (related to lattice defects of sp3 carbon atoms) 
and the G band (related to surface stretching vibrations of sp2 carbon 
atoms) ( Ravichandran et al., 2026 ). The I

values of LCC  2, LCC  3, 
and LCC  4 are 3.34, 5.44, and 5.74, respectively. With increasing ce -
sium acetate doping concentration, the ratio gradually increases, and 
the disorder of the carbon materials is enhanced. This is because a 
sufficient amount of cesium acetate decomposes into cesium carbonate, 
cesium oxide, and metallic cesium during the carbonization process. 
These components disrupt the graphitic order of the carbon framework, 
creating pores and resulting in a highly disordered structure. This highly 
disordered structure sacrifices some conductivity but provides abundant 
specific surface area and defect-active sites.
Fig. 5 (a) shows the nitrogen-doped carbon material prepared with 
urea alone, which presents a smooth surface without a pore structure. In 
the absence of templates and activators, the carbon material fails to 
activate, resulting in an underdeveloped pore structure and a low spe -
cific surface area. Fig. 5 (b – e) display distinct pores and layered struc -
tures after cesium acetate treatment, and the abundant pore structure 
facilitates the incorporation of nitrogen atoms into the carbon skeleton. 
The layered structure in Fig. 5 (c) is stacked more densely, with a smaller 
interlayer spacing, which prevents the collapse of the carbon structure 
during carbonization. Fig. 5 (f) presents the SEM image of LCC  1. This 
sample uses the same cesium acetate dosage as the other groups but 
lacks the secondary carbonization process.

This indicates that LCNC  1 material contains extremely rich and 
concentrated ultramicropores ( < 0.7 nm) and micropores (0.7 – 2 nm) 
with a narrow-concentrated pore size distribution. These pores are the 
main source of its ultra-high specific surface area and account for the 
increase in adsorption capacity observed in its isotherm at extremely 
low pressures. Between 2 and 10 nm, the curve drops to near zero, with 
almost no observable peaks, indicating that the material contains few 
mesopores. The flat adsorption and narrow H4 hysteresis loop in the 
medium pressure region are caused by the narrow-slit space formed by 
the aggregation of these micropores, rather than independent meso -

no contribution of pore volume in the macroporous region, indicating

3.2. Supercapacitive behavior of electrodes
The resulting porous carbon was further processed into electrodes to 
evaluate its potential for supercapacitor applications. In cyclic voltam -
metry (CV) testing, all samples containing the template exhibited 
approximately rectangular curves ( Figure S2 ), indicating that their 
charge storage mechanism is primarily based on double-layer capaci -
tance (EDLC) and is highly reversible. In samples with low-quality ra -
tios, such as LCC  1 and LCC  2, this indicates that the amount of 
template agent used is relatively low. Their current response is moder -
ate, better than the template-free sample LC but inferior to the high- 
quality sample. Among high-quality samples, LCC  3, LCC  4, and 
LCC  6 exhibit the highest current response. Especially for the LCC  3 
sample, it can still maintain a current density close to 60 A g
 1 
and a 
good rectangular shape at a high scanning rate of 200 mV s
 1
, indicating 
the highest specific capacitance and the best rate performance. In the 
constant current charge discharge (GCD) test, the curves of all samples 
showed an approximately symmetrical triangular shape ( Figure S3 ), 
with no obvious voltage plateau in the charge discharge curves, indi -
cating that the charge storage process is mainly dominated by reversible 
ion adsorption/desorption at the electrode/electrolyte interface, and the 
contribution of Faraday pseudocapacitance is very small, which is highly 
consistent with the results of previous CV analysis. According to the 
charging and discharging time, LCC  3 exhibits the highest specific 
capacitance at a current density of 0.5 A g
 1
, reaching 396 F g
 1
; the 
other samples (LCC  1, LCC  2, LCC  4, and LCC  6) recorded values of 
219.5, 299.5, 279, and 214.5 F g
 1
, respectively, under the same con -
ditions, all of which are lower than this value. The performance inflec -
tion point occurs at LCC  4 (1:4 lignin-to-cesium acetate), where the 
electrochemical performance decreases significantly, indicating that 
LCC  3 is already the optimal mass ratio. Continuing to increase the 
proportion of cesium acetate leads to a decrease in specific capacitance, 
due to excessive use of the template agent, which results in excessive 
etching and destroys the microporous structure, causing micropores to 
merge into mesopores or even macropores, and decreasing the total 
specific surface area. At the same time, the continuity of the carbon 
skeleton is disrupted, the conductivity decreases, the mechanical 
strength deteriorates, and ultimately leads to a decline in electro -
chemical performance.
Fig. 8 (a, b) visually shows the comparison between the GCD curve of 
LCC at a current density of 0.5 A g
 1 
and the CV curve at a scan rate of 
5 mV s
 1 
under different cesium acetate ratios. LCC  3 material has the 
longest charge-discharge time and the best rate performance. The per -
formance of LCC  2 and LCC  4 materials is slightly weaker. The former 
is due to an insufficient amount of template agent, while the latter is due 
to an excessive amount, leading to the collapse of the pore structure and 
affecting their electrochemical performance. The specific capacitance of 
the LCC at different current densities was calculated from the GCD 
curves; Fig. 8 (c) and Table 5 provide clear illustrations of the corre -
sponding values for the porous carbon electrode material at various 
current densities under different cesium acetate ratios. The capacitor 
performance of double-layer capacitors is closely related to their specific 
surface area, pore volume, and conductivity. Therefore, the optimal 
electrochemical performance of LCC  3 is attributed to its large specific 
surface area, layered porous structure, and superior conductivity, which 
provide more activation sites and a faster charge-transfer rate. Fig. 8 (d) 
shows the cycling stability curve of LCC  3 at a current density of 
10 A g
 1. 
As shown in the figure, the LCC  3 electrode exhibits relatively 
stable capacity over the first 1500 cycles, and the rich microporous 
carbon material demonstrates good chemical stability and mechanical 
strength. Short-term charge-discharge cycles are insufficient to damage 
its carbon framework. In the initial cycle, there is a slight "activation" 
process. The electrolyte better wets all the pores, and some initially 
difficult-to-access closed micropores are "opened". The slight increase in 
capacitance may offset the downward trend, resulting in overall stabil -
ity. After 1500 cycles, the capacity gradually decreases, and under 
continuous electrochemical polarization, solvation ions in the electro -
lyte will repeatedly "squeeze" into micropores of very similar size. This

extracted. Over time, this retention effect accumulates, blocking more

cles, the capacity tends to stabilize, leaving relatively large micropores 
and mesopores with low kinetic resistance to ion entry and exit, as well

On these pores and surfaces, the ion insertion/extraction process reaches 
a dynamic equilibrium that can be maintained for a long time. There -
fore, the capacitance value no longer decreases significantly but remains 
stable ( K ¨a ¨arik et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2023 ). Furthermore, in a 6 M 
KOH solution, since the test voltage range (  1 – 0 V) covers the onset 
potential of the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER), HER will continue 
to occur during long-term cycling when the carbon material has a low 
hydrogen evolution overpotential, resulting in the formation of H ₂ 
bubbles. Bubbles adhering to the electrode surface physically block 
contact with the electrolyte, and when they detach, they may strip away 
active material. At the same time, local OH ⁻ consumption leads to pH 
fluctuations, accelerating material corrosion. Concentrated KOH reacts 
with the surface of the carbon material during long-term cycling, 
generating soluble carbonates or organic acid salts, which also 
contribute to electrode mass loss ( He et al., 2016 ). Finally, the specific 
capacitance of LCC  3 in the three-electrode system after 5000 consec -

, with a capacitance retention rate 
of 89%.

carbonate are used as template agents to prepare high-performance

precursors to form carbonaceous materials. Although the exact mecha -
nism of this effect is not fully understood, it is believed that different ion 
sizes play different roles. The larger size of cesium ions results in weaker 
binding forces with anions in the reaction medium, thereby enhancing 
their activity. Cs atoms are much larger than K atoms, leading to greater 
distortion of the carbon network and higher SSA. Cesium ions can 
effectively interact with oxygen-containing functional groups in organic 
compounds, promoting their elimination and forming covalent net -
works. For example, cesium ions can effectively catalyze dehydration 
and decarboxylation, accelerate condensation reactions, and activate 
carbonyl to generate enol anions, thereby promoting substitution, 
addition, or macrocyclic reactions ( Dijkstra et al., 1987; Flessner and 
Doye, 1999; Galli, 1992; Nishiyama et al., 2009 ). Research has found 
that the ethylene ketone produced by the pyrolysis of cesium acetate 
may also serve as a carbon precursor, which rapidly polymerizes, 
crosslinks, and condenses into a carbon skeleton at high temperatures. 
Cesium salts promote dehydroaromatization and stabilize carbon in -
termediates during this process. In addition, the activation process of Cs 
compounds can be carried out at significantly lower temperatures ( ≈
600 
◦
C), while K or Na compounds ( > 800 
◦
C) cannot, due to the lower 
melting point and decomposition temperature of Cs compounds. 
Therefore, Cs oxides and metals can be generated at lower temperatures 
and act as powerful activators. At the same time, the addition of lignin as 
the main carbon source in this experiment improved the utilization rate 
of the cesium element. The inorganic cesium salt produced by in-situ 
pyrolysis is in close contact with carbon-based substances as an in-situ 
template to promote the formation of pore structure. At higher tem -
peratures, the decomposition, melting, and volatilization of the cesium 
salt promote the formation of more open microporous and mesoporous 
structures, thereby increasing the specific surface area of the material 
and optimizing its pore structure. Table 8 compares the specific capac -
itance performance of the material in this study with that of porous 
carbon prepared from biomass feedstocks using different template 
agents, as reported in other literature.
In order to verify the feasibility of using N doping to further enhance 
the electrochemical performance in this experiment, a series of porous 
carbon materials were prepared by changing the mass ratio of lignin to 
urea (from 1:0.5 – 1:3), and their electrochemical performance as 
supercapacitor electrode materials was evaluated using cyclic voltam -
metry (CV) ( Figure S4 ). All curves showed a rectangular shape, indi -
cating that the material exhibits typical double-layer capacitance. The 
CV curve of LCNC showed a wide oxidation-reduction peak in the 
voltage range of  0.7 to  0.40 V, attributed to the Faradaic reactions of 
nitrogen- and oxygen-containing groups and indicating its pseudoca -
pacitive properties ( Huang et al., 2024 ). According to the image ob -
tained through constant current charge discharge (GCD) testing 
( Figure S5 ), LNC exhibits the lowest specific capacitance and worst rate 
performance due to the lack of a template agent for pore formation, low 
specific surface area, and poor pore structure, resulting in low ion 
accessibility and high internal resistance. As shown in Figure S5c , 
LCNC  1 has the longest discharge time among all samples, and the ratio 
of lignin, urea, and cesium acetate reaches the optimal equilibrium. The 
template agent creates the optimal pore structure, while an appropriate 
amount of nitrogen doping provides pseudocapacitance, resulting in a 
synergistic effect and yielding an ideal electrode material with both high 
energy and high power density.

4. Conclusion
Overall, we have successfully prepared lignin-based supercapacitor 
electrode materials using cesium acetate as both a template and an 
activator, thereby promoting the formation of a hierarchical porous 
structure. The LCC  3 material obtained has a specific surface area of 
3423.15 m
2 
g
 1
. The prepared electrode material has a capacity of 
396 F g
 1 
(0.5 A g
 1
) in a three-electrode system, with a yield of up to 
40%. While inheriting the advantages of the cesium acetate template, it 
successfully reduces production costs and improves electrochemical 
performance. The subsequent nitrogen-doping experiments also pro -
vided new ideas for the low-cost preparation of high-performance 
electrode materials using the cesium acetate template method. The 
LCNC  1 material prepared maintained a high specific surface area of 
3168.22 m
2 
g
 1
, and exhibited a higher specific capacitance (278 F g ⁻ ¹ 
at 0.5 A g ⁻ ¹) than LCC  1 (219.5 F g ⁻ ¹ at 0.5 A g ⁻ ¹), demonstrating the 
benefit of nitrogen doping. In the three-electrode system, after 5000 
charge-discharge cycles, the LCC  3 electrode material retains 88% of its 
initial capacitance, demonstrating good long-term stability. These re -
sults confirm the enormous potential of lignin-based supercapacitor 
electrode materials prepared with cesium acetate as a template for 
constructing high-performance energy storage device electrodes.

Valorization of pistachio shell biomass into potassium- and fluorine-doped 
porous carbon through pyrolysis for supercapacitor applications
Yavuz Yardım
a
, Cafer Saka
b , *
a
Faculty of Pharmacy, Van Yüzüncü Yıl University, Van, Türkiye
b
Faculty of Health Sciences, Siirt University, Siirt, Türkiye
ARTICLE INFO
Keywords:
Pistachio shell biomass
Chemical activation
K/F doping
Porous carbon
Supercapacitor electrode
ABSTRACT
In this study, pistachio shell biomass was valorized into a high-performance porous carbon material through 
controlled pyrolysis followed by KOH chemical activation and subsequent potassium/fluorine (K/F) modifica -
tion. The influence of dual K/F doping on the structural evolution, surface chemistry, and electrochemical 
behavior of pistachio shell-derived activated carbon (PSAC) was systematically investigated. XRD and Raman 
analyses revealed partial graphitization accompanied by increased defect density after K/F incorporation, as 
evidenced by the appearance of a broadened (002) diffraction peak at ~26
◦
in the XRD pattern and an increased 
Raman I D/ IG ratio compared to pristine PSAC, while FTIR and XPS confirmed significant modification of surface 
functional groups and successful introduction of K, F, and oxygen-containing species. Textural characterization 
demonstrated that K/F doping induced pore widening and the development of a hierarchical pore structure, with 
a decrease in BET surface area from 483 to 383 m² g ⁻ ¹ accompanied by a substantial increase in average pore 
radius from 1.65 to 3.94 nm. Electron microscopy analyses showed that K/F modification resulted in rougher, 
more heterogeneous surfaces and a more uniform layered morphology at the nanoscale. Electrochemical eval -
uation in aqueous electrolytes revealed that K/F-doped PSAC exhibited significantly enhanced charge-transfer 
kinetics, lower interfacial resistance, and improved ion diffusion compared to pristine PSAC. The modified 
electrode delivered a high specific capacitance of 188 F g ⁻ ¹ at 0.5 A g ⁻ ¹ and maintained excellent rate capability 
and cycling stability, retaining 88.2 % of its initial capacitance after 10 000 charge – discharge cycles. Kinetic 
analysis indicated that K/F doping strengthened diffusion-controlled charge storage without shifting the 
mechanism toward purely capacitive behavior. The results demonstrate that dual K/F modification effectively 
tailors the pyrolysis-derived carbon framework and surface chemistry, offering valuable insights into the design 
of biomass-derived carbons for advanced electrochemical energy storage applications.
1. Introduction
The rapid growth of portable electronics, electric vehicles, and 
renewable energy technologies has intensified the demand for advanced 
energy storage systems that can deliver high power density, long cycle 
life, and excellent operational safety. Among various energy storage 
devices, electrochemical supercapacitors have attracted considerable 
attention owing to their fast charge – discharge capability, high power 
output, and superior cycling stability compared to conventional batte -
ries. However, their relatively low energy density remains a critical 
challenge, motivating extensive research into novel electrode materials 
with optimized structure and surface chemistry [1 – 5] . Porous carbon 
materials are widely regarded as the most promising electrode 
candidates for supercapacitors due to their large specific surface area, 
tunable pore structure, high electrical conductivity, and chemical sta -
bility [6,7] . In particular, biomass-derived activated carbons have 
emerged as sustainable and cost-effective alternatives to conventional 
carbon materials, offering abundant resources and environmentally 
benign processing routes. Agricultural wastes such as nut shells, fruit 
peels, and lignocellulosic residues have been successfully converted into 
high-performance activated carbons through chemical activation stra -
tegies [8 – 13] .
Among various activation methods, potassium hydroxide (KOH) 
activation is especially effective in generating highly porous carbon 
frameworks with well-developed microporosity and large surface areas. 
The activation process involves redox reactions between carbon and

potassium species, leading to pore formation, lattice expansion, and 
partial graphitization. These structural features are highly favorable for 
electric double-layer capacitance by providing abundant ion-accessible 
surfaces [14] . Nevertheless, purely microporous carbons often suffer 
from ion transport limitations at high current densities, highlighting the 
need for further structural and chemical optimization. Heteroatom 
doping has proven to be an effective strategy to enhance the electro -
chemical performance of carbon-based electrodes. The incorporation of 
heteroatoms such as N, S, P, F, or alkali metals can modify the electronic 
structure, increase defect density, improve surface wettability, and 
introduce additional electroactive sites. These effects collectively 
contribute to enhanced charge transfer kinetics, reduced internal resis -
tance, and improved rate capability [4,11,15–18] . Recent advances in 
heteroatom doping have demonstrated that simultaneous incorporation 
of multiple dopants into carbon matrices can synergistically enhance 
supercapacitor performance by improving electronic conductivity, 
defect density, surface wettability, and ion transport. Multi-heteroatom 
co-doped carbons (e.g., N/O, N/S, B/N/O/P systems) have been widely 
studied and shown to yield higher specific capacitance and cycling 
stability than single doped analogs due to increased active sites and 
modulated charge distribution within the carbon framework [19,20]
Within this broader context, alkali metal–halogen dual doping repre -
sents a promising yet relatively underexplored class of dopant combi -
nations. Although specific reports on potassium–fluorine (K/F) co-doped 
carbons for supercapacitors are limited, fluorine doping itself has been 
shown to significantly enhance surface polarity and wettability in car -
bon materials, leading to improved electrolyte interaction and charge 
storage behavior [19] . Fluorine incorporation into carbon hosts creates 
polar C–F bonds that not only introduce additional electrochemically 
active sites but also modify local electronic structures, facilitating 
enhanced ion adsorption and transport. Likewise, alkali metal dopants 
such as potassium have been recognized for their ability to alter elec -
tronic density and defect characteristics in carbon frameworks, which 
can contribute to improved conductivity and capacitive kinetics [21] . 
These multi-dopant strategies, including emerging alkali-halogen sys -
tems such as K/F, are attracting increasing research interest for devel -
oping high-performance carbon electrodes with balanced energy and 
power characteristics for next-generation supercapacitors. In particular, 
potassium doping has been reported to promote pore widening and 
improve electrical conductivity, while fluorine doping can induce strong 
electronegativity effects, surface polarization, and enhanced electrolyte 
affinity [22–24] . Despite growing interest in heteroatom-doped carbons, 
studies exploring the synergistic effects of dual K/F doping in 
biomass-derived activated carbons remain limited. The simultaneous 
incorporation of potassium and fluorine is expected to not only tailor 
pore architecture but also stabilize the electrode–electrolyte interface 
and promote efficient ion diffusion across the carbon framework. Such 
modifications are particularly beneficial for aqueous supercapacitor 
systems, where ion transport kinetics and interfacial resistance critically 
influence performance [25,26] . Among various biomass precursors, 
pistachio shells — the rigid, lignified outer layer of the pistachio nut — 
represent an abundant agricultural waste with substantial cellulose and 
lignin content, making them suitable for conversion into porous carbon 
materials. Pistachio shells have been explored not only for carbon 
electrode fabrication but also for adsorption and composite material 
applications, highlighting their versatility as a sustainable material 
source. Their relatively high carbon content and structural robustness 
make them particularly attractive for conversion into activated carbons 
with desirable textural properties. Several studies have demonstrated 
the feasibility of using pistachio shell biomass to produce activated 
carbon with high surface area and well-developed pore structures. For 
example, activated carbons prepared from pistachio shells via 
microwave-assisted KOH activation exhibited BET surface areas 
exceeding 700 m² g⁻¹ with significant total pore volumes, which were 
leveraged for adsorptive applications and confirm the suitability of this 
waste biomass for generating highly porous materials [27] . In addition 
to adsorption applications, pistachio shell-derived carbons have been 
investigated for hydrogen storage, where activated porous carbons 
showed appreciable hydrogen uptake capacities, confirming the broad 
utility of pistachio shell carbons beyond conventional adsorbents [28] . 
The use of pistachio shell derived carbon in electrochemical energy 
storage has also been explored. A recent student project reported that 
KOH-activated pistachio shell carbon exhibited high specific capaci -
tance and energy density values in supercapacitor tests, establishing a 
foundation for further optimization of activation conditions and elec -
trode design [29] . Beyond simple activated carbon, pistachio shell 
biomass has also been used to produce advanced carbon materials for 
lithium–sulfur batteries, demonstrating that pistachio shell–derived 
carbons can serve as efficient conductive matrices in diverse energy 
storage chemistries [30] . In addition to energy storage, pistachio shell 
waste has been investigated for other high-value applications. For 
example, biochar derived from pistachio shells has been used as a 
feedstock for reinforcing conductive polymer composites and as an 
adsorbent for pollutant removal, illustrating the broad potential of this 
biomass beyond energy systems [31] . The intrinsic porosity and me -
chanical strength of pistachio shell carbon make it a promising candi -
date for composite electrode materials in flexible or multifunctional 
energy devices as well. Despite these advances, there remains a need to 
tailor pistachio shell–derived carbons for optimized electrochemical 
performance in supercapacitors, particularly through dual modification 
strategies that enhance both pore architecture and surface chemistry. 
Chemical activation using KOH is widely recognized for producing 
carbons with abundant micropores and high specific surface areas, but 
micropore-dominated structures may limit ion transport at high char -
ge–discharge rates. Despite significant progress in dual heteroatom 
doping strategies for carbon-based supercapacitor electrodes, most re -
ported systems rely on combinations of nonmetallic elements such as 
N/O, N/S, or B/N, which primarily enhance pseudocapacitance and 
surface reactivity through similar electronegativity-driven mechanisms. 
In contrast, dual-doping systems composed of electropositive metals and 
highly electronegative nonmetals remain far less explored, particularly 
in the context of porous carbon electrodes. K/F dual doping is particu -
larly promising because it introduces a fundamentally different 
charge-regulation mechanism compared to conventional dual-doping 
systems. Potassium, as an alkali metal with strong electron-donating 
ability, can increase local electron density, promote charge delocaliza -
tion, and reduce electronic resistance within the carbon framework. 
Conversely, fluorine, owing to its extremely high electronegativity, in -
duces strong surface polarization through C–F bonding, thereby 
enhancing wettability and electrolyte affinity. The coexistence of these 
two dopants enables simultaneous tuning of bulk electronic conductivity 
and interfacial ion accessibility, a balance that is difficult to achieve 
using conventional nonmetal–nonmetal doping combinations. Further -
more, K/F dual doping has the potential to influence pore evolution and 
defect formation during carbonization and activation processes, leading 
to hierarchical pore architectures that are particularly favorable for 
diffusion-controlled charge storage. However, systematic investigations 
into K/F co-doped porous carbons remain scarce, and the synergistic 
effects of alkali metal–halogen interactions on pore structure, electronic 
modulation, and electrochemical performance have not yet been fully 
elucidated. This lack of mechanistic understanding constitutes a clear 
research gap and motivates the present study.
Therefore, heteroatom doping strategies — including the introduc -
tion of potassium and fluorine — have emerged as effective approaches 
to increase surface reactivity, electrical conductivity, and ion accessi -
bility by inducing defects and modifying surface polarity.
In this work, porous activated carbon derived from pistachio shell 
biomass (PSAC) was synthesized via KOH activation and subsequently 
modified through K/F doping to obtain a structurally and chemically 
optimized electrode material. Comprehensive structural and surface 
characterizations—including XRD, Raman spectroscopy, FTIR, SEM, 
TEM, BET, EDS, and XPS—were employed to elucidate the effects of K/F

2. Materials and methods
2.1. Synthesis of PSAC and K/F-Doped PSAC
Pistachio shells were collected from a local market in Siirt, Turkey, 
and used as the biomass precursor. The raw shells were thoroughly 
washed with distilled water to remove surface impurities and dried at 
ambient conditions. After drying, the cleaned shells were ground into a 
fine powder using a laboratory grinder. Chemical activation was carried 
out by impregnating the pistachio shell powder with potassium hy -
droxide (KOH) at a mass ratio of 1:1 (biomass:KOH). The impregnation 
mixture was maintained under static conditions for 24 h to ensure ho -
mogeneous penetration of the activating agent. The impregnated sample 
was subsequently subjected to pyrolysis at 600 
◦
C for 2 h under a ni -
trogen atmosphere to prevent oxidation. After cooling to room tem -
perature, the obtained carbonized product was treated with 1 M HCl 
solution to remove residual inorganic species and potassium compounds 
formed during activation. The sample was then washed repeatedly with 
deionized water until a neutral pH was reached, followed by drying in a 
convection oven at 75 
◦
C. The resulting activated carbon was denoted as 
PSAC.
K/F-doped PSAC was prepared via a hydrothermal modification 
process. PSAC was mixed with potassium fluoride (KF) at a mass ratio of 
1:0.5, and an appropriate amount of urea was added as a nitrogen- 
containing auxiliary reagent. The mixture was dispersed in distilled 
water and stirred on a magnetic stirrer for 30 min to obtain a homoge -
neous suspension. The suspension was then transferred to a Teflon-lined 
stainless-steel autoclave and subjected to hydrothermal treatment at 150 
◦
C for 4 h.
After completion of the hydrothermal reaction, the product was 
cooled naturally to room temperature, thoroughly washed several times 
with deionized water to remove residual salts and unreacted species, and 
dried in an oven at 75 
◦
C. The final product was labeled as K/F-doped 
PSAC.
2.2. Characterization methods
The crystalline structure of the prepared samples was analyzed using 
X-ray diffraction (XRD, PANalytical Empyrean) with a Cu K α radiation 
source ( λ = 1.5406 Å). Diffraction patterns were recorded over a 2 θ 
range of 10 – 90
◦
at room temperature to evaluate the degree of graphi -
tization and structural ordering of the carbon materials. Raman spec -
troscopy was employed to investigate the defect structure and graphitic 
nature of the samples. Raman spectra were collected using a laser 
excitation wavelength of 532 nm over the range of 800 – 2000 cm ⁻ ¹ . The 
intensity ratio of the D band to the G band (ID/IG) was used to assess the

K/F doping. Fourier transform infrared (FTIR, Bruker VERTEX 70 v) 
spectroscopy was used to identify surface functional groups present on 
the carbon materials. FTIR spectra were recorded in the range of 
400 – 4000 cm ⁻ ¹ using the ATR method, providing insight into oxygen- 
and heteroatom-containing surface functionalities. The surface 
morphology and microstructural features of the samples were examined 
using scanning electron microscopy (SEM, Zeiss Sigma 300) equipped 
with an energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) detector for 
elemental analysis. SEM images were obtained at various magnifications 
to observe surface roughness, pore distribution, and morphological 
changes induced by K/F modification. Transmission electron micro -
scopy (TEM, Hitachi HighTech HT7700) was performed to further 
investigate the internal structure and nanoscale morphology of the 
carbon materials. TEM images were collected to evaluate the layered 
structure, particle dispersion, and distribution of nanosized features 
within the carbon matrix. Textural properties, including specific surface 
area, pore volume, and pore size distribution, were determined by ni -
trogen adsorption – desorption measurements conducted at  196 
◦
C 
(Quantochrome Autosorp). Prior to analysis, the samples were degassed 
under vacuum at elevated temperature to remove adsorbed species. The 
specific surface area was calculated using the Brunauer – Emmett – Teller 
(BET) method, while pore size distribution was obtained using the 
Barrett – Joyner – Halenda (BJH) model. X-ray photoelectron spectros -
copy (XPS, Specs-Flex) was employed to analyze the surface elemental 
composition and chemical states of the samples. XPS measurements 
were performed using Al K α radiation as the excitation source. Survey 
scans were used to quantify elemental composition, while high- 
resolution spectra of C 1 s, O 1 s, K 2p, and F 1 s were recorded to 
elucidate surface bonding configurations and confirm successful K/F 
incorporation.
2.3. Electrochemical measurements
All electrochemical experiments were carried out on a Metrohm 
Autolab PGSTAT128N system operated through Nova 2.1.6 software. A 
conventional three-electrode arrangement was used, incorporating a 
glassy carbon electrode (GCE) modified with the prepared carbon ma -
terials as the working electrode, Ag/AgCl as the reference, and a plat -
inum wire serving as the counter electrode. To fabricate the active layer, 
18 mg of PSAC or K/F-doped PSAC powders were dispersed together 
with 2 mg of PVDF binder in 2 mL of N,N-dimethylacetamide. The 
mixture was sonicated for four hours to obtain a uniform slurry. Sub -
sequently, 5 μ L of this dispersion was carefully applied onto a freshly 
polished GCE surface, and the coated electrode was dried in two steps 
under infrared heating to remove residual solvent and promote strong 
attachment of the film. The resulting electrodes are referred to as PSAC- 
GCE and K/F doped PSAC-GCE, with the loading estimated from the 
known suspension concentration and the applied drop volume. Elec -
trochemical characterization was conducted in 1 M H ₂ SO ₄ solution. 
Cyclic voltammetry (CV) was recorded at scan rates between 5 and 
50 mV/s to evaluate the charge-storage profile. Galvanostatic char -
ge – discharge (GCD) measurements were conducted to evaluate capaci -
tive performance under constant-current conditions. For the three- 
electrode configuration, tests were performed within a potential win -
dow of 0 – 0.5 V, while the two-electrode (symmetric) device was tested 
from 0 to 0.8 V. Both systems were examined at current densities 
ranging from 0.5 to 2.0 A/g. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy 
(EIS), collected in the 100 kHz - 0.1 Hz frequency domain using a 10 mV 
perturbation, provided insight into ion transport and interfacial resis -
tance. Together, these measurements enabled a detailed assessment of 
the kinetics, capacitive contributions, and overall electrochemical 
behavior of the synthesized carbon electrodes.
3. Results and discussion
3.1. Analytical methods
The XRD patterns of PSAC and the K/F-doped PSAC both display the 
typical broad diffraction features associated with amorphous, turbos -
tratic carbon, rather than sharp crystalline peaks ( Fig. 1 a). Specifically, 
two diffuse bands centered around 2 θ ≈ 22 – 26
◦
and 42 – 45
◦
are 
observed, corresponding to the (002) and (100) reflections of disordered 
carbon networks. Such broad, low-intensity peaks are widely reported 
for chemically activated biomass-derived carbons, where KOH activa -
tion disrupts graphitic stacking and increases porosity (see literature on 
KOH activated carbon XRD patterns [32] . The absence of sharp crys -
talline carbon peaks indicates limited long-range graphitic order, 
consistent with previous studies showing that KOH activation produces 
mostly amorphous carbon structures with enhanced defect densities and 
microporosity beneficial for charge storage in supercapacitors (e.g., 
KOH-activated AC showing broad peaks at ~24
◦
and ~44
◦
in XRD) [33] . 
Such disordered carbon domains increase ion accessibility and support 
electric double layer formation, essential for high specific capacitance in 
supercapacitor applications. When comparing the PSAC and K/F-doped 
PSAC, subtle differences in peak intensity and position can be linked to 
the incorporation of potassium and fluorine. The slight increase in (002) 
intensity and minor shift toward lower angles suggest modified inter -
layer spacing or increased defect concentration due to dopant incorpo -
ration. A quantitative analysis of the XRD patterns reveals a discernible 
shift in the (002) diffraction peak upon K/F dual doping. For pristine 
PSAC, the (002) reflection is located at 2 θ ≈ 26.1
◦
, corresponding to an 
interlayer spacing (d ₀₀₂ ) of 0.341 nm, calculated using Bragg ’ s law (d =
λ /2sin θ ). After K/F doping, the (002) peak shifts to a lower angle of 2 θ 
≈ 25.6
◦
, indicating an increased interlayer spacing of 0.347 nm. This 
expansion of the interlayer distance suggests a partial disruption of 
graphitic layer stacking induced by heteroatom incorporation and defect 
formation. In particular, the introduction of potassium species and 
fluorine-related functional groups can weaken π – π interactions between 
adjacent graphene layers, leading to lattice distortion and expanded 
layer separation. Such interlayer expansion is favorable for electro -
chemical charge storage, as it facilitates electrolyte ion intercalation and 
diffusion between carbon layers, thereby enhancing ion transport ki -
netics and diffusion-controlled capacitance contributions. While no 
distinct crystalline phases corresponding to potassium or fluorine com -
pounds appear in the XRD, this behavior is consistent with literature on 
heteroatom and metal doping in carbon matrices, where dopants are 
atomically dispersed or bonded to the carbon structure without forming 
separate crystalline phases [19,34] . The XRD analysis confirms that both 
PSAC and K/F-doped PSAC possess highly disordered carbon structures 
with short-range graphitic domains. The lack of sharp crystalline peaks, 
combined with broad turbostratic features, reflects the structural 
changes induced by KOH activation and heteroatom doping. Such 
structural characteristics — disorder, high defect density, and increased 
active surface — are widely accepted as favorable for supercapacitor 
electrode performance, owing to improved electrolyte interaction and 
charge storage dynamics. The FTIR spectra of PSAC and K/F-doped 
PSAC provide important information regarding the surface functional 
groups and chemical modifications induced by KOH activation and 
subsequent K/F doping( Fig. 1 b), supporting the structural observations 
obtained from XRD analysis. Both samples exhibit a broad absorption 
band in the region of 3200 – 3600 cm ⁻ ¹ , which is typically assigned to the 
stretching vibrations of hydroxyl ( – OH) groups originating from 
surface-adsorbed moisture, phenolic groups, and residual 
oxygen-containing functionalities. Such – OH groups are commonly re -
ported in biomass-derived activated carbons and are known to enhance 
electrolyte wettability and ion diffusion in supercapacitor electrodes 
[14]
Weak bands observed around 2900 – 2850 cm ⁻ ¹ correspond to the 
stretching vibrations of aliphatic C – H bonds. The low intensity of these

more pronounced feature observed for PSAC suggests a relatively higher

PSAC, changes in intensity and band shape in this region indicate al -

involve partial reduction of oxygen groups or electronic interactions 
between heteroatoms and the carbon lattice. Similar FTIR behavior has 
been reported for heteroatom-modified activated carbons used in elec -
trochemical energy storage [36]
Bands appearing in the 1400 – 1200 cm ⁻ ¹ range are generally 
assigned to C – O stretching vibrations of phenolic, alcoholic, and ether 
groups. The modification of these bands in the K/F-doped PSAC spec -
trum suggests chemical interactions between potassium/fluorine species 
and surface oxygen functionalities. Furthermore, absorption features 
below 1100 cm ⁻ ¹ may be associated with C – O – C vibrations and, in 
doped samples, possible C – F bonding.
The FTIR analysis confirms that both PSAC and K/F-doped PSAC 
possess abundant oxygen-based surface functional groups, while K/F 
doping leads to noticeable modifications in surface chemistry. These 
findings are fully consistent with the XRD results, which indicate pre -
dominantly amorphous carbon structures without crystalline impurity 
phases. The combination of structural disorder and tailored surface 
functionality is expected to enhance ion adsorption, interfacial charge 
transfer, and pseudocapacitive contributions, thereby improving the 
electrochemical performance of these materials when employed as 
supercapacitor electrodes. The Raman spectra of PSAC and K/F-doped 
PSAC exhibit two prominent bands located at approximately 
1352 cm ⁻ ¹ and 1570 – 1580 cm ⁻ ¹ , corresponding to the D and G bands of 
carbon materials, respectively ( Fig. 1 c). The D band originates from the 
breathing modes of sp² carbon rings that become Raman-active in the 
presence of structural defects, edges, and disorder, whereas the G band is 
associated with the in-plane stretching vibration of sp²-hybridized car -
bon atoms in graphitic domains. These bands are widely used to eval -
uate the degree of structural disorder and graphitization in activated 
carbons and carbon-based electrode materials [37,38] . Based on the 
provided intensity (or peak area) values, the ID/IG ratio of PSAC was 
calculated to be approximately 0.32. This relatively low ID/IG value 
suggests that although PSAC is predominantly amorphous, it still con -
tains a certain proportion of ordered sp² carbon domains. Such behavior 
is typical for KOH-activated biomass-derived carbons, where chemical 
activation generates a porous and defect-containing structure while 
partially preserving short-range graphitic ordering. Similar ID/IG values 
have been reported for activated carbons derived from agricultural 
waste and used as supercapacitor electrodes, where a balance between 
conductivity and surface disorder is required for efficient electric 
double-layer capacitance [39,40] . In contrast, the K/F-doped PSAC 
shows a significantly increased ID/IG ratio of approximately 0.93, 
indicating a substantial rise in defect density and structural disorder 
after doping. The incorporation of potassium and fluorine atoms into the 
carbon framework introduces lattice distortions, additional edge sites, 
and heteroatom-related defects, which enhance the D-band contribution 
relative to the G band. The slight downshift of the G band from 
1579 cm ⁻ ¹ in PSAC to 1574 cm ⁻ ¹ in the K/F-doped sample further re -
flects changes in the electronic environment of sp² carbon domains, 
which are commonly attributed to charge transfer effects and hetero -
atom – carbon interactions. Similar G-band shifts and increases in ID/IG 
ratios have been extensively reported for heteroatom-doped porous 
carbons, including fluorine- and alkali-metal-modified carbons, used in 
electrochemical energy storage systems [39] . The Raman intensity ratio

Consistently, Raman spectra show an increased ID/IG ratio relative to

which balances enhanced electrical conductivity with abundant defect

The nitrogen adsorption – desorption isotherms(a) and pore size dis -

of PSAC and K/F-doped PSAC ( Fig. 2 ) and their evolution after chemical 
modification. As shown by the adsorption isotherms, both samples 
exhibit a sharp uptake at low relative pressures (p/p ⁰ < 0.1), indicating 
the presence of abundant micropores generated during KOH activation. 
This behavior is characteristic of chemically activated biomass-derived 
carbons and is commonly associated with the development of a high 
specific surface area suitable for electric double-layer charge storage 
[14] . For pristine PSAC, the adsorption capacity increases steadily with 
relative pressure and shows a noticeable rise near p/p ⁰ ≈ 0.9 – 1.0, which 
suggests the coexistence of micropores and a fraction of mesopores or 
macropores. This hierarchical pore structure is further confirmed by the 
pore size distribution curve, where a dominant contribution is observed 
in the micropore region below 2 nm, together with a minor distribution 
extending into the mesoporous range. The calculated BET surface area of 
PSAC is relatively high at 483 m² g ⁻ ¹ , with an average pore radius of 
1.65 nm, indicating that micropores are the main contributors to the 
overall surface area. Such micropore-dominated carbons are known to 
provide a large number of active sites for ion adsorption, which is 
favorable for achieving high capacitance in supercapacitors [40] . In 
comparison, the K/F-doped PSAC exhibits a lower overall nitrogen up -
take across the entire pressure range, resulting in a reduced BET surface

distribution, which shows a shift toward larger pore widths and a sig -
nificant increase in the average pore radius to 3.94 nm. The decrease in 
surface area accompanied by pore widening suggests that the incorpo -
ration of potassium and fluorine species leads to partial pore enlarge -
ment or merging of micropores into mesopores during the doping 
process. Similar trends have been reported in heteroatom- or 
alkali-metal-modified activated carbons, where dopant-induced etching 
and framework rearrangement result in reduced surface area but 
improved pore accessibility [8] . From an electrochemical standpoint, 
although a high BET surface area is beneficial, the presence of accessible 
mesopores plays a crucial role in facilitating rapid ion transport, espe -
cially at high charge – discharge rates. Mesopores act as ion-buffering 
reservoirs that shorten diffusion pathways toward micropores, thereby 
improving rate capability and cycling stability in supercapacitors. 
Therefore, the textural evolution observed for K/F-doped PSAC, namely 
the transition from a predominantly microporous structure to a more 
mesopore-rich architecture, is expected to enhance electrolyte pene -
tration and ion mobility despite the reduction in surface area. This 
structure – property relationship has been widely discussed in the liter -
ature on porous carbon electrodes for supercapacitors [36] . The nitro -
gen adsorption – desorption and pore size distribution analyses indicate 
that PSAC possesses a high surface area with dominant microporosity, 
while K/F doping induces pore widening and increases the average pore 
size at the expense of total surface area. When considered together with 
the XRD, FTIR, and Raman results, these findings suggest that 
K/F-doped PSAC offers a more balanced pore structure combining suf -
ficient surface area with improved ion transport pathways, making it a 
promising electrode material for high-performance supercapacitor ap -
plications.( Fig. 3 )
The SEM micrographs of PSAC(a, b , c) reveal a porous and hetero -
geneous surface morphology characterized by irregularly shaped pores 
and a non-uniform texture. The presence of well-developed pores with 
varying sizes confirms the effectiveness of KOH activation in creating a 
highly porous carbon framework from pistachio shell biomass. This 
heterogeneous and porous morphology is typical of chemically activated 
carbons derived from lignocellulosic precursors and is beneficial for 
electrochemical applications, as it provides a large accessible surface 
area for electrolyte ion adsorption and charge storage.
In comparison, the SEM images of the K/F-doped PSAC exhibit a 
noticeably rougher and more heterogeneous surface morphology. The 
carbon matrix appears more irregular, with a higher degree of surface 
corrugation and disrupted pore walls, indicating that the doping process 
induces additional structural modifications. Moreover, the presence of a 
larger number of bright regions in the SEM images suggests the incor -
poration or redistribution of potassium- and fluorine-containing species 
on the carbon surface, which can lead to localized variations in electrical 
conductivity or electron density. Similar observations have been re -
ported in doped carbon materials, where brighter contrasts in SEM im -
ages are often associated with regions enriched in heteroatoms or 
inorganic residues. The comparison of SEM morphologies indicates that 
while PSAC possesses a porous and heterogeneous structure, K/F doping 
further increases surface roughness and heterogeneity. These morpho -
logical changes are expected to enhance the electrochemical perfor -
mance of the doped material by increasing surface reactivity, improving 
electrolyte wettability, and providing additional active sites for ion 
adsorption, thereby supporting its suitability as a supercapacitor elec -
trode material. The EDS analysis provides clear evidence of the 
elemental composition and successful chemical modification of PSAC 
and K/F-doped PSAC. For pristine PSAC, the spectrum indicates that 
carbon is the dominant element, accounting for 78.96 %, while oxygen 
constitutes 21.04 % of the total composition. This relatively high oxygen 
content is typical for biomass-derived activated carbons produced via 
KOH activation and can be attributed to the presence of surface oxygen- 
containing functional groups such as hydroxyl, carbonyl, and carboxyl 
species. These oxygen functionalities are known to enhance surface 
polarity and electrolyte wettability, which are advantageous for elec -
trochemical charge storage. In contrast, the EDS results for the K/F- 
doped PSAC show a noticeable change in elemental composition. The 
carbon content decreases to 70.10 %, accompanied by a reduction in 
oxygen content to 17.04 %, while potassium and fluorine are clearly 
detected at 7.9 % and 1.03 %, respectively. The presence of potassium

The TEM images of PSAC reveal a heterogeneous microstructure in 
which nanosized particles are irregularly distributed both on the carbon 
layers and in the regions outside the layered domains( Fig. 4 a, b). These 
randomly dispersed nanoparticles and the uneven contrast observed 
across the layers indicate a non-uniform carbon framework, which is 
typical for biomass-derived activated carbons produced by chemical 
activation. The coexistence of layered carbon regions and disordered 
nanoscale features suggests the presence of locally stacked graphene- 
like sheets together with amorphous carbon domains, reflecting the 
inherently heterogeneous nature of PSAC. In contrast, the TEM micro -
graphs of K/F-doped PSAC show a noticeably more homogeneous 
appearance of the carbon layer surfaces( Fig. 4 c, d). The layered struc -
ture appears more continuous and uniform, while nanosized particles 
are predominantly accumulated along the edges of the carbon layers 
rather than being randomly distributed. This preferential localization of 
nanoparticles at the layer boundaries suggests that K/F doping in -
fluences the redistribution of inorganic or dopant-related species during 
thermal treatment, promoting their migration toward energetically 
favorable edge sites. Such edge-enriched nanoparticle accumulation is 
often associated with enhanced defect density and modified surface 
chemistry at the layer margins. The TEM observations indicate that 
while PSAC exhibits a heterogeneous nanoscale structure with randomly 
distributed particles, K/F doping leads to a more ordered layer surface 
with nanosized particles concentrated at the layer edges. These struc -
tural features are expected to be beneficial for electrochemical appli -
cations, as homogeneous layer surfaces can facilitate electron transport, 
while edge-located nanoparticles and defects provide additional active 
sites for ion adsorption and interfacial charge storage, thereby 
enhancing the performance of K/F-doped PSAC as a supercapacitor 
electrode material.

over the 0 – 800 eV range(a), over the 250 – 310 eV range(b), over the 
600 – 700 eV range(c), confirming the elemental composition at the 
surface. In PSAC, carbon is the dominant element (86.64 at%) with 
oxygen present at 13.07 at%, reflecting oxygen-containing functional 
groups such as C – O, C
–
– O and surface hydroxyls typical of chemically 
activated carbons exposed to air or activation agents. High oxygen 
content in activated carbons has been widely reported to arise from 
various oxygen functionalities that contribute to electrolyte wettability 
and surface polarity, as observed in XPS studies of carbon materials (e.g., 
O1s peaks at ~531 – 533 eV for oxygen species in carbon matrices) [45] . 
After K/F doping ( Fig. 5 d), the survey spectrum shows a clear decrease 
in carbon (70.00 at%) and oxygen (10.94 at%), accompanied by the 
emergence of potassium (17.21 at%), fluorine (0.69 at%) and nitrogen 
(1.16 %). The appearance of K and F signals confirms successful het -
eroatom incorporation into the carbon surface during the doping pro -
cess. Alkali metal elements such as potassium can significantly influence 
XPS binding energy referencing and chemical state interpretation due to 
their reactivity and interaction with surrounding carbon and oxygen 
species [22,46] . High-resolution deconvolution of the C1s/K2p region 
yielded five peaks at 282.76, 283.80, 285.11, 285.47, and 287.21 eV. 
Peaks near ~284 – 285 eV are typically assigned to graphitic C – C/C
–

(sp²) and slight shifts or lower-BE components can reflect conductive 
graphitic environments or screening by adjacent alkali metals, while 
higher-BE components ( ≈ 285.5 – 287.5 eV) are assigned to carbon bound 
to oxygen in forms such as C – O, C
–
– O and O – C
–
– O; this pattern is 
consistent with mixed sp² domains and oxygenated carbon species in 
activated carbons and with reported C1s fits in the literature [22] . 
Because K2p signals lie close to the C1s region and potassium can exist in 
different chemical states (intercalated/ionic or metalaceous surface 
residues), simultaneous fitting of C1s and K2p is appropriate and the 
pronounced K at% indicates that potassium species (for example K ⁺ 
bound to oxygenated sites or K-containing residues) substantially 
modify the surface chemical environment and electronic screening 
observed in the C1s lineshape [22,47,48] . The possible incorporation of 
nitrogen originating from urea used during the K/F-assisted activation 
process was carefully examined by XPS analysis. As revealed by the XPS 
survey spectrum, in addition to C, O, K and F, a distinct N 1 s signal is 
clearly observable, confirming the successful introduction of nitrogen 
species into the carbon framework. Quantitative surface elemental 
analysis shows that the nitrogen content is 1.16 at%, while the total 
detected surface elements account for 98.84 at%, indicating reliable 
compositional analysis. Although the nitrogen content is relatively low, 
this result is fully consistent with the role of urea as an auxiliary 
nitrogen-containing reagent rather than a primary nitrogen precursor. 
During the high-temperature activation process, most 
nitrogen-containing species are thermally decomposed and removed, 
while a small but chemically meaningful fraction remains incorporated 
into the carbon matrix, most likely in the form of pyridinic, pyrrolic, 
and/or graphitic nitrogen species. From a structural and electrochemical 
point of view, even such a low level of nitrogen doping can significantly 
influence the surface chemistry and electronic structure of carbon ma -
terials. The incorporated nitrogen species introduce additional defect 
sites and electron-rich centers, enhance surface polarity and wettability, 
and facilitate electrolyte ion accessibility. More importantly, nitrogen 
dopants are expected to act synergistically with K and F dopants, where 
K and F mainly contribute to pore formation, interlayer expansion and 
strong surface polarization, while nitrogen species improve electronic 
conductivity and interfacial charge transfer characteristics. This syner -
gistic heteroatom co-doping effect is believed to be one of the key factors 
responsible for the improved electrochemical performance of the 
K/F/N-doped PSAC electrode.
XPS signals for potassium typically appear in the K 2p region and can 
indicate the presence of potassium in ionic states (e.g., K – O or K +
intercalated environments) rather than metallic potassium. Potassium 
doping in carbon frameworks is often associated with charge donation to 
the carbon lattice, which can increase electron density near the Fermi 
level and enhance electronic conductivity. While specific reports on K – C 
bonding in carbon electrodes are relatively few, heteroatom-doping re -
views demonstrate that alkali metals incorporated into carbon structures 
can alter electronic properties, create defects, and improve charge- 
transfer pathways. These modifications reduce kinetic barriers and can 
improve ion transport within the carbon matrix, aiding in both capaci -
tive and diffusion-controlled storage [19,49] .
The O1s spectrum ( Fig. 5 e) decomposes into three components at 
530.11, 531.62 and 535.55 eV, which point to multiple oxygen envi -
ronments: lower-BE O1s components (~530 – 531 eV) are commonly 
attributed to more oxidic or carbonyl-like oxygen (e.g., metal-oxide-like 
O or C
–
– O), mid-BE components (~531 – 532 eV) to hydroxyl/ether or 
C – O species [50] , and the higher-BE shoulder ( ≈ 533 – 536 eV) often re -
flects adsorbed water, peroxide-like species or weakly bound organ -
ics/carbonates. The multiplicity and positions of these O1s components 
therefore corroborate the presence of several oxygen functional groups 
whose relative abundances are altered after K/F treatment. For fluorine 
( Fig. 5 f), the F1s peaks at 685.49 and 687.99 eV are within the range 
reported for covalent and semi-ionic C – F bonding (commonly observed 
near ~686 – 688 eV) rather than metal-fluoride species (which typically 
appear at lower BE ~682 eV) [51 – 53] . The presence of two F1s com -
ponents suggests heterogeneous fluorine environments (for example a 
mixture of covalent C – F and more ionic or semi-ionic F – C environments, 
or different local binding geometries at edge vs basal sites), consistent 
with XPS studies of fluorinated carbons and fluorine-modified surfaces. 
Even the relatively small F at% detected by survey XPS can therefore 
indicate chemically meaningful surface fluorination that modifies local 
electronegativity and charge distribution [54 – 56] . In the F 1 s XPS 
spectrum, the peaks consistent with fluorine bound to carbon in C – F 
configurations were observed. Fluorine incorporation in carbon is 
widely recognized to produce both covalent and semi-ionic C – F bonds. 
Semi-ionic C – F bonds, in particular, introduce localized charge polari -
zation due to the high electronegativity of fluorine, which enhances
