chemical activity in carbon electrodes. Studies on fluorine-doped car -
bons confirm that the presence of semi-ionic C – F bonding increases 
surface polarity and electron-accepting character, thereby strengthening 
interaction with electrolyte ions and enhancing kinetic performance in 
energy storage applications [19,57] .
The XPS results indicate that K/F doping converts a mainly C – O 
functionalized PSAC surface into a more complex, heteroatom-rich 
surface chemistry featuring significant potassium incorporation and 
low but chemically diverse fluorine species. These changes are expected 
to influence electronic structure (local charge transfer and screening), 
surface polarity and wettability, and the density and nature of active 
sites available for ion adsorption — factors that help explain the com -
plementary Raman, FTIR and electrochemical behavior observed for the 
doped material. The combined presence of electronegative fluorine and 
electropositive potassium dopants therefore exerts complementary ef -
fects on the carbon host: F-related species increase surface polarity and 
wettability by introducing charged sites, whereas K-related species 
contribute to enhanced electronic conductivity and defect generation. 
Both effects have been shown, in various heteroatom-doped carbon 
systems, to reduce ion diffusion resistance and enhance electrolyte 
accessibility, particularly in hierarchical pore structures. Enhanced 
wettability in doped carbon electrodes is frequently linked to improved 
electrolyte adsorption and faster ion migration, which directly influence 
overall electrochemical performance [58] . Finally, when interpreting 
the absolute binding energies, it is important to consider referencing 
issues and charging effects (C1s referencing, sample conductivity, and 
presence of alkali metals can shift apparent BEs), so differences of a few 
tenths of an eV should be evaluated in the context of charge referencing 
and chemical environment rather than as unique new chemical states 
[59 – 61] .
3.2. Electrochemical aspects' performance
Fig. 6 illustrates the cyclic voltammograms of the PSAC-GCE (A) and 
K/F-doped PSAC-GCE (B) electrodes recorded in 1 M H ₂ SO ₄ within the 
potential range of 0 – 0.5 V, which was determined to be the most stable 
window for capacitive operation. Both electrodes display nearly rect -
angular CV shapes over scan rates of 5 – 50 mV/s, confirming that their 
charge-storage behavior is largely governed by electric double-layer 
capacitance. The preservation of this geometric profile at increasing 
scan rates indicates rapid ion transport and efficient charge propagation 
within the porous carbon structures. A clear distinction between the two 
materials becomes evident when comparing the enclosed voltammetric 
areas: the K/F-doped PSAC-GCE exhibits a markedly larger integrated 
area than the pristine PSAC-GCE, signifying its superior charge-storage 
capability. This enhancement originates from the dual modification 
achieved through K and F incorporation. The K/F doping process is 
known to enlarge pore channels, increase surface oxygenated or 
heteroatom-derived functional groups, and improve the overall con -
ductivity of the carbon matrix. These combined effects lead to a higher 
electrochemically accessible surface area and more active sites available 
for ion accumulation. Consequently, the K/F-doped PSAC electrode 
demonstrates significantly improved capacitive performance, high -
lighting its potential for use in advanced electrochemical energy-storage 
systems.
The specific capacitance (C ₛ ) of the prepared electrodes was deter -
mined from the cyclic voltammetry measurements using Eq. (1) : 
C

where I is the current (A), v is the applied scan rate (mV/s), and m 
represents the mass of the electroactive material (g). Calculations based 
on this relationship revealed a clear improvement in capacitive behavior 
after introducing K/F dopants into the carbon matrix. The unmodified 
PSAC-GCE exhibited specific capacitances of 92, 59, 57, and 42 F/g at 
scan rates of 5, 10, 25, and 50 mV/s, respectively. Under the same 
experimental conditions, the K/F-doped PSAC-GCE delivered markedly 
higher capacitances of 158, 124, 89, and 85 F/g. These values, deter -
mined from the anodic current response at + 0.5 V, indicate an 
enhancement of roughly 1.5 times compared to the pristine material. 
The superior performance of the K/F-doped electrode can be attributed 
to several synergistic effects generated by the doping process: increased 
electronic conductivity within the carbon framework, a higher density 
of electroactive surface sites, improved ion-accessible porosity, and 
possible contributions from surface redox activity associated with het -
eroatom functionalization. Collectively, these improvements result in 
more efficient charge storage [62] . The K/F-doped PSAC material 
demonstrates significant promise for high-performance electrochemical 
energy-storage applications.
The electrochemical behavior of the K/F-doped PSAC electrode was 
evaluated in acidic (1 M H ₂ SO ₄ ), neutral (1 M KCl), and alkaline (1 M 
KOH) aqueous electrolytes in order to clarify the role of electrolyte 
environment on capacitive performance. Cyclic voltammetry measure -
ments were conducted at a scan rate of 25 mV s ⁻ ¹ using a conventional 
three-electrode configuration within a potential window of 0 – 0.5 V, 
which was selected based on preliminary stability tests. In all

without distinct redox peaks, indicating that the charge storage mech -
anism is mainly governed by electric double-layer capacitance (EDLC) 
through rapid and reversible ion adsorption at the electrode – electrolyte 
interface. Such nearly ideal rectangular voltammograms are character -
istic of porous carbon electrodes operating under EDLC-dominated 
behavior [40] . Clear pH-dependent differences are observed among 
the three electrolytes, reflecting the strong influence of ion type, ionic 
mobility, and electrode surface chemistry. In acidic and neutral media, 
the CV profiles maintain well-defined rectangular shapes, suggesting 
efficient ion transport and low internal resistance within the porous 
carbon network. By contrast, the CV curve recorded in alkaline elec -
trolyte shows noticeable distortion, particularly a sharp increase in 
current density above ~0.3 V. This behavior can be attributed to po -
larization effects and the relatively slower diffusion of hydroxide ions, 
which possess a larger hydrated radius and lower mobility compared to 
protons, thereby limiting their access to narrow micropores [63] . 
Among the investigated electrolytes, 1 M H ₂ SO ₄ provides the most 
favorable capacitive response. This superior performance arises from the 
high ionic conductivity of sulfuric acid electrolytes, as well as the 
exceptionally small hydrated radius of protons, which enables deeper 
penetration into microporous carbon structures and promotes faster 
charge accumulation. Proton transport is known to be significantly 
faster than that of larger alkali metal ions, leading to enhanced power 
capability and improved utilization of the internal surface area [36] . 
Similar electrolyte-dependent trends have been widely reported for 
activated carbon-based supercapacitors, where acidic electrolytes 
consistently outperform neutral and alkaline systems in terms of 
capacitance and rate capability [64] . The charge-storage behavior of the 
K/F-doped PSAC electrode originates from a combination of 
surface-controlled capacitive processes and diffusion-influenced con -
tributions associated with ion transport within the porous framework. 
While the absence of pronounced redox peaks confirms 
EDLC-dominated behavior, the deviation from ideal rectangularity at 
higher potentials — especially in alkaline media — suggests that ion 
diffusion resistance and surface heterogeneity also play a role. Such 
mixed capacitive behavior is commonly observed in 
heteroatom-modified porous carbons, where surface chemistry and pore 
architecture jointly govern electrochemical response [1] . To determine 
the dominant mechanism, the relationship between peak current ( i ) and 
scan rate ( ν ) was analyzed using the well-established power-law 
expression ( Eq. 2 ): 
i = a ν

where i and v usual meaning, a is a constant, and b is the kinetic 
parameter calculated from the slope of the log i versus log ν plot. The 
magnitude of b provides useful mechanistic information: values near 
0 – 0.5 indicate diffusion-limited processes, whereas values approaching 
0.5 – 1.0 suggest that surface-driven capacitive effects are predominant. 
Based on this analysis, the PSAC-GCE yielded a b value of 0.69, while the 
K/F-doped PSAC-GCE produced a value of 0.63. Both values fall in the 
intermediate range, confirming that the electrodes store charge through 
a mixed mechanism. Although capacitive behavior accounts for a sig -
nificant fraction of the response, a measurable diffusion-related contri -
bution is also present, reflecting the combined influence of accessible 
porous structure and ion-transport limitations in the carbon materials.
To gain deeper insight into the charge-storage mechanism, the cur -

PSAC-GCE remained lower (12.0 – 30.2 %) than that of the undoped 
electrode. This trend suggests that K/F modification does not shift the 
mechanism toward predominantly capacitive storage; instead, it 
strengthens diffusion-controlled processes. Such behavior is likely 
associated with improved ion transport within the porous framework, 
increased pore accessibility, and the presence of additional 
heteroatom-derived electroactive sites. These mechanistic findings align 
well with the substantial improvements observed in overall capacitance 
and rate capability for the K/F-doped PSAC electrode.
The strengthened diffusion-controlled contribution revealed by 
Dunn ’ s model for the K/F-doped PSAC electrode can be directly corre -
lated with the combined effects of hierarchical pore evolution and 
doping-induced surface chemistry. Nitrogen adsorption – desorption 
analysis demonstrated that K/F modification induces significant pore 
widening, evidenced by the increase in average pore radius from 1.65 to 
3.94 nm, leading to the development of a hierarchical micro -
– mesoporous architecture. While micropores provide abundant sites for 
charge accumulation, the newly generated mesopores act as ion- 
buffering reservoirs that facilitate electrolyte penetration and shorten 
ion diffusion pathways toward the inner microporous domains. This 
hierarchical pore network effectively alleviates diffusion resistance 
under dynamic charging conditions, thereby enhancing diffusion- 
controlled charge storage rather than purely surface-limited capacitive 
processes. In parallel, Raman and XPS analyses confirm that K/F doping 
introduces a high density of structural defects and heteroatom-related 
active sites, including K-associated oxygen functionalities and 
covalent/semi-ionic C – F bonds. These defects disrupt local graphitic 
ordering and generate energetically favorable adsorption sites, which 
promote stronger ion – surface interactions and extend ion residence time 
within the carbon framework. Moreover, the presence of potassium 
species contributes to local electronic screening and improved ionic 
accessibility, while fluorine-induced surface polarization enhances 
electrolyte affinity and ion migration across the pore walls. As a result, 
the charge-storage process becomes increasingly governed by diffusion- 
mediated ion transport within the hierarchical porous network rather 
than instantaneous surface adsorption. Therefore, the enhanced 
diffusion-controlled contribution observed after K/F doping arises from 
the synergistic interplay between mesopore-enriched pore architecture 
and defect-rich surface chemistry, which together facilitate deeper ion 
penetration, sustained diffusion, and efficient utilization of the internal 
carbon structure during electrochemical cycling.
The kinetic analysis indicates that K/F dual doping strengthens 
diffusion-controlled charge storage rather than shifting the mechanism 
toward purely surface-limited capacitive behavior. This enhancement 
originates from the distinct yet complementary roles played by potas -
sium and fluorine in regulating ion transport and interfacial kinetics. 
Potassium contributes primarily by modifying the bulk transport char -
acteristics of the carbon framework. As an electropositive alkali metal, 
potassium species act as electron donors and are preferentially located at 
defect sites, pore edges, or oxygen-coordinated environments. Such 
incorporation can expand interlayer spacing and promote pore widening 
during activation, leading to a more accessible internal pore network. 
The enlarged diffusion pathways and reduced ion-transport resistance 
enable electrolyte ions to penetrate deeper into the carbon matrix, 
thereby enhancing diffusion-controlled charge storage associated with 
ion migration within the porous structure. In contrast, fluorine pre -
dominantly influences interfacial ion dynamics. The high electronega -
tivity of fluorine induces strong surface polarization through C – F 
bonding, increasing surface energy and electrolyte wettability. This

defect-rich regions, facilitating sustained ion diffusion along internal 
surfaces rather than instantaneous adsorption at the outer surface. As a 
result, charge storage increasingly involves diffusion-mediated ion 
transport processes instead of ideal capacitive accumulation.
Fig. 7 shows the GCD curves of the PSAC and K/F-doped PSAC 
electrodes recorded in 1 M H ₂ SO ₄ at different current densities. Both 
materials exhibit nearly symmetric triangular profiles within the 
0.5 – 2.0 A/g range, confirming ideal capacitive behavior and good 
charge – discharge reversibility. The slight deviation from linearity dur -
ing discharge can be attributed to internal resistance (IR) effects, which 
arise from electrode – electrolyte contact resistance, ion transport limi -
tations, and inherent solution resistance. Compared with the pristine 
electrode, the K/F-doped PSAC displays noticeably longer discharge 
times, reflecting improved ion mobility and reduced overall resistance.
The specific capacitance (C ₛ ) was calculated from the GCD curves 
using Eq. 4 : 
C
s
= I × Δ t / m × Δ V                                                                      (4)
where I is the discharge current, Δ t the discharge time, m the mass of 
active material, and Δ V the applied potential window.
Based on galvanostatic charge – discharge measurements, the PSAC 
electrode exhibits specific capacitances of 104, 100, 97, and 66 F g ⁻ ¹ at 
current densities of 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, and 2.0 A g ⁻ ¹ , respectively. Under the 
same operating conditions, the K/F-doped PSAC electrode delivers 
significantly enhanced capacitance values of 188, 138, 136, and 
100 F g ⁻ ¹ , representing an improvement of approximately 1.5 times 
compared to the pristine material. Such a pronounced enhancement is 
consistent with electrochemical trends commonly observed in chemi -
cally modified porous carbons, where surface chemistry and pore 
structure optimization lead to improved charge-storage efficiency [1] . 
With increasing current density, both electrodes show a progressive 
decline in specific capacitance, which can be primarily attributed to 
kinetic limitations associated with ion transport. At high char -
ge – discharge rates, electrolyte ions cannot fully access narrow micro -
pores within the limited time frame, resulting in partial utilization of the 
available surface area and increased diffusion resistance. This phe -
nomenon has been extensively reported for microporous carbon elec -
trodes and is regarded as an intrinsic limitation of high-rate 
supercapacitor operation [66] . Despite this inevitable decrease, the 
K/F-doped PSAC electrode maintains substantially higher capacitance 
retention across all current densities, demonstrating superior rate 
capability relative to PSAC. This behavior can be attributed to multiple 
synergistic factors induced by K/F modification. First, surface chemical 
alteration enhances electrolyte wettability, facilitating more effective 
penetration of ions into the porous network. Improved wettability has 
been identified as a key determinant of high-rate electrochemical per -
formance in biomass-derived and chemically activated carbons [8] . 
Second, the introduction of potassium and fluorine contributes to 
structural reorganization and increased defect density, which can 
improve electrical conductivity by promoting partial graphitic ordering 
and facilitating electron transport through interconnected carbon do -
mains. Similar conductivity enhancements have been reported in 
heteroatom-doped porous carbons, where electronic structure modula -
tion leads to reduced internal resistance and improved power perfor -
mance. Furthermore, K/F doping induces pore widening and the 
formation of a more favorable hierarchical pore structure, combining 
micropores for charge storage with mesopores that serve as 
ion-buffering reservoirs. Such hierarchical architectures are widely 
recognized as critical for achieving both high capacitance and excellent 
rate capability, as they significantly shorten ion diffusion pathways 
under high-current operation [25] . The prolonged discharge times, 
enhanced capacitance retention, and improved rate performance 
observed for the K/F-doped PSAC electrode highlight the effectiveness 
of K/F modification in optimizing both surface chemistry and pore ar -
chitecture. These results demonstrate that K/F-doped PSAC is a highly 
promising electrode material for advanced supercapacitor applications 
requiring high energy density and excellent power capability.
Long-term electrochemical stability is a key requirement for the 
practical deployment of supercapacitor electrode materials. To evaluate 
cycling durability, the K/F-doped PSAC electrode was subjected to 
10000 consecutive galvanostatic charge – discharge cycles at a current 
density of 2.0 A g ⁻ ¹ within a potential window of 0 – 0.5 V (vs. Ag/AgCl). 
After prolonged cycling, the electrode retained 88.2 % of its initial 
specific capacitance, indicating excellent structural and electrochemical 
stability. Comparable levels of capacitance retention have been reported 
for robustly engineered porous carbon electrodes and are generally 
considered indicative of long operational lifetimes in aqueous super -
capacitor systems [67] . Although the K/F-doped PSAC electrode ex -
hibits excellent cycling stability with 88.2 % capacitance retention after 
10,000 charge – discharge cycles, a gradual capacitance decay of 
approximately 12 % is observed. This loss can be attributed to several 
factors commonly associated with long-term electrochemical cycling of 
porous carbon electrodes. First, repeated ion insertion and extraction 
during prolonged cycling can induce partial blockage or collapse of 
ultramicropores, particularly in defect-rich regions, thereby reducing 
the number of accessible active sites for charge storage. Second, the 
gradual restructuring or passivation of surface functional groups, 
including heteroatom-related defect sites, may weaken ion – surface in -
teractions over extended cycling. Additionally, minor increases in

segments.text:
internal resistance caused by electrode/electrolyte interface evolution, 
such as electrolyte decomposition or accumulation of by-products at 
pore entrances, can hinder ion diffusion and contribute to capacitance 
fading. Mechanical stress generated by continuous ion transport within 
the hierarchical porous network may also lead to subtle structural 
degradation, especially at edge sites and defect zones. Despite these 
effects, the relatively small capacitance loss observed demonstrates the 
robust structural integrity and electrochemical stability of the 
K/F-doped PSAC electrode, confirming its suitability for long-term 
supercapacitor applications.
The nearly identical shapes of the first and last GCD curves further 
confirm the highly reversible nature of the charge – discharge process and 
the absence of significant internal resistance buildup during cycling. 
Such behavior suggests that the electrode – electrolyte interface remains 
stable and that ion transport pathways are preserved throughout 
extended operation. Similar observations have been associated with 
stable carbon frameworks that resist pore collapse, surface passivation, 
and active material degradation under repetitive electrochemical stress 
[68] . The high capacitance retention also implies that the porous ar -
chitecture of the K/F-doped PSAC remains largely intact, with no evi -
dence of severe pore blockage or loss of electrochemically active surface 
area. This durability can be attributed to the beneficial effects intro -
duced by K/F modification, including improved electrical conductivity 
and enhanced mechanical integrity of the carbon network. 
Potassium-assisted structural reorganization has been shown to 
strengthen carbon frameworks, while heteroatom incorporation can 
stabilize surface functional groups and suppress undesirable side re -
actions during long-term cycling [69] . Moreover, the presence of 
heteroatom-derived surface functionalities can promote the formation 
of a more stable electrode – electrolyte interface, reducing irreversible 
reactions and mitigating performance decay during repeated char -
ge – discharge processes. Such interfacial stabilization effects have been 
widely reported for doped carbon electrodes operating in aqueous 
electrolytes and are considered crucial for achieving durable super -
capacitor performance [70] . The excellent cycling stability demon -
strated by the K/F-doped PSAC electrode confirms its ability to maintain 
structural integrity and electrochemical functionality over extended 
operation. These results highlight the strong potential of K/F-doped 
PSAC as a durable and reliable carbon-based electrode material for 
long-life, high-efficiency supercapacitor applications.
To contextualize the electrochemical performance of the K/F-doped 
PSAC electrode, its specific capacitance, rate capability, and cycling 
retention are compared with representative biomass-derived carbon 
electrodes reported in the literature ( Table 1 ). Although K-doping or F- 
doping alone in biomass carbons is less commonly studied than N or 
multi-heteroatom co-doping, some works demonstrate that activation/ 
heteroatom strategies involving potassium compounds significantly 
improve porosity, surface area, and EDLC behavior in supercapacitors. 
For example, biomass-derived carbon activated with potassium citrate 
shows enhanced pore development and conductivity, leading to high 
capacitance and good stability (potassium citrate activation approach) 
[71] . Similarly, F co-doping strategies in porous carbon (often with 
other heteroatoms such as N) have been demonstrated to modify surface 
defects and wettability, enhancing ion transport and stability in carbon 
electrodes [72] . Compared to these reported biomass carbon systems, 
the K/F dual-doped PSAC in this work delivers a balanced performance 
in terms of specific capacitance, rate capability, and long-term cycling 
stability, underscoring the synergistic benefits of alkali metal – halogen 
dual doping.
EIS was employed to investigate the interfacial properties and 
charge-transport behavior of the electrodes using a 10 mV AC pertur -
bation. The experimental spectra were fitted with the Melik-Gaykazyan 
equivalent circuit model using Nova 2.1.6 software. The 
Melik – Gaykazyan equivalent circuit was employed to fit the EIS spectra 
because it more accurately represents the electrochemical response of 
highly porous carbon electrodes with hierarchical pore architectures. 
Unlike the classical Randles circuit, which assumes a relatively flat and 
homogeneous electrode – electrolyte interface and is mainly suited for 
faradaic systems with well-defined charge-transfer reactions, the 
Melik – Gaykazyan model explicitly accounts for distributed ionic trans -
port and non-ideal capacitive behavior commonly observed in porous 
carbon materials. In particular, the inclusion of constant phase elements 
(CPEs) and multiple resistive components in the Melik – Gaykazyan cir -
cuit allows for differentiation between bulk electrolyte resistance, pore 
resistance, and interfacial charge-storage processes occurring at 
different length scales within the porous network. This is especially 
relevant for the K/F-doped PSAC electrode, which exhibits a hierarchical 
micro – mesoporous structure and significant surface heterogeneity 
induced by heteroatom doping. Therefore, the Melik – Gaykazyan 
equivalent circuit provides a more physically meaningful representation 
of ion transport, pore diffusion, and non-ideal capacitive responses in 
the present system, enabling reliable extraction of parameters related to 
internal resistance and diffusion-controlled processes in porous carbon 
electrodes.
As illustrated in Fig. 3 , both the Nyquist plots and the extracted 
fitting parameters reveal pronounced changes in impedance character -
istics following K/F modification of the PSAC electrode. For the pristine 
PSAC-GCE, the charge-transfer resistance (Rct) was calculated to be 44.8 
Ω , indicating moderate electron-transfer kinetics at the electro -
de – electrolyte interface. After K/F doping, Rct decreased sharply to 4.93 
Ω , corresponding to an approximate 92 % reduction. Such a significant 
decrease reflects substantially accelerated interfacial charge transfer, 
which can be attributed to enhanced electrical conductivity and the 
introduction of additional electroactive sites induced by potassium and 
fluorine incorporation. Similar dramatic reductions in Rct have been 
reported for chemically modified porous carbons, where heteroatom

resistance (Rs) decreases markedly from 34.1 Ω for PSAC-GCE to 5.04 Ω 
for the K/F-doped electrode, indicating improved electrolyte accessi -
bility and more effective electrical contact between the electrode surface 
and the electrolyte. Lower Rs values are commonly associated with 
improved wettability and reduced interfacial resistance, both of which 
are critical for achieving high-rate performance in aqueous super -
capacitor systems [75] . The constant phase element (CPE), which ac -
counts for non-ideal capacitive behavior arising from surface roughness 
and heterogeneity, decreases from 209 to 98.2 μ Mho ⋅ s ⁿ after K/F doping. 
This reduction suggests a modification of surface morphology and a 
more uniform charge-distribution environment at the electrode inter -
face. Such CPE evolution has been widely linked to changes in pore

together, the EIS results demonstrate that K/F doping significantly im -

accelerating charge-transfer kinetics, and facilitating ion diffusion. 
These impedance characteristics are essential for high-power operation 
and long-term reliability, confirming that K/F-modified PSAC provides a 
highly favorable electrode architecture for advanced supercapacitor

discharge time. At a current density of 0.5 A/g, the SSC achieved an 
energy density of 4.3 Wh/kg and a power density of 199 W/kg. Even at 
2.0 A/g, the device preserved an energy density of 3.1 Wh/kg while 
delivering 320 W/kg, highlighting its excellent rate capability. This 
superior behavior is attributed to the optimized pore structure and 
enhanced ion accessibility imparted by K/F modification. Cycling sta -
bility ( Fig. 9 D) demonstrated that the device retained 86.2 % of its 
initial capacitance after 10000 continuous cycles at 2.0 A/g, indicating 
robust electrochemical durability. The remarkable retention can be 
linked to the structural reinforcement, improved conductivity, and sta -
bilized electrode – electrolyte interface provided by K/F doping. It should 
be noted that the cycling stability values reported for the K/F-doped 
PSAC electrode depend on the electrochemical configuration 
employed. The capacitance retention of 88.2 % after 10,000 cycles re -
fers to measurements conducted in a three-electrode system, where the 
intrinsic stability of the electrode material is evaluated under idealized 
conditions. In contrast, the slightly lower retention of 86.2 % observed 
in the symmetric two-electrode device reflects the performance of a 
practical full-cell configuration, in which additional factors such as in -
ternal resistance, electrode – electrode interactions, and electrolyte po -
larization contribute to enhanced performance decay. Such differences 
between three-electrode and symmetric device measurements are 
commonly reported in supercapacitor studies and do not indicate 
inconsistency in the electrochemical behavior of the K/F-doped PSAC 
material. Overall, the combination of favorable energy – power charac -
teristics, reliable rate performance, and long-term cycling stability po -
sitions the K/F-doped PSAC-based symmetric device as a strong 
candidate for next-generation, high-durability energy storage systems.
4. Conclusions
In this work, pistachio shell biomass was successfully converted into 
a porous activated carbon through controlled pyrolysis and KOH 
chemical activation, followed by K/F modification to tailor its structural 
and surface properties. Comprehensive characterization revealed that 
K/F doping significantly altered the carbon framework by inducing 
partial graphitization, increasing defect density, and modifying surface 
functional groups, while simultaneously promoting pore widening and 
the development of a hierarchical pore structure. Although a moderate 
decrease in BET surface area was observed after K/F modification, the 
substantial increase in average pore size facilitated improved electrolyte 
accessibility and ion transport. Electrochemical analyses demonstrated 
that K/F-doped PSAC exhibited markedly enhanced charge-transfer ki -
netics, lower interfacial and solution resistances, and improved ion 
diffusion compared to pristine PSAC. These features resulted in signifi -
cantly higher specific capacitance, superior rate capability, and excel -
lent long-term cycling stability, with 88.2 % capacitance retention after 
10 000 charge – discharge cycles. Kinetic analysis confirmed that K/F 
modification strengthens diffusion-controlled charge storage without 
shifting the mechanism toward purely surface-controlled capacitive 
behavior. The results highlight the effectiveness of dual K/F modifica -
tion in optimizing both the pyrolysis-derived carbon structure and sur -
face chemistry. This study demonstrates that pistachio shell waste can be 
transformed into a high-performance and durable electrode material, 
offering a sustainable and scalable strategy for the development of 
advanced carbon-based supercapacitors and reinforcing the value of 
agricultural biomass in energy storage applications.

N, O‑Codoped Porous Carbon Derived from Longan Shells for High-
Performance Supercapacitor Electrodes
Guangfeng Cui, Yingying Guan, Ningning Huang, Yang Zhao, and Huan Wang*
Cite This: ACS Appl. Energy Mater. 2025, 8, 7002−7012
 Read Online
ACCESS
Metrics & More
 Article Recommendations *
sı Supporting Information
ABSTRACT: Biomass-derived porous carbon offers an eco-
friendly solution for energy storage, but challenges persist in
optimizing the pore structure and electrochemical stability. In this
study, we present a novel approach for fabricating nitrogen−
oxygen-codoped porous carbon (NOPC) electrodes derived from
sustainable longan shells, designed for electrical double-layer
capacitors (EDLCs). The N
3
OPC-3 electrode, optimized through
high-temperature activation and surface doping with urea and nitric
acid, exhibits outstanding electrochemical properties, achieving a
specific capacitance of 463 F·g
−1
at a current density of 0.5 A·g
−1
in
a 6 M KOH electrolyte during a three-electrode test. Furthermore,
the symmetric supercapacitor based on N
3
OPC-3 exhibits a high
energy density of 31.9 W h·kg
−1
at a power density of 700 W·kg
−1
, as well as an exceptional cycling stability, retaining 89% of its
initial capacitance after 10,000 cycles. These superior performance characteristics can be attributed to the well-developed 3D
hierarchical porous structure, which enhances ion diffusion, and the synergistic effects of nitrogen and oxygen doping, which
promote pseudocapacitive behavior and improve electronic conductivity. The results highlight the potential of biomass-derived
materials as sustainable, high-performance electrode materials for energy storage applications, offering an eco-friendly alternative to
traditional carbon sources while addressing the growing need for efficient and scalable energy storage systems.
KEYWORDS: longan shell-derived porous carbon, nitrogen and oxygen codoping, hydrothermal method, supercapacitor electrode,
sustainable energy storage
1. INTRODUCTION
In light of the escalating global energy demands and constraints,
the scientific community has intensified efforts to harness
renewable energy sources as sustainable alternatives to fossil
fuels. However, conventional renewable energy sources such as
solar, wind, hydropower, and biomass exhibit intermittent
production patterns, leading to challenges in providing a stable
and continuous energy supply year-round.
1−3
As a result, the
introduction of an energy-efficient storage device is required.
Supercapacitors (SCs) have emerged as a promising class of
energy storage devices, effectively bridging the gap between
traditional dielectric capacitors and electrochemical batteries
and enabling efficient energy management due to their unique
ability to deliver rapid charge and discharge, combined with
relatively high energy density and exceptional cycle stability.
4−6
Carbon-based capacitors, specifically electrical double-layer
capacitors (EDLCs), dominate the commercial landscape,
owing to their simplicity, high power density, and better cycle
life.
7,8
Their superior performance is primarily influenced by the
design of the electrode materials, with a focus on the
development of porous channels that facilitate rapid ion
migration while enhancing material conductivity.
9,10
The
operating principle of EDLCs relies on the reversible spatial
separation of electrons and ions at the interface between the
electrode material and the electrolyte, occurring at nanometer-
scale distances under the influence of an applied electric
field.
11,12
In this context, increasing the specific surface area
(SSA) of the electrode material is a critical factor in optimizing
the energy storage and charge−discharge performance of
EDLCs.
Porous carbon has become an ideal electrode material for
EDLCs due to its high SSA, excellent conductivity, and
structural adjustability, which are crucial for enhancing energy
storage capabilities.
13,14
Among the various carbon sources,
biomass-derived carbon materials, such as those obtained from
peels,
15,16
shells,
17,18
timber waste
19,20
and other agricultural
residues, offer a sustainable, cost-effective alternative to
traditional carbon sources while delivering exceptional electro-
chemical performance. Numerous studies have shown that

maximizing energy density, power density, and lifespan of
EDLCs depends on optimizing the morphology, pore structure,
and heteroatom doping of carbon-based cathode materials.
21−24
Two strategies could be employed to achieve the above goals:
(1) manufacture biomass-derived carbon materials with well-
defined hierarchical porous structures to increase SSA and create
efficient ion diffusion pathways; (2) incorporating heteroatoms
(N, O, S, B, etc.) to introduce additional pseudocapacitance
through chemical modifications. Li et al. successfully synthesized
N/O-enriched PC using eucalyptus bark via molten salt and
KOH activation, achieving a significant increase in specific
capacitance from 350 F·g
−1
to 483.5 F·g
−1
.
25
Yang et al. prepared
PC by coactivation of sugar cane bagasse and beef bone powder,
which showed an outstanding specific capacitance of 397.9 F·g
−1
at 0.5 A·g
−1
, along with a capacitance retention of 63.7% after
20,000 cycles.
26
Li et al. synthesized PC from lotus seedpods,
rice husk, reed straw, and corn cob, respectively, by two-step
KOH activation without templates, which could provide the
highest specific capacitance of 419 F·g
−1
at 0.5 A·g
−1
.
27
Despite
the significant potential of biomass-derived carbon materials as
electrodes for SCs, several challenges remain. The naturally
porous structure of biomass-derived carbons tends to consist
primarily of three-dimensional carbon blocks with limited
interconnected pore networks, which leads to low utilization of
SSA and inadequate electrical conductivity, impeding the overall
electrochemical performance. Moreover, the uneven distribu-
tion of heteroatoms in biomass precursors hinders the
achievement of uniform doping. Therefore, there is an urgent
need to develop simple and efficient strategies for precursor
structure design and surface control to enable fine structure
turning of biomass.
In this study, nitrogen and oxygen-codoped porous carbon
(NOPC) was successfully synthesized using low-cost and
sustainable longan shells as the biochar precursor, potassium
citrate as the activator, and nitric acid and urea for surface
element modification. The optimized N
3
OPC-3 features an
open porous structure and abundant surface active sites,
effectively promoting ion diffusion and enhancing redox
reactions, with a specific capacitance of 463 F·g
−1
at a current
density of 0.5 A·g
−1
. Furthermore, the N
3
OPC-3-based EDLC
demonstrates excellent energy and power performance,
achieving an energy density of 31.9 W h·kg
−1
at a power density

−1
and retaining an 89% capacity stability after
10,000 cycles. Our study offers a cost-effective approach for
preparing N, O-codoped porous carbon electrodes, which
provides a novel pathway for the high-value utilization of longan
shell waste biomass resources.
2. EXPERIMENTAL SECTION
2.1. Preparation of Spongy Longan Shell-Derived Porous
Carbon (PC). The PC was prepared through one-step carbonization
and activation of potassium citrate using long-span shell powder. First,
the longan shell was washed with water and ethanol to eliminate
impurities and then dried and finely powdered. Subsequently, a mixture
of 0.5 g of longan shell powder and 1.5 g of potassium citrate was
thoroughly pulverized and transferred to a corundum crucible, followed
by heating in a tube furnace at 800 °C for 2 h under a pure N
2
atmosphere. The final black powdery products were washed with dilute
HCl and deionized water and then dried to obtain a series of PC-x (1, 2,
3, 4) materials, where x denotes the mass ratio of potassium citrate to
longan shell powder.
2.2. Preparation of NOPC by the Hydrothermal Method.
Initially, 1 g of PC was ultrasonically dispersed in 40 mL of 1 M HNO
3
and stirred for 2 h. The suspension was then transferred to a PTFE-lined
hydrothermal kettle and preoxidized at 130 °C for 3 h. The samples
were rinsed with distilled water and dried, yielding a black powder,
designated as OPC-3. Then, 1.5 g of urea and 0.5 g of OPC-3 were
ultrasonically dispersed in 40 mL of distilled water and heat-treated at
180 °C for 10 h with the same operation. The resulting sample was
labeled as N
y
OPC-3, where y denotes the mass ratio of urea to that of
OPC-3. Additionally, nitrogen-doped longan shell-derived porous
carbon without HNO
3
preoxidation treatment, named N
3
PC-3, was
prepared using the same procedure as a control experiment. The
preparation process of the NOPC composites is described in Scheme 1.
Material characterization and electrochemical measurements were
performed as detailed in the Supporting Information.
3. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
3.1. Morphological and Structural Characterizations.
Figure 1 presents the microscopic morphology and pore
structure of PC-x, OPC-3, and N
3
OPC-3, as observed through
scanning electron microscopy (SEM). Longan shell powder
after activation with potassium citrate shows an irregular blocky
structure with a pronounced spongy-porous appearance. As an
organic weak base salt, potassium citrate has an activation
mechanism similar to that of potassium hydroxide, while offering
the added advantages of being nontoxic and having a low
environmental impact during synthesis and processing.
28,29
This
makes it a safer and more sustainable choice for various
applications. The alkali metal component etches both the
surface and interior of the carbon material at elevated
temperatures, creating additional pores. At the same time, the
gases released during pyrolysis, including CO
2
and H
2
O, help to
further enhance the pore formation within the carbon matrix.
Additionally, the organic fraction of potassium citrate
[(C
6
H
5
O
7
)
3−
] acts as an additional carbon source, assisting in
the pyrolysis of the longan shell powder and promoting the
development of a more defined porous structure. The degree of
porosity and the resultant structure formed in the longan shell
powder varied significantly with different mass ratios of
potassium citrate to the precursor. When small amounts of
potassium citrate (1:1 and 2:1) were applied, the resulting
carbon materials exhibited relatively low porosity, with the
surface appearing less developed in terms of pore formation
(Figure 1a,b). In contrast, when the potassium citrate to
precursor mass ratio was increased to 3:1, the resulting carbon
materials exhibited an optimal porous sponge-like morphology
(Figure 1c), which features a unique multiscale porous structure
with a high SSA, facilitating enhanced electrolyte storage,
shortening ion diffusion paths, and promoting electrochemical
processes.
30,31
However, as shown in Figure 1d, an excess of
potassium citrate leads to the formation of a looser and less
structured carbon material resembling stacked carbon nano-
sheets. This structural change is likely due to the excessive
amount of potassium citrate [(C
6
H
5
O
7
)
3−
], which alters the
pyrolysis process, potentially causing the material to undergo
excessive dissolution and reassembly, to the detriment of energy
storage applications. Further, SEM images of the samples
following nitric acid (HNO
3
) preoxidation treatment and urea
doping (Figure 1e,f) reveal that these processes do not
significantly alter the microstructural features of the carbon
materials. Despite these modifications, the overall morphology
of the carbon materials remains largely intact, suggesting that the
structural integrity of the carbon remains well preserved
throughout these post-treatment processes. Additionally,
carbon, nitrogen, and oxygen elements are uniformly distributed
within the N
3
OPC-3 structural framework (Figure 1g−i).
The mesoporous structure within electrode materials plays a
pivotal role in determining capacitive behavior as it allows
electrolyte ions to pass freely and form double electric layers at
the pore walls, thereby significantly augmenting charge storage
capability.
32,33
To analyze the porous structure of the synthetic
material in detail, we performed a SSA test. Figure 2 displays the
N
2
adsorption−desorption isotherms and the BJH pore size
distribution curves for the samples. The N
2
desorption
isotherms in Figure 2a indicate that all samples exhibit type IV
adsorption isotherms when the relative pressure (P/P
0
) exceeds
0.2, which is characteristic of mesoporous materials. Notably,

PC-3 displays an H4 hysteresis loop, which suggests an irregular
pore structure characterized by the coexistence of both micro-
and mesopores. The reduction in specific surface area observed
in the aqueous mixtures of the phosphates in the aqueous
complexes of OPC-3 and N
3
OPC-3 is primarily due to the
combined effects of strong acid treatment and prolonged
exposure to high temperature and pressure during preparation.
The strong acid treatment, particularly with nitric acid, can
partially dissolve the carbon matrix, leading to a loss of surface
area. Simultaneously, the high temperature and pressure
conditions may cause structural collapse, further reducing
porosity and specific surface area. However, these harsh
conditions are essential for activating the carbon structure and
introducing functional groups, which are critical for enhancing
the material’s performance. The determined BET surface areas
and pore properties of the prepared samples are summarized in
Table 1. As expected, the BET surface area of PC-x increased
with the proportion of the activator used. The increase in surface
area is a clear indication of the enhanced pore development as a
result of the high-temperature activation process, which
promotes the formation of additional pores and surface area
for charge storage. Figure 2b depicts the BJH pore size
distribution curves of PC-x, OPC-3, and N
3
OPC-3, where the
average pore size of the materials is predominantly concentrated
between 1.9 and 3.8 nm, with a minor proportion of large pores,
further suggesting the existence of a hierarchical pore structure
with both micro- and mesopores. This hierarchical structure
effectively prevents pore blockage and enhances the electrolyte
permeability. The abundance of micropores provides numerous
active sites for ion adsorption, increasing specific capacitance,
while the mesopores and macropores serve as ion transport
channels, reducing diffusion resistance and facilitating the rapid
movement of electrolyte ions. The highest BET surface area
recorded for PC-3 was an impressive 1546 m
2
·g
−1
, indicating a
substantial development of pore structures during the activation
of longan shell powder at high temperatures. This remarkable
surface area is crucial for enhancing the electrochemical
performance of supercapacitors as it provides more active sites
for charge storage. Combined with SEM results, it was
confirmed that potassium citrate contributes to the formation
of a well-developed pore network, which is essential for
optimizing the electrochemical performance of electrode
materials.
The surface chemical properties of the as-prepared N
3
OPC-3
were analyzed using X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS),
as depicted in Figure 3, while Figure S1 (Supporting
Information) illustrates the possible formation of nitrogen and
oxygen functional groups on its surface. The full-scan spectrum
(Figure 3a) reveals a reduced carbon (C) content alongside an
increased presence of nitrogen (N) and oxygen (O) elements in
N
3
OPC-3 compared to PC-3, which is primarily attributed to
the nitric acid oxidation and urea treatment during synthesis. For
N
3
OPC-3, C 1s high-resolution XPS spectra (Figure 3b) can be
deconvoluted into four characteristic peaks at 284.8 eV, 285.8
eV, 288.7 and 292.1 eV, corresponding to C−C and C�C, C−
N, C�O, and COOH bonds, respectively.
34
Figure 3c shows
the deconvoluted four N-associated groups from the N 1s high-
resolution XPS spectra corresponding to pyridine N (N-6, 399.0
eV), pyrrole N (N-5, 400.1 eV), quaternary ammonium N (N-
Q, 401.5 eV), and N oxide (N-X, 405.7 eV), respectively. N-6
and N-5 are known for enhancing pseudocapacitors, which
contribute to the enhancement of electronic conductivity and
the active site of redox reactions, thereby improving the charge
storage capacity. N-Q introduces positive charges into the
carbon lattice, further enhancing electronic conductivity, while
N-X improves wettability and electrolyte interaction, leading to
an overall improvement in electrochemical performance.
35
In
the O 1s high-resolution XPS spectra (Figure 3d), three O-
linked components of C�O, C−O, and COOH were fitted at
531.1, 532.7, and 537.1 eV, respectively, and by combining the
contributions of C�O, C−O, and COOH groups, the material
achieves superior hydrophilicity, contributing to a more open
and accessible pore structure, which is beneficial for ion diffusion
during charge and discharge cycles.
36
As a result, the synergistic
effects of nitrogen and oxygen functional groups (Figure 4)
enhance the material’s electrochemical properties by improving
charge storage capacity, ion transport, and electrolyte
interaction, significantly improving both the energy and power
density of the device.
3.2. Electrochemical Characterizations. First, a series of
systematic experiments were conducted to optimize the
properties of the carbon materials at each synthesis step. As
illustrated in Figure S2, different mass ratios of potassium citrate
were used to prepare the series of samples labeled PC-x (x = 1, 2,
3, and 4, respectively). Among these, PC-3 was found to exhibit
the highest energy storage capacity, as evidenced by the CV and
GCD curves, which is primarily attributed to the higher surface
area to adsorb more ions and thus increase the capacitance as
well as the optimal pore structure that ensures efficient ion
transport, thus improving the overall performance of the
supercapacitor. Figure S3 shows the effect of different
concentrations of nitrogen doping on the electrochemical
properties of carbon materials, with the results indicating that
the optimal ratio of urea can effectively enhance the electro-
chemical properties of carbon materials.
To systematically assess the influence of doping elements on
the energy storage performance of the synthesized carbon
materials, electrochemical measurements were performed by
using a three-electrode system, with the samples tested as single
electrodes in a 6 M KOH electrolyte (Figure S4). Figure 4a
shows the CV curves of PC-3, N
3
PC-3, OPC-3, and N
3
OP-3 at a
scan rate of 10 mV·s
−1
. As illustrated in the figure, the CV curve
for N
3
OP-3 exhibits the largest enclosed area, which is indicative
of a higher capacitance. The curve also displays an irregular
shape with noticeable humps, which suggests that the combined
presence of oxygen and nitrogen atoms in the material induces
additional pseudocapacitance. It is worth noting that the CV
curves of samples doped directly with urea without oxidation

curves exhibit nearly symmetric charge−discharge profiles with
minimal voltage drops across increasing current densities,
indicative of low internal resistance and high conductivity
within the electrode material. Moreover, the minimal
deformation in both CV and GCD curves across the tested
ranges demonstrates the excellent rate capability and rapid ion
transport ability of the N
3
OPC-3 electrode material. Due to the
unique combination of heteroatoms and carbon atoms, this
material not only retains the high stability characteristics of
traditional carbon materials but also exhibits enhanced
pseudocapacitive properties that improve capacitance. This
performance arises from the synergistic effect of the hierarchical
porous structure and heteroatom dopants, where the unique
combination of heteroatoms and a carbon matrix enables the
material to retain the high stability of traditional carbon
materials while exhibiting enhanced pseudocapacitive properties
that boost capacitance.
Figure 4e depicts the cycling stability test results of the
N
3
OPC-3 electrode over 10,000 cycles at a scan rate of 200 mV·
s
−1
in a three-electrode system. Notably, the electrode retains
93.5% of its initial capacitance after 10,000 cycles, highlighting
the exceptional stability of the N
3
OPC-3 electrode material with
its structural integrity and robust electrochemical performance
even under prolonged cycling conditions. Figure 4f illustrates
the specific capacitance of carbon materials obtained under
different treatment conditions and measured at varying scan
rates. Among the samples, N
3
OPC-3 demonstrates the highest
specific capacitance, primarily due to the oxidation with HNO
3
and subsequent doping with urea, which introduces abundant
oxygen and nitrogen functional groups into the carbon matrix. It
is noteworthy that the decrease in specific capacitance at higher
current densities, such as 10 A·g
−1
, can be attributed to the
limitation of ion diffusion at elevated current densities. At these
high current densities, ions may not fully penetrate the pores of
the electrode material, particularly the micropores, due to
increased diffusion resistance. As a result, the charge storage
capacity and the specific capacitance are reduced.
To further investigate the dynamic charge-storage behavior of
the N
3
OPC-3 electrode, the contribution rates of surface and
insertion capacitance were quantitatively analyzed using CV
curves, based on eqs S5 and S6. Among these parameters, the
slope of the linear fit (denoted as b in Figure 4g) serves as a
crucial metric for evaluating electrochemical kinetics, typically
ranging between 0.5 and 1. A b value of 0.5 signifies a low
diffusion-limited process, while a value near 1 suggests a fast
surface-controlled charge storage mechanism. The calculated b
value for N
3
OPC-3 is approximately 0.86, suggesting that both
surface- and diffusion-controlled mechanisms contribute to the
overall charge-storage process. However, given its proximity to
1, the results indicate that surface-controlled behavior plays a
dominant role in the electrochemical response of the electrode.
In addition, the quantitative contributions of surface and
insertion capacitances are presented in Figure 4h,i. As the scan
rate increases from 20 mV·s
−1

−1
, the proportion of
surface capacitance rises significantly from 58.2% to 88.1%. This
trend can be attributed to the fact that at higher scan rates, ion
diffusion within the electrode material becomes increasingly
restricted, thereby enhancing the dominance of the surface
electrochemical activity.

electrode samples was evaluated through EIS testing with a

The Ragone plot in Figure 6f shows that N
3

3
OPC-
3 outperforms most other biomass-based PC assembled SCs,
exhibiting both higher energy and power densities, as compared
to the reported values in Table 2. This superior performance can
be attributed to the tailored properties of N
3
OPC-3, including
its optimized porous structure, high SSA, and effective
functional group modifications, which contribute to excellent
electrochemical performance, making it an ideal candidate for a
high-performance energy storage device. Specifically, N
3
OPC-3-
based EDLC achieves an impressive energy density of 31.9 W h·
kg
−1
at a power density of 700 W·kg
−1
. Notably, even at an
ultrahigh power density of 7000·W kg
−1
, the energy density
remains substantial at 22.3 W h·kg
−1
, further underscoring the
practicality of the N
3
OPC-3-based symmetric device for high-
performance energy storage applications. The cycling perform-
ance data (Figure 6g) reveals that the symmetrical super-
capacitor based on N
3
OPC-3 retains 89% of its initial
capacitance after 10,000 cycles at 20 A·g
−1
, highlighting its
remarkable cycling stability and suitability for practical
applications.
4. CONCLUSION
In summary, NOPC has been successfully fabricated, derived
from sustainable longan shells as an electrode material for SCs.
The optimized N
3
OPC-3, synthesized using a combination of
high-temperature activation and hydrothermal doping with urea
and nitric acid, possesses a 3D hierarchical porous structure with
micropore-dominated pore size and nitrogen- and oxygen-rich
functional groups, facilitating efficient ion diffusion and
enhanced Faradaic redox reactions, significantly improving
both energy and power densities. Consequently, N
3
OPC-3
exhibited a high specific capacitance of 463 F·g
−1
at 0.5 A·g
−1
and a long cycling stability of 93.5% (after 10,000 cycles at 200
mV·s
−1
). The EDLC based on N
3
OPC-3 delivered an ultrahigh
capacity of 134 F·g
−1
at 1 A·g
−1
and maintained a high capacity
of 94 F·g
−1
at 10 A·g
−1
. Moreover, the device exhibited a
maximum energy density of 31.9 W h·kg
−1
at a power density of
700 W·kg
−1
and an extremely long cycling performance (89%
capacitance retention after 10,000 cycles at 20 A·g
−1
). These
findings have a certain reference significance for different
biomass precursors used as energy storage materials and provide
a feasible idea for the production of green energy storage
devices.

In Situ Polymerization of PANI to Uniformly Coat Lignin-Based
Carbon Fibers for High-Performance Supercapacitors
Kejia Wang, Junhao Dai, Wanting Zhu, Jingru Liu, Zhexuan Gu, Xinran Wang, Xin Tong, Huifang Zhao,
Daliang Guo, Tianzhong Yuan, and Jing Li*
Cite This: ACS Appl. Polym. Mater. 2026, 8, 14936−14949
 Read Online
ACCESS
Metrics & More
 Article Recommendations *
sı Supporting Information
ABSTRACT: Lignin is abundant and renewable, and its high-value utilization in carbon-based
supercapacitor electrodes has attracted considerable attention. However, pure lignin-based
carbon fibers (LCFs) have insufficient active sites, and direct loading of polyaniline (PANI)
easily causes agglomeration, limiting their electrochemical performance. In this work, LCFs were
prepared from lignin and polyacrylonitrile (PAN) via electrospinning, preoxidation, and
carbonization, and were then combined with PANI through three different methods to
systematically compare their effects on the composite properties. Results show that in situ
polymerization achieves a uniform PANI coating on LCFs, alleviating agglomeration. The Is-
LCFs-PANI-3 sample exhibits a specific capacitance of 287.36 F g
−1
at 0.5 A g
−1
, with 86%
retention after 3000 cycles. The assembled symmetric supercapacitor has a device capacitance of
69.02 F g
−1
and 78% retention after 3000 cycles. This work provides a route for the high-value
utilization of lignin and the development of high-performance supercapacitor electrodes.
KEYWORDS: lignin-based carbon fibers, polyaniline, in situ polymerization, sodium lignosulfonate, supercapacitors,
electrochemical properties
1. INTRODUCTION
With the continuous progress of the global energy transition,
efficient, green and sustainable energy storage technologies have
become a research hotspot in the energy field. As a type of
energy storage device, supercapacitors exhibit broad application
prospects in portable electronic devices, vehicles and other fields
owing to their high power density, fast charge−discharge rate
and long cycle life. As the core component, electrode materials
directly determine the energy storage performance of super-
capacitors.
1−3
At present, research on electrode materials has
focused on low-cost, environmentally friendly and high-
performance biomass-based materials.
4,5
Ternary composites
combining polyaniline with Mg-doped orange peel biochar and
CuO have attained a remarkable specific capacitance of 702.8 F
g
−1
, which validates the great application potential of biomass-
carbon/polyaniline electrode systems.
6
As an abundant natural
polymer, lignin exhibits the advantages of wide sources, low cost
and biodegradability. LCFs prepared from lignin can serve as
ideal electrode substrate materials for supercapacitors.
7−9
However, pure LCFs suffer from low specific capacitance and
insufficient active sites, making it difficult to meet the demands
of high-performance energy storage. Therefore, further mod-
ification is required to optimize their electrochemical perform-
ance.
10,11
Conducting polymers have become an important
modification strategy to improve the electrochemical perform-
ance of carbon-based materials owing to their outstanding
pseudocapacitive properties. Among them, PANI is widely used
in electrode modification due to its facile synthesis, high
theoretical specific capacitance and excellent environmental
stability.
12−14
Meanwhile, the improvement of specific capaci-
tance of LCFs composites also relies on appropriate preparation
processes and auxiliary modification. As a dispersant, sodium
lignosulfonate (LS) can effectively improve the dispersion of
PANI, prevent the agglomeration of active materials, further
enrich the active sites of electrode materials, and achieve the
synergistic energy storage of electric double-layer capacitance
and pseudocapacitance.
15,16
Matrix-free supramolecular PANI/
HEDP/LS hydrogel electrodes built upon noncovalent
synergistic interactions between LS and PANI can effectively
avoid extra resistance loss introduced by insulating polymer
matrices such as PVA.
17
In recent years, Liu et al.
18
prepared N-doped carbon
nanofibers from lignin and PAN via electrospinning combined
with carbonization, and achieved high nitrogen-content doping
through in situ coating of PANI. The results showed that the as-
prepared lignin-based N-doped carbon nanofibers exhibited a
specific surface area of up to 483.1 m
2
g
−1
and a nitrogen doping
content as high as 6.31 wt %. A specific capacitance of 199.5 F

−1
, with a
capacitance retention of 82% after 1000 cycles at 4 A g
−1
. Batista
et al.
19
prepared carbon fiber/PANI composites via in situ
polymerization of aniline on carbon fibers at room temperature.
The results showed that N and O heteroatoms on the carbon
fiber surface provided catalytic active sites for aniline polymer-
ization, and molecular oxygen as an oxidant enabled the
formation of conductive PANI without additional reagents. The
composite used as a supercapacitor electrode achieved a specific
capacitance of 235 F g
−1
at 0.1 A g
−1
, which is 26% higher than
pure carbon fiber. Han et al.
20
developed redox-active LS-
functionalized PANI-based hydrogel electrodes incorporated
into a chitosan/PAAM double-network scaffold; the assembled
devices possessed an ultrawide operating temperature window
from −30 to 90 °C and photothermal self-heating capability to
relieve low-temperature capacitance attenuation. Fei et al.
21
further developed lignin cross-linked hydrogel electrolytes
matched with PANI@carbon cloth electrodes to assemble
textile supercapacitors with dual pressure and bending sensing
functions besides energy storage capacity. However, the
majority of existing studies focus on a single preparation
method and lack a systematic comparison of different routes.
Moreover, the synergistic combination of LCFs, PANI
modification and process optimization has not been fully
realized, leaving room for further improvement in the specific
capacitance and stability of electrode materials.
Based on this, in the present study, LCFs were fabricated from
lignin via electrospinning-preoxidation-carbonization. LCFs-
PANI composite electrodes were then prepared using three
different methods: direct impregnation, LS-assisted impregna-
tion, and in situ polymerization. The novelty of this work lies in
the construction of uniformly coated PANI/LCFs composites
via in situ polymerization, which creates efficient ion transport
channels and intimate interfacial contact. This uniform
morphology directly reduces the IR drop and enhances the
rate capability, establishing a clear structure-performance
correlation. Compared with conventional impregnation meth-
ods, this approach significantly improves electrochemical
performance. The chemical role of LS is clarified: its sulfonate
groups ensure effective PANI dispersion, its phenolic/carbonyl
groups contribute pseudocapacitance, but its nonconjugated
backbone limits electronic conduction, introducing additional
impedance at high current densities. The distinct deposition
mechanisms are also elucidated physical adsorption for
impregnation versus surface-initiated growth for in situ
polymerization. By systematically investigating the effects of
the three methods on the structure and electrochemical
performance, the best-performing electrode was selected and
assembled into a symmetric supercapacitor, achieving syner-
gistic energy storage combining electric double-layer capaci-
tance and pseudocapacitance. This work aims to provide
guidance for the high-value utilization of lignin and the design
of low-cost, high-performance electrode materials for energy
storage.
2. MATERIALS AND METHODS
2.1. Experimental Materials
Lignin (MW = 5000, purity: ≥90%) was purchased from Jinan Yanghai
Environmental Protection Materials Co, Ltd. Polyacrylonitrile (PAN,
MW = 100000), aniline (AN, AR), sulfuric acid (H
2
SO
4
, AR),
hydrochloric acid (HCl, AR) and sodium lignosulfonate (LS) were
purchased from Macklin Biochemical Co, Ltd. (Shanghai). N,N-
Dimethylformamide (DMF, AR) was obtained from Chengdu Kelong
Chemical Co, Ltd. Ammonium persulfate (APS, AR) was supplied by
Aladdin Reagent Co, Ltd. (China). All reagents were used as received
without further purification.
2.2. Experimental Methods
2.2.1. Preparation of LCFs-PANI Composite Electrode
Materials. LCFs were fabricated as shown in Figure 1a. A 20 wt %
DMF solution (lignin:PAN = 2:1) was electrospun into fibrous mats,
vacuum-dried at 80 °C for 12 h. Preoxidation proceeded in air at 220 °C
(0.2 °C/min, 2 h), followed by carbonization under N
2
at 800 °C (3
°C/min, 1 h). Upon cooling, carbon fibers were cut into 1 × 1.5 cm

22
PANI powder was prepared by
chemical oxidative polymerization. Precooled AN and APS dilute HCl
solutions were mixed dropwise in an ice bath and reacted at 0 °C for 3 h
to form green precipitates. The product was washed to neutrality,
vacuum-dried at 80 °C and ground to obtain PANI powder.
23
Three
approaches were employed for fabricating LCFs-PANI electrodes. First,
impregnation (Figure 1b). LCFs were immersed in PANI hydrochloric
acid dispersions under controlled conditions. Samples with graded
PANI loadings were named Imp-LCFs-PANI-1, Imp-LCFs-PANI-2,
Imp-LCFs-PANI-3 and Imp-LCFs-PANI-4 in ascending order of PANI
content. Second, LS-assisted impregnation (Figure 1c). LS (mass ratio
1:0.5) was mixed into PANI dispersion for better stability. LCFs were
impregnated to produce the LS-modified sample series with different
PANI loadings.
15
The samples were denoted Imp-LCFs-PANI-LS-1,
Imp-LCFs-PANI-LS-2, Imp-LCFs-PANI-LS-3 and Imp-LCFs-PANI-
LS-4 with rising PANI loading. Lastly, in situ polymerization (Figure
1d) was conducted on LCFs. Samples with different PANI contents
were fabricated by tuning reaction parameters and named Is-LCFs-
PANI-1, Is-LCFs-PANI-2, Is-LCFs-PANI-3 and Is-LCFs-PANI-4. All
products were washed with HCl to a clear supernatant and dried at 40
°C prior to testing. Table 1 summarizes detailed raw material dosages of
each series.
2.2.2. Characterization and Performance Testing. Fourier
transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR, Nicolet iS50, Thermo Fisher
Scientific Inc., USA) was used to analyze the chemical structures of
lignin and PAN in the wavenumber range of 4000−500 cm
−1
.
Thermogravimetry-Fourier transform infrared spectrometry (TG-
FTIR, Nicolet iS50 + TGA2, Thermo Fisher + METTLER, USA) was
applied to investigate the pyrolysis behavior of lignin and PAN. Tests
were performed under nitrogen atmosphere from 50 to 800 °C at a
heating rate of 10 °C/min.
Water contact angle of the carbon fiber felt with a flat surface was
measured at room temperature using a contact angle measuring
instrument (DSA30, KRU
̈
SS, Germany) under the condition of a set
water droplet volume of 7 μL.
Scanning electron microscopy (SEM, Hitachi Regulus 8100, Japan)
equipped with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) was
employed to characterize LCFs and LCFs-PANI composites at an
accelerating voltage of 5−10 kV.
Raman spectrometer (Horiba LabRAM HR Evolution, Japan) was
used to characterize the molecular structure and graphitization degree
of the samples.
X-ray diffraction (XRD, Ultima IV, Japan) was utilized to analyze the
crystal structures of PANI, LS, LCFs and LCFs-PANI composites over
the 2θ range of 5−80° at a scanning rate of 5°/min.
X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS, K-Alpha, Thermo
Scientific, USA) was performed to determine the surface chemical
composition and elemental valence states of the samples.
Electrochemical measurements were conducted at room temper-
ature on an Autolab PGSTAT204 workstation. A three-electrode
system was employed with LCFs/LCFs-PANI as binder-free working
electrodes, Ag/AgCl as the reference electrode, a Pt sheet as the counter
electrode, and 1 M H
2
SO
4
as the electrolyte. Cyclic voltammetry (CV),
galvanostatic charge−discharge (GCD), and cycling stability tests were
performed using 1 × 1.5 cm electrode slices. A symmetric super-
capacitor was assembled with two identical Is-LCFs-PANI-3 electrodes
for two-electrode evaluation. CV tests were carried out in a 0−1 V
potential window at scan rates of 5−100 mV s
−1
. This window was
selected because it is below the potential for oxygen evolution in 1 M
H
2
SO

3.2. Morphological Characteristics
SEM and EDS were employed to visualize the surface
morphology and elemental distribution of the LCFs-PANI
composites, revealing how different preparation methods
influence PANI coating uniformity�a critical factor for ion
accessibility and charge transfer. Figure 4a shows that LCFs
possess a continuous and intact fibrous morphology. The
interwoven fibers construct a loose 3D network without obvious
particles or agglomerates. Such smooth and clean surfaces
provide a favorable substrate for PANI loading.
22
Water contact
angle tests confirm the hydrophobic nature of LCF surfaces. The
poor wettability restricts electrolyte infiltration, thereby limiting
the electrochemical performance of pristine LCF electrodes.
31
Despite the hydrophobic surface of LCFs that limits electrolyte
infiltration, their 3D network affords sufficient channels for
electrolyte and ion transport. Figure 4b illustrates the
morphology of Imp-LCFs-PANI-3 prepared by direct impreg-
nation, with other samples of different PANI loadings displayed
in Figure S1a−c. Increasing PANI deposition aggravates surface
accumulation and poor coating uniformity, causing severe
agglomeration and pore blockage at high loadings. Although
PANI decoration improves surface wettability compared with
pure LCFs, partial hydrophobicity remains. Excessive PANI
agglomeration hinders electrolyte penetration and ion migra-
tion, covers internal active sites, and thus restricts electro-
chemical performance improvement.
32
The introduction of LS
dispersant greatly improves PANI dispersion in the Imp-LCFs-
PANI-LS series. Figure 4c presents the morphology of Imp-
LCFs-PANI-LS-3, and the microstructures of other loading
samples are shown in Figure S1d−f. Low PANI loading yields
uniformly dispersed fine particles. Increased loading induces
slight particle stacking but no severe large-scale agglomeration as
observed in direct impregnation. Contact angle tests verify that
LS modification switches the surface from hydrophobic to
hydrophilic, achieving full electrolyte wetting and improved
surface wettability.
33
However, partial particle accumulation still
occurs at high PANI loadings, increasing electrolyte transport
resistance. By contrast, the in situ-polymerized Is-LCFs-PANI
series exhibits optimal morphological features across all
loadings. Figure 4d shows Is-LCFs-PANI-3, where PANI
forms a uniform, continuous coating on carbon fibers while
completely preserving the original 3D network pore structure
without pore blockage. SEM images at different magnifications

ensure efficient charge transport. Nevertheless, the agglom-

interfacial bonding and reduce electrolyte wettability, which
further leads to an increased voltage drop and a decline in
specific capacitance.

3.3. Structural and Chemical Composition Characterization
XRD, Raman, and XPS analyses were performed to probe the
crystalline structure, graphitic ordering, and surface chemical
states of the composites. XRD confirms PANI loading and
reflects structural ordering of the carbon framework; Raman
evaluates the graphitization degree and defect density, which are
closely linked to electronic conductivity; XPS identifies surface
chemical states and interfacial interactions between PANI and
LCFs. Figure 6a−c display the XRD patterns of LCFs-PANI
composites. LCFs show a broad and weak diffraction peak near
2θ = 23°, corresponding to the (002) crystal plane of amorphous
carbon, indicating that LCFs are dominated by an amorphous
carbon structure with low crystallinity. PANI exhibits character-
istic diffraction peaks near 2θ = 20° and 25°, corresponding to
the intrinsic crystalline structure of ordered PANI chains. LS
shows sharp crystalline peaks near 2θ = 30° and 45°.
37,38
All
samples in the Imp-LCFs-PANI series retain the broad
amorphous carbon peak of LCFs near 2θ = 23°, accompanied
by a slight shift toward higher angles and a significant increase in
intensity. This results from the overlap of PANI characteristic
peaks with the carbon fiber (002) peak, indicating successful
loading of PANI onto the carbon fiber surface. As PANI loading
increases, the peak intensity near 2θ = 20° and 25° gradually
rises, indicating an increasing proportion of PANI deposited on
the carbon fiber surface. On the basis of retaining the broad
amorphous carbon peak, the Imp-LCFs-PANI-LS series exhibits
superimposed characteristic signals of both PANI and LS. Weak
sharp peaks near 2θ = 30° and 45° correspond to crystalline
diffraction of LS, while enhanced intensity near 2θ = 20° and 25°
reflects the crystalline signal of PANI, indicating the coloading of
LS and PANI on carbon fibers. The introduction of LS does not
damage the carbon fiber framework and only produces weak
crystalline peaks, suggesting dispersion. The Is-LCFs-PANI
series shows a broad amorphous carbon peak similar to that of
the impregnation samples, with stronger and sharper peaks near
2θ = 20° and 25°, indicating the formation of PANI on the
carbon fiber surface via in situ polymerization.

This advantage is attributed to its uniform and continuous PANI
coating with intimate interfacial contact. Notably, while LS
serves as a dispersant to improve PANI distribution and its
oxygen-containing functional groups contribute additional
pseudocapacitance at low current densities, its low intrinsic
conductivity can hinder charge transport�particularly at high
current densities. This is consistent with the lowest I
D

(1.04) of Is-LCFs-PANI-3 from Raman analysis (Figure 6d),
revealing its highest electronic conductivity among all

52−54,55
These results indicate that optimal loading
and uniform coating via in situ polymerization are key to
balancing high capacitance with good rate capability. In Table 3,
our Is-LCFs-PANI-3 electrode delivers a specific capacitance of
287.36 F g
−1
at 0.5 A g
−1
, outperforming all compared samples,
and this superior performance is achieved at higher current
densities than some reported works. In terms of cycling stability,
our electrode maintains 86% of its initial capacitance after 3000
cycles, which is superior to most of the reported
values.
18,19,22,56−58
Is-LCFs-PANI-3 with optimal comprehensive electrochem-
ical performance was tested via CV, GCD and cycling stability
measurements, with Imp-LCFs-PANI-3 and Imp-LCFs-PANI-
LS-3 measured identically for comparison (Figure S4). With
scan rates increasing from 5 to 100 mV s
−1
, (Figure 9a) Is-LCFs-
PANI-3 maintains well-defined pseudocapacitive redox features
and quasi-rectangular CV profiles. The gradually enlarged CV
area confirms synergistic double-layer and pseudocapacitive
energy storage, as well as superior charge transport kinetics and
electrochemical reversibility.
59
Figure 9b presents the GCD
curves of Is-LCFs-PANI-3 at various current densities. As the
current density increases from 0.5 A g
−1
to 5 A g
−1
, all curves
maintain an approximately mirror-symmetric shape and exhibit
distinct pseudocapacitive charge−discharge plateaus, reflecting
excellent rate capability and highly reversible electrochemical
reactions. In comparison, the electrochemical performance of
Imp-LCFs-PANI-3 (Figure S4a,c) shows severe distortion of
CV curves at high scan rates and poor symmetry in GCD
profiles, indicating serious PANI agglomeration from direct
impregnation that impedes charge transport. For Imp-LCFs-
PANI-LS-3 (Figure S4b,d), although the electrochemical curves
are improved, the CV curves still exhibit lower compactness at
high scan rates and less obvious GCD plateaus relative to Is-
LCFs-PANI-3. This further demonstrates that LS merely
alleviates PANI aggregation and cannot reproduce the unique
structural advantages of in situ polymerization.
45
By contrast,
directly impregnated Imp-LCFs-PANI-3 shows severely dis-
torted high-rate CV curves and asymmetric GCD profiles owing
to PANI agglomeration hindering charge transport. Although LS
modification improves the electrochemical performance of Imp-
LCFs-PANI-LS-3, its high-rate CV response and GCD plateaus
remain inferior to Is-LCFs-PANI-3. These results confirm that
LS merely mitigates PANI aggregation and cannot replicate the
structural superiority of in situ polymerization.
60
The outstanding electrochemical performance of Is-LCFs-
PANI-3 can be explained by its unique structural advantages.
Figure 10 schematically illustrates the ion/electron transport
pathways in PANI-coated LCFs. The uniform PANI coating and
porous fiber network facilitate efficient ion diffusion and
electron transport, correlating with the superior electrochemical
performance of Is-LCFs-PANI-3. The complementary charac-
terization results collectively establish a clear structure−
property-performance correlation. SEM/EDS reveals that in
situ polymerization yields the most uniform and continuous
PANI coating, providing intimate interfacial contact and
efficient ion/electron transport pathways. XRD confirms the
presence of ordered PANI structures on the carbon fiber surface,
while Raman demonstrates the lowest defect level (I
D
/I
G
= 1.04)
for Is-LCFs-PANI-3, indicating the highest graphitic order and
electronic conductivity. XPS further verifies the interfacial
interactions between PANI and LCFs. These structural and
interfacial features collectively account for the superior electro-
chemical performance of Is-LCFs-PANI-3, including the highest
specific capacitance, smallest IR drop, and stable cycling
performance. A symmetric supercapacitor using Is-LCFs-
PANI-3 as both electrodes was constructed to evaluate practical
potential. The device retains quasi-rectangular CV contours and
distinct redox peaks from 5 to 100 mV s
−1
(Figure 9d). Its GCD
curves display symmetric triangular shapes with noticeable
plateaus (Figure 9e), delivering 69.02 F g
−1
at 0.5 A g
−1
. A
capacitance retention of 78% is obtained after 3000 cycles at 5 A
g
−1
(Figure 9f), confirming great stability for energy storage
applications.
61
4. CONCLUSIONS
In this work, we systematically compared three preparation
routes�direct impregnation, LS-assisted impregnation, and in
situ polymerization�for constructing lignin-based carbon
fiber/polyaniline composite electrodes, and investigated the
influence of preparation method on the structural and
electrochemical properties. The results demonstrate that in
situ polymerization produces a uniform and continuous PANI
coating on the carbon fiber surface. The optimal sample, Is-

systematically demonstrate its advantages, offering a feasible
route for the high-value utilization of lignin and the development
of low-cost, high-performance electrodes for energy storage.
