segments.text: Fig. 7 presents the EIS curves of AC, ZnO, and the AC-ZnO composite electrode. The EIS data were fitted using Z -view software, with the corresponding electronic circuit shown in the inset images of Fig. 7A and B for before and after 10 000 cycles. The intercept in the high-frequency region corresponds to the solution resistance ( R s ), indicating the overall resistance of the electrochemical system. The semicircle in the high-frequency region represents the charge-transfer resistance ( R ct ) at the electrode–electrolyte interface, whereas the linear region at low frequencies is associated with the diffusion of electrolyte ions within the electrode structure. 91 The cycling stability test was conducted at a current density of 5 A g −1 to evaluate the long-term durability of the electrode under high-rate charge–discharge conditions. Stability testing at higher current densities provides a more rigorous assessment of structural integrity, electrochemical reversibility, and ion-transport stability during prolonged cycling. Therefore, the cycling performance at 5 A g −1 offers a reliable indication of the practical durability of the AC-ZnO electrode. All electrodes show a negligible semicircle diameter, suggesting very low R ct before and after 10 000 cycles ( Fig. 7A and B ). The R ct values for the AC, ZnO, and AC-ZnO electrodes are very low, namely 0.05 or 0.054 Ω, 0.061 or 0.068 ohm, and 0.035 or 0.036 ohm, respectively, before and after 10 000 cycles ( Fig. 7A and B ).

segments.text: The AC-ZnO electrode exhibits a lower R ct due to the synergistic effects between AC and ZnO NPs, along with rapid ion interactions at defect-rich active sites. 92 The intercepts on the EIS curves are 1.64, 1.78, and 1.32 ohms, representing the equivalent series resistance ( R s ) of AC, ZnO, and AC-ZnO electrodes before 10 000 cycles. After 10 000 cycles, R s slightly increases to 1.72, 1.88, and 1.34 ohms. The Warburg diffusion curve indicates the ion diffusion rate on the electrode surface, with slope values of 1.28, 1.22, and 2.04 for AC, ZnO, and AC-ZnO, confirming that enhanced ion diffusion occurs in the composite electrode due to its porous structure. The shift of the Nyquist plot toward lower X -axis intercept values for the AC-ZnO electrode indicates a reduction in internal resistance and improved charge-transfer kinetics resulting from the synergistic interaction between AC and ZnO. The lower R s and R ct values of the composite electrode confirm enhanced electrical conductivity and faster electron transfer at the electrode/electrolyte interface. Furthermore, the steeper low-frequency slope suggests improved ion diffusion and more ideal capacitive behavior, which collectively contribute to the superior electrochemical performance of the AC-ZnO electrode. After 10 000 cycles, the slope of AC and ZnO decreases to 1.24 and 1.16, respectively, while the slope of AC-ZnO increases to 2.12, demonstrating that the composite electrode's excellent capacitive performance results from enhanced ion diffusion.

segments.path: D:\机器学习-超级电容器\三电极端点扩充_20261018\new_sources\PMC13400085\main.xml
segments.text: The cycling stability and specific capacitance retention are crucial for the practical use of the prepared electrode in energy storage devices. Fig. 7C–E illustrates the specific capacitance retention and coulombic efficiency of the AC, ZnO, and AC-ZnO electrodes over 10 000 charge–discharge cycles. Among the investigated electrodes, the AC-ZnO electrode exhibits superior cycling stability, retaining 89.98% of its initial specific capacitance with a coulombic efficiency of 91.36% after 10 000 cycles. In comparison, the ZnO and AC electrodes retain 75.34% and 83.54% of their initial specific capacitance, respectively, corresponding to coulombic efficiencies of 78% and 75% after 10 000 cycles. These results demonstrate the enhanced electrochemical stability and reversibility of the AC-ZnO composite electrode.

segments.path: D:\机器学习-超级电容器\三电极端点扩充_20261018\new_sources\PMC13400085\main.xml
segments.text: The excellent cycling stability of the AC-ZnO electrode can be attributed to the high electrical conductivity of AC and the rapid redox reactions of ZnO. In addition, the high surface area and porous structure facilitate enhanced ion transport and provide abundant active sites for ion interactions, resulting in superior electrochemical performance during prolonged cycling. It is important to note that the relatively low capacitance retention and coulombic efficiency of the ZnO electrode are primarily due to particle agglomeration and restricted ion diffusion during long-term cycling. Furthermore, rapid redox reactions may lead to a gradual reduction in the number of accessible active sites for ion interactions during repeated charge–discharge cycles. In contrast, the synergistic combination of electrical double-layer capacitance and pseudocapacitive behavior enables the AC-ZnO electrode to exhibit outstanding cycling stability, maintaining excellent electrochemical performance even after 10 000 cycles at a current density of 5 A g −1 .

segments.path: D:\机器学习-超级电容器\三电极端点扩充_20261018\new_sources\PMC13400085\main.xml
segments.text: The excellent cycle life of the AC-ZnO electrode is due to the high electrical conductivity of AC and rapid redox reactions in ZnO. The maximum surface area and porous structure support optimal ion interactions and charge storage in the composite electrode, showing excellent performance during long cyclic processes. The low capacitance retention and coulombic efficiency of the ZnO electrode are due to nanoparticle agglomeration and small pores, which limit ion diffusion during extended cycling. Rapid redox reactions reduce the active sites available for ion interactions during electrochemical performance. However, the combination of electrical double-layer capacitive behavior and pseudocapacitive behavior allows the AC-ZnO electrode to demonstrate superior cycle life, even after 10 000 cycles at 5 A g −1 . SEM images of the AC-ZnO electrode after 10 000 cycles (Fig. S2) confirm the structural stability of the electrode materials.

segments.path: D:\机器学习-超级电容器\三电极端点扩充_20261018\new_sources\PMC13400085\main.xml
segments.text: The charge storage behavior and kinetics can be examined from CV curves by performing calculations using Dunn's model equations. 83,84 8 i = av b 9 i ( V ) = k 1 v + k 2 v 1/2 where k 1 and k 2 are variable parameters and i represents the current response at different scan rates ( v ). The b value is determined from the slope of the eqn (8) (log( i ) versus log( v )) plot by observing the current at a fixed potential for various scan rates, as shown in Fig. 8A–C . Typically, the electrode displays electrical double-layer capacitive behavior if the b value is one, while the ab value of 0.5 indicates pseudocapacitive behavior. Values between 0.5 and 1 suggest hybrid supercapacitive behavior. 93 The AC electrode exhibits maximum b values of 0.79, 0.98, and 1.01 at 0.6, 0.8, and 0.9 V, confirming electrical double-layer capacitive behavior ( Fig. 8A ). The ZnO electrode shows pseudocapacitive behavior, with b values of 0.57, 0.64, and 0.68 at these voltages ( Fig. 8B ). Interestingly, the AC-ZnO composite displays hybrid supercapacitor behavior, with b values of 0.67, 0.79, and 0.82 at 0.6, 0.8, and 0.9 V ( Fig. 8C ). This hybrid behavior results from the electrical double-layer capacitance of AC alongside pseudocapacitance from ZnO. The hybrid charge-storage behavior of the AC-ZnO composite arises from the synergistic combination of electrical double-layer capacitance (EDLC) and pseudocapacitance. 94 The porous activated carbon framework provides a high surface area and a conductive network for rapid electrolyte-ion adsorption and electron transport, resulting in dominant capacitive-controlled charge storage. Meanwhile, ZnO contributes additional charge storage through reversible faradaic redox reactions, which account for the diffusion-controlled component observed in Dunn's analysis. Consequently, the coexistence of these two charge-storage mechanisms enables the AC-ZnO electrode to exhibit enhanced electrochemical performance and hybrid supercapacitive behavior.

segments.text: Moreover, the electrical double layer and pseudocapacitive behavior curves and contributions (due to surface-controlled and diffusion-controlled processes) can also be simulated using the following equations. 95 10 where k 1 and k 2 parameters correspond to surface-controlled (capacitive) and diffusion-controlled (diffusive) contributions acquired from the slope and intercept of the plot of versus v 1/2 . The diffusive and capacitive currents collectively contribute to generating the total current response of said electrode. Therefore, these currents should be significant to produce a large current by said electrode at the specified scan rate. Fig. 8D–F shows that the experimental curve is contributed by the diffusive and capacitive curves of AC, ZnO, and AC-ZnO electrodes measured at 100 mV s −1 , respectively. The AC shows the maximum capacitive current response as compared to ZnO and AC-ZnO. The ZnO shows a larger diffusive current response, whereas AC-ZnO exhibits approximately similar capacitive and diffusive current responses. The presence of oxygen causes a diffusion process in ZnO and the AC-ZnO electrode. The AC-ZnO electrode shows hybrid behavior due to the electrical double-layer capacitive behavior of AC and pseudocapacitive behavior of ZnO.

segments.text: Fig. 8H–J shows the diffusive and capacitive contributions for AC, ZnO, and AC-ZnO electrodes at various scan rates: 10, 20, 40, 60, 80, and 100 mV s −1 . The AC displays higher capacitive contributions of 62.53, 70.24, 76.95, 80.34, 82.52, and 84.07%, compared to ZnO (10.07, 13.67, 18.29, 21.52, 24.05, and 26.15%) and AC-ZnO (22.06, 28.58, 36.15, 40.94, 44.46, and 47.23%) at these scan rates. The maximum capacitive contributions in AC are due to small pores and high electrical conductivity. The formation of composites between AC and ZnO introduces more structural defects, a larger surface area, and a porous structure, leading to improved performance of the AC-ZnO electrode. The increasing capacitive behavior indicates excellent rate capability, rapid charge transfer, and storage capacity of the optimal sample.

segments.path: D:\机器学习-超级电容器\三电极端点扩充_20261018\new_sources\PMC13400085\main.xml
segments.text: The AC-ZnO sample was used to assemble an asymmetric device with a 1 M H 2 SO 4 electrolyte to evaluate its performance in energy storage applications. First, CV curves were recorded at 10, 20, 30, 50, 70, 100, and 150 mV s −1 within a potential range of 0–1 V ( Fig. 9A ) to analyze its capacitive behavior. The CV curves are nearly rectangular at all scan rates, indicating excellent stability, rate capability, reversibility, and superior capacitive performance of the assembled device. Similarly, GCD curves were obtained at different current densities of 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 10, and 20 A g −1 ( Fig. 9B ). The triangular symmetric shape persists across all current densities, confirming the EDLC behavior of the asymmetric device. The C s values of the assembled device are 149, 133, 126, 111, 98, 82, and 66 F g −1 at 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 10, and 20 A g −1 , respectively ( Fig. 9C ). The discharge time gradually decreases with increasing current density due to limited ion adsorption at the electrode surface. At higher current densities, ion diffusion is restricted and ion penetration decreases, leading to lower C s (specific capacitance) values. Additionally, E d and P d are critical parameters for assessing the performance of the asymmetric device in practical applications. A maximum E d of 20.66 Wh kg −1 and a minimum P d of 500 W kg −1 are observed for the device ( Fig. 9D ).

segments.path: D:\机器学习-超级电容器\三电极端点扩充_20261018\new_sources\PMC13400085\main.xml
segments.text: The superior electrochemical performance is due to high surface area, maximum porosity, and a hierarchical network that provides effective pathways for rapid ion movement at the AC-ZnO electrode. The solution resistance ( R s ), charge transfer resistance ( R ct ), and ion diffusion rate within the assembled device were also examined through EIS analysis, covering a frequency range from 0.01 Hz to 100 kHz ( Fig. 9E ). The presence of a nearly vertical EIS curve confirms ideal capacitive behavior. A small semicircle in the high-frequency region indicates a low R ct of 0.06 ohms, confirming fast ion movement at the electrode–electrolyte interface. The R s is 0.95 ohms, with a Warburg diffusion slope of 4.45, showing low resistance due to the high electrical conductivity of the AC-ZnO electrode. To verify these electrochemical results, a long-term cycling stability test was performed for 5000 cycles ( Fig. 9F ). The device retained 97% of its C s and showed a coulombic efficiency of 100%, demonstrating excellent reversibility and stability.

segments.path: D:\机器学习-超级电容器\三电极端点扩充_20261018\new_sources\PMC13400085\main.xml
segments.text: The superior electrochemical performance of the AC-ZnO composite is closely related to its structural and morphological characteristics. The incorporation of ZnO into the activated carbon matrix generates additional electrochemically active sites, while the porous and interconnected structure facilitates electrolyte penetration and ion transport. Moreover, the increased specific surface area and pore volume enhance electrolyte accessibility and charge-storage capability. These features collectively promote efficient electron transport, faster ion diffusion, and improved charge-transfer kinetics, resulting in higher specific capacitance, lower internal resistance, enhanced rate capability, and excellent cycling stability of the AC-ZnO electrode.

segments.path: D:\机器学习-超级电容器\三电极端点扩充_20261018\new_sources\PMC13400085\main.xml
segments.text: In conclusion, activated carbon was produced from rice straw waste and then combined with ZnO nanoparticles prepared via a hydrothermal method. The materials were characterized using XRD, Raman, FTIR, BET, SEM, and TEM to analyze their crystal structure, vibrational modes, functional groups, surface area, surface morphology, and microstructures, respectively. The peak intensity, crystallite size, and d -spacing decreased due to the formation of the AC-ZnO composite. The AC-ZnO composite exhibited a higher specific surface area of 578 m 2 g −1 compared with 201 and 255 m 2 g −1 for AC and ZnO, respectively. It achieved a maximum specific capacitance of 244 F g −1 at 0.5 A g −1 . The AC, ZnO, and AC-ZnO retained 83.54%, 75.34%, and 89.98% of their initial capacitance after 10 000 cycles. The AC-ZnO displayed hybrid supercapacitive behavior. The assembled device demonstrated a specific capacitance of 149 F g −1 , energy density of 20.66 Wh kg −1 , and power density of 500 W kg −1 at 1 A g −1 , with 97% capacitance retention and 100% coulombic efficiency after 5000 cycles. These results demonstrate that the AC-ZnO nanocomposite is a promising electrode material for high-performance supercapacitor applications.

segments.text:

Preparation of microwave-assisted expired
honey-derived electrodes with excellent
performance for supercapacitors
Xinting Yu, †a Yuxin Zhu, †b Yunqiang Zhang* b and Mei Li* b
Microwave and hydrothermal methods were employed to prepare expired honey-based biochar,
respectively, followed by KOH activation, carbonization and Co 2+ catalysis. The eﬀect of microwave
heating and the mechanism of Co 2+ catalysis were investigated using XRD, Raman, XPS and BET results.
The biochar heated using microwave technology has interconnected pores, a higher specific surface
area (1404.6 m 2 g/C0 1), a greater macropore volume (1.081 cm 3 g/C0 1), oxygen-rich atoms (9.71 at%), and
highly graphitized structural characteristics, compared with that obtained using a hydrothermal method
which has a lower specific surface area (451.2 m 2 g/C0 1) and a lower oxygen atom content (8.71 at%).
Due to its dominant structural characteristics, supercapacitors (SCs) based on as-prepared expired
honey biochar (CMC) exhibit superior capacitive performance, including ultra-high capacitance (up to
780.3 F g
/C0 1 at a current density of 0.2 A g /C0 1) and good cycling stability (over 96.7% capacitance
retention at 10.0 A g /C0 1 after 10 000 cycles of constant current charge and discharge) in a three-
electrode system containing 2.0 M H 2SO4 electrolyte solution. The excellent electrochemical properties
and eﬃcient synthesis of biomass-derived carbon materials provide an economical and feasible strategy
for large-scale production of high-performance electrodes.
1. Introduction
Researchers are looking for eﬃcient and low-cost alternative
clean energy sources, including lithium ion batteries, lithium
sulfur batteries, sodium ion batteries, zinc ion batteries, fuel
cells, and supercapacitors (SCs).
1–5 Supercapacitors are widely
studied for their high capacity and ability to meet the growing
energy demand due to their stable cycle performance, high
energy conversion efficiency and distinctive power density.
6
However, their low energy density significantly limits their
further application as the main energy source, and the specific
capacitance (C
sp) and operating voltage ( DV) of the electrode are
the key factors affecting the energy density. 7,8 Since carbon
materials efficiently store and release electrical energy through
electrostatic interactions between electrolyte ions and the elec-
trode surface, their C
sp can be improved by increasing the
effective specific surface area (SSA). 9,10 The fractional micro–
meso–macroporous structure is more advantageous, which can
effectively improve the ion accessible specific surface area of
materials and the kinetics of electrochemical reactions.
11 Meso-
pores and macropores can be used for the storage of electrolyte
ions to shorten the ion transport path, so that electrolyte ions
can be transferred from mesopores and macropores to micro-
pores, which greatly increases the ion diffusion rate and
effectively improves the capacitance and rate performance of
materials.
12,13 Furthermore, increasing attention has been paid
to enhancing the wettability and pseudocapacitance of carbon
materials by doping with various heteroatoms (such as N, O, S,
B, and P) to enhance the electrochemical performance.
14,15
In practical applications, biochar materials are promising
electrodes due to the low-cost recycling of biomass waste and
eﬃcient energy storage, and great research eﬀorts have been
focused on tailoring advanced porous biochar electrodes for
achieving a tunable pore structure, higher available SSA and
higher conductivity.
16–18 Heat treatment of biomass materials
with KOH activation at high temperature is one of the most
important ways to increase their surface area and adjust
their pore structure, but most biochar-based SCs show poor
capacitance (usually below 300 F g
/C0 1).19–21 Long-time high-
temperature treatment destroys electrochemically-active func-
tionalities.
22 Besides, conventional high-temperature heating
methods are relatively limited in producing high-quality mate-
rials, due to obvious thermal gradients, slow reaction kinetics

segments.text:
8282 |  New J. Chem., 2026, 50, 8281–8288 This journal is © The Royal Society of Chemistry and the Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique 2026
and inhomogeneous heating. 23 Thus, developing short-time or
low-temperature carbonization processes is crucial for obtaining
functional carbon with rich functionalities. Recently, microwave
heating techniques have become effective methods to prepare
micro- and nanomaterials. Microwave irradiation induces dipole
rotation and ionic conduction at the molecular level, leading to
homogeneous and quick thermal reactions with low thermal
gradients.
24 Compared with conventional heating techniques,
microwave heating techniques provide advantages such as higher
heating/reaction rates, more homogeneous thermal transmission
and easier formation of porous structures.
25,26
In this work, a three-dimensional (3D) interconnected porous
carbon (IPC) with a high O and N atom content was fabricated
through a developed microwave-assisted activation method from
biomass waste. Expired honey, as waste biomass, can enhance
resource utilization through reuse while its high glucose and
fructose content provides abundant oxygen-containing functional
groups, conferring an additional pseudocapacitive eﬀect.
27,28
The as-prepared three-dimensional interconnected porous
carbon from expired honey exhibits a large accessible SSA
(1404.6 m
2 g/C0 1), an ordered hierarchical porous structure,
and a high level of heteroatomic doping. Benefiting from the
synergistic eﬀects of the above merits, the as-made carbon
materials exhibit a large gravimetric specific capacitance ( C
sp)
of 508.2 F g /C0 1 at a current density of 1.0 A g /C0 1 in 2.0 M H 2SO4,
high rate capability (78.2% capacitance retention at 10.0 A g /C0 1),
and excellent cycling stability (96.7% capacitance retention
after 15 000 cycles). In addition, a high energy density of
24.7 W h kg
/C0 1 at a power density of 102.9 W kg /C0 1 was obtained
in a 2.0 M H 2SO4 electrolyte, which shows its potential as a
promising electrode for biochar-based SCs in practical applica-
tions. The present work presents a simple and economic way to
obtain biochar-based electrodes for high-performance SCs and
advances our understanding of eﬀective strategies to engineer
the microstructure of carbonaceous materials.
2. Experimental section
2.1. Material synthesis
Expired honey was placed in a microwave reactor for heating to
prepare high-quality biochar. Specifically, the honey was six
months past its labeled expiration date and exhibited natural
crystallization and a higher solid content (determined with an
Abbe refractometer) compared to fresh honey. The micro-
wave reactor (model XH-300UL) was operated at a frequency
of 2450 MHz in continuous mode. The temperature was moni-
tored using an infrared sensor, and the sample was heated at
180 1C (with a fluctuation of /C6 5 1C) under a constant power of
200 W for 4 hours. After heating, the sample was washed with
deionized water and dried. An appropriate amount of the dried
sample was then immersed in a solution containing KOH and a
certain concentration of Co(NO
3)2, stirred for 6 hours, and
subsequently dried. The obtained product was placed in a tube
furnace and sintered under an argon atmosphere, with the
temperature ramped from room temperature to 700 1C at a rate
of 5 1C min
/C0 1. After cooling to room temperature, the sample
was immersed in 0.1 M HCl solution and washed with deio-
nized water until neutral, and the final product was denoted as
CMC. For comparison, the sample prepared using the same
microwave heating method without Co(NO
3)2 immersion was
labeled as MC. The sample prepared by heating in a conven-
tional drying oven with Co(NO
3)2 immersion was designated as
CHC, while the counterpart without Co(NO 3)2 immersion was
labeled as HC.
2.2. Material characterization
A scanning electron microscope (SEM, Hitachi S4800) equipped
with an energy dispersive spectrometer (EDS, Oxford) and
a transmission electron microscope (TEM, JEM-2100) were
employed to investigate the microstructure and morphology
of the samples. The Fourier-transform infrared spectra (FTIR)
of the samples were recorded with a TENSOR 27 FTIR spectro-
meter using KBr pellets. The X-ray diﬀraction (XRD) patterns of
the samples were recorded using a D8-ADVANCE (Bruker AXS,
Germany) X-ray diﬀractometer (Cu K a radiation, l = 1.5406 Å)
with a scan rate of 10 1C min
/C0 1. The Raman spectra were
recorded on a laser confocal micro-Raman spectrometer (Lab
RAM HR800) with an excitation wavelength of 532 nm, and the
argon ion laser source ranged from 400 to 2600 cm
/C0 1. The X-ray
photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) measurements were per-
formed with a multifunctional imaging electron spectrometer
(Thermo ESCALAB 250XI) with a monochromatic source of
Al-Ka (1253.6 eV photons). The S
BET and pore size were deter-
mined by the Brunauer–Emmett–Teller (BET) and Barrett–
Joyner–Halenda (BJH) methods, respectively.
2.3. Electrochemical measurements
The two and three electrode cell systems were designed to eval-
uate the electrochemical performance of the prepared electrode
materials in 2.0 M H
2SO4 aqueous electrolyte. For electrode
preparation, 80.0 wt% active material, 10.0 wt% acetylene black

3. Results and discussion
This work proposes a novel and feasible heating strategy to
obtain a three-dimensional (3D) interconnected porous carbon
(IPC) electrode for high-performance SCs, and Scheme 1 pre-
sents a schematic diagram of the preparation of expired honey-
based biochar with a high oxygen atom content. Instead of
traditional heating techniques, expired honey was heated in a
microwave reactor at 180 1C for 4 h to gain high quality biochar,
followed by activated carbonization at 700 1C after impregna-
tion in a KOH and Co(NO
3)2 solution. Molten KOH and Co 2+
catalytic graphitization treatment were employed under high-
temperature-activated carbonization, enabling the successful
in situ fabrication of O-doped interconnected hierarchical por-
ous carbon from honey. A large number of pores were gener-
ated by KOH activation, inevitably resulting in the reduction of
graphitization, while the addition of Co
2+ improved the graphi-
tization degree by converting it to cobalt oxide and metallic
cobalt during carbonization to transform the amorphous
carbon into graphitized carbon.
29,30 After the removal of the
residues of KOH, Co and its compounds with hydrochloric acid,
a carbon material characterized by rich porosity, a large surface
area, and abundant oxygen-rich functional groups was
obtained and named CMC. In order to highlight the eﬀects of
the heating method and Co
2+ treatment, expired honey was
subjected to hydrothermal heating and microwave heating,
respectively, and the diﬀerence with Co
2+ or not was compared.
Samples were prepared by microwave heating without cobalt
nitrate addition (MC), by hydrothermal heating with cobalt
nitrate addition (CHC) and by hydrothermal heating without
cobalt nitrate addition (HC). Expired honey biochar samples
prepared only through hydrothermal and microwave treatment
are called BH and BM, respectively.
The surface morphology and microstructure of the as-
prepared carbonaceous materials were investigated by SEM
and TEM, with the results shown in Fig. 1, and Fig. S1 and S2
in the SI. As is shown in Fig. S1, honey biochar demonstrates
smooth surface microspheres with a diameter in the range of
4.0–10.0 mm after hydrothermal and microwave heating. The
four samples a display blocky morphology in Fig. 1a, c, e and g,
while the morphologies in detail exhibit significant differences
especially at greater magnifications, as shown in Fig. 1b, d, f
and h. Samples HC and CHC show a karst cave–like morphol-
ogy with rough walls, while the existence of pores can be seen in
CHC in Fig. 1. As shown in Fig. 1f, MC possesses plenty of
columnar bumps completely different from the karst cave–like
morphology of HC, which is attributed to the different heating
methods to obtain biochar at different heating levels. But the
SEM image of CMC in Fig. 1h exhibits apparent macropores
ranging from hundreds of nanometers to micron size. KOH is
reported to have strong perforating capability for biomass
precursors by reacting with carbon, leading to the release of a
gas product that introduces porosity; meanwhile molten KOH,

and increase the quality of activated carbon compared with
conventional chemical activation methods. 31 The formed por-
ous structure is favorable for ion penetration, which shortens
the path of ion transport between mesopores, micropores and

32 The TEM images of these samples (Fig. S2) all

stantiating the aforementioned analysis. Correspondingly,
energy-dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) analysis demonstrates
the homogeneous distribution of C, N, and O within CMC
(Fig. 1i–l).
The detailed structural features of the obtained carbon
materials were investigated employing Brunauer–Emmett–
Teller (BET) analysis. As shown in Fig. 2a, there is a sharp rise
in the low pressure P/P
0 (0–0.017), and there is an obvious
hysteretic loop in the high pressure P/P0 (0.45–0.90), which is
the characteristic isotherm combined with type I and IV
adsorption curves, indicating that micropores, mesopores and
macropores exist in CMC and MC. It is worth noting that the
SSA of the sample CMC is 1404.6 m
2 g/C0 1, higher than that of
MC (1154.5 m 2 g/C0 1). The key is that the extra removal of Co 2+ in
CMC increases the vacancy in the porous carbon material and
the effective area of contact between the material and the
electrolyte ions. Similarly, the SSA (452.1 m
2 g/C0 1) of CHC was
higher than that of HC (420.5 m 2 g/C0 1), which also supported
this result. As shown in Table S1, compared with CHC
(451.2 m
2 g/C0 1) prepared by the hydrothermal method, CMC
possesses a higher SSA (1404.6 m 2 g/C0 1) after microwave heat-
ing, which can be attributed to the high-quality precursor
formed via molecular-level microwave heating. Analogously,
HC and MC samples obtained only by different heating meth-
ods also have the same trend; the SSA of MC obtained by
microwave heating is larger than that of HC. CMC exhibits a 3D
interconnected porous structure with the increase of the SSA in
the micropores, mesopores and macropores after microwave
heating, as shown in Fig. 2b. Barrett–Joyner–Halenda (BJH)
analysis reveals a hierarchical porous structure within CMC,
which endows the material with rapid reaction kinetics and
superior capacitive performance. Notably, the significantly
increased number of mesopores not only offers more accom-
modation sites for electrolyte ions but also shortens their
diffusion paths to the micropores.
The phase compositions of HC, CHC, MC, CMC were
characterized by XRD analysis (Fig. 2c). Two primary peaks at
21.41and 44.41 are observed which correspond to the (002) and
(101) planes of graphitic carbon.
33 The ratio of (002) to (101)
peak intensities ( I(002)/I(101)) was calculated for each sample to
assess changes in crystallinity. Compared to CMC, CHC exhib-
ited a smaller I(002)/I(101) ratio, indicating decreased crystallinity
after microwave treatment due to increased porosity. Conver-
sely, CMC underwent graphitization catalyzed by Co ions at
elevated temperatures,
34 resulting in an enhanced I(002)/I(101)
ratio relative to MC. The two distinctive peaks at 1343 and
1600 cm
/C0 1 in the Raman spectra in Fig. 2d can be assigned to
the D-band, which corresponds to disordered sp 2-hybridized
carbon atoms, and the G-band, which relates to the graphitic
mode of carbon materials.
35,36 The samples of CMC showed a
moderate ID/IG value of 1.175 compared to HC ( ID/IG = 1.101),
CHC (ID/IG = 1.053) and MC ( ID/IG = 1.191), indicating that Co 2+
can balance the graphitization degree reduced by KOH activa-
tion. KOH activation and Co 2+ catalytic graphitization promote
the formation of the honey-based biochar with an appropriate
pore structure and graphitization degree, consistent with XRD
results.
XPS analysis was performed to characterize the chemical
and electronic states of HC, CHC, MC and CMC with the results
shown in Fig. S3, Fig. 3 and Tables S2–S4. The Co 2p XPS
spectral data of the intermediate product post-carbonization
and pre-acid pickling verified the existence of Co
2+ ions. The
XPS spectra show that the as-prepared samples mainly contain
the elements C, N, and O, without any Co observed, which was
fully removed. The acid-washed CMC samples were analyzed
using inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS),
and the results showed that the residual cobalt content was less
than 0.05 wt% (Table S2), confirming the removal of Co. The
elemental atomic ratios of the samples are shown in Table S3,
and all samples possess a high oxygen content, which can
effectively improve the electrochemical reactivity of the mate-
rial in the charge/discharge process. In the high-resolution C 1s
spectrum of the as-prepared samples shown in Fig. 3a, d, g and
j, the four peaks centered at 284.5 /C6 0.1, 285.1 /C6 0.1, and
287.8 eV refer to C–C/C QC, CQO, and C–O/C–N, respectively.
The high-resolution N 1s spectrum in Fig. 3b, e, h and k
consists of three peaks with binding energies of 398.8 /C6 0.2,
400.2 /C6 0.1, and 401.9 eV, corresponding to pyridinic-N (N-6),
pyrrolic-N (N-5), and quaternary-N (N-Q), respectively. The N-Q
as a sign of the graphitization degree contributes greatly to the
increased conductivity and electron transfer of the carbonac-
eous materials.

CHC and CMC both exhibit a significant increase in the

4. Conclusions
In this work, expired honey was heated at the molecular level by
microwave heating to obtain high-quality precursor materials,
and honey-based derived carbon (CMC) was further prepared
by KOH-activated carbonization and Co
2+ catalytic graphitiza-
tion. CMC demonstrated a three-dimensional interconnected
porous structure with a large SSA (1404.6 m
2 g/C0 1) and large pore
volume (1.081 cm 3 g/C0 1), which can increase the eﬀective con-
tact area between the material and the electrolyte ions and
provide enough active sites for the rapid redox reaction;
Oxygen-rich atoms (9.71 at%) can improve the wettability of
the electrode material and provide substantial pseudocapaci-
tance, and the improvement in the graphitization degree pro-
motes electron conduction, which is assisted by Co
2+. Due to
the above dominant structural characteristics, CMC shows
superior capacitive performance (up to 780.3 F g
/C0 1 at 0.2 A g /C0 1)
and good cycle stability (over 96% capacitance retention
after 15 000 constant-current charge and discharge cycles at
10.0 A g
/C0 1). The excellent electrochemical properties and rapid
and eﬃcient synthesis of expired honey-based carbon materials
provide an economical and feasible strategy for large-scale
production of high-performance porous carbon.

A synchronous activation-graphitization route for the 
preparation of highly graphitized porous biomass carbon 
from raisins for supercapacitor applications 
Ni Zhao, Weibin Cui* 
Key Laboratory of Electromagnetic Processing of Materials, Ministry of Education, 
Northeastern University, Shenyang 110819, China 
 
*Corresponding author’s e-mail: cuiweibin@epm.neu.edu.cn 
 
Abstract. An innovative single-step synthesis route that transforms raisin biomass into 
highly graphitized porous carbon with exceptional electrochemic al properties for 
supercapacitor applications is reported. This approach uniquely  combines KOH 
activation with K₂FeO₄-catalyzed graphitization in a unified th ermal treatment, 
eliminating the need for sequential processing steps characteri stic of conventional 
methods Structural characterization confirmed the successful sy nthesis of highly 
graphitized carbon, as evidenced by XRD patterns showing charac teristic (002) and 
(101) diffraction peaks and Raman spectroscopy yielding an I G/ID ratio of 0.98. The 
material exhibited exceptional textural properties, including a BET surface area of 2315 
m2g-1 and a total pore volume of 1.34 cm 3g-1, indicative of a well-developed porous 
architecture. Electrochemical testing demonstrated outstanding performance, with the 
biomass-derived porous carbon el ectrode achieving 323.1 F g -1 at 0.5 A g -1. This 
scalable synthesis strategy facilitates sustainable production of high-performance 
carbon materials for advanced energy storage applications, comb ining economic 
viability with environmental benefits. 
1. Introduction 
Recent advances in sustainable energy storage have highlighted biomass-derived carbons as promising 
electrode materials, owing to the ir renewable nature and tunabl e physicochemical properties [1-3]. The 
degree of graphitization is a key research metric in the study of biomass carbon compounds. The stability 
and electrical conductivity of carbon-based materials can be im proved with a higher degree of 
graphitization. A lot of work has been done to improve the grap hitization of carbon-based materials. 
Conventional graphitization methods rely on extreme conditions (>2500 °C) or mechanical stress, which 
inevitably compromise porosity and increase energy consumption.  However, both techniques 
necessitate severe experimental settings and invariably result in porosity loss [4, 5]. Fortunately, catalysts 
like Fe, Co, Ni, and Mn can drastically lower graphitizing temp eratures (below 1000 °C) [6, 7] . 
Conventional synthesis of porou s graphitic biocarbons typically  employs sequential steps involving 
transition metal catalysts (e.g., Fe/Co/Ni nitrates or chloride s) coupled with chemical activators (KOH 
or ZnCl₂) for pore formation [8-10]. However, the multi-step process is time-consuming, and most o f the 
reagents listed above are toxic and caustic. 
Here, we propose a one-step stra tegy to achieve simultaneous ac tivation and graphitization of 
raisins using K2FeO4 and KOH for the preparation of AGC. Here, K 2FeO4 was used as a graphitizing 
catalyst (Fe), and KOH was used as an activating porogen to con vert biomass precursors into porous 
carbon. The AGC electrodes demonstrated exceptional electrochemical characteristics because of their 
well-designed pores and integrated conductive network. For usag e in energy storage applications, this 
technique presents a great deal of potential for the large-scal e, inexpensive, sustainable production of 
carbon compounds from biomass.

2. Experimental section 
2.1. Synthesis of electrode materials 
8 g of raisins were washed with deionized water, acid-treated ( 2 M HNO₃, 24 h), and carbonized at 
400 °C (2 °C/min, 4 h, Ar). The carbonized material was mixed with K₂FeO₄ and KOH (1:3:1 ratio) by 
ball milling (30 min), then activated at 800 °C (5 °C/min, 2 h, Ar flow: 50 mL/min). 
2.2. Electrochemical tests on AGCs in 2 M H2SO4 
Electrochemical measurements used a three-electrode system (Pt counter, Ag/AgCl reference) in 2 M 
H₂SO₄ at 25±1°C. Working electrodes contained 80% AGC, 10% acet ylene black, and 10% PVDF 
binder pressed onto Ni foam (1 cm², 3.0 mg loading). After dryi ng, electrodes were soaked for 1 hour 
in N₂-purged electrolyte. Tests employed a CHI760D workstation with current densities from 0.5 to 10 
A/g⁻¹ (5 cycles each for stabilization). 
3. Results and Discussion 
3.1. Formation mechanism of AGC 
 
 
Figure 1. Preparation of the activation-graphitization carbon. (a) Optical photograph of raisins. (b) Product after 
pre-carbonization. (c) Schematic of mixing process and (d) activation-graphitization process. (e) Optical 
photograph of product AGC-FK. 
The proposed one-pot synthesis strategy (Figure 1) utilizes KOH  as a dual-functional agent for both 
chemical activation and oxygen scavenging, while K₂FeO₄ serves as the graphitization catalyst by 
providing Fe species. During thermal treatment, KOH undergoes d ecomposition above 700 °C to yield 
reactive metallic potassium and CO₂, which subsequently partici pate in concurrent pore-forming and 
graphitization processes. The metallic potassium facilitates ex tensive carbon matrix etching to create 
porous structures, while the liberated CO₂ and Fe species syner gistically promote carbon layer 
rearrangement into ordered graphitic domains through a series o f redox-mediated solid-gas reactions. 
This coupled activation-graphitization mechanism enables the simultaneous development of hierarchical 
porosity and enhanced crystallinity in the biomass-derived carb on material [11, 12]. The carbon matrix 
undergoes structural expansion during activation, generating ex tensive micropores through combined 
chemical etching and physical expansion. Concurrently, K₂FeO₄ undergoes stepwise thermal reduction: 
transforming to Fe₂O₃ at 400 °C, then to Fe₃O₄ (500-700 °C), an d ultimately to metallic Fe, which 
catalyzes the conversion of amorphous carbon to graphitic structures[13].  
3.2. Morphological and structural characterization 
SEM is used to analyze the sampl es' microstructure and morpholo gy. The inactivated pre-carbonized 
samples have a dense bulk shape and few pores on their surface,  as can be shown (Figure 2a). During 
the activation and graphitizing processes, abundant pores were created (Figure 2 b-d). A continuous

promote electrolyte penetration and increase the number of electrochemically active sites. 
 
Figure 2. SEM images of (a) pre-carbonized carbon, (b) AGC-F, (c) AGC-K, (d) AGC-FK. 
Raman and XRD are used to characterize the graphitization of th e samples. The usual (002) and 
(101) reflections of graphitic  carbon are represented by two di ffraction peaks at 2θ of 26.3° and 44.5° 
in Figure 3a, respectively, whereas for AGC-F and AGC-K the dif fraction peaks representing graphite 
are significantly weaker, indicating that it is poorly graphitized and has an amorphous carbon structure. 
Therefore, the XRD results indicate that the AGC-FK samples synthesized by the one-step method have 
a good degree of graphitization. Raman spectroscopy also proved  the graphitic structure (Figure 3b). 
Raman spectroscopy characterizati on revealed distinct vibration al modes: the D-band (1350 cm⁻¹) 
directly relates to the degree of structural defects and disorder in sp²-carbon, while the G band at ~1580 
cm⁻¹ arises from in-plane vibrations of ordered graphitic structures. Quantitative analysis of the intensity 
ratio (I G/ID) yielded values of 0.98, 0.96, and 0.94 for AGC-FK, AGC-F, and  AGC-K samples, 
respectively, indicating their relative graphitization degrees.  Notably, the Raman spectra of AGC-FK 
show narrower D and G bands compared to the other samples, which confirms that the AGC-FK samples 
exhibit a higher degree of graphitization. 
 
Figure 3. Structural characterization of the synthesized carbons: (a) XRD diffraction patterns demonstrating 
crystallinity, (b) Raman spectra showing graphitic features, (c) N₂ physisorption isotherms revealing porosity 
characteristics, and (d) pore size distribution profiles for AGC-FK, AGC-F, and AGC-K samples. 
Nitrogen adsorption-desorption is used for analyzing porosity at 77 K. TAs is observed; the AGC-
FK sample exhibits a typical t ype IV adsorption-desorption isot herm, centered at 3.5 nm (Figure 3d), 
with well-developed plateau periods and dramatic adsorption inflection points at low relative pressures. 
These features suggest the presence of mesopores and micropores . Furthermore, the AGC-FK sample 
showed a significant overall pore volume of 1.34 cm3g-1, with the micropore accounting for 0.40 cm3g-
1, and a substantial BET surface area of 2315 m2g-1. The energy storage capacity of AGC-FK is enhanced 
by its wide accessible surface area as well as appropriate pore  size distribution, which are mostly 
attributed to the micropores and mesopores. These features prom ote ion adsorption and electrolyte 
penetration. Conversely, AGC-F and AGC-K samples exhibited typi cal type I adsorption-desorption 
isotherms at low relative pressures and well-developed plateau periods, with a smaller BET surface area 
of 1114 m2g-1, total pore volume of 0.62 cm 3g-1 for AGC-F, and a BET surface area of 0.62 cm 3g-1 for 
AGC-K, which was 2056 m2g-1 with a total pore volume of 1.16 cm3g-1. This suggests that the activation 
pore-making process of AGC is mainly undertaken by KOH, and K2FeO4 acts as a graphitization catalyst. 
XPS analysis was used to furthe r study the characteristics of t he nitrogen and oxygen groups of 
carbon materials (Figure 4). The co-existence of C, N, and O is confirmed by the XPS survey spectrum, 
which is displayed in Figure 4a. According to the spectra fitte d to each element, the majority of the

3.3. Electrochemical performance of AGC electrodes 
The AGC-FK electrodes' CV curves (Figure 5a) were recorded between -0.6 V and 0.2 V at various scan 
rates (2~100 mV s -1). The CV curves displayed a symmetric rectangle with a mild hu mp widening, 
indicating that the pseudo-capacitance of oxygen-containing fun ctional groups was constrained and 
electrochemical double-layer capac itance (EDLC) predominated. T he reduced surface area and pore 
volume of the AGC-F, in contrast, result in a lower current as seen in the CV curve. Ion transport 
obstruction is the reason for the fusiform shape of the AGC-K e lectrode's CV curve. The GCD curves 
of the AGC-FK electrode (Figure 5b) showed a triangular symmetry and a small voltage drop as a result 
of the dominant EDLC activity. Additionally, at 0.5 A g−1, it provided a specific capacitance of 323.1 F 
g−1, while the AGC-F and AGC-K electrodes (Figure 5c) displayed specific capacitances of 110.8 F g−1 
and 214.1 F g−1. The enhanced capacitance of AGC-FK is mainly caused by its la rger surface area and

pore volume. Galvanostatic charge-discharge is used to further investigate the cycle stability of AGCs 
at a current density of 1 0  A g −1 (Figure 5d). The AGC-FK electrode maintained 96.3% capacitance  
retention after 10,000 cycles at 10 A g -1 (Figure 5d), demonstrating outstanding cycling stability. The 
galvanostatic charge-discharge curves after 2000, 4000, 6000, 8000, and 10000 cycles inserted in Figure 
6d corroborate the AGC-FK's cycling endurance, since they stay virtually symmetric as before the cycles. 
EIS was also used to analyze the electron/ion transport mechani sm of AGC electrodes. As shown in 
Figure 5e, the EIS spectra are obtained and fitted with an equi valent electric circuit. The EIS plot of 
AGC-FK shows vertical straight lines in the low-frequency band, indicating low ion diffusion resistance. 
Two characteristics were present at higher frequencies: (1) low  combined series resistance (Rs) due to 
electrode materials' intrinsic resistance, electrolyte ionic re sistance, and electrode-current collector 
contact resistance;(2) the small semicircle in the EIS plot cor responds to the charge transfer resistance 
(Rct). The hierarchical porous architecture enhances capacitive  performance by facilitating rapid ion 
transport through interconnected microporous channels, thereby optimizing charge transfer kinetics. 
The high specific capacitance of AGC-FK (323.1 F g-1) is attributed to its hierarchical pore structure 
(micropores for charge storage and mesopores for ion transport)  and high graphitization degree (IG/ID~ 
= 0.98), as confirmed by Raman and BET analysis. The dominant p yridinic-N and pyrrolic-N (66.8%) 
in XPS spectra (Table 1) further  enhance pseudocapacitance thro ugh Faradaic reactions. Additionally, 
the low Rct value (Figure 5e) correlates with the continuous ca rbon skeleton observed in SEM (Figure 
2d), facilitating rapid electron transfer. 
 
Figure 5. Electrochemical characterization of the carbon electrodes: (a) CV plots at 100 mV s⁻¹, (b) GCD plots 
at 1 A g⁻¹, (c) Rate-dependent capacitance retention, (d) Cycling stability at 10 A g⁻¹ (10,000 cycles), and (e) EIS 
plots (10 mHz-100 kHz) for AGC-FK, AGC-F, and AGC-K samples. 
4. Conclusions 
This study demonstrates a sustainable one-pot synthesis of highly graphitized porous carbon from raisin 
biomass, where K₂FeO₄/KOH synergistically mediates simultaneous  activation-graphitization. The 
optimized AGC-FK material exhibits superior structural characte ristics (IG/ID = 0.98, S BET = 2315 m² 
g⁻¹, Vtotal = 1.34 cm³ g⁻¹) and exceptional electrochemical performance (323.1 F g⁻¹), establishing a new 
paradigm for designing high-perfo rmance, eco-friendly supercapa citor electrodes from renewable 
precursors.

Yousheng Tao1,4,* 
1College of Materials Science and Engineering, Sichuan University, Chengdu, 610064, China; 
2School of Chemistry and Chemical Engineering, Guangxi University, Nanning, 530004, China; 
3Physical Chemistry Department, National Research Centre, Cairo, P.O. 12622, Egypt; 4MNR Key 
Laboratory of Salt Lake Resources and Environment, Institute of Mineral Resources, Chinese  
Academy of Geological Sciences, Beijing, 100037, China 
 Abstract: Introduction: Supercapacitors have shown substantial promise in electrochemical energy 
storage devices, where porous carbon materials demonstrate exceptional potential applications in 
their electrodes owing to their large specific surface area, high electrical conductivity, and rationally 
tunable pore architectures. 
Methods: Sodium lignosulfonate and graphene oxide-based porous carbon materials (LC/rGO) were 
prepared and characterized. The electrochemical performance of the samples was investigated with 
three-electrode configurations. 
Results: LC/rGO demonstrated mesoporous architecture and excellent electrochemical performance. 
The kinetic analysis on the electrochemical properties of the materials revealed an electric double-
layer capacitance dominated energy storage mechanism. 
Discussion: XRD and Raman analysis on the structures of the as-prepared carbon materials suggest-
ed a relatively high degree of defects and disorder. Investigations on the morphology, the pore size 
distributions and the surface chemistry of the samples demonstrated that the materials had a high 
specific surface area, mesporous structures and multi-atomic doping of nitrogen and oxygen func-
tional groups. All these features could be taken into account for the high electrochemical perfor-
mance of carbon. 
Conclusion: LC/rGO as an electrode material demonstrated a high specific capacitance of 296 F g
-1 
at 0.1 A g -1 and outstanding cycling stability with 97% of the initial capacitance after 10,000 cycles 
at 5 A g -1 in a 6 M KOH electrolyte. The assembl ed symmetric supercapacitor using the as-
synthesized materials exhibited energy density of 10.6 Wh kg -1 at 300 W kg-1 and cycling stability of 
95% capacitance after 10,000 charge-discharge cycles, promising for supercapacitor applications.

chemical performance of biomass-derived carbons, 
heteroatom doping with nitrogen, sulfur, and oxy-
gen has been developed [12-20]. These chemical 
modifications lead to significant improvements in 
specific capacitance and/or cycling stability of bi-
omass-derived carbon materials for supercapacitor 
applications. Lignin, one of the most abundant ar-
omatic polymers on Earth and a major byproduct 
of the paper industry, has attracted extensive atten-
tion from researchers for the preparation of porous 
carbon [21]. Pang et al. successfully prepared in-
terconnected hierarchical porous carbon by direct-
ly carbonizing sodium lignosulfonate without ad-
ditional template agents or activators, achieving a 
specific capacitance of 247 F g
-1 at 0.05 A g-1 [12]. 
With chemical activation and/or heteroatom dop-
ing, the pore structures of sodium lignosulfonate-
derived porous carbon materials can be effectively 
tuned, significantly enhancing their electrochemi-
cal performance. Sun et al. prepared highly porous 
carbon materials doped with N, O, and S atoms by 
using sodium lignosulfonate and humic acid sodi-
um as precursors, boric acid as a template, and 
KOH activation, achieving a specific capacitance 
of 318.3 F g
-1 at a current density of 0.5 A g -1  
[13]. Ye et al . directly converted sugarcane ba-
gasse and graphene oxide into nitrogen-doped car-
bon spheres using a hydrothermal carbonization 
process with sodium hydroxide/urea aqueous solu-
tion, achieving a specific capacitance of 226.8 F g
-
1 at a current density of 0.5 A g -1, with 83.9% re-
tention after 10,000 cycles [14].  
 Graphene oxide (GO) tends to stack, signifi-
cantly reducing its specific surface area. Introduc-
ing templates or supporting materials such as car-
bon nanofibers and carbon nanohorns can con-
struct three-dimensional porous structures for the 
diffusion channels of electrolyte ions, improving 
their electrochemical performance [22-24]. Re-
cently, a few studies combining reduced GO with 
lignin to obtain porous carbon materials were re-
ported. With a two-step process involving hydro-
thermal reaction and high-temperature carboniza-
tion, Jiang et al . fabricated graphene-templated 
lignin-derived porous carbon materials for high-
performance supercapacitors. It showed a specific 
capacitance of 330 F g -1 at 1 A g -1, an energy den-
sity of 11.3 Wh kg -1 at a power density of 254 W 
kg-1, and cycling stability of 100% after 10,000 
cycles [25]. 
 In this study, we used sodium lignosulfonate, 
melamine, and graphene oxide to prepare porous 
carbon materials with potassium hydroxide activa-
tion. The carbons as an electrode demonstrated a 
specific capacitance of 296 F g
-1 at 0.1 A g -1 and 
cycling stability with 97% of the initial capaci-
tance after 10,000 cycles at 5 A g
-1 in a 6 M KOH 
electrolyte. The assembled symmetric supercapaci-
tor using the prepared carbon materials exhibited 
an energy density of 10.6 Wh kg
-1 at 300 W kg -1 
and cycling stability with 95% capacitance after 
10,000 charge-discharge cycles.  
2. MATERIALS AND METHODS 
 Sodium lignosulfonate and melamine (Alad-
din), potassium hydroxide (Chengdu Ding Sheng 
Times Technology Co., Ltd.), hydrochloric acid 
and N-methyl-2-pyrrolidone (Chengdu Kelong 
Chemicals Co., Ltd.), acetylene black and polyvi-
nylidene fluoride (Taiyuan LiZhiyuan Technology 
Co., Ltd.) were used for the preparation of sam-
ples. All chemicals were of analytical grade and 
used without further purification. 
 Graphene oxide (GO) was prepared according 
to the improved Hummers method. GO was dis-
persed ultrasonically in water (2 mg/mL) for use. 
Five grams of sodium lignosulfonate was added to 
80 mL of deionized water, followed by the addi-
tion of GO. The mixture was stirred for 0.5 hours 
to produce a homogeneous mixture. A total of 3g 
of a dried mixture of sodium lignosulfonate and 
GO was then mixed with melamine and KOH in a 
mass ratio of 1:0.75:0.5. It was then heated in a 
furnace at 800°C for 1 hour under a nitrogen at-
mosphere. The product was soaked in a 2M HCl 
aqueous solution for 12 hours, followed by wash-
ing with water and ethanol. The samples were ob-
tained after drying and named as LC/rGO.  
 The structures of samples were studied by X-
ray diffraction (XRD) with a radiation of the cop-
per target Cu kα (Empyrean) and Raman spectros-
copy (Horiba Scientific LabRAM HR Evolution). 
The morphologies of the samples were analyzed 
by scanning electron microscopy (SEM) (Hitachi 
S-4800). The pore size distributions of the samples 
were characterized by nitrogen adsorption and de-
sorption at 77 K using a gas sorption analyzer (mi-
cromeritics ASAP 2460). 
 In order to evaluate the electrochemical charac-
teristics of the materials as electrodes in aqueous

ducted using a CHI660E electrochemical work-
station (Shanghai Chenhua Instrument Co., Ltd., 
China) with a standard three-electrode system in a 
6M KOH aqueous solution. A platinum sheet (Pt, 
1.0 cm²) and a mercury/mercury oxide (Hg/HgO) 
electrode were used as the counter and reference 
electrodes, respectively, while the carbon material 
electrode served as the working electrode. The 
specific capacitance involved in this experiment 
was calculated from the galvanostatic charge/  
discharge (GCD) curves using the following for-
mula (1): 
          (1) 
Cg is the specific capacitance (F·g-¹); I is the dis-
charge current (A);
/g1t is the discharge time (s); m 
is the mass of active material (g); /g1V is the 
charge-discharge voltage. 
3. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION 
 The XRD pattern of the samples is shown in 
Fig. ( 1). It exhibited a broad diffraction peak at 
23.6° and a weak diffraction peak at 44°, corre-
sponding to the (002) and (100) planes of carbon 
materials, respectively. Raman spectrum of the 
representative samples, as shown in Fig. ( 2), had 
the D and G bands at 1336 cm
-1 and 1590 cm -1, 
respectively, representing the degree of disorder 
and graphitization in the material [26]. The I
D/IG 
value of LC/rGO samples was 1.04, suggesting 
that the carbon materials had a relatively high de-
gree of defects and disorder. The addition of mel-
amine during the activation process was beneficial 
to increase the defect density [27].  
 The morphology and the pore size distributions 
of the samples were studied with FE-SEM and ni-
trogen adsorption and desorption at 77 K, respec-
tively, as shown in Figs.  (3 and 4). The porous 
structures of the carbon materials were observed. 
The activation and gases generated during the de-
composition of melamine at high temperatures 
could create nano-pores, enriching the pore struc-
tures of the carbon materials [28]. The materials 
had a specific surface area of 2011 m
2g-1, and their 
pore size distribution (PSD) indicated mainly 
mesopores of 2-5 nm width. It was worth mention-
ing that the mesoporous structures would be bene-
ficial for ion transport and facilitate the rapid reali-
zation of kinetic reactions [29]. The elemental 
mapping images of LC/rGO samples demonstrated 
that the C, O, N, and S elements were uniformly 
distributed (not shown). Analyzed with XPS, the 
surface chemistry of LC/rGO materials showed 
diffraction peaks at 284.8 eV (C 1s), 531.5 eV (O), 
and 400.1 eV (N), respectively, suggesting the 
doping of O and N elements in the carbon frame-
work, consistent with the elemental mapping. The 
high-resolution N 1s spectrum of LC/rGO revealed 
various nitrogen-containing functional groups, in-
cluding pyridinic nitrogen (N-6, 398.4 eV), pyra-
zolic nitrogen (N-5, 400.1 eV), quaternary nitro-
gen (N-Q, 401.2 eV), and nitrogen oxides (N-x, 
402.9 eV). The high-resolution S 2p spectrum of 
LC/rGO exhibited three fitted peaks corresponding 
to C-S-C (2p
3/2) at 164.0 eV, C-S-C (2p 1/2) at 
165.4 eV, and C-SOx at 168.5 eV. The surface 
composition of LC/rGO was found to be 85.3 at.% 
C, 6.5 at.% O, 7.9 at.% N and 0.3 at.% S. 
 As shown in Fig. ( 5), cyclic voltammetry (CV) 
investigations were performed on the samples, 
with the voltage window set between -1 V and 0 
V, and the scan rate increased from 1 mV s
-1 to 
100 mV s-1. The CV curves of all materials exhib-
ited rectangular shapes, indicating that the capaci-
tance was mainly dominated by the double-layer 
charge storage mechanism [30]. As the scan rate 
increased, the CV curves maintained their shapes, 
suggesting that the materials had excellent ion 
transport capacity and reversibility. This was be-
cause their mesopores removed the restrictions of 
ion storage and diffusion [22, 30, 31]. Additional-
ly, slight humps were observed at -0.8V and  
-0.2V, indicating redox reactions during charge-
discharge processes, which were attributed to the 
pseudo-capacitance caused by heteroatom doping 
[32, 33]. The LC/rGO electrode materials were 
further assembled into an aqueous symmetric su-
percapacitor, using 6 M KOH as the electrolyte, 
with two LC/rGO electrode sheets of the same 
mass serving as the positive and negative elec-
trodes. The galvanostatic charge/discharge (GCD) 
investigation confirmed that the working voltage 
of LC/rGO reached 1.4 V in the symmetric super-
capacitor, which had a specific capacitance of 52.9 
F g
-1 at a current density of 0.5 A g -1. A cyclic 
voltammetry (CV) study with a scan rate of 50 mV 
s
-1 indicated the device had maximum energy den-
sity of 10.6 Wh kg -1 and a corresponding power 
density of 300 W kg -1. When the energy density 
was 7.7 Wh kg -1, the power density reached 5,995 
W kg-1.

STUDY LIMITATIONS 
 Despite the high electrochemical performance 
of the as-prepared materials demonstrated by the 
EDLC symmetric device, the relatively low energy 
density remains one of the main areas of study for 
their practical applications [34-36]. 
CONCLUSION 
 In summary, sodium lignosulfonate and gra-
phene oxide-based porous carbon were prepared 
using a facile method. The materials had a high 
specific surface area and featured mesoporous 
structures and multi-atomic doping of nitrogen and 
oxygen functional groups. Benefiting from their 
mesopores, LC/rGO composites exhibited high 
performance as electrode materials for supercapac-
itors. It demonstrated a specific capacitance of 296 
F g
-1 at a current density of 0.1 A g -1 and showed 
outstanding cycling stability, losing only 3% of its 
initial capacitance after 10,000 cycles. A symmet-
ric supercapacitor with two electrodes of the same 
mass of LC/rGO exhibited an energy density of 
10.6 Wh kg -1 at a power density of 300 W kg -1. 
The excellent electrochemical properties of these 
materials highlight their significant potential for 
applications in sustainable energy resources. 
AUTHORS’ CONTRIBUTIONS 
 The authors confirm their contribution to the 
paper as follows: BY and GT carried out the ex-
periments, did the data collection and analysis and 
wrote the draft. QL, JS, YW and NAF contributed 
to the improvement of the study. YT supervised 
the research. They have meticulously reviewed all 
results and unanimously approved the final version 
of the manuscript.
